Initially created: 2025-11-27T21:55:00.599+09:00 by schwermann Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into $lang.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the $lang translation.
5. The target language is $lang.
Input text:

p.seg: Those who possess land and govern the people
must focus on the four seasons,
and secure the granaries.
When a state is wealthy,
people from afar will come;
when the land is fully cultivated,
the people will settle and stay.
When granaries are full,
people understand礼节 (lǐjié);
when well-fed and clothed,
they know荣辱 (róngrǔ).
When superiors observe proper norms,
family bonds are strong;
when the four cardinal virtues are upheld,
the ruler's orders are carried out.
Thus, the key to reducing punishments
lies in prohibiting frivolous crafts;
the measure to secure the state
is to cultivate the four virtues;
the way to guide the people
is to honor spirits and deities,
revere mountains and rivers,
respect ancestral temples,
and venerate elders and traditions.
Neglecting the timing of heaven
prevents wealth from growing;
neglecting the advantages of earth
leaves granaries unfilled.
If fields lie waste and barren,
the people become idle;
if superiors lack restraint,
the people become reckless.
If frivolous crafts are not banned,
the people become decadent;
if the two sources are not controlled,
punishments multiply.
Without honoring spirits and deities,
the common people remain unenlightened;
without revering mountains and rivers,
authoritative commands go unheeded;
without respecting ancestral temples,
the people defy their superiors;
without venerating elders and traditions,
filial piety and fraternal duty are incomplete.
If the four virtues are not upheld,
the state will perish.
Right: The Ode of the State.
The state has four cardinal virtues;
if one is broken, it tilts;
if two are broken, it is in danger;
if three are broken, it collapses;
if all four are broken, it is destroyed.
A tilt can be corrected,
danger can be stabilized,
a collapse can be rebuilt,
but destruction cannot be restored.
What are the four cardinal virtues?
The first is礼 (lǐ),
the second is义 (yì),
the third is廉 (lián),
the fourth is耻 (chǐ).
礼 (lǐ) means not overstepping bounds,
义 (yì) means not self-advancing,
廉 (lián) means not concealing evil,
耻 (chǐ) means not following wrongdoing.
Thus, not overstepping bounds
ensures the security of superiors;
not self-advancing
prevents cunning and deceit among the people;
not concealing evil
leads to integrity in conduct;
not following wrongdoing
prevents wicked deeds from arising.
Right: The Four Cardinal Virtues.
What makes governance effective
is conforming to the people's hearts;
what makes governance fail
is opposing the people's hearts.
The people dislike toil and hardship,
so I give them ease and joy;
the people dislike poverty and lowliness,
so I enrich and honor them;
the people dislike danger and downfall,
so I preserve and secure them;
the people dislike extinction and death,
so I nurture and multiply them.
If you can give them ease and joy,
they will endure toil and hardship for you;
if you can enrich and honor them,
they will bear poverty and lowliness for you;
if you can preserve and secure them,
they will face danger and downfall for you;
if you can nurture and multiply them,
they will risk extinction and death for you.
Thus, penalties and punishments cannot intimidate their will,
killing and execution cannot subdue their hearts.
So if punishments are numerous but they feel no fear,
orders will not be carried out;
if killings are many but their hearts are not won,
the position of superiors is endangered.
Therefore, by fulfilling their four desires,
those afar will draw close of their own accord;
by imposing their four dislikes,
even the near will rebel.
Hence, to know that giving is taking
is the treasure of governance.
Right: The Four Accordances.
Establish the state on unshakable ground.
Store in inexhaustible granaries.
Keep in unfailing treasuries.
Issue orders from the source of flowing water.
Employ the people in non-contentious positions.
Make clear the paths that lead to certain death.
Open the gates that lead to certain gain.
Do not attempt what cannot be achieved.
Do not seek what cannot be obtained.
Do not dwell where one cannot endure.
Do not practice what cannot be repeated.
To establish the state on unshakable ground
means to entrust it to the virtuous.
To store in inexhaustible granaries
means to focus on the five grains.
To keep in unfailing treasuries
means to cultivate mulberry, hemp, and rear the six domestic animals.
To issue orders from the source of flowing water
means to make orders conform to the people's hearts.
To employ the people in non-contentious positions
means to let each do what they excel at.
To make clear the paths that lead to certain death
means to enforce strict penalties.
To open the gates that lead to certain gain
means to be trustworthy in rewards and honors.
Not to attempt what cannot be achieved
means to measure the people's strength.
Not to seek what cannot be obtained
means not to force the people into what they detest.
Not to dwell where one cannot endure
means not to seize temporary gains for one generation.
Not to practice what cannot be repeated
means not to deceive the people.
Thus, entrusting to the virtuous
ensures the state's security.
Focusing on the five grains
ensures sufficient food.
Cultivating mulberry and hemp,
rearing the six domestic animals,
ensures the people's wealth.
Making orders conform to the people's hearts,
ensures authoritative orders are carried out.
Letting the people each do what they excel at,
ensures that resources are complete.
Enforcing strict penalties,
keeps the people away from evil.
Being trustworthy in rewards and honors,
makes the people undaunted by difficulties.
Measuring the people's strength,
ensures that affairs are accomplished without fail.
Not forcing the people into what they detest,
prevents deceit and falsehood from arising.
Not seizing temporary gains for one generation,
prevents resentment among the people.
Not deceiving the people,
ensures that subordinates are close to their superiors.
Right: The Eleven Canons.
To treat a family as a village,
the village cannot be managed;
to treat a village as a state,
the state cannot be managed;
to treat a state as the world,
the world cannot be managed.
Treat a family as a family,
a village as a village,
a state as a state,
the world as the world.
Do not say they are not of the same clan,
and thus ignore those who are distant;
do not say they are not from the same village,
and thus dismiss those from afar;
do not say they are not of the same state,
and thus reject those from other lands.
Be like the earth and sky—
impartial and without favoritism;
be like the moon and sun—
embodying the ruler's integrity.
The reins to guide the people
lie in what the ruler values;
the gate to lead the people
lies in what the ruler prioritizes;
the path to summon the people
lies in what the ruler likes and dislikes.
Thus, if the ruler seeks something,
the ministers will obtain it;
if the ruler craves something,
the ministers will consume it;
if the ruler favors something,
the ministers will adopt it;
if the ruler detests something,
the ministers will conceal it.
Do not掩盖 your faults,
nor alter your standards,
or the worthy will not assist you.
Speak in the chamber and fill the chamber;
speak in the hall and fill the hall—
this is called the sage king.
Walls and moats
are insufficient for firm defense;
weapons and strength
are inadequate to face enemies;
vast lands and abundant wealth
are not enough to win the masses;
only those with the Dào
can prepare against calamity before it forms,
thus disaster does not sprout.
The world does not worry about lacking ministers,
but worries about having no ruler to command them;
the world does not worry about lacking wealth,
but worries about having no one to distribute it.
Therefore, those who understand timing
may be established as leaders;
those who are selfless
may be appointed to governance;
those who discern timing and scrutinize utility,
and can prepare officials,
may be upheld as rulers.
The sluggish fall behind affairs;
those stingy with wealth lose their close ones;
those who trust petty men lose scholars.
Above are the six relationships and five laws.
Second discourse.
The mountain,
being the highest among things,
is like benevolence,
the highest conduct of a ruler;
kindness, the highest conduct of parents;
loyalty, the highest conduct of ministers;
filial piety,
the highest conduct of children and wives.
Thus, if the mountain is high and does not crumble,
sacrificial sheep will come;
if the ruler is benevolent and does not slacken,
the people will support him;
if parents are kind and do not slacken,
children and wives will be obedient;
if ministers are loyal and do not slacken,
rank and emolument will come;
if children and wives are filial and do not slacken,
a fine reputation will follow.
Therefore, with unwavering high integrity,
what is desired will be attained;
if slackened, it will not.
Hence it is said: "If the mountain is high and does not crumble,
sacrificial sheep will come;"
"If the abyss is deep and does not dry up,
jades will be cast to the utmost."
The abyss,
being the source of all things,
if deep and undried,
will attract jades cast into it.
The ruler,
is whom people look up to for livelihood.
If broad-minded, pure, and generous without harshness or envy,
the people will adhere to him.
Parents,
are from whom children and wives receive instruction;
if kind, benevolent, and teaching without losing reason,
children and wives will be filial.
Ministers,
are those employed by the ruler;
if they exert full effort in serving above,
they will satisfy the ruler.
Children and wives,
are whom parents rely on for comfort;
if filial, respectful, and obedient to parents,
they will satisfy them;
thus, if the abyss dries up without water,
jades will not be cast.
If the ruler is harsh and not generous,
the myriad people will not adhere.
If parents are violent and without kindness,
children and wives will not be close.
If ministers are obsequious and not loyal,
they will face humiliation and poverty.
If children and wives do not comfort parents,
disaster and sorrow will arrive;
therefore, if the abyss does not dry up,
what is desired will come;
if dried,
it will not,
hence it is said:
"If the abyss is deep and does not dry up,
jades will be cast to the utmost."
Heaven does not change its constancy;
it covers all things,
regulates cold and heat,
moves the sun and moon,
orders the stars and constellations—
this is Heaven's constancy,
governed by principle,
ending and beginning anew.
The ruler shepherds the myriad people,
governs the world,
oversees all officials—
this is the ruler's constancy,
governed by law,
ending and beginning anew.
Harmonizing descendants,
uniting relatives—
this is parents' constancy,
governed by righteousness,
ending and beginning anew.
Sincerity, respect, loyalty, and trust—
this is ministers' constancy.
Serving their ruler thereby,
ending and beginning anew.
Loving parents and providing well,
mindful of respect and heeding teachings—
this is children and wives' constancy,
serving their parents thereby,
ending and beginning anew.
Thus, if Heaven does not lose its constancy,
cold and heat arrive in season,
the sun, moon, stars, and constellations follow their sequence.
If the ruler does not lose his constancy,
the ministers understand their duty,
and all officials fulfill their tasks.
If parents do not lose their constancy,
descendants are harmonious and obedient,
and relatives rejoice together.
If ministers do not lose their constancy,
affairs are without error,
and official duties are well managed.
If children and wives do not lose their constancy,
then old and young are orderly, and close and distant are harmonious.
Therefore, upholding constancy brings order;
losing it brings chaos.
Heaven has never changed its way of order,
hence it is said:
"Heaven does not change its constancy."
Earth does not alter its principles;
Earth nurtures all things—
this is Earth's principle.
Governing and pacifying the common people—
this is the ruler's principle.
Teaching and protecting family affairs—
this is parents' principle.
Remonstrating uprightly and dying for integrity—
this is ministers' principle.
Exerting full effort in support and care—
this is children and wives' principle.
The earth does not alter its principles,
thus all things are born.
The ruler does not alter his principles,
thus the people are at peace.
Parents do not alter their principles,
thus household affairs are managed.
Ministers do not alter their principles,
thus the ruler is without faults;
children and wives do not alter their principles,
thus parental care is fully provided;
Therefore, those who follow principles are secure,
those who do not use principles are endangered.
The earth has never altered,
this is the reason for its stability;
Hence it is said:
"The earth does not alter its principles."
Spring, autumn, winter, and summer
do not change their seasons,
this is constant from ancient times to the present.
In spring,
yang energy begins to ascend,
thus all things are born.
In summer,
yang energy fully ascends,
thus all things grow.
In autumn,
yin energy begins to descend,
thus all things are harvested.
In winter,
yin energy fully descends,
thus all things are stored;
Therefore, growth occurs in spring and summer,
storage and harvesting in autumn and winter,
these are the seasons of the four periods.
Rewards and punishments,
are the ruler's seasons.
The four seasons never fail to give life and take it,
the ruler never fails to reward and punish;
Hence it is said:
"Spring, autumn, winter, and summer,
do not change their seasons."
Heaven covers all things and governs them,
earth carries all things and nurtures them,
the four seasons grow all things and store them,
from ancient times to the present,
their way has not changed,
Therefore it is said:
"Ancient and present are one."
When the flood dragon obtains water,
its divinity can be established;
The flood dragon,
is the divine creature of water,
riding on water,
its divinity is established,
losing water,
its divinity is lost.
The ruler,
is the one with authority in the world,
gaining the people, his authority is established,
losing the people, his authority is lost.
The flood dragon waits to obtain water before establishing its divinity,
the ruler waits to gain the people before completing his authority,
Therefore it is said:
"When the flood dragon obtains water,
its divinity can be established."
When tigers and leopards dwell in darkness,
their awe can be respected.
Tigers and leopards,
are the fiercest of beasts,
residing in deep forests and vast marshes,
then people fear their awe and respect them.
The ruler,
is the one with power in the world,
dwelling deeply, people fear his power;
Therefore, if tigers and leopards leave their darkness and approach people,
people can capture them and diminish their awe.
If the ruler leaves his gates and presses close to the people,
the people will轻视 him and despise his power.
Therefore it is said:
"Tigers and leopards rely on darkness,
and their awe can be respected."
Wind and rain have no fixed direction,
yet resentment and anger do not reach them.
Wind,
is what blows things;
what the wind blows,
does not avoid noble or humble, beautiful or ugly.
Rain,
is what moistens things;
where the rain falls,
does not avoid small or large, strong or weak.
Wind and rain are utterly impartial and without selfishness,
their movement has no constant direction,
though people may be blown or soaked,
none bear them resentment;
Therefore it is said:
"Wind and rain have no fixed direction,
yet resentment and anger do not reach them."
Nobility lies in having means to enforce orders,
humility lies in having means to forget lowliness.
The reason why the ruler's orders are followed when issued,
and prohibitions stop when declared,
is that he must order what the people desire,
and prohibit what the people detest.
The nature of people is to desire life and detest death,
to desire benefit and detest harm,
Therefore, if the ruler orders what gives life and benefits people,
then orders are followed;
if he prohibits killing and harming people,
then prohibitions are effective.
The reason orders are followed,
is that the people delight in his governance.
Thus orders are carried out,
Therefore it is said:
"Nobility lies in having means to enforce orders."
The reason why the ruler can make subordinates exert their strength and draw close to him,
is that he must bring benefits and eliminate harms for the world,
Thus his virtue and favor extend to all under heaven,
his kindness and generosity enrich all things,
fathers and sons can thereby be secure,
all living beings can thereby be nurtured,
Therefore the myriad people joyfully exhaust their strength,
and delight in being used by their superior,
at home they focus on fundamentals and work diligently,
to fill the granaries,
abroad they fulfill their duties and die fighting enemies,
to secure the altars of soil and grain,
though toilsome, humble, and disgraceful,
they dare not complain.
This is how the humble forget their lowliness.
Therefore it is said:
"Humility lies in having means to forget lowliness."
Longevity, premature death, poverty, and wealth,
do not come without reason.
If daily routines are timely,
eating and drinking moderate,
cold and heat appropriate,
then the body benefits and lifespan increases.
If daily routines are untimely,
eating and drinking immoderate,
cold and heat inappropriate,
then the body is burdened and lifespan diminished.
If people are lazy and extravagant, they become poor;
if diligent and frugal, they become rich;
Nothing comes vainly,
there must be a cause for it,
Therefore it is said:
"Longevity, premature death, poverty, and wealth,
do not come without reason."
The one who carries out orders
embodies the ruler's dignity.
When laws are established and the people rejoice in them,
when orders are issued and the people carry them out,
when laws and orders align with the people's hearts,
like tally slips matching perfectly,
then the ruler's dignity is enhanced,
Therefore it is said:
"Carrying out orders
embodies the ruler's dignity."
Accepting instructions
moves reputation.
If the superior does not interfere,
the people will naturally apply themselves.
The enlightened ruler's governance of the world,
calms his people without disturbing them,
gives them rest without toiling them;
Without disturbance,
the people naturally follow order;
Without toil,
the people naturally apply themselves,
Therefore it is said:
"When the superior does not interfere,
the people naturally apply themselves."
Holding the ceremonial vessel without speaking,
yet the temple court is already well-ordered.
When a ruler establishes his standards and measures,
sets forth the divisions of duties, clarifies
his laws and models,
and governs his people
without prioritizing words,
then the people follow the right path.
What is called "holding the Shǔ"
refers to a sacrificial vessel.
Hence it is said:
"Holding the Shǔ without speaking,
yet the temple court is well-ordered."
"The wild geese cry qiangqiang,"
and the people sing of them.
"The majestic wild geese,"
are admired for their beauty.
Their beauty
is why the people sing of them.
Virtue and righteousness
are the beauty of conduct.
The beauty of virtue and righteousness
is why the people delight in them.
What the people sing of and delight in
are beautiful conduct, virtue, and righteousness.
And the enlightened ruler possesses these, like the majestic wild geese.
Hence it is said:
"The wild geese majestic,
the people sing of them;
the many officers dignified,
the Yīn people are transformed by them."
"Dignified"
means sincere, solemn, decisive in affairs.
"Many officers"
means many wise elders.
King Wén of Zhōu was sincere, solemn, and decisive,
so the state was well-governed.
His ministers understood principles and assisted the ruler,
so the ruler was enlightened.
The ruler enlightened and the state well-governed,
the entire realm benefited from his kindness,
and the Yīn people raised their heads to gaze at King Wén,
wishing to be his subjects;
hence it is said:
"The many officers dignified,
the Yīn people are transformed by them."
#Zhòu's failures.
When Zhòu was the ruler,
he exhausted the people's strength,
seized their wealth,
endangered and killed them,
and imposed unjust and cruel decrees
upon the hundred surnames.
He dispatched brutal envoys
throughout the world;
thus, his high ministers did not draw close,
the common people hated and resented him,
and the world rebelled against him,
wishing instead to be subjects of King Wén—
this was Zhòu's own doing.
Hence it is said:
"Zhòu's failures."
The words of flying thistledown
are not among what is honored;
without standards and models,
rules and measures, drifting and unsettled,
this is called the words of flying thistledown. The words of flying thistledown
an enlightened ruler does not heed.
Words without measure
an enlightened ruler does not accept.
Hence it is said:
"The words of flying thistledown are not among what is honored."
The gathering of swallows and sparrows,
the path being followed, one does not look back.
When the path is followed, then ruler and ministers are close,
father and son are at peace,
and all living things thrive;
thus, the enlightened ruler's task
lies in following the path,
not looking back at small things;
swallows and sparrows
are among the smallest of things;
hence it is said:
"The gathering of swallows and sparrows,
the path being followed, one does not look back."
Pure sacrificial animals, jade tablets, and discs
are not enough to please ghosts and spirits.
The enlightened ruler's actions and stillness accord with principle and righteousness,
his commands follow the people's hearts,
his executions match the crimes,
and his rewards match the achievements.
Thus, even without using sacrificial animals, jade tablets, and discs to pray to ghosts and spirits,
the ghosts and spirits aid him,
heaven and earth support him,
and his undertakings bring blessings.
The chaotic ruler's actions lose righteousness and principle,
his commands go against the people's hearts,
his executions do not match the crimes,
his rewards do not match the achievements,
so even if he uses sacrificial animals, jade tablets, and discs to pray to ghosts and spirits,
the ghosts and spirits do not aid him,
heaven and earth do not support him,
and his undertakings bring disaster;
hence it is said:
"Sacrificial animals, jade tablets, and discs are not enough
to please ghosts and spirits."
The ruler's achievements have a foundation;
what use are precious goods?
What the ruler uses to achieve merit
is wealth and strength;
thus, when the state is rich and the army strong,
the feudal lords submit to his governance,
neighboring enemies fear his might,
and even without using precious goods to serve the feudal lords,
they dare not attack him.
What the ruler incurs as fault
is poverty and weakness;
thus, when the state is poor and the army weak,
in battle he does not win,
in defense he is not secure,
and even if he offers famous vessels and heavy treasures to serve neighboring enemies,
he cannot escape the peril of death and destruction;
hence it is said:
"The ruler's achievements have a foundation;
what use are precious goods?"
Yì's way
is not archery;
Yì,
an expert archer of antiquity,
adjusted his bow and arrows and firmly maintained them;
in handling his bow,
he assessed the high and low,
having a way that ensured hitting the mark,
thus he could shoot often and hit often.
The enlightened ruler is like Yì:
he harmonizes his laws,
examines what to abolish and establish and firmly maintains them,
having a way that ensures good governance,
thus he can undertake much and succeed often.
The way
is why Yì always hit the mark,
and why the ruler always achieves good governance.
Archery
is the releasing of arrows from the bowstring;
hence it is said:
"Yì's way is not archery."
Zàofǔ's technique
is not driving;
Zàofǔ,
an expert at driving horses,
carefully tended his horses,
regulated their food and drink,
measured their strength,
and assessed their running,
thus he could cover long distances without the horses tiring.
The enlightened ruler is like Zàofǔ:
he skillfully governs his people,
measures their strength,
assesses their abilities,
thus he achieves merit without the people being distressed or harmed;
so the technique
is why Zàofǔ covered long distances,
and why the ruler achieves merit and fame.
Driving
is handling the reins;
hence it is said:
"Zàofǔ's technique is not driving."
Xīzhòng's skill
is not carving;
when Xīzhòng made chariots and tools,
whether square, round, curved, or straight,
all matched the compass, square, hook, and line,
so the parts fit together perfectly,
were durable and efficient in use,
and the finished products were solid.
The enlightened ruler is like Xīzhòng:
his words and actions
all match methods and calculations,
so all principles align,
and high and low are close.
The ingenuity of Xī Zhòng
is what enabled him to create vessels,
just as the ruler employs it to govern.
The carving and cutting
are but the work of the axe and knife.
Hence it is said:
"Xī Zhòng's ingenuity
lies not in the carving and cutting."
To attract the distant, one makes no special effort;
to draw close the near, one speaks no special words.
Only the nightwalker possesses this uniquely.
When people benefit, they come;
when harmed, they leave.
People follow profit
as water flows downward,
choosing no particular direction.
Thus, to attract people,
first establish benefits for them,
and though unsummoned, they will come of themselves.
If what they detest is set up,
though summoned, they will not come.
Hence it is said:
"To attract the distant, one makes no special effort."
Governing the people as parents do,
they will feel affection and love.
Guide them with pure sincerity,
and treat them with substantial care.
Though not proclaiming "I am close to the people,"
the people will be close.
Governing the people as enemies,
they will become distant.
If the guidance lacks sincerity,
and treatment is insubstantial,
with deceit and falsehood arising together,
though proclaiming "I am close to the people,"
the people will not be close.
Hence it is said:
"To draw close the near, one speaks no special words."
The enlightened ruler causes the distant to come and the near to be close
by acting from the heart.
The so-called nightwalker
is one whose heart acts.
If one can practice virtue from the heart,
then none under heaven can contend with him.
Hence it is said:
"Only the nightwalker uniquely possesses this!"
On the lowlands of the plain,
what height is there?
To be a ruler yet cruel,
a parent yet violent,
a minister
yet disloyal, a child or spouse
yet unfilial—these four are great faults of humanity.
With great faults upon oneself, even minor virtues cannot make one worthy.
The so-called plain refers to low marshlands.
Even with small mounds, it cannot be considered
high. Hence it is said: the lowlands of the plain
have no height.
In the curves of the great mountain,
what depth is there?
To be a ruler yet benevolent,
a parent yet kind,
a minister yet loyal,
a child or spouse yet filial—
these four are lofty conducts of humanity.
With lofty conducts upon oneself,
even minor faults
do not make one unworthy.
The so-called great mountain
is the highest among mountains.
Even with small curves,
they are not considered deep.
Hence it is said:
"In the curves of the great mountain,
what depth is there?"
Those who slander and flatter
should not be entrusted with great responsibilities.
Defaming the worthy is called slander,
praising the unworthy is called flattery.
If such persons are employed,
the ruler's clarity is obscured,
and words of defamation and false praise arise.
Entrusted with great tasks,
they will fail, and calamity will arrive.
Hence it is said:
"Those who slander and flatter,
should not be entrusted with great responsibilities."
Those of great vision can be partnered for far-reaching endeavors;
those who consider worries can be partnered to attain the Way.
Those whose plans are hasty and worries are immediate
should be let go and not summoned.
When an enlightened ruler considers affairs,
those who plan for the world are called visionary ministers.
Visionary ministers cause all within the seas to receive
their beneficence, which spreads throughout the world, and later generations enjoy their achievements long after, with benefits growing over time.
Hence it is said: visionary ministers can be partnered for far-reaching endeavors.
The sage chooses what can be spoken before speaking,
and what can be done before acting.
To seize profit that later brings harm,
or seize pleasure that later brings sorrow—
the sage does not do such things.
Thus, the sage in choosing words must consider the burdens,
in choosing actions must consider the worries.
Hence it is said:
"Those who consider worries can be partnered to attain the Way."
Petty persons
distort the Way to gain favor,
cater to the ruler's wishes to seek fleeting pleasure,
and covet profit to seize gains.
Such people,
though they may gain quickly,
will also face calamity swiftly.
Thus, the sage rejects and does not employ them.
Hence it is said:
"Those whose plans are hasty and worries are immediate,
should be let go and not summoned."
Promoting the enduring allows for long-term vision;
advocating what brings long-term benefit to the world
is called promoting the enduring.
Promoting the enduring benefits many,
and the influence of virtue and righteousness is far-reaching.
Hence it is said:
"Promoting the enduring allows for long-term vision."
The magnitude of capacity is what the multitude relies upon;
Heaven's capacity is great,
thus it can cover all things.
Earth's capacity is great,
thus it can carry all things.
The ruler's capacity is great,
thus he can accommodate much and the multitude can rely on him.
Hence it is said: the magnitude of capacity is what the multitude relies upon.
To be cherished by people,
one must steadfastly practice virtue without weariness.
Wealth, honor, dignity, and prominence
are what people return to and delight in,
and every ruler desires them.
Thus, to have the people cherish and delight in oneself,
one must practice the Way and virtue without weariness,
and the people will cherish and delight in him.
Hence it is said:
"To be cherished by people,
one must steadfastly practice virtue without weariness."
Matters that are inevitably obtained
are not reliable.
When the sage seeks affairs,
he first examines their principle and righteousness,
and considers their feasibility.
Thus, if righteous, he seeks them;
if unrighteous, he stops.
If feasible, he seeks them;
if not feasible, he stops.
Therefore, the affairs he obtains
are often treasures for life.
When petty persons seek affairs,
they do not examine their principle and righteousness,
nor consider their feasibility.
Even unrighteous, they seek them;
even unfeasible, they seek them.
Thus, the affairs they obtain
are never reliable.
Hence it is said:
"Matters that are inevitably obtained
are not reliable."
Words that are inevitably promised
are not trustworthy.
When the sage makes a promise,
he first examines its principle and righteousness,
and considers its feasibility.
If righteous, he promises;
if unrighteous, he refrains.
If feasible, he promises;
if not feasible, he refrains.
Thus, his promises are always trustworthy.
The petty person promises even what is unjust,
promises even what is impossible,
and upon speaking, always makes a promise,
hence their promises are not necessarily trustworthy;
thus it is said:
"Words that are always promised,
are not enough to be trusted."
Those who are cautious in small matters do not achieve great standing;
being cautious within one family,
they establish themselves within that family;
cautious within one village,
they establish themselves within that village;
cautious within one state,
they establish themselves within that state;
cautious throughout the world,
they establish themselves throughout the world;
Therefore, if what they are cautious about is small,
then what they establish is also small;
if what they are cautious about is great,
then what they establish is also great;
thus it is said:
"Those cautious in small matters do not achieve great standing."
Those who are picky about food do not fatten their bodies.
The sea does not refuse water,
hence it can achieve its vastness.
The mountain does not refuse earth and stones,
hence it can achieve its height.
The enlightened ruler does not disdain people,
hence he can gather his multitude.
The scholar does not disdain learning,
hence he can achieve sageliness.
Being picky,
means disliking many things.
Remonstrance,
is what secures the ruler.
Eating,
is what fattens the body.
If the ruler dislikes remonstrance, he is not secure;
if a person is picky about food, they do not fatten;
thus it is said:
"Those picky about food do not fatten their bodies."
Those who have words that are not discarded,
must align with heaven and earth.
Speaking of morality, loyalty, trustworthiness, filial piety, and fraternal duty—
these are words that are not discarded.
Heaven is fair and impartial,
hence it covers all, beautiful and ugly.
Earth is fair and impartial,
hence it carries all, small and great.
Words that are not discarded,
are fair and impartial,
hence the worthy and unworthy are all employed;
thus, words that are not discarded
align with the impartiality of heaven and earth;
therefore it is said:
"Those who have words that are not discarded,
must align them with heaven and earth."
A cliff of three rèn,
is a great difficulty for humans,
yet monkeys drink from it;
the enlightened ruler appoints things to office,
employing their strengths,
not their weaknesses,
hence affairs are always accomplished,
and achievements are always established.
The chaotic ruler does not know that each thing has its strengths and weaknesses,
and demands they be complete in all.
In planning affairs and determining matters,
distinguishing and clarifying rites and righteousness,
are human strengths,
but weaknesses of the monkey;
climbing high and traversing danger,
are strengths of the monkey,
but weaknesses of humans;
to demand of humans what monkeys excel at,
hence his orders fail and demands are not met,
thus it is said:
"A cliff of three rèn,
is a great difficulty for humans,
yet monkeys drink from it."
Therefore it is said, boasting and favoring专制,
are the calamity of undertaking affairs.
The enlightened ruler in undertaking affairs,
employs the wisdom of the sage,
uses the strength of the multitude,
and does not rely solely on himself;
hence affairs succeed and blessings arise.
The chaotic ruler considers himself wise,
and does not follow the wisdom of the sage,
boasts and strives for personal achievement,
and does not use the strength of the multitude,
relies solely on himself,
and does not heed correct remonstrance.
Hence affairs fail and calamities arise;
thus it is said:
"Boasting and favoring专制,
are the calamity of undertaking affairs."
Even if one does not travel the wilds,
one does not neglect one's horse;
the horse,
is what one rides to travel the wilds,
hence even if not traveling the wilds,
the feeding and care of the horse
are never neglected.
The people,
are what one uses for defense and battle,
hence even if not defending or battling,
the governance and care of the people
are never neglected;
thus it is said:
"Even if one does not travel the wilds,
one does not neglect one's horse."
Those who can give without taking,
are the counterparts of heaven and earth.
Heaven gives birth to the four seasons,
earth gives birth to all wealth,
to nurture all things,
without taking anything;
The enlightened ruler is the counterpart of heaven and earth,
teaching the people according to the seasons,
encouraging them in farming and weaving,
to enrich the people's livelihood,
without boasting of his achievements,
without privatizing the benefits;
thus it is said:
"Those who can give without taking,
are the counterparts of heaven and earth."
The lazy and weary fall behind,
being negligent and disrespectful,
in serving the ruler, it is disloyal,
in serving parents, it is unfilial,
in undertaking affairs, it leads to failure,
hence it is said:
"The lazy and weary fall behind."
Those without breadth seem divine;
the divine is within,
the lagging are at the door;
those within are about to act,
those at the door are about to wait.
At dawn, be vigilant without slack,
lest later you meet calamity.
If you forget your duties in the morning,
by evening you lose your achievements.
Using compass and square, circles and squares are formed;
using inches and feet, length and shortness are measured;
using laws and methods, the people are governed peacefully;
hence affairs not exceeding principle in breadth,
their success seems divine;
thus it is said:
"Those without breadth seem divine."
Serving the ruler without full effort,
leads to punishment.
Serving parents without full effort,
leads to lack of closeness.
Receiving instruction and asking about learning without increased effort,
leads to no accomplishment.
Hence, if one does not strive diligently for advancement in the morning,
by evening there are no achievements to see,
thus it is said:
"If you forget your duties in the morning,
by evening you lose your achievements."
When evil qi enters inward,
the proper complexion fades.
If inner feelings are sincere and truthful,
then reputation and fame are beautiful.
If conduct is careful and respectful,
then honor and prominence follow.
If inwardly there is no true feeling,
then reputation and fame are foul.
If conduct is negligent and disrespectful,
then disgrace and humiliation arise.
Therefore it is said:
"When evil qi assails inward,
the proper complexion fades."
If the ruler is not a ruler,
then the minister is not a minister.
If a ruler does not understand the principles governing the relationship between sovereign and subject to properly guide his ministers,
then the ministers will not know the duties of being a subject to serve their lord.
Hence it is said:
"If the sovereign is not sovereign-like,
then the ministers will not be minister-like."
If the father is not father-like,
then the son will not be son-like.
If a father does not understand the principles governing the relationship between father and son to educate his children and bring them into order,
then the children will not know the way of being a son to serve their father.
Hence it is said:
"If the father is not father-like,
then the son will not be son-like."
When those above lose their proper position,
those below will overstep their bounds.
When superiors and subordinates are not harmonious,
commands will not be carried out.
When sovereign and ministers are close,
superiors and subordinates are harmonious,
and the myriad people are united,
then when the ruler issues commands the people carry them out,
and when superiors impose prohibitions the people do not violate them.
When sovereign and ministers are not close,
superiors and subordinates are not harmonious,
and the myriad people are not united,
then commands will not be carried out,
and prohibitions will not be observed;
hence it is said:
"When superiors and subordinates are not harmonious,
commands will not be carried out."
If clothing and cap are not proper,
then the attendants will not be respectful;
if words are trustworthy,
actions are dignified,
and clothing and cap are proper,
then the ministers and subordinates will be respectful.
If words are disrespectful,
actions are deficient,
and clothing and cap are slovenly,
then the ministers and subordinates will despise him;
hence it is said:
"If clothing and cap are not proper,
then the attendants will not be respectful,
if advancing and retreating lack decorum,
then government orders will not be carried out.
Decorum is
the standard pattern for all things.
Laws and measures are
the model for the myriad people.
Ritual and righteousness are
the model for honor and humility.
Therefore, if actions have decorum then commands are carried out,
if without decorum then commands are not carried out;
hence it is said:
"If advancing and retreating lack decorum,
then government orders will not be carried out."
Both cherishing and awe-inspiring,
then the way of the ruler is complete.
The ruler,
if gentle, kind, generous, and tolerant,
then the people will love him.
If orderly, strict, and dignified,
then the people will fear him.
Thus if the people love him they will be close,
if they fear him they will be employed.
When the people are close and can be employed,
this is what the ruler urgently needs;
hence it is said:
"Both cherishing and awe-inspiring,
then the way of the ruler is complete."
If he does not make them happy,
then they will not share his sorrow;
if he does not give them life,
then they will not die for him.
If the ruler can bring peace to his people,
then the people will serve their ruler as they serve their parents,
so when the ruler has sorrow they share it,
when he has difficulties they die for him.
If the ruler regards the people as dirt,
then the people will not serve him,
when the ruler has sorrow they will not share it,
when he has difficulties they will not die for him;
hence it is said:
"If he does not make them happy,
then they will not share his sorrow,
if he does not give them life,
then they will not die for him."
What goes out does not reach,
what comes in does not arrive.
The reason why the people defend and fight to death without decline is that
what the superiors bestow upon the people is generous;
thus if the superiors bestow generously,
then the people's repayment to the superiors is also generous;
if the superiors bestow meagerly,
then the people's repayment to the superiors is also meager;
thus to bestow meagerly but demand generously,
the ruler cannot obtain this from his ministers,
the father cannot obtain this from his son;
hence it is said:
"What goes out does not reach,
what comes in does not arrive."
What the Dào speaks of is one,
but its applications differ.
The Dào is
that which supports all things,
enabling them to grow and nurture,
and each to complete its nature and destiny.
Thus some use it to govern a village,
some use it to govern a state,
some use it to govern the world.
Hence it is said:
"What the Dào speaks of is one,
but its applications differ."
There are those who hear the Dào and are fond of governing a family -
they are people of one family.
There are those who hear the Dào and are fond of governing a village -
they are people of one village;
those who hear the Dào and use it to govern one village,
making fathers and sons close,
making brothers harmonious,
correcting customs and habits,
making the people delight in their superiors,
and be content with their land,
becoming the mainstay of one village -
they are people of the village;
hence it is said:
"There are those who hear the Dào and are fond of governing a village -
they are people of one village."
There are those who hear the Dào and are fond of governing a state -
they are people of one state.
There are those who hear the Dào and are fond of governing the world -
they are people of the world.
There are those who hear the Dào and are fond of settling all things -
they are the match of Heaven and Earth.
When the Dào departs,
the people do not come;
when the Dào arrives,
the people do not leave;
the people's following of one who possesses the Dào
is like hunger preceding food,
like cold preceding clothing,
like heat preceding shade;
thus when there is the Dào the people return to him,
when there is no Dào the people leave him;
hence it is said:
"When the Dào departs,
the people do not come.
When the Dào arrives,
the people do not leave."
What the Dào establishes,
the body transforms.
The Dào is
that by which we transform our body and reach correct principle,
thus when the Dào is in the body,
then words naturally accord,
actions naturally correct,
serving the ruler naturally loyal,
serving the father naturally filial,
dealing with people naturally reasonable;
hence it is said:
"What the Dào establishes,
the body transforms."
Maintaining fullness is with Heaven,
safety and danger are with people.
The way of Heaven is
full without overflowing,
flourishing without declining,
the enlightened ruler models himself on the way of Heaven,
thus noble without arrogance,
wealthy without extravagance,
acting with principle without laziness,
thus able to long maintain nobility and wealth,
long possess the world without losing it;
hence it is said:
"Maintaining fullness is with Heaven."
An enlightened ruler is one who rescues the world from calamity
and stabilizes the world in times of peril.
To rescue from calamity and stabilize peril,
one must rely on the service of all the people,
and only then can it be accomplished.
Hence it is said:
"Stability and peril depend on the people."
If the measures of Heaven are lost,
even fullness will surely dry up.
With vast territory and a wealthy state,
a populous people and strong soldiers,
this is a state at the peak of fullness;
yet even at such fullness,
without virtuous generosity to stabilize it,
without rules and measures to govern it,
then the state ceases to be its state,
and the people cease to be its people.
Therefore it is said:
"If the measures of Heaven are lost,
even fullness will surely dry up."
When superiors and subordinates are not in harmony,
even stability will turn to peril.
If ministers do not feel close to their ruler,
and the common people do not trust their officials,
superiors and subordinates are estranged and discordant,
so even if they seem secure,
peril is bound to arise.
Hence it is said:
"When superiors and subordinates are not in harmony,
even stability will turn to peril."
One who desires to rule the world
but loses the Way of Heaven,
cannot attain rulership over the world.
If a ruler possesses the Way of Heaven,
to guide his people,
then the people will be of one mind in serving their superior,
thus enabling him to achieve nobility, wealth, and long-lasting rule over the world.
If the Way of Heaven is lost,
then the people will rebel and disobey,
so the ruler is endangered and cannot long rule the world;
therefore it is said:
"One who desires to rule the world,
but loses the Way of Heaven,
cannot attain rulership over the world."
When one attains the Way of Heaven,
affairs proceed as if naturally;
when the Way of Heaven is lost,
even if established, there is no stability.
Once the Way is attained,
none know how it was done;
once the task is accomplished,
none perceive its influence.
It is stored without form—
such is the Way of Heaven.
If a ruler diligently studies methods and techniques,
and earnestly practices correct principles,
then transformation and progress advance daily,
leading to great achievements,
yet foolish people remain unaware.
A disorderly ruler indulges in excess and depravity,
daily acting without the Way,
proceeding to ruin and extinction without self-awareness;
therefore it is said:
"None know how it was done,
once the task is accomplished,
none perceive its resting place,
stored away without form."
For those who doubt the present,
examine antiquity;
for those who do not know the future,
look to the past.
The ancient Three Sovereigns and Five Hegemons
all were rulers who benefited
from the Way of Heaven.
Thus they attained personal honor and eminence
with descendants receiving their beneficence.
Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì
all were rulers who harmed the world,
thus they suffered personal hardship and injury
with descendants inheriting their calamities. Hence it is said: For those who doubt
the present, examine antiquity,
for those who do not know the future, look to the past.
The manifestation of all affairs
differs in course but converges in outcome,
this unity persists through past and present.
Shénnóng taught plowing to grow grain,
thereby benefiting the people.
Yǔ personally dredged waterways,
leveling heights and bridging lows,
thereby benefiting the people.
Tāng and Wǔ campaigned against the unprincipled,
executing the violent and chaotic,
thereby benefiting the people.
Thus, though the actions of enlightened kings differ,
their benefit to the people is the same;
therefore it is said:
"The undertaking of all affairs,
though arising differently, converges in outcome,
this unity persists through past and present."
When a green timber beam collapses the roof,
no resentment arises;
but when a young child removes tiles,
a kind mother takes up the rod.
If a beam bends from being unseasoned,
and cannot bear the load, causing the roof to collapse,
people do not resent it,
for such is the natural principle.
A young child,
beloved by a kind mother,
if removing tiles against principle,
will be whipped by the mother;
thus, when actions follow principle,
even a collapsed roof draws no resentment.
When actions defy principle,
removing tiles warrants whipping;
hence it is said:
"A green beam collapsing the roof
draws no resentment.
A young child removing tiles
brings the kind mother's rod."
At the ultimate of Heaven's Way,
the distant draw near of themselves;
when human affairs arise,
even close kin create resentment.
By practicing Heaven's Way,
enacting public principle,
the distant draw near spontaneously.
Abandoning Heaven's Way,
pursuing private deeds,
then mother and child resent each other;
therefore it is said:
"At the ultimate of Heaven's Way,
the distant draw near of themselves;
when human affairs arise,
close kin create resentment."
All things towards humanity
show no private closeness,
no private distance.
The skillful have surplus,
while the clumsy suffer lack.
In ancient times, King Wǔ's territory did not exceed a hundred lǐ,
his troops numbered no more than ten thousand,
yet he could triumph in battle and conquer,
establishing himself as Son of Heaven,
and the world calls him a sage king
because he knew the method of accomplishing it.
Jié and Zhòu were honored as Sons of Heaven,
possessed the wealth of the entire realm,
held vast territories,
commanded numerous troops,
yet they died and their states perished,
becoming scorned by the world,
because they did not know the method of accomplishing it;
thus, those who can accomplish it
can turn small into great,
humble into noble;
those who cannot accomplish it,
even as Sons of Heaven,
will still be overthrown;
therefore it is said:
"The skillful have surplus,
while the clumsy suffer lack."
Those whose deeds accord with Heaven receive Heaven's aid,
those whose deeds oppose Heaven face Heaven's opposition.
Those aided by Heaven,
though small, will surely become great;
those opposed by Heaven,
though seeming successful, will surely fail.
In ancient times, King Wǔ,
was assisted by Heaven,
so although his territory was small and his people few,
he still became the Son of Heaven.
Jié and Zhòu,
were opposed by Heaven,
so although their territories were vast and their people numerous,
they still met with distress, humiliation, and death;
Hence it is said:
"Those assisted by Heaven,
though small will surely become great.
Those opposed by Heaven,
though great will surely be diminished."
Those who follow Heaven achieve merit,
those who oppose Heaven incur misfortune,
and cannot be restored.
The cunning of the crow,
though clever is not intimate;
in dealing with people,
if one is mostly deceitful and insincere,
stealing everything opportunistically,
it is called a crow-gathered friendship;
a crow-gathered friendship,
though initially joyful,
will later turn to mutual reproach;
hence it is said:
"A crow-gathered friendship,
though clever is not intimate."
An unvalued bond,
though firm will surely loosen.
In the application of the Dào,
its value lies in being valued.
When a sage forms bonds with others,
he observes how they serve their ruler above,
and how they serve their parents within,
there must be a discernible principle,
only then does he form the bond;
forming a bond without following principle,
will later lead to mutual betrayal;
hence it is said:
"An unvalued bond,
though firm will surely loosen.
In the application of the Dào,
its value lies in being valued."
Do not ally with the impossible,
an enlightened ruler consults with sages,
thus his plans succeed.
When he undertakes affairs with them,
thus his affairs are accomplished.
A chaotic ruler consults with the unworthy,
thus his plans fail.
When he undertakes affairs with them,
thus his affairs are ruined.
When plans fail and affairs are ruined,
this is the fault of allying with the impossible,
hence it is said:
"Do not ally with the impossible."
Do not force the incapable,
an enlightened ruler measures what people are capable of,
and then employs them;
thus when ordering what people can do,
the orders are carried out;
when employing people for what they can do,
affairs are accomplished.
A chaotic ruler does not measure people's capabilities,
ordering what people cannot do,
thus his orders are abandoned;
employing people for what they cannot do,
thus his affairs are ruined.
When orders are issued but abandoned,
and undertakings fail,
this is the crime of forcing the incapable,
hence it is said:
"Do not force the incapable."
Do not instruct the unknowing.
To mad and deluded people,
if one instructs them on the duty between ruler and minister,
the principles of father and son,
the distinctions of noble and base,
they do not believe the words of the sages,
but instead harm and injure them,
thus the sage does not instruct them;
hence it is said:
"Do not instruct the unknowing."
Allying with the impossible,
forcing the incapable,
instructing the unknowing,
is called labor without merit.
Undertaking affairs with the unworthy,
then affairs are ruined.
Employing people for what they cannot do,
then orders are abandoned.
Instructing mad and deluded people brings harm to oneself;
hence it is said:
"Allying with the impossible,
forcing the incapable,
instructing the unknowing,
is called labor without merit."
Friendship that shows its giving,
is almost not intimate;
affection that shows its love,
is almost not bonded;
virtue that shows its bestowal,
is almost not repaid.
What all quarters return to,
is one whose heart acts.
Always using words to proclaim one's giving to others,
one's love for others,
one's virtue towards others,
using this to make friends,
then there is no intimacy,
using this to form bonds,
then there is no connection.
Using this to have virtue towards others,
then there is no repayment,
hence it is said:
"Friendship that shows its giving,
is almost not intimate.
Affection that shows its love,
is almost not bonded.
Virtue that shows its bestowal,
is almost not repaid,
what all quarters return to,
is one whose heart acts."
A state ruled alone,
is toilsome and full of calamities;
an enlightened ruler does not use his own wisdom,
but employs the wisdom of sages;
he does not use his own strength,
but employs the strength of the multitude;
thus using the wisdom of sages to ponder,
there is nothing unknown.
Using the strength of the multitude to undertake affairs,
there is nothing unaccomplished.
Able to set aside oneself and rely on the wisdom and strength of all under Heaven to act,
then the body is at ease and blessings are many.
A chaotic ruler uses only his own wisdom,
and does not employ the wisdom of sages;
he uses only his own strength,
and does not employ the strength of the multitude,
thus his body is toilsome and calamities are many;
hence it is said:
"A state ruled alone,
is toilsome and full of calamities."
The ruler of an isolated state,
is lowly and lacks authority.
An enlightened ruler internally practices his laws and measures,
externally practices his principles and righteousness,
thus neighboring states are close to him,
and allied states trust him;
if there is trouble, neighboring states worry for him,
if there is difficulty, neighboring states rescue him.
A chaotic ruler internally loses his people,
externally is not trusted by neighboring states,
if the state has trouble, none worry for him,
if there is difficulty, none rescue him;
both externally and internally failing,
isolated and without partisans,
thus the state is weak and the ruler humiliated;
hence it is said:
"The ruler of an isolated state,
is lowly and lacks authority."
A woman who acts as her own matchmaker,
is disgraceful and not trusted.
An enlightened ruler in governing all under Heaven,
must employ sages,
and only then will all under Heaven be well-governed.
A woman seeking a husband's family,
must use a matchmaker,
and only then will the family matter be accomplished.
Thus governing all under Heaven without employing sages,
then all under Heaven will be disorderly and the people not intimate.
Seeking a husband's family without using a matchmaker,
then it is shameful and people do not trust it.
Hence it is said:
"A woman who acts as her own matchmaker,
is disgraceful and not trusted."
When one feels affection without having seen him,
one may go to him.
An enlightened ruler,
whom people have not seen,
yet feel affection for,
possesses the way to make the people affectionate.
Thus his position is secure and the people go to him.
Hence it is said:
"When one feels affection without having seen him,
one may go to him."
When one does not forget him over time,
one may come to him.
Yáo and Shùn were enlightened rulers of antiquity.
The world supported them tirelessly,
praised them without weariness,
and did not forget them over long ages,
because they possessed the way to make people remember.
Thus their positions were secure and the people came to them.
Hence it is said:
"When one does not forget him over time,
one may come to him."
When the sun and moon are not bright,
it is not that Heaven has changed.
The sun and moon illuminate all things,
but if Heaven has many clouds,
and there are numerous obstructions covering them,
then the sun and moon are not bright.
The ruler is like the sun and moon.
If many ministers act treacherously,
using selfish means to obstruct the ruler,
then the ruler cannot clearly observe his subordinates.
The true conditions of the subordinates
cannot reach upward,
so treacherous evils increase daily,
and the ruler becomes increasingly obscured.
Hence it is said:
"When the sun and moon are not bright,
it is not that Heaven has changed."
When high mountains are not visible,
it is not that Earth has changed.
Mountains
are the highest of things.
If the terrain is dangerously filthy and not level,
then mountains cannot be seen.
The ruler is like mountains.
If his attendants form many cliques to surround him,
then the ruler cannot be seen.
Hence it is said:
"When high mountains are not visible,
it is not that Earth has changed."
Words that cannot be repeated -
the ruler does not speak them.
When a ruler's speech does not oppose the people's hearts,
nor contradict principle and righteousness,
his words are sufficient to pacify the world,
and people only fear he will not speak them again.
If his speech severs the affection between father and son,
alienates the way between ruler and minister,
and harms the multitude of the world,
these are words that cannot be repeated.
Therefore an enlightened ruler does not speak them.
Hence it is said:
"Words that cannot be repeated -
the ruler does not speak them."
Actions that cannot be repeated -
the ruler does not perform them.
When a ruler's personal conduct is upright,
treating people with courtesy,
meeting others with reason,
and actions emanating from his person
become models for the world,
people only fear he will not repeat them.
If his personal conduct is not upright,
treating people with violence,
meeting others without trust,
and actions emanating from his person
become laughingstocks for the world,
these are actions that cannot be repeated.
Therefore an enlightened ruler does not perform them.
Hence it is said:
"Actions that cannot be repeated -
the ruler does not perform them."
All words that cannot be repeated
and actions that cannot be repeated
are major prohibitions for those who possess states.
Words that cannot be repeated
are untrustworthy words.
Actions that cannot be repeated
are harmful and violent actions.
Therefore, speaking without trust,
the people will not adhere;
acting with harm and violence,
the world will resent.
When the people do not adhere
and the world resents,
this is where destruction arises from.
Therefore enlightened rulers prohibit this.
Hence it is said:
"All words that cannot be repeated,
actions that cannot be repeated,
are major prohibitions for those who possess states."
In a state of ten thousand chariots,
the military cannot be without leadership;
with vast territory,
the countryside cannot be without officials;
with numerous prosperous people,
the government cannot be without leadership;
holding the lives of the people,
the court cannot be without governance.
When the land is extensive but the state poor,
it is because the wilderness is not opened;
when the people are numerous but the military weak,
it is because the people have nothing to strive for.
Therefore, if non-essential production is not prohibited,
the wilderness will not be opened;
if rewards and punishments are not trustworthy,
the people will have nothing to strive for.
When the wilderness is not opened
and the people have nothing to strive for,
externally they cannot respond to enemies,
internally they cannot firmly defend.
Hence it is said, having the title of ten thousand chariots
but not the utility of a thousand chariots,
and seeking that authority not be diminished,
is impossible.
When the land is opened but the state poor,
it is because boats and carriages are ornate,
and towers and pavilions extensive;
when rewards and punishments are trustworthy but the military weak,
it is because the masses are used lightly,
making the people labor.
When boats and carriages are ornate
and towers and pavilions extensive,
then taxes are heavy;
when the masses are used lightly
and the people made to labor,
then the people's strength is exhausted.
When taxes are heavy,
then subordinates resent superiors;
when the people's strength is exhausted,
then commands are not carried out.
When subordinates resent superiors
and commands are not carried out,
and seeking that enemies do not plot against oneself,
is impossible.
Those who wish to govern the world
must carefully utilize their state;
those who wish to govern their state
must carefully utilize their people;
those who wish to govern their people
must carefully exhaust their people's strength.
Without means to nurture them,
then when they leave, it cannot be stopped;
without means to govern them,
then when they stay, they cannot be employed.
When distant people come and do not leave,
there are means to nurture them;
when the people are numerous and can be unified,
there are means to govern them.
When seeing what is acceptable,
show delight with evidence;
when seeing what is unacceptable,
show dislike with form.
If rewards and punishments are trustworthy regarding what is seen,
even regarding what is unseen,
would they dare to act?
When they see something commendable,
they rejoice without evidence;
when they see something objectionable,
they dislike without form.
If rewards and punishments are not trustworthy in what is seen,
yet expect the unseen to be transformed by them,
it is unattainable.
Generous love and benefits
are sufficient to endear them;
enlightened wisdom and rituals
are sufficient to educate them.
The ruler personally practices to lead by example,
establishes standards to regulate them,
appoints teachers in villages to guide and explain.
Then reinforce with laws and decrees,
encourage with rewards and honors,
and discipline with penalties and punishments.
Thus, when the people are all pleased to do good,
then violent and disorderly conduct has no way to arise.
The land produces wealth only at seasons,
the people's labor has its limits,
yet the ruler's desires are endless.
Using the seasonal and the limited
to support a ruler of endless desires,
without measures arising between them,
then superiors and inferiors will resent each other.
Hence, there are ministers who kill their rulers,
and sons who kill their fathers.
Therefore, if taking from the people is moderate,
and spending has its limits,
the state, though small, will surely be secure;
if taking from the people is immoderate,
and spending is unchecked,
the state, though large, will surely be in peril.
Land that is not cultivated
is not our land;
people who are not governed
are not our people.
In governing the people,
one must feed them according to their accumulated merits,
and this cannot be without careful consideration.
Those with many merits receive more sustenance,
those with few merits receive less,
those without merits receive none.
If there are those with merits but not fed,
then the people will alienate from the ruler;
if there are those with many merits but fed little,
then the people will not exert effort;
if there are those with few merits but fed much,
then the people will become deceitful;
if there are those without merits yet fed freely,
then the people will rely on luck.
Thus, alienation, lack of effort,
deceit, and reliance on luck
lead to failure in undertakings,
and inability to respond to enemies.
Therefore it is said,
assess abilities to assign offices,
distribute emoluments and grants,
this is the key to guiding the people.
When the fields compete with the markets for people,
households compete with the treasury for goods,
money competes with grain for value,
and the countryside competes with the court for governance—
thus, if the fields do not accumulate weeds,
it is because farming is prioritized;
if the treasury does not hoard goods,
it is because they are stored among the people;
if the market has no excess stalls,
it is because households are self-sufficient;
if the court does not convene crowds,
it is because villages manage their own affairs.
Hence, fields without weeds,
treasury without hoards,
market without excess,
court without crowds—
this is the pinnacle of governance.
Human nature does not differ,
thus the people's sentiments can be understood and managed.
Examine what they like and dislike,
then their strengths and weaknesses can be known;
observe their associations,
then their worthiness or unworthiness can be discerned.
If these two are not missed,
then the people's capabilities can be assessed and appointed.
The defense of the land lies in the cities,
the defense of the cities lies in the soldiers,
the defense of the soldiers lies in the people,
the defense of the people lies in grain.
Thus, if the land is not cultivated,
the cities will not be secure.
If one cannot govern oneself,
how can one govern others?
If one cannot govern others,
how can one govern a family?
If one cannot govern a family,
how can one govern a village?
If one cannot govern a village,
how can one govern a state?
If one cannot govern a state,
how can one govern the world?
The world
is the foundation of the state;
the state
is the foundation of the village;
the village
is the foundation of the family;
the family
is the foundation of the individual;
the individual
is the foundation of the self;
the self
is the foundation of governance.
Thus, if the ruler does not prioritize fundamental tasks,
then non-essential production will not be prohibited;
if non-essential production is not prohibited,
then the people will neglect seasonal duties and undervalue land's benefits;
undervaluing land's benefits
yet seeking fields to be cultivated,
and granaries to be full,
is unattainable.
If merchants are in court,
then goods and wealth flow upward;
if women discuss public affairs,
then rewards and punishments are untrustworthy;
if men and women lack distinction,
then the people have no sense of shame.
Goods flowing upward,
untrustworthy rewards and punishments,
and people without shame—
yet expecting the people to endure hardship,
and soldiers to die for duty,
is unattainable.
If the court is not solemn,
noble and base not distinguished,
elders and young not separated,
measures not carefully set,
clothing without hierarchy,
and superiors and inferiors transgress boundaries—
yet expecting the people to respect the ruler's decrees,
is unattainable.
If the ruler favors deceit and trickery,
and ministers compete in levying taxes,
making the people opportunistic and uniform,
then the people will resent and complain,
and expecting them to be loyal to the ruler,
is unattainable.
Having land but not attending to fundamental tasks,
ruling a state but unable to unify the people,
yet expecting the ancestral temple and state altars to be secure,
is unattainable.
If the ruler relies on divination,
and frequently uses shamans and healers,
then ghosts and spirits will repeatedly cause havoc.
Thus, when achievements are not made,
and fame is not renowned,
the worries in such efforts are three:
some rule alone,
some are poor and lowly,
some have days that are insufficient.
For a one-year plan,
nothing is better than planting grains;
for a ten-year plan,
nothing is better than planting trees;
for a lifetime plan,
nothing is better than nurturing people.
Plant once and harvest once: this refers to grain.
Plant once and harvest ten times: this refers to trees.
Plant once and harvest a hundred times: this refers to people.
If I cultivate them,
their use will be as if divine;
undertakings will proceed as if by magic—
this is the gateway for a king.
In general, those who govern the people
should ensure that men commit no wicked deeds,
and women engage in no lewd affairs.
Men committing no wicked deeds is due to education;
women engaging in no lewd affairs is due to instruction.
When education and instruction become customs,
punishments can be reduced—
this is the rule.
In general, those who govern the people
desire the people to be upright.
To desire the people to be upright,
then minor vices must be prohibited.
Minor vices are what give rise to major vices.
If minor vices are not prohibited,
yet one expects major vices not to harm the state,
this is unattainable.
In general, those who govern the people
desire the people to have ritual propriety.
To desire the people to have ritual propriety,
then minor rituals must be carefully observed.
If minor rituals are not carefully observed in the state,
yet one expects the common people to practice major rituals,
this is unattainable.
In general, those who govern the people
desire the people to have righteousness.
To desire the people to have righteousness,
then minor righteousness must be practiced.
If minor righteousness is not practiced in the state,
yet one expects the common people to practice major righteousness,
this is unattainable.
In general, those who govern the people
desire the people to have integrity.
To desire the people to have integrity,
then minor integrity must be cultivated.
If minor integrity is not cultivated in the state,
yet one expects the common people to practice major integrity,
this is unattainable.
In general, those who govern the people
desire the people to have a sense of shame.
To desire the people to have a sense of shame,
then minor shames must be rectified.
If minor shames are not rectified in the state,
yet one expects the common people to uphold major shames,
this is unattainable.
In general, those who govern the people,
desiring the people to carefully observe minor rituals,
practice minor righteousness,
cultivate minor integrity,
rectify minor shames,
and prohibit minor vices—
this is the way to discipline the people.
The people carefully observing minor rituals,
practicing minor righteousness,
cultivating minor integrity,
rectifying minor shames,
and prohibiting minor vices—
this is the foundation of governance.
In general, those who govern the people
desire the people to be governable.
To desire the people to be governable,
then laws must be emphasized.
Laws are what establish the court.
To establish the court,
then ranks and robes must be valued.
If ranks and robes are bestowed on the unrighteous,
then the people will despise those ranks and robes;
if the people despise the ranks and robes,
then the ruler will not be respected;
if the ruler is not respected,
then his commands will not be carried out.
Laws are what mobilize the people's labor.
To mobilize the people's labor,
then salaries and rewards must be substantial.
If salaries and rewards are given to the undeserving,
then the people will disdain those salaries and rewards;
if the people disdain the salaries and rewards,
then the ruler has no means to encourage the people;
if the ruler has no means to encourage the people,
then his commands will not be carried out.
Laws are what utilize the people's abilities.
To utilize the people's abilities,
then appointments to office must be carefully considered.
If appointments to office are not carefully considered,
then the people will be estranged from governance;
if the people are estranged from governance,
then principles will not reach upward;
if principles do not reach upward,
then the lower will resent the upper;
if the lower resent the upper,
then commands will not be carried out.
Laws are what govern the people's lives and deaths.
To govern the people's lives and deaths,
then punishments must be carefully deliberated.
If punishments are not carefully deliberated,
then there will be favoritism and avoidance;
if there is favoritism and avoidance,
then the innocent will be killed and the guilty pardoned;
if the innocent are killed and the guilty pardoned,
then the state cannot avoid treacherous ministers.
Thus, if ranks and robes are despised,
salaries and rewards are devalued,
the people are estranged from governance,
and treacherous ministers initiate troubles—
this is called the teaching that ruins a state.
There are three factors that determine a state's order or chaos;
killing, execution, and punishments
are insufficient to rely on.
There are four factors that determine a state's safety or peril;
city walls, moats, and natural barriers
are insufficient to defend it.
There are five factors that determine a state's wealth or poverty;
light taxes,
reduced levies
are insufficient to depend on.
Governing a state has three fundamentals,
securing a state has four stabilizers,
and enriching a state has five tasks.
These five tasks are the five constants.
There are three things the ruler must carefully examine:
first, virtue not matching the position;
second, achievement not matching the salary;
third, ability not matching the office.
These three fundamentals
are the roots of order and chaos.
Therefore, if in the state there are those whose virtue and righteousness are not evident at court,
they should not be given high positions;
if there are those whose achievements and efforts are not seen in the state,
they should not be granted generous salaries;
if there are those who, in handling affairs, are not trusted by the people,
they should not be appointed to high offices.
Thus, having abundant virtue but a low position is called an excess;
having meager virtue but a high position is called a fault.
It is better to have an excess with a noble man
than to have a fault with a petty man.
An excess with a noble man
brings shallow resentment;
a fault with a petty man
brings deep calamity.
Therefore, if in the state there are those whose virtue and righteousness are not evident at court yet hold high positions,
then good ministers will not advance;
if there are those whose achievements and efforts are not seen in the state yet have generous salaries,
then diligent ministers will not be encouraged;
if there are those who, in handling affairs, are not trusted by the people yet hold high offices,
then talented ministers will not be employed.
If the three fundamentals are carefully examined,
then subordinates will not dare to make demands.
If the three fundamentals are not carefully examined,
then treacherous ministers will rise to the top,
and sycophants will control authority.
In this case,
clarity is blocked above,
and governance is obstructed below,
the right path is abandoned,
and wicked affairs daily grow.
When the three fundamentals are thoroughly examined,
then fawning courtiers hold no power in the state,
no prisoners are seen on the roads,
the distant and estranged have no concealed grievances,
and the orphaned and widowed have no hidden sufferings.
Hence it is said:
"Punishments are few, governance is minimal,
the court does not need to assemble the masses."
End of the three fundamentals.
There are four things a ruler must be cautious about:
first, if one possesses great virtue but does not attain benevolence,
they should not be entrusted with the authority of the state;
second, if one sees the worthy but cannot yield to them,
they should not be given a high position;
third, if one avoids punishing relatives and the noble,
they should not be put in charge of the military;
fourth, if one does not value fundamental tasks,
does not devote effort to land benefits,
and lightly imposes taxes,
they should not be entrusted with cities and towns.
These four priorities
are the foundation of safety and danger.
Hence it is said:
"If ministers and chancellors do not gain the support of the masses,
the state is in danger;
if high officials are not harmonious and united,
the state is in danger;
if the military commander is not sufficiently feared,
the state is in danger;
if the people do not cherish their livelihoods,
the state is in danger."
Therefore, if one possesses great virtue and attains benevolence,
they will hold the state and gain the masses;
if one sees the worthy and can yield,
then high officials will be harmonious and united;
if punishments do not avoid relatives and the noble,
then authority extends to neighboring enemies;
if one values fundamental tasks,
devotes effort to land benefits,
and imposes taxes heavily,
then the people will cherish their livelihoods.
The four consolidations.
There are five things a ruler must attend to:
first, if mountains and marshes are not saved from fire,
and plants and trees cannot grow,
the state will be poor;
second, if ditches and canals are not completed through narrow passes,
and obstructed waters do not settle in their storage,
the state will be poor;
third, if mulberry and hemp are not cultivated in the fields,
and the five grains are not suited to their land,
the state will be poor;
fourth, if the six domestic animals are not raised in households,
and melons, gourds, vegetables, and all fruits are not fully provided,
the state will be poor;
fifth, if craftsmanship competes in engraving and carving,
and women's work is excessive in ornate patterns,
the state will be poor.
Hence it is said:
"If mountains and marshes are saved from fire,
and plants and trees are cultivated and grow,
the state will be rich;
if ditches and canals are completed through narrow passes,
and obstructed waters settle in their storage,
the state will be rich;
if mulberry and hemp are cultivated in the fields,
and the five grains are suited to their land,
the state will be rich;
if the six domestic animals are raised in households,
and melons, gourds, vegetables, and all fruits are fully provided,
the state will be rich;
