on the right, hold the five flavors,"
this refers to the distinction between ruler and minister.
The ruler issues commands effortlessly,
thus stands on the left;
the minister undertakes labor strenuously,
thus stands on the right.
The five tones differ in sound but can harmonize,
this means the ruler's commands are not arbitrary,
and all is compliant,
compliant so that orders are implemented and governance achieved.
The five flavors differ in substance but can blend,
this means the minister's labors are not arbitrary,
and all is attained,
attained so that efforts focus and wealth abounds.
Thus, when the ruler issues commands,
he rectifies the state without equalizing desires,
unifies care without solely affirming his own views;
When the king bestows without selfishness,
then all within the seas will come as guests.
When ministers exert their strength,
unite in loyalty without contending for profit,
do not neglect their duties nor claim fame;
when they share respect without jealousy,
then husband and wife will harmonize and encourage each other.
If the ruler loses the musical notes, the wind and pitch pipes will drift,
and drifting leads to chaos and ruin.
If ministers depart from the flavors, the hundred surnames will not be nourished,
and if the hundred surnames are not nourished,
the multitude will scatter and perish.
When ruler and ministers each fulfill their roles,
the state will be tranquil,
hence it is called "non-virtue."
"Embrace the plumb line, level, and marking cord,
abundantly prepare compasses and axles,
reduce flow to achieve great completion,
this is the node of timely virtue."
The plumb line straightens by supporting what is bent;
the level evens by breaking down what is rugged;
the marking cord enters crooked and emerges straight.
This speaks of the system established by sage rulers and worthy assistants.
Broad yet without loss,
thus preparing abilities without omission.
The state remains the same state,
the people remain the same people,
yet Jié and Zhòu perished through chaos,
while Tāng and Wǔ prospered through order.
Manifest the Way to teach,
clarify laws to set expectations,
and the people's rise to goodness is like transformation,
such were the achievements of Tāng and Wǔ.
Abundantly preparing compasses and axles
means forming axles.
When axles are well-formed,
they fit large spaces without looseness,
enter small spaces without obstruction,
like seeking footprints for shoe lasts,
how could there be misfit?
Good fit
means good preparation,
it is immortals,
thus there is no lack.
Therefore, those who expound teachings take this as example.
Heaven nourishes,
without measure or limit;
Earth transforms and generates,
without boundary or shore.
What is called right without wrong,
wrong without right,
right and wrong
must interact.
If one believes in what is right,
there must be what cannot be预先 planned,
and what cannot be anticipated.
Yet one will face it unprepared.
Thus the sage broadens knowledge and multiplies views,
storing the Way to await events,
when things come, he responds according to their form,
and both straight and curved are preserved.
Reduce,
means exhaust;
flow,
means initiate.
When all aspects are completely addressed,
nothing is left unprepared.
Hence it is said:
Reduce flow to achieve great completion.
The method of achieving success
must have great standards.
It must be comprehensive in virtue,
discerning in timing,
the encounter of timely virtue
is the convergence of events,
like matching tally tokens.
Therefore it is said:
This is the node of timely virtue.
"Gather living things in spring,
pick melons in autumn,
dwell in shade in summer,
reside in sunlight in winter."
This speaks of how the sage's movement and stillness, opening and closing,
bending and stretching, fullness and humility,
taking and giving must follow the timing.
Act when the time is right,
remain still when it is not.
Thus ancient scholars had intentions but did not reveal them openly.
So they refined their governing words,
keeping them hidden in secrecy.
When worthy men live in chaotic times,
knowing the Way cannot be practiced,
they suppress themselves to avoid punishment,
and remain silent to seek exemption.
Avoiding it is like seeking coolness in summer,
warmth in winter,
thus avoiding harm from extreme heat or cold.
Not because they fear death and are disloyal.
Forcing speech leads to humiliation,
without adding to achievements or benefits,
advancing injures the dignity of the ruler,
retreating harms the life of a minister,
making it highly disadvantageous.
Thus they withdraw without abandoning principles,
cultivate their work without ceasing study,
awaiting clear understanding.
Thus Wēizǐ did not participate in Zhòu's disaster,
but was enfeoffed in Sòng,
becoming the master of Yīn.
The ancestors were not extinguished,
later generations did not cease.
Hence it is said:
The virtue of great worthies endures.
"Brightness leads to wisdom,
wisdom leads to brightness,
exuberance leads to decline,
bright wisdom leads to great practice."
This speaks of monopolizing beauty, dominating splendor, and self-exaltation,
using arrogance to override others,
people's failure often starts from this.
Therefore sages record it on bamboo slips,
transmitting to inform later generations
saying:
"Exuberance means flourishing;
decline means falling.
Those who flourish without falling
have never existed.
Thus those who possess the Way
do not balance their scales to the full,
do not fill their measures to the brim,
do not rely on their music,
do not reach their limits.
When rank is noble, they respect scholars;
when emolument is rich, they focus on giving;
when merit is great, they do not boast;
when achievement is illustrious, they do not boast.
Name and reality have long been at odds,
thus severed without interaction,
the wise know they cannot maintain both,
so they choose one.
Thus they remain secure without worry.
"Be poisonous but not angry,"
this means stopping rage quickly
to achieve resolution.
"Resent but do not speak,"
means one must be cautious in speech:
if words are not周密,
they instead harm oneself.
"Desire but do not scheme,"
means schemes must not be泄露,
if schemes are泄露, disaster is extreme.
Acting on rage quickly
leads to completion, without law
thieves arise,
if words are轻浮 and schemes泄露,
disaster will surely reach oneself.
Therefore it is said:
"Be poisonous but not angry,
resent but do not speak,
desire but do not scheme."
"Greatly measure and gauge,
like waking sleep,
like twilight dawn,"
means deep contemplation to question oneself,
silent reflection to carefully consider.
Rely on worthy talents,
employ the benevolent and good,
once clearly
understanding the principles of advantage and harm,
it is like removing a blindfold.
Hence it is said:
like waking sleep,
like twilight dawn,
like Áo's position under Yáo.
"Do not seek out the glib,"
means do not employ glib-tongued people,
for employing glib-tongued people
leads to the proliferation of selfish deeds.
"Do not harbor flatterers,"
means do not listen to flattery,
for listening to flattery leads to deceiving superiors.
"Do not nurture the cruel,"
means do not employ the violent,
for employing the violent harms the people.
"Do not observe through slander,"
means do not listen to slander,
for listening to slander causes the loss of capable men.
Acting selfishly, deceiving superiors, harming the people, and losing capable men—
when these four are practiced,
they harm the ruler's righteousness and cause the loss of correctness.
As for those who serve as rulers,
once they have lost their righteousness and correctness,
they rely on them to build their reputation;
as for those who serve as ministers, they are disloyal and corrupt,
striving for rank and emolument,
disturbing customs and ruining the age,
to steal comfort and cherish pleasure.
Even if they expand their authority,
it can only last a short while.
Therefore it is said:
"Without correctness, expansion leads to ruin."
Thus the people of old
blocked such paths,
obstructed such ways,
guarded and cultivated things.
Therefore, they recorded it on bamboo slips,
transmitting it to inform later generations, saying:
The resentment it causes is deep,
hence authority is entirely lost.
"Not using their small efforts"
refers to emptiness.
When a person lacks goodness,
it is called emptiness.
All that is rigid and unyielding without movement,
dammed and blocked without flow,
will inevitably miss the timing,
and missing the timing leads to abandonment and failure.
Heaven-planted correctness without error,
cannot be considered worthy,
straightforward yet incapable,
cannot be praised.
What is worthy and admirable in a sage
is their ability to follow changes and transformations.
Like an abyssal spring that never runs dry,
subtle and restrained yet flowing and extending,
thus the virtue's flowing moisture evenly
benefits all things.
Therefore it is said:
The sage aligns with heaven and earth.
"Birds fly by the plumb line."
This refers to the principle of the great person.
When birds fly,
they must return to the mountains and gather in the valleys.
Not returning to the mountains leads to exhaustion,
not gathering in the valleys leads to death.
The locations of mountains and valleys
are not necessarily straight and direct.
Yet returning to the mountains and gathering in the valleys,
though winding, are winding,
they are named by the plumb line.
Considering that a bird starts from the north,
intending south and reaching the south;
starts from the south,
intending north and reaching the north—
if the general intention is achieved,
minor imperfections are not considered damaging.
Therefore, the sage admires and records this,
saying:
A road of a thousand miles
cannot be straightened with a string;
a city of ten thousand households
cannot be leveled with a level.
This means the actions of a great person
need not follow prior constants,
establishing righteousness is called worthy.
Hence, when superiors evaluate their subordinates,
they must not lose this method.
"Juān chōng,"
refers to the heart,
and the heart desires loyalty;
"Mò héng,"
refers to the ears and eyes,
and the ears and eyes desire uprightness.
Central correctness
is the foundation of governance.
The ears manage hearing,
hearing must follow careful listening,
listening attentively is called acuity.
The eyes manage sight,
sight must follow careful observation,
observing discerningly is called clarity.
The heart manages thought,
thought must follow appropriate speech,
speaking aptly is called wisdom.
Acuity and clarity leading to wisdom
result in breadth,
breadth without confusion,
thereby facilitating governance.
Governance that benefits the people,
benefits encourage them,
encouragement leads to auspiciousness.
Hearing without caution
and without attentiveness is not acute,
not attentive and not acute leads to error.
Sight without discernment is not clear,
without discernment and not clear leads to faults.
Thought without attainment is not wise,
without attainment and not wise leads to obscurity.
Errors and faults with obscurity bring worry,
worry leads to craftiness and harshness,
craftiness and harshness lead to perilous governance.
Perilous governance harms the people,
harm breeds resentment,
resentment leads to misfortune.
Therefore it is said:
Juān chōng mò héng,
means facilitating governance and benefiting the people.
"Do not incur its misfortune,"
means maintaining central correctness with accumulated caution.
"Do not approach your desires,"
means the downfall of a ruler often
comes from greed for gold, jade, horses, and women,
and indulging in love for grain, money, and goods.
Heavy exactions from the common people
cause myriad people to resent and complain.
"Distance your worries,"
means the loss of a ruler's state
often comes from approaching pleasures.
Establishing excessive beauty,
and externally indulging in galloping and hunting,
internally indulging in beautiful women and lewd music,
leading those below to become negligent and lazy, losing their way,
all officials losing their proper course,
then chaos arises and the state is lost.
"High is their dwelling,
perilous the peak with no rescue,"
this means exalting oneself in loftiness and fullness,
and fond of boasting with elegance;
the ruler, flourishing and positioning himself as worthy,
and self-proclaiming as mighty.
Hence, flourishing must lead to loss and might to defeat.
When the ruler, already flourishing and positioning himself as worthy,
controls the scholars and people,
the state becomes troubled and chaotic,
the hearts of the myriad people full of resentment,
this ensures their inevitable downfall.
Like casting oneself from a ten-thousand-ren mountain into a deep abyss,
death without revival is certain.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not approach your desires,
but distance your worries,
high is their dwelling,
perilous the peak with no rescue."
"Can be shallow or deep,
can sink or float,
can be curved or straight,
can speak or be silent."
This refers to the essence of intention and achieving merit.
"Heaven does not have one season,
earth does not have one benefit,
people do not have one affair.
Therefore, established endeavors must be many and divided,
names and positions must have diverse methods.
The wise examine affairs,
hence they are not confined to things, but comprehensively understand the Way."
The Dào is that which
penetrates to the highest heights,
encompasses the boundless infinite,
and operates through all living beings.
Therefore, those who argue based on a single saying,
examine a single governance,
or focus on a single affair
may grasp partial explanations,
but cannot achieve comprehensive understanding.
The sage, through this, knows that words cannot cover everything,
thus broadly practices governance
while considering their meanings;
knowing that affairs cannot be all handled simultaneously,
thus establishes names for theories
and compares their effectiveness.
The year has spring, autumn, winter, and summer,
the month has upper, middle, and lower periods,
the day has morning and evening,
the night has dusk and dawn,
constellations and stars in sequence,
each has its own governance.
Hence it is said:
Heaven does not provide one season alone.
Mountains high and rocky,
deep springs and vast flows,
springs flow abundantly yet never exhaust,
lakes receive streams yet never overflow,
high and low, fertile and barren,
each suitable for different things.
Hence it is said:
Earth does not provide one benefit alone.
Regions have their customs,
states have their laws,
food and drink have different flavors,
clothing varies in colors,
ages use different tools,
standards and measures,
weights and measurements,
each category has its completion.
Hence it is said:
Humans do not engage in one affair alone.
These are the norms of various affairs,
their details cannot be fully exhausted.
"Correct in observation",
means examining beauty and ugliness,
distinguishing good and bad,
must be done with care.
Maintaining distinctions without confusion,
thus governance remains without regret.
"Steady in practice",
means staying in one's position,
walking one's path,
performing one's duties,
then people keep to their roles without disorder,
thus preserving order and achieving good outcomes.
"Deep in traces",
means clear rules and manifest plans,
constant moral principles,
then later generations follow reason without confusion,
thus reputation never ceases.
"Heaven and earth have both danger and ease,
like a drum having its stick,
when tapped, it sounds."
This means if there is singing,
there must be harmony,
the harmony without error,
thus exhausts the way of heaven and earth.
Shadow doesn't straighten crooked objects,
echo doesn't beautify ugly sounds,
therefore the sage understands things' nature,
must respond according to their kind.
Thus the gentleman cautiously minds what comes first.
"Heaven and earth are the bag of all things,
Zhòuhé contains heaven and earth."
Heaven and earth wrap all things,
thus called the bag of all things.
The meaning of Zhòuhé,
penetrates above heaven,
sinks below earth,
extends beyond the four seas,
enveloping heaven and earth,
making one bundle.
Scattered to the space between,
cannot be named yet exists.
So large it has no outside,
so small it has no inside.
Hence it is said
it contains heaven and earth.
Its meaning wasn't transmitted,
one classic described it, not fully in one volume,
yet classics cannot fully govern it.
Rich in content makes wealth,
timely expression makes appropriateness.
And the way of the sage,
values wealth with appropriateness.
What is appropriateness?
Rooted in governance without error,
operating affairs without fixed method,
responding to change without mistake is called appropriateness.
Change reaches everywhere,
nothing fails to respond,
fundamentals correct without resentment,
thus it is named "Zhòuhé".
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Dào in heaven is the sun;
in humans, it is the heart."
Hence it is said:
With qì there is life,
without qì there is death,
life depends on qì;
with names there is order,
without names there is chaos,
order depends on names.
Essential sayings state:
"Love them, benefit them,
help them, secure them,
these four stem from Dào.
Emperors and kings using these,
bring order to the world.
Emperors and kings
discern what comes first and last:
putting people and land first
brings success,
putting nobility and pride first
brings failure.
Therefore ancient kings
carefully ordered priorities.
Rulers cannot be careless about nobility,
cannot be careless about people,
cannot be careless about wealth.
Care for nobility lies in promoting worthies;
care for people lies in appointing officials;
care for wealth lies in attending to land.
Thus rulers' humility, honor, lightness, and weight
lie in these three,
which cannot be neglected.
The state has treasures,
has instruments,
has utilities.
City walls,
strategic passes,
stored provisions,
are treasures;
sage wisdom,
is the instrument;
pearls and jades,
are minor utilities.
Ancient kings valued treasures and instruments
but lightly regarded utilities,
thus could rule the world.
Two things live without dying,
four things perish without establishment:
joy,
anger,
hatred,
desire,
are what ruin the world,
and worthies seldom have them.
Doing good,
is not true goodness.
Thus goodness cannot be forced.
Therefore ancient kings valued true goodness.
Kingly rulers accumulate among people,
hegemonic rulers accumulate among warriors,
declining rulers accumulate among nobles,
doomed rulers accumulate among women, pearls and jades,
thus ancient kings carefully considered their accumulations.
Urge it, urge it,
for all things serve as teachers.
Do it, do it,
for all things have their timing.
Strengthen it, strengthen it,
for all things provide essence.
There are three governing conditions in a state:
those who govern others,
those who are governed by others,
and those who cannot govern others
nor are governed by others.
How can this be known?
When virtue flourishes and righteousness is honored,
and one does not impose titles upon others;
when the population is large and the military strong,
yet the state does not create troubles or provoke disasters;
when major events occur in the world,
and one prefers to let the state act last;
such a one
is a governor of others.
When virtue does not flourish,
righteousness is not honored,
and one imposes titles upon others;
when the population is not large,
the military not strong,
yet the state creates troubles and provokes disasters;
relying on allied states,
seeking fame and profit;
such a one
is governed by others.
Advancing when others advance,
retreating when others retreat,
laboring when others labor,
resting when others rest,
with every advance, retreat, labor, and rest
synchronized with others;
such a one
cannot govern others,
nor can others govern them.
Loving someone deeply, yet unable to benefit them;
hating someone deeply, yet unable to harm them.
Thus, the ancient kings valued appropriateness
and thoroughness.
Thoroughness means not revealing through words,
not showing through expressions,
like a dragon or a snake,
transforming five times in a day—
this is called thoroughness.
Hence, the ancient kings did not equate one with two,
did not act alone,
nor monopolize achievements.
The ancient kings did not bind themselves with ties,
nor knot alliances.
For ties can be undone,
and knots can be broken.
Thus, closeness
lies not in ties or knots.
The ancient kings did not engage in transactional friendships,
nor parcel out territory,
to rule the world.
The world cannot be altered,
but can be directed with a whip.
Timing and righteousness
are what guide actions.
With no extra eyes to see clearly,
no extra ears to hear keenly,
thus
they could uphold the dignity of the Son of Heaven.
So it is with official duties.
Timing captures heaven,
righteousness captures people.
With both timing and righteousness,
one can grasp heaven and people.
The ancient kings did not use ferocity to guard borders,
so borders were secure;
secure borders
led to friendly neighboring states;
friendly neighbors,
then actions were appropriate.
People naturally harbor mutual hatred,
human hearts are fierce,
hence laws were established.
Laws stem from ritual,
ritual stems from order.
Order and ritual are the Way.
All things await order and ritual to be settled.
All things
arise from yin and yang and are viewed in threes,
so the ancient kings, based on this triad, carefully considered what to adopt and discard.
Treating the humble as humble,
humility cannot be attained;
treating the noble as noble,
nobility cannot be attained.
Jié and Shùn exemplify this.
This is what the ancient kings valued most.
What, when gained, ensures life,
and when lost, ensures death?
Why?
Only nothingness. Gaining it,
Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wénwǔ, and Xiàojǐ
relied on it to achieve greatness,
and the world depends on it for life.
Thus, the ancient kings esteemed it.
One day without food,
liken to a lean year;
three days without food,
liken to a famine;
five days without food,
liken to a devastation;
seven days without food,
no state or land remains;
ten days without food,
no kin or kind survive, all perish.
The ancient kings valued sincerity and trust. Sincerity and trust
are the bonds of the world.
Worthy officials do not rely on royal lineage,
scholars do not rely on external power.
Plain benefits are not taken as merit,
plain preparations are not used for gain.
Thus, preserving the state,
stabilizing the altars of soil and grain,
lies in the swiftness of strategy.
The sage uses their mind,
vast and round like chaos,
obscure with no entry point,
tangled like messy threads,
hesitating as if following order.
Therefore it is said,
for those who desire knowledge, provide knowledge;
for those who desire profit, provide profit;
for those who desire courage, provide courage;
for those who desire nobility, provide nobility.
If they desire nobility
and I honor them,
people say I am courteous;
if they desire courage
and I encourage them,
people say I am respectful;
if they desire profit
and I benefit them,
people say I am benevolent;
if they desire knowledge
and I inform them,
people say I am wise.
Be cautious, be cautious,
subtle and varied in approach,
ponder every action,
do not let others discern your intentions,
always be prepared for sudden events.
To be trustworthy is benevolence.
To be undeceived is wisdom.
With both wisdom and benevolence,
one is called a complete person.
The lowly naturally serve the noble,
the unworthy naturally serve the worthy.
The reason the noble can achieve nobility
is by serving the lowly despite their nobility;
the reason the worthy can achieve worthiness
is by serving the unworthy despite their worthiness.
The ugly is the substance of beauty;
the lowly is the substance of nobility;
the humble is the substance of honor.
Thus, the ancient kings valued them.
Heaven employs through timing,
earth employs through resources,
humans employ through virtue,
spirits employ through omens,
beasts employ through strength.
What is called virtue
means taking the lead.
Thus, nothing is better than leading with virtue,
and nothing is better than responding to adversaries by holding back.
The ancient kings, using one yin and two yang, achieved hegemony;
using all yang, achieved kingship;
using one yang and two yin, led to decline;
using all yin, led to ruin.
Measure not by quantity,
weigh not by lightness or heaviness,
gauge not by shortness or length;
without examining these three,
one cannot undertake great endeavors.
Can one be cautious?
Can one be diligent?
Can one conceal and lie low?
Can one cultivate millet?
Can one grow wheat?
If spring does not produce, can summer yield nothing?
The former kings used affairs to forge alliances,
and virtue to unite people.
If these two are not harmonized,
then nothing is accomplished,
and there is no intimacy.
Generally, a state perishes
because of its strengths;
a person's self-loss
is due to their own strengths.
Thus, good swimmers die in weirs and ponds,
good archers die in the open fields.
Life depends on food,
governance depends on affairs.
Without good deeds yet having good governance—
from ancient times to the present,
this has never occurred.
The many overcome the few,
the swift overcome the slow,
the brave overcome the timid,
the wise overcome the foolish,
good overcomes evil,
righteousness overcomes unrighteousness,
the Way of Heaven overcomes the absence of the Way of Heaven.
Of these seven victories, the multitude is valued;
those who apply them throughout life are numerous.
If a ruler favors ease and desires,
losing himself and his state,
it is perilous; if his virtue is insufficient to win over his people,
it is perilous; if he emphasizes punishments and belittles his scholars,
it is perilous; if feudal lords borrow his authority long without realizing their limits,
it is perilous; if in advanced age he does not respect his rightful heir,
it is perilous; if he hoards stores, letting them pile up and rot,
without sharing with others, it is perilous.
Human endeavors are of three kinds:
those of governance,
those of shame,
and those of action.
Actions are of two kinds:
correcting and examining.
When these five are achieved, the world is well-governed.
If names are correct, there is order;
if names are skewed, there is chaos;
without names, there is death.
Thus, the former kings valued names.
The former kings won the world,
treating the distant with ritual,
the near with embodiment.
Embodiment and ritual
are the means to win the world;
distance and proximity
are how the boundaries of the world are distinguished.
What increases daily yet worries of being insufficient
is loyalty;
what decreases daily yet worries of excess
is desire.
More loyalty, less desire—
this is wisdom,
the broad path for ministers.
For a minister,
if without merit to the state,
his family is rich while the state is poor—
this is a great crime for a minister;
for a minister,
if without merit to the state,
his rank is exalted while the ruler is debased—
this is a great crime for a minister.
To be noble and wealthy without merit to the state—
could it be due to exalting the worthy?
In the hearts of the masses,
love is the beginning of hatred,
virtue is the root of resentment.
In serving parents,
when wife and children are present,
filial piety declines;
in serving the ruler,
with prosperous endeavors
and a wealthy household,
conduct declines;
when ranks and emoluments are full,
loyalty declines.
Only the worthy are not so.
Thus, the former kings did not allow fullness.
When a fu or hu measure is full,
people level it;
when people are full,
Heaven levels them.
Hence, the former kings avoided fullness.
The ruler holds contrariety,
the ministers hold compliance.
The former kings esteemed honor and disgrace,
for honor and disgrace lie in action.
Heaven has no private love,
no private hatred.
Those who do good receive blessings,
those who do evil receive misfortunes.
Misfortunes and blessings depend on action,
so the former kings valued action.
Clear rewards are not wasteful,
clear punishments are not violent.
When rewards and punishments are clear,
it is the pinnacle of virtue.
Thus, the former kings valued clarity.
The Way of Heaven is vast, and the emperors and kings utilize it; love and hate—
through love and hate, the world can be secured,
and closure must be firm.
The writings of the former kings
are revered in the heart,
yet the masses do not understand this.
Thus, with affairs, it is engagement;
without affairs, it is also engagement.
I fear affairs,
not wishing to engage in them;
I fear speech,
not wishing to engage in it.
Therefore, at sixty years of age, I am old and stammer.
Great walls must not be left incomplete,
outer walls must not have external passage,
neighborhoods must not have transverse access,
gates must not be left unclosed,
palace walls and barriers
must not be left unrepaired.
For if great walls are incomplete,
then rebellious traitors will plot;
if outer walls have external passage,
then evildoers and escapees will emerge;
if neighborhoods have transverse access,
then plunderers and thieves will not cease;
if gates are unclosed,
allowing free passage inside and out,
then men and women will lack distinction;
if palace walls are unprepared,
barriers not firm,
even with valuable goods,
they cannot be guarded.
Thus, when circumstances prevent wrongdoing,
then the treacherous become honest;
when prohibitions and penalties are威严,
then the negligent become orderly;
when laws and decrees are clear,
then barbarians dare not offend;
when rewards are trustworthy and certain,
then the meritorious are encouraged;
when teachings and customs are widespread,
then ruler and people transform unconsciously.
Therefore, with an enlightened ruler above,
punishments are few and penalties rare—
not that punishable acts go unpunished,
nor that culpable acts go unpenalized;
an enlightened ruler
closes the gates,
blocks the paths,
obscures the tracks, preventing people from accessing places of depravity and wrongdoing.
Thus, the people's path of righteousness and good conduct
becomes as if innate.
Hence, with few crimes and penalties, the people are well-governed.
Walk through the fields,
observe the plowing and weeding,
calculate the farming efforts,
and the state of hunger or fullness can be known.
If the plowing is not deep,
the weeding not diligent,
the land not suited to its use,
the fields overgrown with weeds,
the tilled land not necessarily fertile,
the wasteland not necessarily barren,
estimating the fields by the crowded population,
with many weedy fields and few cultivated ones—
even without flood or drought,
it is the landscape of a hungry state.
If the population is sparse under such circumstances,
then it is insufficient to guard the territory;
if the population is dense under such conditions,
then the state will be impoverished and the people hungry;
encountering floods or droughts under these conditions,
the masses will scatter and cannot be gathered.
When the people are insufficient for defense,
their city walls are not secure;
when the people are hungry, they cannot be sent to battle;
if the masses scatter and cannot be gathered,
the state will become ruins.
Therefore it is said:
A ruler who possesses land and governs a state
but does not devote effort to plowing and weeding,
is a parasitic ruler.
Hence it is said:
Travel through its fields,
observe its plowing and weeding,
calculate its agricultural affairs,
and the state's condition of hunger or satiety can be known.
Travel through its mountains and marshes,
observe its mulberries and hemps,
calculate the production of its six domestic animals,
and the state's condition of poverty or wealth can be known.
When mountains and marshes are vast,
then vegetation easily becomes abundant;
when soil is fertile and rich,
then mulberries and hemps easily multiply;
when pasture grass is plentiful and widespread,
then the six domestic animals easily prosper.
Though mountains and marshes be vast,
if there are no restrictions on vegetation;
though the soil be fertile,
if mulberries and hemps are not counted;
though pasture grass be abundant,
if the six domestic animals are taxed,
this is closing the gate to wealth.
Therefore it is said,
"If seasonal goods do not flourish,
even with abundant gold and jade,
it is called a poor state."
Hence it is said:
"Travel through its mountains and marshes,
observe its mulberries and hemps,
calculate the production of its six domestic animals,
and the state's condition of poverty or wealth can be known."
Enter the state's cities,
look at its palaces and buildings,
observe its carriages, horses, and clothing,
and the state's condition of extravagance or frugality can be known.
When the state's walls are large but the fields are shallow and narrow,
the countryside cannot sufficiently nourish its people;
when the city's domain is large but the population is sparse,
the people cannot sufficiently guard the city;
when the palace complex is large but the dwellings are few,
the rooms cannot sufficiently fill the palace;
when dwellings are numerous but inhabitants are few,
the people cannot sufficiently occupy the rooms;
when granaries are few but towers and pavilions are numerous,
the stores cannot sufficiently supply the expenses.
Therefore it is said,
"When the ruler has no reserves but the palaces are beautiful,
when common households have no reserves but clothing is ornate,
when carriage riders adorn themselves for show,
when pedestrians mix colorful patterns,
when fundamental resources are few but peripheral uses are many,
this is the custom of an extravagant state."
When the state is extravagant, expenditures are wasteful;
when expenditures are wasteful, the people become poor;
when the people are poor, cunning schemes arise;
when cunning schemes arise, wicked crafts emerge.
Thus the source of treachery and evil,
arises from insufficiency and want;
the source of insufficiency and want,
arises from extravagance;
the source of extravagance,
arises from lack of measure.
Therefore it is said:
"Examine measurements and limits,
regulate clothing,
economize on wealth and expenditures,
prohibit excessive luxury,
these are urgent matters for governing a state."
Those who do not understand such calculations,
cannot be employed to administer the state.
Hence it is said:
"Enter the state's cities,
look at its palaces and buildings,
observe its carriages, horses, and clothing,
and the state's condition of extravagance or frugality can be known."
Assess crop failures and famines,
calculate military conscription and corvée labor,
observe towers and pavilions,
measure state expenditures,
and the state's condition of solidity or emptiness can be known.
Generally, for a population of ten thousand households,
the arable land,
fifty li square,
should be sufficient.
For fewer than ten thousand households,
supplementing with mountains and marshes is acceptable;
for more than ten thousand households,
reducing mountains and marshes is acceptable.
When the fields are fully cultivated yet the people have no reserves,
the state's territory is small and arable land is shallow;
when half the farmland is cultivated yet the people have surplus food and abundant grain,
the state's territory is large and arable land is extensive;
when the state's territory is large but the fields are not cultivated,
the ruler favors goods and the ministers favor profits;
when land reclamation is extensive but the people have insufficient means,
the ruler's taxes are heavy,
draining their stores.
Therefore it is said,
"When grain travels three hundred li,
the state lacks one year's reserves;
when grain travels four hundred li,
the state lacks half a year's reserves;
when grain travels five hundred li,
the masses will have hungry faces.
When one-third of the harvest is lost,
it is called a minor disaster;
after three years of minor disasters comes a major disaster;
during a major disaster
the masses will have only husks to eat.
With a one-tenth military conscription,
three-tenths not engaged in productive work,
then one-third of the harvest is lost.
When one-third of the harvest is lost,
and there are no previous reserves,
then on the roads there will be abandoned corpses.
With a one-tenth military conscription,
unrelieved for three years,
and no surplus food,
then the people will sell their children."
Therefore it is said:
"Though mountains and forests be nearby,
though vegetation be lush,
palaces and buildings must have limits,
prohibitions and harvesting must have their seasons,
why is this?"
The answer is:
"Large trees cannot be felled alone,
large trees cannot be lifted alone,
large trees cannot be transported alone,
large trees cannot be placed on thin walls."
Therefore it is said,
"Though mountains and forests be vast,
though vegetation be lush,
prohibitions and harvesting must have their seasons;"
though the state be prosperous,
though gold and jade be abundant,
palaces and buildings must have limits;
though rivers and seas be vast,
though ponds and marshes be extensive,
though fish and turtles be plentiful,
nets and traps must have proper regulations,
boats and nets cannot provide all wealth.
This is not from partiality to vegetation or affection for fish and turtles,
but from aversion to diverting people from grain production.
Therefore it is said,
"The reason former kings restricted work in mountains and marshes,
was to concentrate the people on grain production."
The people cannot eat without grain,
grain cannot grow without land,
land cannot be productive without people,
people without labor cannot generate wealth.
The source of talent,
arises from applying effort;
the source of effort,
arises from bodily labor.
Therefore if the ruler spends wealth without end,
this means the people labor without rest.
Hence it is said,
"When towers and pavilions face each other,
those above and below resent each other."
When the people have no surplus stores,
prohibitions cannot be effectively enforced;
when the masses have leftover grain bundles,
battles cannot be surely won;
when there are emaciated corpses on the roads,
defense cannot be securely maintained.
Thus, if orders are not necessarily carried out,
prohibitions not necessarily enforced,
battles not necessarily won,
defense not necessarily secure,
then peril and downfall will follow.
Hence it is said:
"By assessing famine conditions,
calculating military conscription,
observing tower pavilions,
and measuring state expenditures,
one can know the虚实 of a state."
Enter the villages and communities,
observe customs and practices,
listen to how the people are transformed by their superiors,
and one can know the order or chaos of a state.
When communities are not separated,
neighborhood gates not established,
coming and going without fixed times,
early and late without restrictions,
then those who plunder, steal,
assault, and commit atrocities
cannot be controlled.
Drinking valley water,
digging wells in alleys,
connecting threshing grounds and gardens,
with trees overgrown,
palace walls crumbling,
gates and doors unbarred,
inside and outside intermingling,
then distinctions between men and women
cannot be properly maintained.
When townships lack senior patrols,
villages lack scholars' lodgings,
seasonal gatherings never convened,
funeral feasts not assembled,
prohibitions and penalties not strict,
then respect for elders and harmony
cannot spontaneously arise.
Thus, if wedding ceremonies are not carefully observed,
the people will not cultivate integrity;
if virtuous candidates are not recommended locally,
scholars will not pursue proper conduct;
if wealth circulates in the state,
laws and decrees will be undermined by officials;
if petitions are granted by superiors,
cliques will form below;
if local officials lack legal systems,
the common people and groups will not obey.
This is how states perish and rulers are assassinated.
Hence it is said:
"Enter the villages and communities,
observe customs and practices,
listen to how the people are transformed by their superiors,
and one can know the order or chaos of a state."
Enter the court,
observe those nearby,
examine the ministers of the court,
assess what the high and low value or disdain,
and one can know the strength or weakness of a state.
If those with many achievements rank high,
while salaries and rewards are low,
then ministers who have long served
will not strive to exert themselves;
if governance merits rank high,
while noble titles are low,
then talented heroes and capable ministers
will not strive to exhaust their abilities.
If favored attendants nearby,
regardless of merit or ability
receive titles and salaries,
then the common people will resentfully
criticize superiors, despising titles and轻视 salaries;
if merchants with gold, jade, and goods,
regardless of aspirations or conduct
receive titles and salaries,
then the ruler's orders will be轻视,
laws and systems destroyed.
If those with powerful connections,
regardless of talent or ability
gain honored positions,
then the people will abandon fundamental conduct and seek external influence.
When those long in service
do not strive to exert themselves,
then soldiers will not fight;
when heroic talents do not strive to exhaust their abilities,
then internal governance will lack distinction;
when the common people resentfully
criticize superiors, despising titles and轻视 salaries,
then the ruler has no means to encourage the masses;
when the ruler's orders are轻视,
laws and systems destroyed,
then the ruler cannot command ministers,
nor ministers serve the ruler;
when the people abandon fundamental conduct and seek external influence,
then the state's true conditions will be fully exposed to enemy states.
Hence it is said:
"Enter the court,
observe those nearby,
examine the ministers of the court,
assess what the high and low value or disdain,
and one can know the strength or weakness of a state."
Establish laws and issue decrees,
govern the masses and employ the people,
consider whether威严 and宽惠
are practiced among the people or not, and one can know the rise or fall of a state.
If laws are emptily established while harm remains distant,
decrees once issued but disobedient remain,
those despising titles and salaries without merit grow rich,
then the masses will必然轻视 decrees
and the ruler's position will be endangered.
Hence it is said,
"Good fields not given to warriors,
in three years the army weakens;
rewards and punishments not trustworthy,
in five years the state is broken;
the ruler selling offices and titles,
in seven years it perishes;
betraying human relations with beastly conduct,
in ten years it is destroyed."
Battles not won,
indicates weakness;
territory reduced on four sides,
absorbed by other states,
indicates breaking;
leaving the capital,
moving the seat of government,
indicates perishing;
possession by a different clan,
indicates destruction.
Hence it is said:
"Establish laws and issue decrees,
govern the masses and employ the people,
consider whether威严 and宽惠
are practiced among the people
or not among the people,
and one can know the rise or fall of a state."
Assess enemies and allies,
measure the ruler's intentions,
examine the state's foundation,
observe what the people produce in surplus or shortage,
and one can know the survival or demise of a state.
When enemy states are strong and allied states weak,
remonstrating ministers die while flattering ministers are honored,
personal favoritism prevails while public laws are destroyed,
then allied states cannot rely on their kinship,
and enemy states do not fear its strength,
heroes feel insecure in their positions,
and long-serving ministers do not cherish their salaries.
Favoring merchants instead of focusing on essential goods,
then the people will idly dwell without storing supplies.
When heroes feel insecure in their positions,
then good ministers depart;
when long-serving ministers do not cherish their salaries,
then soldiers become useless;
when the people idly dwell without storing supplies,
then granaries become empty.
If under such circumstances the ruler makes no changes,
then plunderers, thieves,
destroyers, and aggressors will arise.
Internally, the court lacks good ministers,
soldiers are useless,
granaries empty,
while externally facing strong enemy threats,
then the state will collapse from within.
Therefore it is said:
"By assessing the enemy's strength,
gauging the ruler's intentions,
examining the foundations of the state,
and observing whether the people's production is sufficient or deficient,
one can know which states will survive and which will perish."
Thus through these eight aspects, when observing a ruler's state,
the ruler cannot conceal the true situation.
5.2 Chapter Fourteen: Prohibitions by Law - Outer Discourse Five. When laws and regulations are not subject to debate,
the people will not form private alliances;
when punishments and executions allow no pardon,
the people will not neglect doing good;
when ranks and emoluments are not improperly granted,
subordinates will not create disorder against their superiors.
When these three are preserved by the officials
they become laws,
and when implemented in the state they become customs.
The rest will be governed without need for compulsion.
If the ruler uniformly establishes his standards,
then all officials will abide by his laws;
if the superior clearly proclaims his institutions,
then subordinates will all conform to his measures.
If the ruler does not establish his standards uniformly,
then those below who violate the law
and set up private principles will certainly be numerous.
Thereby people follow their private interests,
abolish the superior's institutions
and pursue what they have heard.
Hence subordinates contend with officials over laws,
and superiors share authority with the ruler,
the state's peril
must inevitably begin from this.
In ancient times, the sage kings governed their people differently:
those who abolished the ruler's laws and regulations
were certainly disgraced.
Those who used abundant wealth and extensive favors
to privately win over the people
were rectified through proper governance and corrected themselves.
After the sage kings perished,
those who received the throne declined.
A ruler who does not understand the way of establishing rulership,
taking it as the state's foundation,
will find many ministers who manipulate subordinates
and captivate people's minds.
If the ruler cannot carefully establish his laws
to serve as standards for subordinates,
then common people who establish private principles
and directly pursue profit will certainly be numerous.
In ancient times, when sage kings governed people,
they did not value them for broad learning,
but desired their harmony and unity
in obeying commands.
The "Great Oath" says:
"Zhòu had millions of ministers,
and also millions of different hearts.
King Wǔ had three thousand ministers but one heart."
Thus Zhòu perished with millions of hearts,
while King Wǔ survived with one heart.
Therefore, the ruler of a state
if he cannot unify people's hearts,
consolidate the state's authority,
align the scholars' righteousness,
and make his governance understood above
to serve as law below,
then even with vast territory and numerous people,
he still cannot achieve security.
When the ruler loses his way,
high ministers will compare their powers
to mutually promote each other in the state,
while petty officials will certainly follow profit to gather together.
Thus they enlist
scholars
throughout the state as their own faction,
practicing public justice for private favors,
advancing by pushing each other before the ruler,
retiring by praising each other among the people,
each benefiting themselves,
forgetting the altars of state,
expanding their positions,
gathering followers into groups,
above obscuring the ruler,
below extorting the people -
these are all ways to weaken the ruler and disorder the state.
Hence the state becomes endangered.
Ways that disorder the state,
alter the state's constants,
and allow arbitrary bestowal of rewards by oneself -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who monopolize state power to deeply extort the people -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those whose persons are not employed by the superior -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who advance to receive salaries from the ruler,
retire to store salaries at home,
perform no official duties,
only work at forming cliques,
privatizing royal officials,
privatizing the ruler's affairs,
removing unsuitable people
and acting privately -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who in self-cultivation do not take kinship as fundamental,
in handling affairs do not take office as primary,
promoting the incapable
and advancing the meritless -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who regard befriending people as their own gift,
regard recommending people as their own achievement,
and share their salaries with appointed officials -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who associate with the profitable and connected while preying on the poor,
lightly taking from their people
but heavily giving to their ruler,
diminishing the superior to attach to subordinates,
perverting law to seek among the people -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those whose employment doesn't match their person,
whose household wealth exceeds their rank,
whose salary is very meager but assets very abundant -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who oppose the world in their conduct,
defy superiors to make a name,
constantly opposing the ruler's laws and institutions to form groups in the state -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who adorn themselves in poverty
and display diligence,
wielding power among the poor and humble,
having no official duties themselves,
no constant livelihood at home,
positioning between superior and subordinate,
discoursing as champions of the people -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who hoard scholars as personal assets,
maintain armor as personal foundation,
nourishing treacherous ministers, privately determined to die,
then making false claims to deeply bargain with the ruler -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who carefully adorn minor details to show the people,
timely discuss major matters to move the ruler,
form distant alliances to surpass groups,
usurp ranks to oversee the court -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who humble themselves to mix with others,
conceal their actions in secrecy,
sneak in sideways and welcome from afar,
evading both ruler and people -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those with deceitful customs and strange rituals,
grand speech and imitated conduct,
making their actions difficult
while highly esteeming themselves -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who guard stores while living idly,
distributing widely to attract crowds,
diligently pursuing their course,
persuading people with goods and wealth,
aiding people to buy reputation,
their persons very quiet,
yet making people seek them -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those whose conduct is depraved yet firm,
speech deceptive yet eloquent,
methods wrong yet extensive,
following evil yet making it attractive -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who take factionalism as friendship,
take concealing evil as benevolence,
take frequent change as wisdom,
take heavy exactions as loyalty,
take venting anger as courage -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
Those who consolidate the state's foundation,
their persons striving to go to superiors,
deeply attaching to feudal lords -
these are prohibited by sage kings.
When a sage king governs the world in person,
his virtuous conduct must have its correctness,
and his moral principles must have their clarity.
Thus, no scholar dares to adopt deceitful customs or aberrant rites
to draw attention to themselves in the state;
none dares to distribute favors or relax discipline,
cultivating connections between high and low,
to privately endear themselves to the people;
none dares to overstep their rank or exceed their office,
fishing for profits or reviving achievements,
to curry favor with their ruler.
In governing the people, the sage king
ensures that in advancement, they have no means to gain undue benefits,
and in retreat, no means to avoid due penalties.
He must make them revert to being content with their positions,
delighting in their communities,
devoted to their duties,
and proud of their reputations,
before he ceases.
Therefore, those who exceed their office and estrange themselves from their group
must be made to suffer harm,
and those who fail in their tasks and neglect their duties
must be made to feel shame.
Thus, the sage king's way of instructing the people
is to guide them with benevolence,
and motivate them with shame,
cultivating their abilities
until they achieve their intended accomplishments.
Hence it is said:
"Decisive and settled,
calm and orderly,
secure and respected,
with actions and measures unchanging—
this is the way of the sage king."
5.3 Chapter Fifteen: On the Importance of Decrees, Outer Discourse Six. Among the vital instruments for ruling a state,
none is more important than decrees.
When decrees are weighty, the ruler is honored;
when the ruler is honored, the state is secure.
When decrees are light, the ruler is demeaned;
when the ruler is demeaned, the state is endangered.
Thus, securing the state lies in honoring the ruler,
and honoring the ruler lies in implementing decrees,
which in turn relies on severe punishments.
When punishments are severe and decrees are carried out,
all officials are fearful;
if punishments are not severe
and decrees are not implemented,
all officials become complacent.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler discerns the foundation of governing the people,
and nothing is more essential than decrees.
Hence it is said:
"Those who undermine decrees shall die,
those who add to decrees shall die,
those who do not implement decrees shall die,
those who delay decrees shall die,
those who disobey decrees shall die."
These five offenses are punishable by death without pardon,
showing that only the decree is to be regarded.
Thus it is said:
"When decrees are weighty, subordinates are fearful."
If the superior is not clear-sighted,
although decrees issue from above,
the decision on their feasibility lies with those below.
When subordinates defy the ruler's orders to assert authority,
and act arbitrarily for personal gain,
how can officials not become complacent?
Moreover, if decrees issue from above,
but the judgment on their feasibility rests with those below,
this means authority is tied to the people.
When authority is tied to the people,
to expect the ruler not to face peril
is impossible.
If those who delay decrees go unpunished,
this teaches the people disrespect.
If those who do not implement decrees are not held accountable,
while those who do are punished,
this teaches the people disobedience.
If officials debate the feasibility of decrees after they are issued,
this divides authority downward.
If those who add or detract are not punished,
this leads the people onto wicked paths.
Under such circumstances,
cunning and flattering individuals
will use this to form private connections;
cliquish persons
will use it to form factions and seek gains;
greedy individuals
will use it to amass goods and wealth;
the timid and weak
will use it to flatter the rich and noble,
serving those in favor; the boastful and arrogant
will use it to buy fame and reputation.
Thus, with a single decree issued,
five paths of wickedness are shown to the people,
and to expect the ruler not to be endangered,
or the people not to be in chaos,
is impossible.
If grain is insufficient,
and non-essential production is not restricted,
the people will inevitably show signs of hunger,
yet artisans pride themselves on ornate carvings and engravings—
this is called perversity.
If cloth and silk are lacking,
and clothing is not regulated,
the people will surely suffer from cold and exposure,
yet women pride themselves on beautiful dresses and embroidered silks—
this is called perversity.
In a state capable of fielding ten thousand chariots and maintaining arms,
if soldiers cannot fight in the field or respond to enemies,
the altars of soil and grain will face the threat of peril and ruin,
yet officers pride themselves on avoiding divided duties—
this is called perversity.
If titles are conferred without regard to ability,
and emoluments granted without regard to merit,
then scholars will have no reason to uphold regulations or die for principles,
and ministers will inevitably engage in external solicitations,
seeking influence,
serving those in favor,
and priding themselves on wealth and nobility as glory—
this is called perversity.
The court should have principled ministers,
the state should have established customs,
and the people should have fundamental livelihoods.
What are principled ministers of the court?
Those who, assessing their own abilities, accept office
without deceiving the superior;
who govern meticulously according to laws and decrees,
without forming cliques;
who exhaust their abilities and efforts
without seeking undue gain,
facing difficulties and hardships
without shunning death;
who receive emoluments not exceeding their merits,
hold positions not beyond their capabilities,
and do not accept empty rewards without substance—
these are the principled ministers of the court.
What are the established customs of the state?
Where likes and dislikes
do not contradict the superior,
and what is valued or despised
does not oppose the decrees;
where there are no acts of defiance above,
no collusive talk below,
no extravagant maintenance,
no clothing beyond one's rank;
where conduct in the villages is careful,
and not contrary to the affairs of the court—
these are the established customs of the state.
What are the fundamental livelihoods of the people?
Raising livestock and planting trees,
focusing on timely grain cultivation,
exerting effort in farming and reclaiming wasteland,
and restricting non-essential activities—
these are the fundamental livelihoods of the people.
Therefore it is said:
"If the court does not value principled ministers,
then favorites will advance,
and the meritless will receive empty rewards;
if wickedness prevails,
the capable cannot reach the top.
If the state does not adhere to established customs,
then subordinates will be disobedient,
and the ruler's decrees will be hard to implement.
If the people do not focus on fundamental livelihoods,
then granaries will be empty,
and resources will be insufficient."
If favorites advance,
and the meritless receive empty rewards;
if wickedness prevails,
and the capable cannot reach the top,
then great ministers will not be harmonious.
If subordinates are disobedient,
and the ruler's commands are hard to enforce,
then emergencies cannot be overcome.
If granaries are empty,
and financial resources insufficient,
then the state has no means to secure its defense.
If any one of these three appears,
then an enemy state will dominate it.
Thus, a state is not strong in vain,
an army does not win in vain,
the people are not used in vain,
and commands are not enforced in vain.
For a state to be strong,
it must rely on the army's victory,
and only then is the state strong.
For an army to be victorious,
it must rely on the people's service,
and only then is the army victorious.
For the people to be used,
it must rely on the enforcement of commands,
and only then are the people used.
For commands to be enforced,
it must rely on the compliance of those close,
and only then are commands enforced.
Therefore, if prohibitions do not apply to the intimate and noble,
punishments are not enforced against the favored,
laws and prohibitions do not punish the serious offenders,
but harm the distant and lowly,
rewards and honors are not bestowed upon the humble,
yet one expects commands to be necessarily enforced,
it is unattainable.
If ability does not reach the officials,
salaries and rewards do not match merit,
decrees go against the people's will,
actions contradict the changes of the times,
the meritorious are not necessarily rewarded,
the guilty are not necessarily punished,
commands are not necessarily enforced,
prohibitions are not necessarily upheld.
If those in high positions have no means to command their subordinates,
yet expect the people to be necessarily used,
it is unattainable.
If generals lack stern authority,
the people's hearts are not unified,
soldiers in formation do not die for the regulations,
troops do not despise the enemy,
yet one expects the army to be necessarily victorious,
it is unattainable.
If internal defense cannot be maintained,
external attacks cannot subdue,
field battles cannot overcome the enemy,
invasions cannot awe the neighboring states,
yet one expects the state to be strong,
it is unattainable.
If virtue does not extend to the weak and small,
might is not trusted by the strong and great,
military campaigns cannot subdue the world,
yet one seeks to hegemonize the feudal lords,
it is unattainable.
If might has a rival to stand with,
arms have a contender to share the struggle,
virtue cannot win over distant states,
commands cannot unify the feudal lords,
yet one seeks to king over the world,
it is unattainable.
Vast territory and wealthy state,
numerous people and strong army,
these are the foundation of hegemony and kingship,
yet they border on peril and ruin.
The way of heaven's cycles,
the changes in human hearts:
the way of heaven's cycles,
when extreme, reverse;
when full, decline;
the changes in human hearts,
when surplus, lead to arrogance;
arrogance leads to slackness and neglect.
Now, arrogance means arrogance towards the feudal lords;
arrogance towards the feudal lords
causes loss of feudal lords abroad;
slackness and neglect
cause chaos among the people at home.
Loss of feudal lords abroad,
chaos among the people at home,
is the way of heaven.
This is the time of peril and ruin.
As for territory, though vast,
do not annex or seize;
do not plunder or rob;
people, though numerous,
do not slacken or neglect,
do not arrogantly oppress inferiors;
state, though wealthy,
do not be extravagant or wasteful,
do not indulge desires;
army, though strong,
do not lightly insult the feudal lords,
when mobilizing the masses and using arms,
must act for the governance of the world,
this is the foundation of rectifying the world
and the way of hegemony and kingship.
The former kings had three instruments for governing the state,
and six destroyers that attack and ruin them.
Enlightened kings could overcome these attacks,
thus, without adding to the three instruments,
they possessed the state and rectified the world.
Chaotic kings could not overcome these attacks,
thus, without diminishing the three instruments,
they possessed the world yet perished.
"What are the three instruments?"
It is said:
"Decrees and commands,
the axe of execution,
salaries and rewards."
"What are the six destroyers?"
It is said:
"Kinsmen,
nobles,
wealth,
beauty,
flattery and cunning,
and objects of pleasure."
"How are the three instruments used?"
It is said:
"Without decrees and commands, there is no way to command subordinates;
without the axe of execution, there is no way to awe the masses;
without salaries and rewards, there is no way to encourage the people."
"How do the six destroyers cause ruin?"
It is said:
"Though disobeying, one can still survive;
though violating prohibitions, one can still be exempt;
though without merit, one can still become wealthy.
If in a state, there are those who disobey yet can survive,
then decrees and commands are insufficient to command subordinates;
if there are those who violate prohibitions yet can be exempt,
then the axe of execution is insufficient to awe the masses;
if there are those without merit yet can become wealthy,
then salaries and rewards are insufficient to encourage the people.
If decrees and commands are insufficient to command subordinates,
the axe of execution insufficient to awe the masses,
salaries and rewards insufficient to encourage the people,
then the people will not act of their own accord.
If the people do not act of their own accord,
then battles cannot be won;
if battles cannot be won,
then defense cannot be secured;
if defense cannot be secured,
then an enemy state will dominate it."
"Then, how would the former kings handle this?"
It is said:
"Do not alter decrees and commands for the six;
do not hesitate or err with the axe of execution for the six;
do not increase or decrease salaries and rewards for the six.
If so,
then near and far are of one mind;
if near and far are of one mind,
then many and few unite their strength;
if many and few unite their strength,
then battles can be surely won,
and defense can be surely secured.
Not for annexation or plunder,
but for the governance of the world,
this is the way to rectify the world."
If not following the law, then affairs lack constancy;
if the law is not enforced, then commands are not carried out.
If commands are issued but not carried out,
then the commands are not lawful;
if laws are established but not implemented,
then those who formulate the laws are not careful;
if careful but not implemented,
then rewards and punishments are too light;
if severe but not implemented,
then rewards and punishments lack credibility,
If one has faith but does not act accordingly,
then they do not lead by example.
Hence it is said:
"If prohibitions are upheld by the ruler himself,
then orders will be carried out among the people."
To hear of the worthy but not promote them,
is perilous;
to hear of the good but not seek it,
is perilous;
to see the capable but not employ them,
is perilous;
to be close to others but not steadfast,
is perilous;
to share plans but become estranged,
is perilous;
to endanger others but lack the ability,
is perilous;
to depose someone and then reinstate them,
is perilous;
to have the means but not act,
is perilous;
to have plenty but not give,
is perilous;
to handle critical matters without secrecy,
is perilous.
If the ruler is not cautious and secretive,
then those who speak honestly and act uprightly are endangered;
if those who speak honestly and act uprightly are endangered,
then the ruler becomes isolated with no loyal supporters;
if the ruler is isolated with no loyal supporters,
then the ministers form cliques and factions.
That the ruler becomes isolated with no loyal supporters,
and the ministers form cliques and factions,
is not the fault of the ministers,
but the error of the ruler.
If the people do not commit serious crimes,
it is because their faults are not great;
if the people do not commit great faults,
it is because the ruler does not pardon them.
If the ruler pardons minor faults,
then the people will commit many serious crimes,
which accumulate from this practice.
Hence it is said:
"If pardons are issued, the people lose respect;
if favors are granted, faults increase daily."
When favors and pardons are bestowed upon the people,
even if prisons are full,
and executions numerous,
wickedness cannot be overcome.
Hence it is said:
"There is no better way with evil than to prohibit it early."
Generally, pardoning
brings small benefits but great harm,
so over time it cannot overcome its calamities.
Not pardoning
brings small harm but great benefits,
so over time it cannot surpass its blessings.
Thus, pardoning is like
dropping the reins of a galloping horse;
not pardoning is like
the lancet for a boil or ulcer.
In civil matters, there may be three reprieves,
but in military matters, not a single pardon.
Favoritism, which involves frequent pardons,
is easy at first but difficult later,
and over time cannot overcome its disasters;
the law,
difficult at first but easy later,
over time cannot surpass its blessings.
Thus, favoritism is the enemy of the people;
the law is the parent of the people.
The highest standard is to establish systems with regulations,
the next is to correct errors when they occur,
so even if there are faults,
they are not too severe.
If faults are pardoned and good deeds overlooked,
then the people are not encouraged.
If faults are not pardoned,
and good deeds are not overlooked,
the way to encourage the people
is thereby applied.
Hence it is said:
"An enlightened ruler is one who decides affairs resolutely."
The ruler has three demands of the people,
and if these three demands are not moderated,
then the ruler's position is endangered.
What are the three demands?
First, to seek;
second, to prohibit;
third, to command.
What is sought must be obtained,
what is prohibited must be stopped,
what is commanded must be carried out.
If much is sought,
little is obtained;
if much is prohibited,
little is stopped;
if many commands are issued,
few are carried out.
If seeking yields no results,
then authority is daily diminished;
if prohibitions are not heeded,
then punishments are scorned;
if commands are not obeyed,
then inferiors encroach upon superiors.
Thus, none can seek much and obtain much,
none can prohibit much and stop much,
none can command much and have much carried out.
Hence it is said:
"If the superior is harsh, the inferiors will not obey;
if the inferiors do not obey and force is applied with punishments,
then the ruler becomes the target of many plots.
When the ruler is plotted against by many,
even if he wishes to avoid danger,
it is impossible.
If decrees are issued
and then altered,
if rituals and righteousness are practiced
and then halted,
if standards are established
and then changed,
if laws and penalties are set
and then shifted,
then,
even if rewards are generous,
the people will not be encouraged;
even if executions are numerous,
the people will not fear.
Hence it is said:
"If the ruler lacks firm resolve,
the inferiors will have doubtful hearts;
if the state lacks constant principles,
the people's strength will not be exhausted,
as is the natural course."
When an enlightened ruler is in power,
none among the people dare establish private opinions and exalt themselves,
the state has no strange severity,
no mixed customs,
no divergent rituals,
and scholars have no private debates.
Those who are arrogant and alter commands,
deviate from norms,
and devise systems,
those who create dissenting views
are all executed,
so the strong are broken,
the sharp are blunted,
the hard are shattered.
Guiding them with the line and ink,
controlling them with executions and penalties,
thus the hearts of all the people submit and follow the superior,
pushing them forward, they go;
leading them, they come.
If there are those below who establish private opinions and exalt themselves,
withdrawing to engage in disputes,
then commands from this point will not be carried out.
Hence it is said:
"If private opinions are established, the ruler's way is debased;
how much more so if there are those who are arrogant and alter commands,
deviate from norms and devise systems,
change customs,
and perverse attire and strange doctrines are still upheld?"
Those above who do not follow the ruler's commands,
below who do not harmonize with the village,
who change and act on their own,
altering the established customs of the state,
are called ungovernable people.
Ungovernable people
are outside the line.
Those outside the line are punished.
Let the worthy be fed according to their ability,
and warriors be fed according to their achievements.
If the worthy are fed according to their ability,
then the ruler is honored and the people follow;
if warriors are fed according to their achievements,
then soldiers disregard hardship and despise the enemy.
If the ruler is honored and the people follow,
and soldiers disregard hardship and despise the enemy,
with these two established in the state,
then the world is orderly and the ruler secure.
When ranks are not respected
and emoluments are not substantial,
one cannot expect others to share in overcoming difficulties and facing dangers,
because the Way is not yet sufficient to attract them.
Therefore, the ancient kings established carriages and crowns
merely to distinguish the noble from the humble,
not seeking their beauty;
they set up ranks and emoluments
to maintain their corresponding attire,
not seeking their splendor.
They ensured that gentlemen lived by the Way,
and commoners lived by their labor.
When gentlemen live by the Way,
the rulers are respected and the people are obedient;
when commoners live by their labor,
wealth is abundant and sustenance is ample.
With rulers respected and people obedient,
wealth abundant and sustenance ample,
when these four are fully embodied,
then awaiting the right time to become a true king is not difficult. , . , , , ; , , . , ; , . , , .
An enlightened ruler establishes ancestral temples,
sufficient for hosting guests and conducting sacrifices,
not seeking their beauty;
builds palaces, towers, and pavilions,
sufficient to shelter from dryness, dampness, cold, and heat,
not seeking their grandeur;
creates carvings and engravings,
sufficient to distinguish the noble from the humble,
not seeking their spectacle.
Thus, farmers do not miss their seasons,
artisans do not fail in their work,
merchants do not lose their profits,
the people have no idle days,
and wealth does not lie stagnant.
Hence it is said:
"Frugality is the Way indeed!
If a decree has not been promulgated, and some people act accordingly,
yet rewards follow,
this is the ruler's arbitrary bestowal.
With arbitrary bestowal by the ruler,
meritorious ministers will resent it;
when meritorious ministers resent it,
and ignorant people engage in reckless actions,
ignorant people engage in reckless actions,
this becomes the root of great chaos.
If a decree has not been promulgated, and punishments are applied,
this is the ruler's arbitrary punishment.
With arbitrary punishment by the ruler, the people will hold life lightly;
when the people hold life lightly, violent individuals will rise,
factions form, and rebellious villains emerge.
If a decree has been promulgated, but rewards do not follow,
this causes the people not to be encouraged,
not to follow regulations,
and not to sacrifice their lives for duty. When the people are not encouraged,
do not follow regulations,
and do not sacrifice their lives for duty,
then battles cannot be won and defenses cannot be secured;
if battles are not won and defenses are not secured,
the state will not be safe.
If a decree has been promulgated, but punishments are not applied,
this teaches the people not to obey.
When the people do not obey,
the strong will assert themselves;
when the strong assert themselves,
the ruler's position is endangered.
Therefore, it is said:
"Laws and institutions must emulate the Way,
commands must be clear and prominent,
rewards and punishments must be trustworthy and meticulous,
this is the standard for rectifying the people."
Generally, the rulers of large states are honored,
while those of small states are humble.
Why are the rulers of large states honored?
What is the reason?
It is said:
"Because those who serve them are many."
Why are the rulers of small states humble?
What is the reason?
It is said:
"Because those who serve them are few."
Thus, if those who serve are many, one is honored;
if those who serve are few, one is humble.
Then, how can a ruler not desire the people to be numerous and serve him?
How to make the people numerous and serve oneself? What to do?
It is said:
"If laws are established and commands are carried out,
then those among the people who serve will be many;
if laws are not established,
and commands are not carried out,
then those among the people who serve will be few."
Therefore, if the laws established
and commands carried out are many,
while those abolished are few,
the people will not criticize;
if the people do not criticize,
they will obey.
If the laws established,
commands carried out,
and those abolished are equal,
then the state lacks constant norms;
if the state lacks constant norms,
the people will act recklessly.
If the laws established
and commands carried out are few,
while those abolished are many,
the people will not obey;
if the people do not obey,
violent individuals will rise, and treacherous evils will emerge.
Considering why the ruler loves the people,
it is for the purpose of using them that he loves them.
If, for the sake of loving the people,
he does not hesitate to destroy laws and compromise commands,
then he loses what is called loving the people.
To love the people in order to use them,
it is clear that the people will not be used.
Those who are good at using the people
may kill them, endanger them,
toil them,
starve them, thirst them;
those who use the people will drive them to these extremes,
yet the people have no one with whom to consider harming themselves,
for the enlightened king is above,
and the Way and laws are practiced in the state,
so the people all abandon their preferences and do what they dislike.
Therefore, those skilled in using the people
do not bestow carriages and crowns lightly,
nor apply axes and execution blades arbitrarily.
Thus,
the worthy are encouraged and the violent are restrained.
When the worthy are encouraged and the violent are restrained,
achievements and fame are established thereafter.
Treading on bright blades,
enduring arrows and stones,
entering water and fire,
to obey the ruler's commands;
the ruler's commands are fully carried out,
prohibitions are entirely enforced,
when led and employed,
the people dare not withhold their strength;
when pushed into battle,
the people dare not cherish their lives.
Daring not to withhold their strength,
only then can they achieve merit;
daring not to cherish their lives,
only then can they be invincible.
Advancing invincibly,
retreating with merit,
thus the masses of the three armies
all preserve their heads,
and parents, wives, and children
remain safe at home.
Therefore, the people cannot be consulted at the beginning,
but can share in the joy of success.
Hence, the benevolent,
the wise, and those who possess the Way,
do not consult with others about the beginning.
No state is small or unfortunate and yet becomes diminished or perishes
without the ruler and ministers having failed in their personal conduct,
or without failures in offices,
legal systems, governance, and education within the state,
or without failures in the strategies of feudal lords externally,
leading to loss of territory and national danger.
No state is large or fortunate and yet achieves merit and fame
without the ruler and ministers having succeeded in their personal conduct,
or without successes in offices,
legal systems, governance, and education within the state,
or without successes in the strategies of feudal lords externally.
Only then are merit established and fame achieved.
Then, how can a state be without the Way?
How can a person be without worthies?
Attaining the Way and guiding by it,
obtaining worthies and employing them,
there will be great expectations for promoting benefits and eliminating harms.
In promoting benefits and eliminating harms,
nothing is more urgent than personal conduct.
and you alone are particularly severe. The harm lies in
the inevitable initial failure of decrees.
When a ruler fails in his decrees and becomes obscured,
once obscured, he is coerced;
once coerced, he is assassinated.
The reason why a ruler is able to be a ruler
is due to his authority.
Thus, if a ruler loses his authority,
then his ministers will control him.
If authority lies below,
then the ruler is controlled by his ministers;
if authority lies above,
then the ministers are controlled by the ruler.
Therefore, the exchange of positions between ruler and minister
occurs when authority lies below.
If it remains with a minister for a year,
