even if the minister is disloyal,
the ruler cannot take it back;
if it remains with a son for a year,
even if the son is unfilial,
the father cannot subdue him.
Hence, the records in the "Spring and Autumn Annals" state:
there are ministers who assassinate their rulers,
and sons who assassinate their fathers.
Therefore, it is said:
"The hall is farther than a hundred lǐ away,
the courtyard is farther than a thousand lǐ,
the gate is farther than ten thousand lǐ."
Now, a walker in one day
can convey information over a hundred lǐ,
yet if there is an affair in the hall,
the ruler may not hear of it in ten days—
this is what is meant by 'farther than a hundred lǐ';
a walker in ten days
can convey information over a thousand lǐ,
yet if there is an affair in the courtyard,
the ruler may not hear of it in a month—
this is what is meant by 'farther than a thousand lǐ';
a walker in a hundred days
can convey information over ten thousand lǐ,
yet if there is an affair at the gate,
the ruler may not hear of it in a year—
this is what is meant by 'farther than ten thousand lǐ.'
Thus, when a request enters but does not exit,
it is called extinction;
when it exits but does not enter,
it is called severance;
when it enters but does not reach,
it is called encroachment;
when it exits but is blocked on the way,
it is called obstruction.
For a ruler who faces extinction, severance, encroachment, or obstruction,
it is not because his doors are barred and guarded,
but because his governance is not being implemented.
Therefore, it is said:
"Decrees are weightier than treasures,
the state takes precedence over relatives,
law is more important than the people,
and authority is more valuable than ranks and emoluments."
Thus, one should not value treasures lightly over decrees,
not put relatives before the state,
not bend the law for the sake of loving the people,
not share authority for the sake of ranks and emoluments.
Hence, it is said:
authority is not something to be given to others.
Governance
means correctness.
Correctness
is what is used to properly determine the destiny of all things.
Therefore, the sage refines his virtue and establishes the mean to generate correctness,
and clarifies correctness to govern the state.
Thus, correctness is what stops excess and reaches what is lacking.
Both excess and deficiency
are not correctness.
Without correctness,
the state is harmed all the same.
Courage without righteousness
harms the military,
benevolence without correctness
harms the law.
Thus, the defeat of an army
arises from lack of righteousness;
the infringement of law
arises from lack of correctness.
Therefore, there are words that are eloquent but not essential,
and actions that are difficult but not good.
Hence, words must hit the essentials,
not merely be eloquent for its own sake;
actions must aim for goodness,
not merely be difficult for its own sake.
Compasses and squares
are the standards for circles and squares.
Even with sharp eyes and skilled hands,
one cannot match the ability of crude compasses and squares to correct circles and squares.
Thus, the skilled can create compasses and squares,
but cannot abolish them to correct circles and squares.
Even a sage can create laws,
but cannot abolish laws to govern the state.
Therefore, even with great wisdom and noble conduct,
to govern by背离ing the law
is to abolish compasses and squares in correcting circles and squares.
Another saying:
The dignity of a ruler
is not because his virtue alone surpasses others';
it is because he is the ruler,
and thus he is honored accordingly,
without daring to debate the high or low of his virtue,
for there is a reason.
It is because his power over life and death
is more urgent than that of the Director of Fate,
enriching the poor
makes people support each other,
honoring the humble
makes people serve each other.
The ruler wields these six to control his ministers,
and the ministers look to these six to serve their ruler.
When ruler and minister meet,
these six are called the stratagem.
If these six remain with a minister for a year,
even if the minister is disloyal,
the ruler cannot take them back;
if they remain with a son for a year,
even if the son is unfilial,
the father cannot take them back.
Hence, the records in the "Spring and Autumn Annals":
there are ministers who assassinate their rulers,
and sons who assassinate their fathers,
who obtain these six,
while the ruler or father is unaware.
When these six are with the minister,
the ruler is obscured.
When the ruler is obscured,
he loses his decrees.
Therefore, it is said:
when a decree enters but does not exit,
it is called obscurity;
when it exits but does not enter,
it is called obstruction;
when it exits but is not implemented,
it is called dragging;
when it enters but does not reach,
it is called flaw.
For a ruler facing dragging,
flaw,
obscurity,
or obstruction,
it is not that he dares to bar his doors and guard his household,
but that his decrees are not being carried out.
The reason for this
is that worthy men do not come and loyal ministers are not employed.
Therefore, a ruler must be cautious with his decrees.
Decrees
are the great treasure of the ruler.
Another saying:
when worthy men do not come,
it is called obscurity;
when loyal ministers are not employed,
it is called blockage;
when decrees are issued but not implemented,
it is called hindrance;
when prohibitions are set but not stopped,
it is called defiance.
For a ruler facing obscurity, blockage, hindrance, or defiance,
it is not that he dares to bar his doors and guard his household,
but that worthies do not come,
and decrees are not implemented.
In general, the people follow their superiors
not by what is said,
but by what is truly favored.
If the superior favors courage,
the people will轻视 death;
if the superior favors benevolence,
the people will轻视 wealth;
thus, what the superior favors,
the people will favor even more.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler knows that the people inevitably take the superior as their heart,
so he establishes laws to govern himself,
and sets standards to correct himself.
Therefore, if those above do not act properly,
the people will not follow.
If the people do not submit to the law and die for the regulations,
the state will surely fall into chaos.
Thus, a ruler with the Way
implements laws and cultivates regulations,
leading the people to submit first.
In evaluating people, there are essential points:
Those who boast of their achievements
are not great men.
Such boasting
signifies arrogance;
arrogance
is emptiness.
Arrogance and emptiness lie in their dealings with things,
and in things, they become constraints.
Boasters
belong to the petty category.
Those who evaluate others contrary to ancient ways
are not noble men.
Those who do not understand antiquity and belittle its achievements
are not wise men.
Those whose moral conduct is not yet cultivated in themselves yet distance themselves from antiquity
are base individuals.
Without resources for affairs,
and who neglect their duties when opportunities arise,
are foolish men.
Those who fish for fame
are not worthy men;
rulers who fish for profit
are not true kings.
Worthy men conduct themselves
forgetting they have fame;
true kings practice their Way,
forgetting their achievements.
The conduct of worthy men
and the Way of true kings
are what they cannot cease from.
Enlightened rulers make the state public and unify the people to heed the world,
while loyal ministers advance directly to discuss their abilities.
Enlightened rulers do not bestow ranks and emoluments privately on their favorites,
and loyal ministers do not falsely claim ability to seek rank and emolument.
If the ruler does not privatize the state,
and ministers do not falsify ability,
those who follow this path,
even if not achieving great order,
are upholding the proper way of guiding the people.
Now, with ministers who falsify ability
serving rulers who privatize the state,
achieving success and renown
has never occurred in past or present.
Those who falsify ability are easy to recognize.
I consider the former kings:
When Shùn possessed the empire,
Yǔ served as Minister of Works,
Xiè as Minister of Education,
Gāo Yáo as Judge,
and Hòu Jì as Minister of Agriculture;
these four men
were worthies of the empire,
yet each still refined one virtue
to serve their ruler.
Now, those who falsify ability,
when serving in office,
all claim to possess the capabilities of these four worthies combined.
From this perspective,
their failure to establish merit and fame
is also easy to understand.
Thus, high ranks and heavy emoluments
they accept without exception,
powerful positions and great offices
they follow without refusal,
serving the ruler in this manner,
these are what are called ministers who falsify ability and usurp benefits.
If the age lacks rulers who make the state public,
then there are no ministers who advance directly;
if there are no rulers who evaluate ability,
then there are no ministers who achieve success.
In the past, during the succession of the Three Dynasties,
how could they have two empires to privatize?
Impoverishing the people and wasting resources
nothing is greater than war;
endangering the state and distressing the ruler
nothing is swifter than war.
These four perils are clear,
yet none in past or present have been able to abolish them.
If war should be abolished but is not,
that is delusion;
if it should not be abolished
yet one seeks to abolish it,
that is also delusion.
Both these cases
harm the state equally.
During the reigns of Huángdì, Táng, and Yú,
the height of imperial virtue,
possessing the empire,
authority rested with one person,
yet at that time,
war was not abolished.
Now, with virtue not matching the Three Emperors,
and the empire not compliant,
to seek to abolish war
is it not difficult?
Thus, what an enlightened ruler masters
is knowing where the perils lie.
When the state is well-governed and the people accumulate resources,
this is called mastery.
Action and stillness,
these are where perils lie.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler carefully attends to what he masters
to prepare for where perils lie.
A fierce and resolute ruler
cannot avoid external calamities;
a weak and timid ruler
cannot avoid internal chaos.
A fierce and resolute ruler metes out punishments lightly,
and the consequence of light punishment
is that those on the right path feel insecure;
when those on the right path feel insecure,
then talented and capable ministers will leave or flee.
Those wise ones who know our true situation
will advise our enemies against us,
and thus external calamities will arrive from this.
Hence it is said:
"A fierce and resolute ruler
cannot avoid external calamities."
A weak and timid ruler hesitates to punish,
and the fault of hesitant punishment
is that those who act evilly do not reform;
when evildoers persist without reform,
then ministers form cliques;
when ministers form cliques,
they conceal the good and promote the evil;
concealing the good and promoting the evil,
then internal chaos arises from this.
Hence it is said:
"A weak and timid ruler
cannot avoid internal chaos."
An enlightened ruler does not endanger the altars of grain and soil for the sake of relatives,
for the altars are closer than kin;
does not change his decrees for the ruler's desires,
for decrees are more revered than the ruler;
does not divide his authority for precious treasures,
for authority is more valuable than treasures;
does not weaken his laws for love of the people,
for the law is what truly loves the people.
6.2 Chapter 17 On Military Methods, Outer Discourses 8. He who illuminates the One becomes sovereign;
he who discerns the Way becomes emperor;
he who comprehends virtue becomes king;
he who plans successfully and wins in war becomes hegemon.
Thus, war,
although not the ultimate Way or highest virtue,
is yet a means to assist kingship and achieve hegemony.
Nowadays, those who employ troops are not so;
they do not understand the balance of military power.
Hence, on the day they raise an army, their territory becomes impoverished,
in battle they are not certain to win,
if they win, many die,
and though they gain land, the state is ruined.
These four
are the calamities of using military force.
When these four calamities befall a state,
it cannot but be endangered.
The book of great strategies says:
On the day of raising an army,
the territory is not impoverished,
in battle victory is certain,
victory is achieved without loss of life,
and gaining land does not ruin the state.
How to achieve these four?
On the day of raising an army,
the territory not being impoverished
is due to accurate calculations.
To be certain of victory in battle
is due to well-defined laws and measures.
To be victorious without casualties
is because training and weapons are well-prepared and sharp,
and the enemy dares not confront them.
To gain territory without the state suffering defeat
is by aligning with the people.
Aligning with the people
means commands and systems can be effectively issued.
With training and weapons well-prepared and sharp,
there is discipline.
With laws and measures well-defined,
there is defense.
When calculations are accurate,
there is clarity.
Governing the masses has its methods,
defeating the enemy has its principles;
examine the methods to understand the principles,
scrutinize the weapons to recognize victory,
and clarify the principles to overcome the enemy.
Stabilize the ancestral temple,
settle men and women,
divide officials into four roles,
then authority and virtue can be established;
establish laws and rituals,
issue commands and decrees,
then you can unify the masses and govern the people.
An army without leadership
cannot anticipate the enemy early.
Without officials in the fields,
there will be no reserves.
Without constant governance,
the subordinates will resent their superiors,
and weapons will not be effective.
Without governance in the court,
rewards and punishments unclear,
the people will disregard their property.
Thus it is said:
Anticipate the enemy early,
and you can act independently;
have reserves,
and you can endure long without exhaustion;
with ingenious weapons,
you can attack without waste;
with clear rewards and punishments,
the brave are encouraged.
If the three commands are without error,
the five instructions are without chaos,
and the nine banners are clearly displayed,
then even in peril there is no harm,
in extremity there is no difficulty.
Thus, one can achieve far-reaching goals through methods,
and control strength through systems.
The three commands:
first, the drum,
which is for assuming duty,
for rising,
for advancing;
second, the gong,
which is for halting,
for retreating,
for disengaging;
third, the flag,
which is for deploying troops,
for controlling troops,
for ceasing troops.
These are called the three commands.
With these three orders, military laws are governed.
The five instructions:
first, instruct their eyes with the shapes and colors of flags;
second, instruct their ears with the signals of commands;
third, instruct their feet with the measures of advance and retreat;
fourth, instruct their hands with the advantages of long and short weapons;
fifth, instruct their hearts with the sincerity of rewards and punishments.
When the five instructions are each practiced,
the soldiers will be brave.
The nine banners:
first, raising the sun banner
means march by day;
second, raising the moon banner
means march by night;
third, raising the dragon banner
means march over water;
fourth, raising the tiger banner
means march through forests;
fifth, raising the bird banner
means march over slopes;
sixth, raising the snake banner
means march through marshes;
seventh, raising the magpie banner
means march on land;
eighth, raising the wolf banner
means march in mountains;
ninth, raising the sack banner
means carry provisions and drive.
Once the nine banners are established,
movements and halts will not err.
The three commands,
five instructions, and nine banners,
begin without origin,
end without limit.
Beginning without origin
is the Dào;
ending without limit
is the Dé.
The Dào cannot be measured,
the Dé cannot be counted.
Thus, being immeasurable
means even the strong cannot scheme against it,
being uncountable
means deceit dare not approach.
When both are fully applied,
movements and halts achieve success.
Advance without others knowing,
strike without others expecting.
Advancing without knowledge,
so none can resist it;
striking unexpectedly,
so none can respond.
Thus, complete victory is achieved without harm.
Teach according to convenience,
act based on advantage.
Teaching has no constant,
action has no constant.
When both are fully applied,
movements yield success.
With weapons perfected and training implemented,
pursuing the fleeing is like a whirlwind,
striking and thrusting like thunder and lightning.
Even impassable terrain cannot be defended,
relying on strongholds cannot hold.
Positioned centrally without rivals,
commands are executed without delay.
With weapons perfected and training implemented,
dispersing without fixed direction,
gathering beyond count.
With training and weapons well-prepared and sharp,
advancing and retreating like thunder and lightning,
without hesitation or exhaustion.
With unified focus,
one moves freely without doubt;
with sharpened soldiers and effective weapons,
one faces difficulties without exhaustion.
Advancing without doubt,
retreating without exhaustion,
the enemy is then at your service.
Scaling mountains and cliffs,
without waiting for hooks or ladders;
crossing rivers and valleys,
without needing boats or oars.
Passing through impassable lands,
attacking reliant strongholds,
entering and exiting alone
with none able to stop it.
Indeed, not entering alone,
yet none can stop it;
indeed, not exiting alone,
so none can restrain it.
The ultimate of namelessness,
exhausted yet unexpected.
Thus, it cannot be doubted as divine.
Nourish them with the Dào,
and the people will be harmonious;
cultivate them with the Dé,
and the people will be united.
Harmonious and united, thus they can cooperate,
cooperating thus they can assemble,
fully cooperative and assembled,
none can harm them.
Establish the one ultimate,
practice the two essentials,
employ the three authorities,
implement the five instructions,
activate the four opportunities,
set the six conducts,
discuss the seven calculations,
maintain the eight responses,
Examine the nine chapters,
each chapter with ten commands.
Thus, one can achieve complete victory and great triumph.
By not defending,
one can secure victory through defense.
Frequent battles weary the soldiers,
repeated victories make the ruler arrogant.
When an arrogant ruler commands weary people,
how can the state avoid peril?
Therefore, the ultimate excellence lies in not fighting,
the next best is to unify through one action.
To crush the great and triumph over the strong,
is the pinnacle of unification.
Disrupting the enemy without resorting to change,
exploiting them without deceit,
defeating them without trickery,
is the essence of unification.
Use substance when near,
employ commands when far,
strength that cannot be measured,
power that cannot be gauged,
spirit that has no limit,
virtue that is unfathomable,
are the origins of unification.
In multitude like timely rain,
in scarcity like a swift wind,
is the culmination of unification.
Controlling the enemy,
is the ultimate in weaponry;
employing the enemy,
is the perfection of training.
Those who cannot procure weapons,
cannot sharpen them against the enemy;
those who cannot complete training,
cannot utilize the enemy.
Those who cannot use the enemy are impoverished,
those who cannot procure weapons are stranded.
Swift use of troops
ensures certain victory.
Advancing and retreating on different paths,
then harm the enemy.
Penetrate deeply to endanger them,
and the soldiers will self-cultivate,
soldiers self-cultivating
leads to unity of heart and strength.
The adept in warfare,
make the enemy as if grasping at emptiness,
as if seizing shadows.
With no setup and no form,
nothing cannot be accomplished;
with no form and no action,
nothing cannot be transformed.
This is what is called the Dào.
As if absent yet present,
as if behind yet ahead,
mere force is insufficient to command it.
Qí Xīgōng begat Prince Zhū'ér,
Prince Jiǔ,
and Prince Xiǎo Bái.
He appointed Bào Shū to tutor Xiǎo Bái,
but Bào Shū declined,
claiming illness and not appearing.
Guǎn Zhòng and Shào Hū went to see him, saying:
"Why do you not appear?"
Bào Shū said:
"There is an old saying:
'No one knows a son better than his father,
no one knows a minister better than his ruler.'
Now the ruler knows my lack of virtue,
hence he has ordered this humble minister to tutor Xiǎo Bái.
I, the humble minister, know I am being cast aside."
Shào Hū said:
"If you firmly decline and do not appear,
I will take responsibility for you unto death,
and surely spare you."
Bào Shū said:
"If you do so,
how could I not be spared?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"That will not do.
Those who uphold the state and ancestral temples,
do not shirk duties,
nor seek idle leisure.
Who will come to rule the state
is still unknown.
You should appear."
Shào Hū said:
"It will not do.
The three of us in regard to the state of Qí,
are like the legs of a tripod;
remove one,
and it surely cannot stand.
I observe that Xiǎo Bái
will certainly not be the successor."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Not so.
The people of the state despise Jiǔ's mother,
and by extension Jiǔ himself,
while pitying Xiǎo Bái for having no mother.
Zhū'ér is elder but lowly,
the outcome is uncertain.
Those who will stabilize Qí,
if not these two princes,
then who else?
Xiǎo Bái's character
lacks petty cleverness, is cautious
yet has great foresight.
None but Yí Wú can accommodate Xiǎo Bái.
If heaven unfortunately brings disaster upon Qí,
even if Jiǔ gains the throne,
affairs will not succeed.
If not you to stabilize the state,
then who will it be?"
Shào Hū said:
"After a hundred years,
when our ruler passes away,
to violate his command
and depose the one he established,
seizing Jiǔ from me,
even gaining the world, I would not live on.
You, brother, share with me the governance of Qí,
receiving the ruler's order without change,
supporting the established without failure,
that is my duty."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I, Yí Wú, as a minister,
will uphold the ruler's command,
serve the state,
and maintain the ancestral temples.
How could I die for just one Jiǔ?
What I, Yí Wú, would die for,
is the state shattered,
the ancestral temples destroyed,
the sacrifices severed—
then I would die for that.
Without these three,
then I, Yí Wú, live.
If I live,
it benefits Qí;
if I die,
it harms Qí."
Bào Shū said:
"Then what should be done?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"You should appear and accept the command."
Bào Shū agreed,
then appeared and accepted the command,
thus tutoring Xiǎo Bái.
Bào Shū asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What course to take?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"As a minister,
if one does not exert full effort for the ruler,
one is not trusted,
if not trusted,
one's words are not heeded,
if words are not heeded,
the state is not stabilized.
Serving the ruler allows no divided loyalty."
Bào Shū agreed.
Xīgōng's maternal younger brother Yí Zhòngnián
begat Gōngsūn Wúzhī,
who was favored by Xīgōng,
his attire and rituals akin to the heir.
When Xīgōng died,
Zhū'ér, being the eldest, became ruler,
known as Xiānggōng.
After Xiānggōng was established,
he demoted Wúzhī,
and Wúzhī became angry.
The duke ordered Lián Chēng and Guǎn Zhìfù to garrison Kuíqiū,
saying:
"Go at the melon season,
and return at the next melon season."
When the garrison duty period ended,
no inquiry from the duke arrived,
and their request for replacement was denied,
so the two men conspired with Gōngsūn Wúzhī to start a rebellion.
Wén Jiāng, wife of Duke Huán of Lǔ,
was a daughter of Qí.
The duke was about to go to Qí,
and traveled together with his wife.
Shēn Yú remonstrated:
"This cannot be.
Women have their homes,
men have their chambers,
they should not defile each other,
this is called propriety."
The duke did not listen,
and thus met with the Marquis of Qí at Luò together with Wén Jiāng.
Wén Jiāng had an affair with the Marquis of Qí,
Duke Huán learned of it,
and reproached Wén Jiāng.
Wén Jiāng informed the Marquis of Qí,
who became angry,
entertained the duke,
and had Prince Péngshēng assist Duke Lǔ
by pressing against his ribs,
and the duke died in his carriage.
Shù Màn said:
"The worthy die for loyalty to resolve doubts,
and the common people find refuge in this;
the wise investigate principles with long-term consideration,
and thus preserve themselves.
Now Péngshēng served his lord doubly,
without speaking exhaustively
but flattering in action, to mock our lord,
causing our lord to lose the rites between relatives, and now
he further forcefully accomplished our lord's calamity,
creating enmity between two states,
can Péngshēng escape this?
The principle of calamity belongs to him.
When a lord carries out calamity in anger,
without fear of worsening relations with kin, allowing
confusion to arise, there is no shame.
How could Péngshēng have stopped it?
If Lǔ demands accountability,
they will certainly name Péngshēng as the cause."
In the second month,
the people of Lǔ informed Qí:
"Our humble lord, fearing your majesty's authority,
dared not remain at ease,
came to restore former amity.
The rites were completed but he did not return,
with no one else to blame,
we ask to use Péngshēng to resolve this."
The people of Qí accordingly killed Péngshēng,
to apologize to Lǔ.
In the fifth month,
Duke Xiāng hunted at Bèiqiū,
and saw a boar.
His attendants said:
"It is Prince Péngshēng."
The duke angrily said:
"How dare Prince Péngshēng appear!"
He shot at it,
the boar stood like a man and cried.
The duke, terrified,
fell from his carriage,
injured his foot and lost his shoe.
Upon returning,
he demanded the shoe from attendant Fèi,
who could not find it,
and was whipped until bleeding.
Fèi ran out,
encountered assassins at the gate,
who seized and bound him.
Fèi bared his back to show them,
the assassins believed him,
and sent Fèi in first,
who hid the duke then went out, fighting
to death in the gateway.
Shízhī Fēnrú died at the base of the steps.
Mèng Yáng took the duke's place sleeping in the bed,
the assassins killed him,
saying:
"This is not the lord,
he does not resemble him."
Seeing the duke's feet beneath the door,
they then killed the duke
and established Gōngsūn Wúzhī.
Bào Shūyá escorted Prince Xiǎobái to flee to Jǔ,
while Guǎn Yíwú and Shào Hū escorted Prince Jiǔ to flee to Lǔ.
In the ninth year,
Gōngsūn Wúzhī was cruel to Yōng Lǐn,
and Yōng Lǐn killed Wúzhī.
Duke Huán entered first from Jǔ,
the people of Lǔ attacked Qí,
to install Prince Jiǔ,
they battled at Gānshí,
where Guǎn Zhòng shot Duke Huán
hitting his hook.
The Lǔ army was defeated,
and Duke Huán ascended the throne.
Thereupon he threatened Lǔ,
forcing them to kill Prince Jiǔ.
Duke Huán asked Bào Shū:
"How shall we stabilize the altars of state?"
Bào Shū said:
"If we obtain Guǎn Zhòng and Shào Hū
then the altars of state will be stabilized."
The duke said:
"Yíwú and Shào Hū
are my enemies."
Bào Shū then explained to the duke their original plan.
The duke said:
"Then can we obtain them?"
Bào Shū said:
"If summoned quickly
then they can be obtained,
if not quick
they cannot be obtained.
Now Lǔ's Shī Bó knows that Yíwú is a man of wisdom,
his plan will certainly be to have Lǔ offer governance to Yíwú.
If Yíwú accepts it,
then they will know how to weaken Qí;
if Yíwú does not accept,
they will know he intends to return to Qí,
and will certainly kill him."
The duke said:
"Then will Yíwú accept governance from Lǔ?
Or not?"
Bào Shū replied:
"He will not accept.
The reason Yíwú did not die for Jiǔ
was because he wished to stabilize Qí's altars of state,
now if he accepts governance from Lǔ,
that would weaken Qí.
Yíwú's service to his lord is without duplicity,
even knowing he would die,
he certainly will not accept."
The duke said:
"Then towards me,
would he be like this?"
Bào Shū replied:
"It was not for you,
but for the former lord.
His relation to you is not as close as to Jiǔ,
he did not die for Jiǔ,
how much more for you?
If you wish to stabilize Qí's altars of state,
then quickly welcome him."
The duke said:
"I fear it is too late,
what can be done?"
Bào Shū said:
"As for Shī Bó's character,
he is sharp but overly cautious.
If you act first,
fearing to incur enmity,
he certainly will not kill them."
The duke said:
"Agreed."
Shī Bó advised the Lord of Lǔ:
"Guǎn Zhòng has wisdom,
if his affairs do not succeed,
now that he is in Lǔ,
you should offer him governance of Lǔ.
If he accepts it
then Qí can be weakened,
if he does not accept
then kill him.
Killing him
will please Qí,
sharing their anger
is still better than doing nothing."
The lord said: "Agreed."
Before Lǔ could carry out the government matter,
an envoy from Qí arrived,
saying:
"Yí Wú and Shào Hū
are enemies of our ruler,
and now they are in Lǔ.
Our ruler wishes to capture them alive.
If they are not obtained,
it means you, sir, are siding with our ruler's enemies."
The lord of Lǔ consulted Shī Bó,
who said:
"Give them to him.
I have heard that the ruler of Qí is cautious yet increasingly arrogant;
even if he obtains worthy men,
how could he necessarily employ them?
And if the ruler of Qí were to employ them,
Guǎnzǐ's affairs would succeed.
Guǎn Zhòng is a great sage of the world;
now if he returns to Qí,
the whole world will turn to him—
how could it be only Lǔ!
If we kill him now,
he is a friend of Bào Shū;
Bào Shū would use this as a pretext to cause trouble,
and you, sir, would certainly be unable to withstand it.
It is better to hand them over."
The lord of Lǔ then had Guǎn Zhòng and Shào Hū bound.
Guǎn Zhòng said to Shào Hū:
"Are you afraid?"
Shào Hū replied:
"Why should I be afraid?
I did not die early
because I was waiting for a settlement.
Now that it is settled,
with you appointed as minister of the left of Qí,
I must be appointed minister of the right.
However,
to serve one who killed our lord
would be to disgrace me again.
You shall be the minister for life,
and I, Hū, shall be the minister for death.
I, Hū, know that by dying, I gain the governance of a state of ten thousand chariots;
thus, Prince Jiǔ can be said to have a minister willing to die.
You, by living, will make the lords hegemon;
thus, Prince Jiǔ can be said to have a minister for life.
The dead accomplish their deeds,
the living achieve their fame;
fame cannot be attained in both ways,
and deeds do not come in vain.
Do your best;
life and death have their destinies."
Then they set out, and upon entering Qí territory,
he cut his throat and died.
Guǎn Zhòng then entered.
A gentleman, hearing of this, said:
"Shào Hū's death
was more worthy than his life;
Guǎn Zhòng's life
was more worthy than his death."
Some say:
The next year,
Duke Xiāng expelled Xiǎo Bái,
who fled to Jǔ.
In the twelfth year,
Duke Xiāng passed away,
and Prince Jiǔ ascended the throne.
The people of the state summoned Xiǎo Bái.
Bào Shū said:
"Why not go?"
Xiǎo Bái replied:
"It cannot be.
Guǎn Zhòng is wise,
and Shào Hū is strong and martial;
even if the people summon me,
I still cannot enter."
Bào Shū said:
"If Guǎn Zhòng could exercise his wisdom in the state,
could the state be said to be in disorder?
And Shào Hū, strong and martial as he is,
how could he alone plot against us?"
Xiǎo Bái said:
"Even if he cannot exercise his wisdom,
does that mean he has none?
Even if Shào Hū cannot command the masses,
are his allies not enough to plot against us?"
Bào Shū responded:
"When a state is in disorder,
wise men cannot manage internal affairs,
and friends cannot unite to assist;
only then can the state be plotted against."
Then he ordered the carriage prepared;
Bào Shū drove, and Xiǎo Bái rode out from Jǔ.
Xiǎo Bái said:
"Those two men
are carrying out the lord's orders;
I cannot test this."
He was about to descend.
Bào Shū stepped on his foot and said:
"The success of our endeavor
lies in this moment;
if it does not succeed,
this old minister will die for it,
and you, my lord, may still
escape."
Then they proceeded.
Upon reaching the outskirts of the city,
Bào Shū ordered twenty chariots to go ahead,
and ten behind.
Bào Shū then informed Xiǎo Bái:
"The state suspects
a few of you, but none can bear to harm this old minister.
If the endeavor fails,
I will block the road."
Bào Shū then made a vow:
"If the endeavor succeeds,
follow my orders;
if it does not succeed,
those who ensure the lord's escape shall be honored,
and the dead shall be below;
I will hold the road with the strength of five chariots."
Bào Shū then led the way,
entered the state,
expelled Prince Jiǔ,
and Guǎn Zhòng shot an arrow at Xiǎo Bái
that hit his belt hook.
Guǎn Zhòng, Prince Jiǔ, and Shào Hū then fled to Lǔ.
Duke Huán ascended the throne,
Lǔ attacked Qí,
but failed to install Prince Jiǔ.
In the first year of Duke Huán,
he summoned Guǎn Zhòng,
who arrived,
and the duke asked:
"Can the state be stabilized?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"If you, my lord, become hegemon and king,
the state will be stabilized;
if you do not become hegemon and king,
the state will not be stabilized."
The duke said:
"I dare not aim so high;
stabilizing the state is enough."
Guǎn Zhòng pressed again,
and the lord said:
"I cannot."
Guǎn Zhòng took his leave from the lord, saying:
"You spared me from death,
which was my fortune.
However, the reason I did not die for Jiǔ
was to stabilize the state.
If the state is not stabilized,
for me to hold office in Qí's government
without having died for Jiǔ
is something I dare not do."
Then he walked out,
reached the gate,
and the duke called Guǎn Zhòng back.
Guǎn Zhòng returned,
and the duke, sweating, said:
"If it must be,
then strive for hegemony."
Guǎn Zhòng bowed twice, touched his head to the ground, rose, and said:
"Today, as you, my lord, commit to hegemony,
I greedily accept the command
and hasten to take my post as minister."
Then he ordered the five officials to carry out their duties.
Another day,
the duke informed Guǎn Zhòng:
"I wish to use the intervals of peace among the lords
to modestly strengthen our weapons and armor."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It cannot be.
The common people are suffering,
you should first benefit the people
and store away your weapons.
Rather than being generous to the military,
it is better to be generous to the people.
The altars of the soil and grain of Qí State are not yet secure,
if you do not start with the people
but start with the military,
externally you will not be close to the feudal lords,
internally you will not be close to the people."
The Duke said:
"Agreed."
Yet the policies could not be implemented.
In the second year,
Duke Huán became more chaotic,
and again told Guǎn Zhòng:
"I wish to strengthen the military."
Guǎn Zhòng again said:
"It cannot be."
The Duke did not listen,
and indeed built up the military.
Duke Huán was drinking in a boat with the Lady of Sòng,
the lady rocked the boat and frightened the Duke.
The Duke was angered,
expelled her,
Sòng took her back and married her to the Marquis of Cài.
The next year,
the Duke angrily
told Guǎn Zhòng:
"I wish to attack Sòng."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It cannot be,
I have heard that if internal governance is not cultivated,
external endeavors will not succeed."
The Duke did not listen,
and indeed attacked Sòng.
The feudal lords raised troops and rescued Sòng,
greatly defeating the army of Qí.
The Duke was angered,
returned and told Guǎn Zhòng:
"I request to repair weapons and armor.
Our soldiers are not trained,
our weapons are not substantial,
hence the feudal lords dared to rescue our enemy.
We must internally repair weapons and armor!"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It cannot be,
Qí State is in danger.
Internally seizing the people's resources,
encouraging soldiers to be brave,
is the root of chaos.
Externally offending the feudal lords,
the people will harbor much resentment.
Righteous scholars
will not enter Qí State,
how can it not be in danger?"
Bào Shū said:
"You must follow Yí Wú's words."
The Duke did not listen,
then ordered within the four borders to repair weapons.
Taxes at passes and markets were increased,
the Duke then used bravery to grant salaries.
Bào Shū said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"In the past,
the Duke promised you hegemony,
now the state is more chaotic,
what will you do?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Our lord is vigilant,
his wisdom often seeks advice,
let us wait a little for him to come to it himself."
Bào Shū said:
"By the time he comes to it himself,
will the state not be lost?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Not yet.
The governance within the state,
I, Yí Wú, still subtly influence,
chaos can still be awaited.
Among the assistants of external feudal lords, since there are none
like us two,
none dare to offend us."
The next year,
at court, struggles for salaries led to mutual stabbings,
those slashed and cutting their throats were endless.
Bào Shū said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"Many in the state have died,
is this not harmful?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"How can it be considered so?
These are all greedy people.
What I, Yí Wú, worry about,
is that righteous men among the feudal lords refuse to enter Qí,
and righteous men in Qí refuse to serve in office.
This is what I, Yí Wú, worry about. As for those who die,
why should I cherish them?"
The Duke again internally repaired the military.
In the third year,
Duke Huán was about to attack Lǔ,
saying:
"Lǔ is close to me,
thus it quickly rescued Sòng,
I will punish it."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It cannot be.
I have heard that a ruler with territory,
if not diligent in military affairs,
not mindful of insults,
not abetting his faults,
then the altars of the soil and grain will be secure.
If diligent in military affairs,
mindful of insults,
abetting his faults,
then the altars of the soil and grain will be in danger."
The Duke did not listen,
raised an army and attacked Lǔ,
reaching Cháng Sháo.
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ raised an army to meet him,
and greatly defeated him.
Duke Huán said:
"My troops are still too few,
if I surround them with three times the number,
how can they withstand me."
In the fourth year,
he repaired the military,
with armored soldiers numbering one hundred thousand,
and five thousand chariots,
said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"Our soldiers are now trained,
our troops are now numerous,
I wish to subdue Lǔ."
Guǎn Zhòng sighed deeply and said:
"Qí State is in danger!
You compete not in virtue but in military might.
Among the states under heaven,
those with armored soldiers numbering one hundred thousand are not few,
if we use a small force to subdue a large one,
internally we will lose our people,
the feudal lords will set up defenses,
our people will resort to deceit,
how can the state hope to avoid danger?"
The Duke did not listen,
and indeed attacked Lǔ.
Lǔ did not dare to fight,
retreated fifty lǐ from the capital and set up a pass there.
Lǔ requested to be treated as within the pass,
to follow Qí,
and Qí would also not invade Lǔ again.
Duke Huán agreed.
The people of Lǔ requested an alliance, saying:
"Lǔ
is a small state,
originally did not carry swords,
now if we carry swords
it will be heard among the feudal lords that we are at war,
you should rather stop.
We ask to lay down our weapons."
Duke Huán said:
"Agreed."
Then ordered his followers not to carry weapons.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It cannot be.
The feudal lords are wary of you,
if you retreat like this, it is acceptable.
If you truly weaken the ruler of Lǔ,
the feudal lords will become more greedy towards you,
in the future when events occur,
small states will become more resolute,
large states will set up defenses,
this is not beneficial for Qí State."
Duke Huán did not heed.
Guǎn Zhòng again remonstrated, saying:
"You certainly must not go. Why
does Lǔ not use military force?
Cáo Guì's character
is resolute and jealous,
and cannot be won over by agreement."
Duke Huán did not listen,
and indeed encountered them.
Duke Zhuāng carried a sword in his robe,
Cáo Guì also carried a sword in his robe,
they ascended the platform,
Duke Zhuāng drew the sword from his robe and said:
"The border of Lǔ is fifty lǐ from the capital,
so it's nothing more than dying here."
With his left hand he seized Duke Huán,
with his right hand pointed to himself,
saying:
"Since death is the same,
let me be killed before the ruler."
Guǎn Zhòng rushed to his lord,
Cáo Guì drew his sword and stood between the two steps, saying:
"The two rulers will change their plans,
let no one advance!"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Give them land,
using the Wèn River as the boundary."
Duke Huán agreed,
and returned with the Wèn River as the boundary.
Duke Huán returned and improved governance,
did not focus on weapons and armor,
strengthened self-defense, avoided conflicts,
acknowledged faults, and disbanded troops.
Five years later,
Sòng attacked Qǐ.
Duke Huán said to Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shū:
"That Sòng,
I have long wanted to attack it,
but what about the other states?
As for Qǐ,
it is descended from enlightened kings.
Now Sòng attacks it,
I wish to rescue it,
is that feasible?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"It is not feasible.
I have heard that if internal affairs are not well-managed,
external acts of righteousness will not be credible.
If you wish to externally promote righteousness,
and take the lead in doing so,
how can you make the other states submit?"
Duke Huán said:
"If we do not rescue them now,
we will have no grounds to attack Sòng later."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The rulers of the states,
should not covet territory.
Coveting territory
inevitably leads to frequent warfare,
frequent warfare
inevitably harms the people,
and when the people suffer, deceit becomes rampant.
Those who act after careful deceit may win,
but deceit leads to loss of trust among the people.
Loss of trust among the people causes chaos,
and internal unrest endangers the ruler.
Therefore, those in ancient times who understood the ways of the former kings
did not compete through military force."
Duke Huán said:
"Then what should be done?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"In my opinion, do not
but send someone with generous gifts to persuade them.
If persuasion fails,
you should accept and enfeoff them."
Duke Huán asked Bào Shū:
"What do you think?"
Bào Shū said:
"Act upon Yíwú's words."
The duke then ordered Cáo Sūn Sù to go as an envoy to Sòng.
Sòng did not comply,
and indeed attacked Qǐ.
Duke Huán built Yuánlíng to enfeoff them,
gave them a hundred chariots,
and a thousand suits of armor.
The following year,
the Dí people attacked Xíng,
the ruler of Xíng fled
and came to Qí,
Duke Huán built Yíyí to enfeoff them,
gave them a hundred chariots,
and a thousand soldiers.
The next year,
the Dí people attacked Wèi, the ruler of Wèi fled and arrived
at Xū,
Duke Huán was about to enfeoff them.
Xí Péng and Bīn Xūwú remonstrated, saying:
"It cannot be done.
The reason these three states were lost was due to their small size.
Now you seek to enfeoff these perished states,
what if all states are lost?"
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What do you think?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"You have the reputation for action,
how can you not have the substance?
You should proceed."
The duke asked Bào Shū again,
Bào Shū said:
"Act upon Yíwú's words."
Duke Huán built Chǔqiū to enfeoff them,
gave them five hundred chariots,
and five thousand suits of armor.
After enfeoffing Wèi,
the next year, Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng what to do next,
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"If you internally improve governance and encourage the people,
you can gain the trust of the states."
The duke agreed.
Then he reduced taxes,
relaxed market and customs duties,
and established a system for salaries and emoluments.
After this was done,
Guǎn Zhòng further requested:
"Inquire about their hardships.
I recommend rewards without punishments,
in five years,
the states can be made to submit."
The duke said:
"Agreed."
Once implemented,
Guǎn Zhòng again requested:
"Regarding the etiquette between states,
have Qí send leopard skins,
and small states reciprocate with deer skins;
Qí send horses,
and small states reciprocate with dogs."
Duke Huán agreed and implemented it.
Guǎn Zhòng further requested rewards within the state and extending to the states,
the duke said:
"Agreed."
It was implemented.
Guǎn Zhòng bestowed rewards within the state,
while the duke rewarded among the states.
If a ruler of any state acted virtuously,
he was congratulated with generous gifts;
from officials down to scholars who did good,
they were congratulated with robes;
any minister of a state
who remonstrated with his ruler wisely,
was acknowledged with a seal,
to validate his words.
After the duke implemented these,
he asked Guǎn Zhòng again:
"What next?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Xí Péng is intelligent and quick-witted,
can be assigned to the eastern states.
Bīn Xūwú is resolute and virtuous,
can be assigned to the western states.
The teachings of Wèi state,
emphasize profit through risky means.
Gōngzǐ Kāifāng's character,
is clever and quick,
but not persistent and fond of beginnings,
can be sent to Wèi.
The teachings of Lǔ cities,
favor closeness and are disciplined in rites.
Jì Yǒu's character,
is respectful and precise,
well-versed in rites,
values small promises,
can be sent to Lǔ.
The teachings of Chǔ state,
are artful in rhetoric and profit-oriented,
not fond of establishing great righteousness,
but prefer small credibility.
Méng Sūn was skilled in teaching,
and eloquent in speech,
but he did not care to establish grand principles,
preferring instead to forge minor alliances.
He could be sent to Chǔ.
Once the smaller states submitted,
and the larger states pledged allegiance,
under such circumstances,
governance could then be implemented."
The ruler said:
"Agreed."
Thereupon, he sent Prince Kāifāng to Wèi,
Jì Yǒu to Lǔ,
and Méng Sūn to Chǔ.
After five years, the feudal lords pledged allegiance.
The Dí people launched an attack,
and Duke Huán informed the feudal lords, saying:
"I request aid to counter the invasion.
The feudal lords agreed,
with the larger states contributing two hundred chariots
and two thousand soldiers;
the smaller states one hundred chariots
and one thousand soldiers."
All the feudal lords consented.
Qí mobilized a thousand chariots,
and troops were dispatched to Yuánlíng,
engaging in battle afterward.
Thus, the Dí were defeated.
Their chariots, armor, and goods
were taken by the smaller states,
while the larger states nearby
divided them by their counties,
without setting foot in their own states.
The northern lords did not come,
so Duke Huán met the southern lords at Shàolíng,
saying:
"The Dí have acted without principle,
violating the Son of Heaven's decrees
to attack smaller states.
For the sake of the Son of Heaven,
and in reverence to Heaven's mandate, I command
that we rescue them from the attack.
The northern lords have not arrived,
showing disobedience to the Son of Heaven above,
and disrespect to the feudal lords below.
I request
to punish the northern lords."
The feudal lords agreed.
Duke Huán then marched north to attack Lìngzhī,
descended Fúzhīshān,
beheaded Gūzhú,
and blocked the Shānróng,
turning to ask Guǎn Zhòng:
"What should we do next?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Instruct the feudal lords to gather food for the people,
and for those whose troops are insufficient,
assist them in mobilizing.
In this way,
governance can then be implemented."
Duke Huán then informed the feudal lords,
that they must secure three years' worth of food,
and use the surplus to repair weapons and armor.
If weapons and armor are insufficient,
report the matter to Qí,
and Qí will assist in mobilization.
After this was carried out,
the Duke again asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What next?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"If you can unite the rulers and ministers, fathers and sons,
then governance can be implemented."
The Duke said:
"How can they be united?"
He said:
"Feudal lords should not arbitrarily appoint concubines as wives,
nor arbitrarily execute high officials,
nor grant salaries without state merit,
nor should they do so arbitrarily,
scholars and commoners should not arbitrarily abandon their wives,
nor build crooked dikes,
nor hoard grain,
nor restrict resources."
After practicing this for a full year,
punishments can then be imposed."
The ruler then promulgated this among the feudal lords,
who agreed,
accepted, and implemented it.
After a full year,
the Wú people attacked Gǔ,
and before Duke Huán had finished informing all the feudal lords,
the armies of the feudal lords had all arrived,
awaiting Duke Huán.
Duke Huán, with a thousand chariots, met the feudal lords at the border,
but before the army arrived,
the Wú people fled.
The feudal lords then disbanded.
Duke Huán returned,
and asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What should we do next?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Governance can now be implemented."
He said:
"From now on, for two years,
if an heir apparent is not known for filial piety,
not known for loving his younger brothers,
not known for respecting the elderly and the virtuous of the state,
and lacks even one of these three,
he may be punished.
For the ministers of feudal lords and state affairs,
if after three years no good deeds are heard of,
they may be penalized.
If the ruler has faults,
and the high officials do not remonstrate,
or if there are virtuous scholars and commoners,
and the high officials do not recommend them,
they may be penalized.
If scholars and commoners are reported by officials for being worthy, filial, and fraternal,
they may be rewarded."
Duke Huán accepted and implemented this,
and the nearby lords all sought his guidance,
with six military assemblies,
and three peaceful assemblies,
ruling for forty-two years.
In the nineteenth year of Duke Huán's reign,
he relaxed the taxes on passes and markets,
taking only one-fiftieth.
Salaries were paid in grain,
and taxes were levied based on land.
Taxes were collected once every two years,
with the best years taking three-tenths,
average years two-tenths,
and poor years one-tenth;
in years of famine, no tax was levied, and in years of scarcity, taxes were relaxed.
Duke Huán appointed Bào Shū to recognize the virtuous among rulers and ministers,
Yànzǐ to recognize the virtuous among those not in office and farmers,
Gāozǐ to recognize the virtuous among artisans and merchants,
Guózǐ as the chief judge,
Xí Péng overseeing the eastern regions,
Bīn Xūwú the western lands,
and Fú Zhèng in charge of residences.
All officials were stationed near the court,
those not in office and farmers near the gates,
and artisans and merchants near the markets.
Every thirty lǐ, a relay station was set up with supplies,
managed by officials.
When feudal lords wished to travel,
and officials accompanied them,
one person was ordered to provide a cart for carrying;
if they stayed overnight,
someone was assigned to tend their horses,
and they ate from the supplies.
Guests and officials exchanged tallies,
and upon reaching the state, the tally fees were paid.
If the tally count was incorrect,
it was a crime.
If a commoner wished to travel to another village,
and the official did not permit it,
after seven days, the official was imprisoned.
If a scholar wished to travel,
and the official did not permit it,
after five days, imprisonment.
If a noble's son wished to travel,
and the official did not permit it,
after three days, imprisonment.
If a county official recommended feudal lords' scholars who were virtuous,
rewards were given based on their ability,
and mistakes were not punished.
Bào Shū was ordered to recommend high officials who encouraged the state,
achieved success without regret,
as the top candidates.
Those who governed well in administration were next;
those who cultivated the wilderness as farmland,
and did not frequently mobilize
or incite lawsuits without arrogance,
were next in rank.
Advising the state,
achieving success but later regretting it;
engaging in governance yet failing to maintain order, with the wilderness
frequently seeing unrest,
inciting litigation and arrogance,
practicing these three constitutes the lowest rank.
Order Yànzǐ to recommend sons of nobles,
who when going out are not reckless,
when at home are not extravagant,
and in friendship respect both young and old,
practicing these three qualifies as the highest recommendation;
achieving two, as medium;
achieving one, as low.
Scholars, who dwell in tranquility,
respect the elderly and the noble,
and in interactions do not breach etiquette,
practicing these three
qualifies as the highest recommendation;
achieving two, as medium;
achieving one, as low.
Farmers, who in agriculture
exert effort diligently,
respond to the wishes of fathers and elder brothers,
and serve the virtuous extensively,
practicing these three
qualifies as the highest recommendation;
achieving two, as medium;
achieving one, as low.
Order Gāozǐ to recommend artisans and merchants,
who respond to the wishes of fathers and elder brothers,
serve elders and care for the aged,
and undertake duties respectfully,
practicing these three
qualifies as the highest recommendation;
achieving two, as medium;
achieving one, as low.
Order Guózǐ to adjudicate cases based on circumstances.
After the three great officers have made their selections,
have the districts implement them.
Guǎn Zhòng came forward and presented his recommendations, ascending
to present them to the ruler,
concluding the year with the ruler's endorsements.
Guǎn Zhòng informed Bào Shū, saying:
"Advising the state, failing to achieve success and regretting it,
engaging in governance without order
and inability, with the wilderness
frequently seeing unrest,
litigation and arrogance,
all three,
are crimes without pardon."
He told Yànzǐ:
"Sons of nobles
living extravagantly,
associating with inferiors,
indulging in fine food and drink,
practicing these three,
are crimes without pardon.
Scholars coming and going without constancy,
not respecting the elderly, but pursuing wealth,
practicing these three,
are crimes without pardon.
Farmers coming and going not responding to fathers and elder brothers,
not exerting effort diligently in agriculture,
not serving the virtuous,
practicing these three,
are crimes without pardon."
He told Gāozǐ:
"Artisans and merchants coming and going not responding to fathers and elder brothers,
undertaking duties disrespectfully,
and opposing the elderly while managing risks,
practicing these three,
are crimes without pardon.
Generally, those without faults toward fathers and elder brothers,
praised in the local community,
recommended by officials,
are employed by the ruler.
If they do good, there is no reward;
if they err, there is no punishment.
If officials do not recommend them, they are cast aside.
Those without faults toward fathers and elder brothers,
but not praised in the local community,
if recommended by officials,
and employed by the ruler,
if good,
receive high rewards;
if not good,
the officials are punished."
The ruler said to Guózǐ:
"In all matters of honor and humility,
at home, be with the father;
abroad, be with the teacher;
in service, be with the ruler.
In all three cases, if encountering a traitor
and not dying for the cause,
or not recognizing the traitor,
there is no pardon.
In adjudicating cases,
if circumstances are exchanged for righteousness,
righteousness for emolument,
and emolument leads to unchecked greed,
it is a crime without pardon.
Guǎn Zhòng assessed the state's resources,
finding two-thirds spent on guests,
and one-third within the state.
Guǎn Zhòng, alarmed, reported this.
The Duke said:
"Does my minister still think this way?
Guests from neighboring states,
if they enter pleased,
and leave praising,
spread a glorious reputation throughout the world;
if they enter displeased,
and leave not praising,
spread a sullied reputation throughout the world.
Soil can produce grain,
wood can become goods.
When grain is exhausted, it can regrow;
when goods are dispersed, they can be regathered.
A ruler,
values reputation as precious;
how can wealth be paramount?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"This shows Your Majesty's wisdom."
The Duke said:
"The people are prepared for military affairs;
I wish to punish the unjust among the great states—is that permissible?"
He replied:
"It is not.
Armor and weapons are not yet sufficient.
I request lightening punishments to strengthen armor and weapons."
Thereupon, those guilty of capital offenses were not executed,
those with penal offenses were not punished,
but made to redeem themselves with armor and weapons.
Capital offenses with one rhinoceros-hide armor and one halberd,
penal offenses with one rib-shield and one halberd,
minor offenses with a weight of gold,
and those litigating without suppression,
settled with a bundle of arrows.
The Duke said:
"Now that armor and weapons are sufficient,
I wish to punish the unjust among the great states—
is it permissible?"
He replied:
"Only by loving within the four borders
can one then oppose the wicked beyond them;
by securing the homes of ministers and officials
can one then endanger rival states;
by granting land to small states
can one then punish the unjust among the great states;
by promoting the worthy and virtuous can one then abolish the people who are negligent of law and base.
Thus, the former kings necessarily had establishments,
and only then could they have abolishments;
necessarily had benefits,
and only then could they have harms."
Duke Huán said:
"The three ancient kings,
having slain their rulers,
now when speaking of benevolence and righteousness,
must take the three kings as the model—
I do not understand the reason for this, why?"
He replied:
"In ancient times, Yǔ brought order to the world,
but by Jié's time it fell into chaos;
Tāng exiled Jié
to secure Yǔ's achievements.
Tāng brought order to the world,
but by Zhòu's time it fell into chaos;
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu
to secure Tāng's achievements.
Moreover, the good attacking the not good,
from ancient times to the present,
has never changed.
Why does Your Majesty doubt it?"
The Duke asked further:
"Ancient states that perished—
what did they lose?"
He replied:
"They only calculate gaining land and treasures,
but do not calculate losing the feudal lords;
they only calculate acquiring wealth and resources,
but do not calculate losing the common people;
they only consider being favored but not being abandoned.
If any one of these three situations occurs,
it is enough to lead to decline,
and if all are present, the state will perish.
Those who in ancient times ruined their states and toppled their altars of grain and soil,
did not intentionally set out to do so;
rather, they invariably found some small pleasure in their actions,
unaware that they were sinking into evil."
Duke Huán said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"I invite you, Zhòngfù,
to my residence." The Duke prepared a banquet for Zhòngfù and was about to toast him,
having dug a new well and purified it with cypress.
After ten days of fasting and purification,
he summoned Guǎn Zhòng.
When Guǎn Zhòng arrived,
the Duke held the wine cup,
and his wife held the wine vessel.
After three rounds of toasts,
Guǎn Zhòng hurried out.
The Duke angrily said:
"I fasted for ten days to toast Zhòngfù,
believing I had acted properly.
Yet Zhòngfù left without informing me—
what is the reason for this?"
Bào Shū and Xí Péng hurried out,
caught up with Guǎn Zhòng on the road,
and said:
"The Duke is angry."
Guǎn Zhòng returned,
entered,
and stood with his back to the screen,
but the Duke did not speak to him;
he advanced slightly into the central courtyard,
and the Duke still did not speak;
he moved closer to the hall,
and the Duke said:
"I fasted for ten days to toast you, Zhòngfù,
thinking I had avoided any fault.
Yet you left without informing me—
I do not know the reason."
He replied:
"I have heard that
those immersed in pleasure are steeped in worry,
those indulging in flavors neglect their conduct,
those negligent at court delay governance,
and those who harm the state endanger the altars of grain and soil.
That is why I dared to leave."
The Duke hastily descended the hall and said:
"I dare not be indolent for my own sake,
but you, Zhòngfù, are advanced in years,
and even I am declining.
I wished to give you a day of comfort."
He replied:
"I have heard that the vigorous should not be idle,
and the aged should not be indolent.
Following the way of Heaven,
one must end well.
The loss of the Three Kings
was not the accumulation of a single day.
How can you, my lord, be indolent?"
Guǎn Zhòng walked out,
and the Duke saw him off with the礼节 of a guest, bowing twice.
The next day,
Guǎn Zhòng attended court,
and the Duke said:
"I wish to hear about the trustworthiness of a ruler."
He replied:
"When the people love him,
neighboring states are close to him,
and all under Heaven trust him,
this is the trustworthiness of a ruler."
The Duke said:
"Good.
May I ask where such trustworthiness begins?"
He replied:
"It begins with cultivating oneself,
proceeds through governing the state,
and is completed in ruling all under Heaven."
The Duke said:
"May I ask about cultivating oneself?"
He replied:
"Guide the blood and vital energy,
to seek longevity,
a sound mind, and virtuous character.
This is cultivating oneself."
The Duke said:
"May I ask about governing the state?"
He replied:
"Promote worthy men from afar,
be kind and loving to the common people,
restore states that have perished abroad,
continue extinguished lineages,
and raise up the orphaned;
lighten taxes and levies,
and mitigate punishments and penalties.
These are the great rites of governing a state."
The Duke said:
"May I ask about ruling all under Heaven?"
He replied: "Enforce laws without harshness,
administer punishments justly without pardon,
have officials who are lenient but not negligent;
even the troubled and stagnant do not lose sight of the law,
past actions do not recur,
and the people can navigate the world freely.
This is ruling all under Heaven."
Duke Huán returned to Qí from Jǔ,
and appointed Bào Shūyá as chief minister.
Bào Shū declined, saying:
your servant, am but an ordinary minister.
If you, my lord, show favor to your servant,
keeping him from cold and hunger,
that is already your generous gift.
But if you must govern the state well,
that is beyond my capability,
and only Guǎn Yíwú can do it.
There are five areas in which I am inferior to Guǎn Yíwú:
in being generous, kind, and loving the people,
I am not as good;
in governing the state without losing hold,
I am not as good;
in being loyal and trustworthy to bond with the feudal lords,
I am not as good;
in establishing rituals and righteousness that can be modeled by all,
I am not as good;
in donning armor and holding the drumstick,
standing at the army gate,
and inspiring the people to greater courage,
I am not as good.
Guǎn Zhòng is like a parent to the people;
if you wish to govern your children,
you cannot abandon their parent."
The Duke said:
"Guǎn Yíwú personally shot at me,
hitting my belt hook,
and nearly caused my death.
Now to employ him—is that acceptable?"
Bào Shū said:
"He acted for the sake of his ruler then.
If you, my lord, pardon and recall him,
he will serve you in the same way."
The Duke said:
"Then how should we proceed?"
Bào Shū said:
"Send someone to request him from Lǔ."
The Duke said:
"Shī Bó
is a cunning minister of Lǔ.
If he knows we intend to employ him,
he will certainly not give him to us."
Bào Shū said:
"Instruct the envoy to say:
'Our ruler has a disobedient minister in your state,
and we wish to request him to execute before our ministers.'
The ruler of Lǔ will surely agree.
Moreover, Shī Bó, knowing
Yíwú's talent,
will surely offer him the governance of Lǔ.
If Yíwú accepts it,
then Lǔ will be able to weaken Qí.
If Yíwú does not accept,
they will know he intends to return to Qí,
and will certainly kill him."
The Duke said:
"Then will Yíwú accept?"
Bào Shū said:
"He will not.
Yíwú serves his ruler with undivided loyalty."
The lord said:
"Would he treat me in the same manner?"
The reply was:
"It was not for your sake,
but for the sake of your late father and the altars of soil and grain.
If you wish to stabilize the ancestral temple,
then urgently request him,
otherwise
it will be too late."
The lord then sent Bào Shū to negotiate a settlement,
saying:
"Prince Jiǔ is a relative.
We ask you to punish him."
The people of Lǔ accordingly killed Prince Jiǔ.
He also said:
"Guǎn Zhòng is an enemy.
We ask to receive him and deal with him to our satisfaction."
The lord of Lǔ agreed.
Shī Bó said to the Marquis of Lǔ:
"Do not give him up.
It is not to execute him,
but to employ his governance.
Guǎn Zhòng is
a worthy man of the world,
a great vessel.
If in Chǔ,
then Chǔ would succeed in the world,
if in Jìn,
then Jìn would succeed in the world,
if in Dí,
then Dí would succeed in the world.
Now if Qí seeks and obtains him,
then he will surely long be a worry to the state of Lǔ.
Why does my lord not kill him and deliver his corpse?"
The lord of Lǔ said:
"Agreed."
He was about to kill Guǎn Zhòng.
Bào Shū presented himself and said:
"To kill him in Qí
is to execute Qí's punishment.
To kill him in Lǔ
is to execute Lǔ's punishment.
Our humble lord
wishes to capture him alive,
to parade him in the state,
as a warning to the ministers;
if not captured alive,
then you would be aligning with the enemy of our lord.
This is not what the ruler of our humble state requested,
and your envoy cannot accept such orders."
Thereupon the lord of Lǔ did not kill him,
but had him bound alive and placed in a cage to be given to Qí.
Bào Shū received him and wept for him, three times raising his voice.
Shī Bó followed and laughed at him,
saying to the senior officials:
"Guǎn Zhòng will certainly not die.
That Bào Shū,
would not harm a worthy man;
his wisdom recognizes worth to accomplish his own aims.
Bào Shū assisted Prince Xiǎo Bái,
entering first to gain the state;
Guǎn Zhòng and Shào Hū supported Prince Jiǔ entering later,
fighting with Lǔ,
able to make Lǔ defeated,
their merit was sufficient. Gaining Heaven's favor or losing it,
their human efforts were the same.
Now Lǔ is afraid,
killed Prince Jiǔ and Shào Hū,
imprisoned Guǎn Zhòng to give to Qí;
Bào Shū knows there will be no further trouble,
and will surely urge Guǎn Zhòng to labor for his lord's concerns,
to display his merit.
The multitude will surely grant him achievements.
The merit of dying by force,
can still be surpassed,
how much more the merit of displaying worth while alive?
What would that be like?
This is to illuminate virtue and serve the lord doubly;
Bào Shū's wisdom
would not miss this."
When they reached the heights of Táng Fù,
Bào Shū purified him and bathed him three times.
Huán Gōng personally welcomed him in the suburbs.
Guǎn Zhòng, with his cap tassels bent and lapels fastened,
had a man hold an axe and stand behind him.
The lord declined the axe three times, then withdrew it.
The lord said:
"Let down the tassels and lower the lapels,
I wish to see you."
Guǎn Zhòng bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
"In response to your grace,
if you kill me in the Yellow Springs,
I would die without decay."
The lord then returned with him,
treated him with ceremony in the temple,
toasted three times and asked about governance,
saying:
"In the past, the former lord Xiāng Gōng
had high towers and broad ponds,
indulged in pleasure and drinking,
hunted with nets and arrows,
and did not attend to state affairs.
He belittled the wise and insulted scholars,
honoring only women,
with nine consorts and six concubines,
and rows of concubines numbering in the thousands.
They ate fine grain and meat,
wore embroidered silks,
while the warriors were cold and hungry.
The warhorses waited until the pleasure carriages were worn out,
the warriors waited for the leftovers of the concubines.
Actors and dwarfs were in front,
while worthy senior officials were behind.
Therefore, the state did not grow daily,
nor expand monthly.
I fear the ancestral temple will not be swept,
the altars of soil and grain will not receive blood sacrifices.
May I ask what should be done about this?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"In the past, our former kings,
King Zhāo and King Mù of Zhōu,
generations modeled on the distant traces of King Wén and King Wǔ,
to establish their fame.
They assembled the elders,
compared and selected among the people those who had the Way,
set up models as guidelines for the people.
Used tallies to correspond,
compared and connected with writing,
traced the root and exhausted the branches.
Encouraged them with rewards and honors,
corrected them with punishments and penalties,
weeded out the disordered and reckless,
bestowed gifts to pacify them,
thus providing a constant framework for the people."
The lord said:
"How is this done?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"In the past, the sage kings governed their people
by dividing the capital into three and the countryside into five,
settling the people's dwellings,
completing the people's tasks,
as guidelines for the people.
Carefully applying the six controls,
thus the people's sentiments can be understood
and the hundred surnames can be governed."
Huán Gōng said:
"What are the six controls?"
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Death, life, nobility, baseness, poverty, wealth—
these are the six controls."
Huán Gōng said:
"How is the capital divided into three?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Divide the state into twenty-one districts:
six districts for merchants and artisans,
fifteen districts for scholars and farmers.
You command eleven districts,
Gāo Zǐ commands five districts,
Guó Zǐ commands five districts,
thus the threefold division forms three armies.
Establish ministers for three offices:
set up three districts for markets,
three clans for artisans,
three overseers for marshes,
three regulators for mountains.
Regulate five households as a track,
each track has a head.
Ten tracks form a neighborhood,
each neighborhood has a director.
Four neighborhoods form a company,
each company has a head.
Ten companies form a district,
each district has a good man.
Five districts have one commander."
Duke Huán said:
"What about the five rural districts?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Organize five households into a unit,
each unit having a head.
Six units form a village,
each village having an administrator.
Ten villages form a district,
each district having a chief.
Ten districts form a canton,
each canton having a director.
Three cantons form a region,
each region having a grand master.
There are five grand masters for the five regions.
Military affairs are managed by the regions,
civil affairs by the cantons,
each maintaining order and compliance,
so there are no transgressors."
Duke Huán said:
"How to settle the people in their dwellings,
and establish their livelihoods?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"The four classes of people—scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants—
are the pillars of the state.
They should not be allowed to live intermingled,
for if they live intermingled, their speech becomes confused,
and their affairs become disordered.
Therefore, the sage kings settled scholars
in quiet places,
farmers near the fields and wilderness,
artisans near government offices,
merchants near marketplaces.
Have the scholars gather and live in communities;
in quiet places, fathers speak of righteousness with fathers,
sons speak of filial piety with sons,
those serving the ruler speak of respect,
elders speak of kindness,
the young speak of fraternal duty.
Day and night they engage in these,
teaching their sons and younger brothers,
so that from a young age they practice them,
their hearts become settled,
and they do not stray upon seeing different things.
Thus,
the teaching of their fathers and elder brothers is accomplished without severity;
the learning of their sons and younger brothers is achieved without toil.
Therefore, the sons of scholars always remain scholars.
Have the farmers gather and live in communities;
they observe the four seasons,
adjust their usage accordingly,
prepare their tools and implements,
such as plows, harrows, and sickles.
When it turns cold,
they clear the fields of weeds,
waiting
for the time to plow,
then deep plowing, even sowing, and quick harrowing.
They weed before the rain, awaiting the seasonal showers.
When the seasonal rain arrives,
they carry their hoes, scythes, and weeding tools,
working in the fields from dawn to dusk,
shedding their outer garments to labor,
distinguishing seedlings from weeds,
arranging the sparse and dense.
They wear straw hats on their heads,
coir capes on their bodies,
bodies soaked and feet muddied,
exposing their skin and hair,
exerting all the strength of their limbs,
to work swiftly in the fields.
From a young age they practice this,
their hearts become settled,
and they do not stray upon seeing different things.
Thus, the teaching of their fathers and elder brothers is accomplished without severity;
the learning of their sons and younger brothers is achieved without toil.
Therefore, the sons of farmers always remain farmers.
Simple and rustic without deceit,
those among them talented enough to become scholars
are truly reliable.
Thus, in farming they produce abundant grain,
in office they yield many worthies;
hence, the sage kings respect and are concerned for the farmers.
(Failure to report this is the fifth offense.)
Have the artisans gather and live in communities;
they select fine materials,
observe the four seasons,
distinguish between quality and coarseness.
They adjust their usage accordingly,
discuss comparisons, plan
designs, and craft utensils,
valuing durability and utility.
They talk about their work,
demonstrate their achievements,
display their skills,
and compete in wisdom.
Day and night they engage in this,
teaching their sons and younger brothers.
From a young age they practice it,
their hearts become settled,
and they do not stray upon seeing different things.
Thus, the teaching of their fathers and elder brothers is accomplished without severity;
the learning of their sons and younger brothers is achieved without toil.
Therefore, the sons of artisans always remain artisans.
Have the merchants gather and live in communities;
they observe famines and shortages,
study national changes,
watch the four seasons,
and monitor local goods,
to understand market prices.
They carry loads on their backs and shoulders,
drive oxen and horses to travel all around;
estimate surpluses and shortages,
calculate values,
using what they have
to exchange for what they lack,
buying low and selling high.
Thus, feathers and plumes arrive without seeking,
bamboo and arrows abound in the state,
rare items come in timely,
and precious goods gather.
Day and night they engage in this,
teaching their sons and younger brothers.
They talk about profit,
show each other timing,
and discuss market knowledge.
From a young age they practice this,
their hearts become settled,
and they do not stray upon seeing different things.
Thus, the teaching of their fathers and elder brothers is accomplished without severity;
the learning of their sons and younger brothers is achieved without toil.
Therefore, the sons of merchants always remain merchants.
Assess the land and adjust taxes accordingly,
then the people will not relocate.
Rectify the military and honor traditions,
then the people will not be lazy.
Allow mountain and marsh resources to be accessed in their seasons,
then the people will not act recklessly.
Equalize hills, plains, mounds, and fields,
then the people will not be confused.
Do not rob the people of their farming seasons,
then the hundred surnames will be wealthy.
Do not overwork sacrificial animals,
then oxen and horses will multiply."
Duke Huán asked further:
"I wish to govern well to achieve timely success under heaven;
is it possible?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"It is."
The Duke said:
"Where should I begin?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Begin with loving the people."
The Duke said:
"What is the way to love the people?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Let the ducal house care for the ducal clan,
families care for their own clans,
connecting them through shared affairs,
and extending emoluments to them,
then the people will be close to one another.
Pardon past offenses,
restore old lineages,
establish heirs for those without,
then the people will multiply.
Reduce punishments,
lighten taxes and levies,
then the people will be wealthy.
Appoint worthy scholars in the cantons,
to teach throughout the state,
then the people will be courteous.
Issue decrees without altering them,
then the people will be upright.
This is the way to love the people."
The Duke said:
"If the people are wealthy and close-knit,
can they then be employed?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Promote wealth and encourage artisans,
to meet the people's needs;
Display strength and honor the worthy,
to inspire the people's wisdom;
Apply punishments without harshness,
to benefit the common folk.
Act without selfishness,
and you will be able to embrace the multitude;
Speak with unwavering honesty,
and your commands will not be exhausted.
This is the way to guide the people."
Huán Gōng said:
"The people are settled in their dwellings,
and affairs are accomplished.
I wish to engage with the feudal lords under heaven,
is it permissible?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Not yet.
The people's hearts are not yet at peace with us."
The Duke said:
"How can we put them at ease?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Revise the old laws,
select the good ones,
and implement them strictly;
Be compassionate to the people,
grant them resources;
Ease governance and labor duties,
respect the common folk,
then the state will be wealthy and the people at peace."
The Duke said:
"With the people at peace,
is it permissible now?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Not yet.
If you, my lord, wish to rectify the military ranks,
and repair armor and weapons,
then the great states will also rectify their ranks,
and repair their armor and weapons.
If you have campaigns to wage,
the ministers of the small feudal states will prepare their defenses.
Thus, it will be difficult to quickly achieve your will under heaven.
If you wish to swiftly gain influence among the feudal lords under heaven,
then your actions must be concealed
and your governance must be embedded."
The Duke said:
"How can this be done?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Establish internal administration while embedding military commands within it.
Create the neighborhoods of Gāo Zǐ,
the neighborhoods of Guó Zǐ,
and the Duke's neighborhoods,
dividing Qí into three parts,
to form three armies.
Select the worthy among the people,
and appoint them as neighborhood chiefs.
The villages will have ranks and files, with squad leaders
issuing commands,
and they will engage in hunting,
using it to administer rewards and punishments,
so the people become versed in military affairs."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, Guǎnzǐ established five households as a unit called 'guǐ',
with a unit leader.
Ten units formed a neighborhood 'lǐ',
with a neighborhood administrator.
Four neighborhoods formed a company 'lián',
with a company leader.
Ten companies formed a township 'xiāng',
with a virtuous overseer.
This became the military command structure.
Thus, five households formed a unit,
five men formed a squad 'wǔ',
led by the unit leader.
Ten units formed a neighborhood,
so fifty men formed a small contingent 'xiǎo róng',
led by the neighborhood administrator.
Four neighborhoods formed a company,
so two hundred men formed a company 'zú',
led by the company leader.
Ten companies formed a township,
so two thousand men formed a brigade 'lǚ', led by the township's
virtuous overseer.
Five townships under one commander,
so ten thousand men formed an army 'jūn',
led by the commander of the five townships.
The three armies
thus had the central army's drum,
Gāo Zǐ's drum,
and Guó Zǐ's drum.
In spring, they hunted, called 'sōu',
to drill the troops.
In autumn, they hunted, called 'xiǎn',
to train the soldiers.
Thus, the organization of squads was settled within the neighborhoods.
