The organization of armies was settled in the outskirts.
Once internal training was complete,
they were not allowed to relocate.
Therefore, the men in the squads,

associating together in adulthood,

enjoying each other's company in daily life,

Thus, in night battles, their voices could be heard,

Their joy and camaraderie made them willing to die for one another.
Therefore, in defense they were firm,

With such thirty thousand trained soldiers, my lord,

In the first month's court assembly,

The administrators, having completed their tasks, withdrew.
The Duke inquired further,

The administrators, having completed their tasks, withdrew.
The Duke inquired again,

The administrators, having completed their tasks, withdrew.
Thereupon, the township leaders retired to cultivate virtue and recommend the worthy.

their critical opinions,

Hence, no gentleman dared speak of short-term gains,

In the first month's court assembly,

Fine metal should be cast into spears, swords, lances, and halberds,

In three years, governance was stabilized,

Yuè, Bā,

Duke Huán became fearful,

The Son of Heaven conveyed his decree to Duke Huán, who did not accept it,

Duke Huán worried about the feudal lords under heaven.

Men and women were not violated,

The Dí people attacked Xíng,

Thereupon, the feudal lords under heaven knew that Duke Huán toiled for their sake,

Duke Huán knew that the feudal lords were submitting to him,

while Qí reciprocated with fine horses.

Therefore, the small feudal lords under heaven,

Duke Huán knew that many small feudal lords under heaven were aligning with him,

He shared their worries when they had worries,

He attacked Tán and Lái but did not annex them,

At Zhōng, he built Wǔlù, Yègài, and Mǔqiū,

His teachings achieved great success.
Therefore, regarding Duke Huán under heaven,
the people of distant states

Thus, the farther his influence spread,

Why was this?
They cherished his civil virtues and feared his military might.
So, by eliminating the unruly,

by securing the three armors,

Therefore, the rulers of great states felt ashamed,

Thus, the rulers of great states
served him as servants,

In this way,
the rulers of great states did not act arrogantly,
and the small feudal lords did not feel inferior.
Hence, the rulers of great states were not proud,
and the small feudal lords were not intimidated.
Thus, he expanded the territories of narrow lands,

By aiding the gentlemen,
he ensured their success;
by aiding the common people,

In this manner,
his governance was smooth at home,

Without resorting to mobilizing armies,

Duke Huán was able to borrow the strategies of his ministers,

With these five men, what achievements

the ways of heaven to pass on to posterity;

This was only possible because there was an enlightened ruler above,

Initially,
Duke Huán welcomed Guǎnzǐ outside the city and questioned him.
Guǎn Zhòng modestly declined,

establishing five districts to promote education,

Duke Huán was greatly pleased.
Thereupon, he fasted for ten days,

Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I am a man deserving of the axe,

To know the affairs of state,
is not my duty."
The Duke said:
"If you, Sir, accept the governance,

if you, Sir, do not accept the governance,

Guǎn Zhòng consented,

Three days later,

The Duke said:

The reply was:
"It is bad, indeed,

The Duke said:

The reply was:
"It is bad, indeed,

The Duke said:

The reply was:
"It is bad, indeed,

The Duke changed countenance and said:

Huán Gōng was in his court,
Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng appeared.

now those swans

sometimes north,

sometimes come,
to all directions without distance,

The next day,

Guǎnzǐ said:
"As you wish."
Thereupon, he ordered the hanging of bell and chime racks,
displayed the music of singing, dancing, reed pipes, and zithers,
and for several decades, dozens of oxen were slaughtered daily.
The ministers remonstrated, saying:
"Sòng is attacking Qǐ,
the Dí are attacking Xíng and Wèi,
my lord must not fail to rescue them."
Huán Gōng said:
"I have food for a thousand years,
but not the lifespan of a hundred years.
Now again I am ill,
let me enjoy myself for a while!
Moreover, they are not attacking my state,
but neighboring states.
You need not concern yourselves."
Sòng had already taken Qǐ,
and the Dí had overrun Xíng and Wèi.
Huán Gōng rose
and walked among the bell and drum stands.
Guǎn Zhòng followed
to the west of the great bell,
where Huán Gōng stood facing south,
and Guǎn Zhòng faced him to the north,
the great bell rang.
Huán Gōng said to Guǎnzǐ:
"Are you enjoying this,
Zhòngfù?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"This is what I call lamentable,
not pleasurable.
I have heard that
in ancient times, those who spoke of pleasure amidst bells and chimes did not do so like this.
Words left their mouths,
and commands were implemented throughout the realm;
they roamed among bells and chimes,
without worries of war on all four sides.
Now in Your Majesty's affairs,
words leave your mouth,
yet commands cannot be implemented throughout the realm;
while among bells and chimes,
you have worries of war on all four sides.
This is what I call lamentable,
not pleasurable."
Huán Gōng said:
"Well said."
Thereupon, he dismantled the displays of bells and chimes,
and abolished the music and dances.
The palace became empty with no one in it.
Huán Gōng said:
"I have dismantled the displays of bells and chimes,
and abolished the music and dances.
May I ask what should be done first for the state,
what actions should be taken?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Sòng attacked Qǐ,
the Dí people attacked Xíng and Wèi,
yet you did not rescue them.
I request to congratulate you on this.
I have heard that
when feudal lords contend for strength,
do not share in that strength with them.
Why does Your Majesty not settle the positions of these three rulers now?"
Thereupon Huán Gōng said:
"Agreed."
He then ordered one hundred chariots,
a thousand soldiers
to enfeoff Qǐ at Yuánlíng;
one hundred chariots,
a thousand soldiers
to enfeoff Xíng at Yíyí;
five hundred chariots,
five thousand soldiers
to enfeoff Wèi at Chǔqiū.
Huán Gōng said:
"I have settled the dwelling places of the three rulers,
what should be done next?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"I have heard that when feudal lords are greedy for profit,
do not share in that profit with them.
Why does Your Majesty not send leopard and tiger skins, and patterned brocades as gifts to the feudal lords,
ordering them to reciprocate with plain silk and deer skins?"
Huán Gōng said:
"Agreed."
Thereupon, he sent leopard and tiger skins, and patterned brocades to the feudal lords,
and the feudal lords reciprocated with plain silk and deer skins.
Thus, his commands were firmly implemented throughout the realm.
After this, the Chǔ people attacked Sòng and Zhèng.
They set fires and burned
the land of Zhèng,
so that damaged city walls could not be rebuilt,
and burned houses could not be repaired;
they caused the people to lose their spouses,
living in dwellings like birds and mice in holes.
They seized Sòng's fields,
blocked two rivers,
preventing the water from flowing eastward;
west of the eastern mountains,
the water rose deep enough to submerge ruined walls,
and only after four hundred lǐ could fields be cultivated.
Chǔ wanted to吞并 Sòng and Zhèng but feared Qí,
considering that the one with numerous people and strong soldiers who could harm them
must be Qí.
Thereupon, the King of Chǔ issued a command within his state:
"The enlightened ruler among men that I recognize,
none is like Huán Gōng;
the worthy minister among subjects that I esteem,
none is like Guǎn Zhòng.
With such an enlightened ruler and worthy minister,
I wish to serve them.
Who can establish relations with Qí for me,
I will not hesitate to enfeoff them as a lord."
Thereupon, the worthy scholars of Chǔ all carried their heavy treasures and silks to serve Qí.
Huán Gōng's attendants,
all received heavy treasures and silks.
Thereupon Huán Gōng summoned Guǎn Zhòng and said:
"I have heard that
he who treats others well,
will be treated well in return.
Now the King of Chǔ treats me extremely well,
if I do not reciprocate,
it would go against the Way.
Why does Father Zhòng not establish relations with Chǔ?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"It cannot be done.
The Chǔ people attacked Sòng and Zhèng:
they set fires and burned the land of Zhèng,
so that damaged city walls could not be rebuilt,
and burned houses could not be repaired;
they caused people to lose their spouses,
living in dwellings like birds and mice in holes;
they seized Sòng's fields,
blocked two rivers,
preventing the water from flowing eastward;
west of the eastern mountains,
the water rose deep enough to submerge ruined walls,
and only after four hundred lǐ could fields be cultivated.
Chǔ wants to吞并 Sòng and Zhèng,
considering that the one with numerous people and strong soldiers
who can harm them,
must be Qí.
This is an attempt to overcome Qí through diplomacy,
and to seize Sòng and Zhèng by force.
If Chǔ takes Sòng and Zhèng
and we do not stop them,
we lose Sòng and Zhèng;
if we stop them,
then we break faith with Chǔ.
To suffer losses internally,
while our troops are strained externally,
is not a wise move."
Huán Gōng said:
"Well said.
Then what should we do?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"I request to raise troops and go south to preserve Sòng and Zhèng,
and issue the order: 'Do not attack Chǔ,
but say you wish to meet with the King of Chǔ.'
When you meet,
then request regarding Zhèng's city walls and Sòng's waters.
If Chǔ agrees,
then we have achieved our aim through diplomatic orders;
if Chǔ does not agree,
then we enforce it through military orders."
Huán Gōng said:
"Well said."
Thereupon, he raised troops and went south to preserve Sòng and Zhèng,
meeting the King of Chǔ at Shàolíng,
and issued the order at the meeting:
"Do not hoard grain,
do not build crooked dikes,
do not arbitrarily depose rightful heirs,
do not make concubines into wives."
He then made the request to Chǔ regarding Zhèng's city walls and Sòng's waters.
The Chǔ people did not agree,
so they retreated seventy lǐ and encamped.
They had the soldiers build a city on the southern land of Zhèng,
establishing the Bǎidài City.
Saying:
"From here northward
to the river,
Zhèng shall build its own cities,
and Chǔ dare not destroy them."
To the east, they opened up Sòng's fields,
between the two rivers,
allowing the water to flow east again,
and Chǔ dared not block it.
Then they went south to attack Chǔ,
crossed Fāngchéng
and crossed the Rǔshuǐ River,
gazing toward Wènshān,
and summoned the rulers of Wú and Yuè from the south.
Then they went west to attack Qín,
north to attack the Dí people,
preserved Duke Jìn in the south to the east,
went north to attack Gūzhú,
and on return, preserved Duke Yān.
He held six military meetings,
three carriage meetings,
assembled the feudal lords nine times,
returned to his position having established hegemony,
repaired the bells and chimes and restored the music.
Guǎnzǐ said:
"This is what I call pleasurable."
The form of a hegemon,
models after heaven and follows earth,
transforms people and changes eras,
establishes systems for all under heaven,
ranks the feudal lords in order,
makes the four seas pay tribute and submit,
timely rectifies the world;
large states are made small,
crooked states are straightened,
strong states are weakened,
heavy states are lightened;
chaotic states are annexed,
tyrannical kings are destroyed:
punish their crimes,
lower their ranks,
stabilize their people,
then rule over them.
To enrich a state is called hegemony,
to unite and rectify the states is called kingship.
The true king possesses unique insight.
Those who share virtue are not to be taken,
those who follow the same way do not become king.
Those who contend for the world,
use might to replace danger and violence,
is the constant practice of kings.
The ruler who governs people follows the Way,
the hegemon and king act in accordance with the times.
When a state is well-ordered and neighboring states lack the Way,
it is the foundation for hegemony and kingship.
The survival of a state,
depends on neighboring states;
the fall of a state,
also depends on neighboring states.
When neighboring states have affairs,
neighboring states may gain from them;
when neighboring states have affairs,
neighboring states may perish because of them.
When the world has affairs,
the sage king benefits.
When the state is in danger,
the sage becomes aware.
The reason the former kings became kings,
was by capitalizing on the improper actions of neighboring states.
Acting improperly,
is why neighboring enemies achieve their ambitions.
Those who wish to wield the power of the world,
must first spread virtue among the feudal lords.
Therefore, the former kings took some and gave some,
yielded in some aspects and were resolute in others,
only then could they wield the power of the world.
Military success depends on power,
power depends on territory.
Thus, when feudal lords gain advantageous terrain,
power follows them;
when they lose advantageous terrain,
power leaves them.
Those who contend for the world,
must first contend for people.
Those who understand the grand scheme gain people;
those who scrutinize petty calculations lose people.
Gaining the masses of the world leads to kingship,
gaining half leads to hegemony.
Therefore, the sage king humbles himself with courtesy to attract the worthy of the world and employs them,
distributes equally to attract the masses of the world and makes them subjects.
Thus, though honored as the Son of Heaven,
rich with all under heaven,
the world does not call him greedy,
because his grand strategy remains.
Using the wealth of the world,
to benefit the people of the world;
with the awe of clear authority,
to unite the power of the world;
through the practice of perfected virtue,
to bond closely with the feudal lords;
by the crime of treachery and flattery,
to punish the hearts of the world;
leveraging the might of the world,
to expand the campaigns of the enlightened king;
attacking rebellious and chaotic states,
rewarding the meritorious for their labors;
honoring the virtue of the wise and sage,
clarifying the actions of the ruler, and thus the common people are settled.
The way the former kings took the world,
was profoundly through great virtue,
which is called benefiting all things.
To keep the state constantly free from trouble,
with both fame and profit arriving,
is divine sageliness;
when the state is in peril and near destruction,
yet able to endure,
is enlightened sageliness.
Therefore, what the former kings emulated,
was divine sageliness;
what they esteemed,
was enlightened sageliness.
A single word that prolongs the state's life,
or if ignored leads to the state's fall,
such words are those of the great sage.
What the enlightened king轻视 is horses and jade,
what he values is governance and military.
If a ruler is not thus,
lightly giving away governance,
but heavily giving away horses;
lightly giving away military,
but heavily giving away jade;
emphasizing the construction of palace gates,
but neglecting the defense of the four borders,
that is the way to decline.
Power,
is what the divine and sage rely on.
Unique insight,
is a sharp weapon of the world;
independent judgment,
is a fortress of subtle secrecy.
These two are what the sage follows.
The sage fears the subtle
while the fool fears the obvious,
the sage's hatred and dislike are internal,
the fool's hatred and dislike are external,
when the sage is about to act
he must know,
the fool reaches danger without avoiding it.
The sage can assist the times,
but cannot defy them.
The wise are good at planning,
but it's better to act in timely fashion.
Those who master timing achieve much with little effort.
Plans without a ruler will flounder,
affairs without preparation will fail.
Therefore, the sage king ensures preparation is complete,
and carefully guards his timing.
With preparation awaiting the time,
with timing initiating affairs,
when the time comes, raise arms.
Cut through the坚固 and attack states,
break the great and control territory,
large at the root and small at the tip,
close in territory but attack afar.
Using the large to lead the small,
the strong to command the weak,
the many to attract the few,
virtue benefiting the common people,
might shaking the world;
orders are followed by feudal lords without opposition,
nearby, none disobey,
afar, none disregard.
The enlightened king is the rectifier of the world, this is principle.
Restrain the strong and aid the weak,
curb violence and stop greed,
preserve the perishing and stabilize the endangered,
continue severed lineages,
this is what the world supports,
what the feudal lords ally with,
what benefits the common people,
therefore the world makes him king.
Wisdom that covers the world,
judgment that is the best of the generation,
talent that stirs the four seas,
are the assistants to the king.
A state of a thousand chariots that maintains its defense,
can make feudal lords its subjects,
and possess the world.
A state of ten thousand chariots that loses its defense,
is no longer its own state.
When all under heaven is orderly
but one alone is chaotic,
that state is no longer its own;
when all feudal lords are united
but one alone is isolated,
that state is no longer its own;
when neighboring states are all secure
but one alone is vulnerable,
that state is no longer its own.
These three,
are signs of a perishing state.
When a state is large but its governance is small,
the state follows its governance;
when a state is small but its governance is large,
the state grows larger.
If large but inactive,
it reverts to smallness;
if strong but unmanaged,
it reverts to weakness;
if populous but unmanaged,
it reverts to few;
if noble but without propriety,
it reverts to lowliness;
if weighty but transgressing bounds,
it reverts to lightness;
if wealthy but arrogant and unrestrained,
it reverts to poverty.
Thus, to observe a state, observe its ruler;
to observe an army, observe its general;
to observe preparedness, observe the fields.
If the ruler appears wise but is not truly wise,
if the general appears worthy but is not truly worthy,
if the people appear to be farming but are not truly farming,
once these three safeguards are lost,
the state is no longer its state.
If the land is vast but unused,
it is called land surplus;
if the people are numerous but unmanaged,
it is called population surplus;
if military might is present but not righteous,
it is called martial surplus.
If these three surpluses are not halted,
the state is no longer its state.
Land vast but uncultivated
is not truly its land;
ministers noble but not subservient
are not truly its ministers;
people numerous but not loyal
are not truly its people.
Those without land yet desiring wealth will worry,
those without virtue yet aspiring to rule will face danger,
those giving little yet seeking much will be isolated.
When superiors are oppressive and inferiors are degraded,
or the state is small but the capital large, regicide occurs.
When the ruler is honored and ministers humble,
when superiors are authoritative and inferiors respectful,
when orders are carried out and people obedient,
that is the pinnacle of governance.
If there were two Sons of Heaven in the world,
the world could not be governed;
if there were two rulers in one state,
the state could not be governed;
if there were two fathers in one family,
the family could not be governed.
Orders, if not elevated, will not be implemented;
if not concentrated, will not be heeded.
The people of Yáo and Shùn were not born orderly,
nor were the people of Jié and Zhòu born chaotic.
Thus, order and chaos lie with the superiors.
The beginning of hegemony and kingship
takes the people as its foundation.
When the foundation is orderly, the state is secure;
when the foundation is chaotic, the state is endangered.
Thus, when superiors are enlightened, inferiors are respectful;
when governance is fair, the people are tranquil;
when officers are trained harmoniously,
the military overcomes enemies;
employing the capable
leads to all affairs being well-managed;
cherishing the benevolent
ensures the ruler's safety;
appointing the worthy
makes the feudal lords submit.
The form of hegemony and kingship
is achieved through excelling in virtue and righteousness,
through excelling in wisdom and strategy,
through excelling in military combat,
through excelling in terrain,
through excelling in actions—
thus, one becomes king.
Those skilled in governing a state
leverage the weight of a large state
to reduce its influence;
leverage the power of a strong state
to weaken its force;
leverage the form of a weighty state
to lighten its stature.
When strong states are numerous,
unite the strong to attack the weak,
to seek hegemony;
when strong states are few,
unite the small to attack the large,
to seek kingship.
If strong states are numerous
yet one speaks of kingly potential,
that is the wisdom of a fool;
if strong states are few
yet one implements hegemonic ways,
that is a plan for failure.
The divine and sagacious observe the forms under heaven,
knowing the timing of action and inaction;
observing the balance of precedence and sequence,
they know the gateways to fortune and misfortune.
When strong states are numerous,
the first to act faces danger,
the later actor gains advantage.
When strong states are few,
the first to act becomes king,
the later actor perishes.
When warring states are numerous,
acting later can lead to hegemony;
when warring states are few,
acting first can lead to kingship.
The heart of a king
is square but not extreme.
Rank does not yield to the worthy,
the worthy do not discriminate by age or select from the masses—
this is coveting great things.
Thus, the form of a king is vast.
The ancient kings contended for the world
with uprightness,
established it
with orderliness,
governed it
with simplicity.
In setting policies and issuing orders,
they followed human principles;
in bestowing ranks and emoluments,
they followed earthly principles;
in undertaking great endeavors,
they followed heavenly principles.
Therefore, in the campaigns of the ancient kings,
they attacked the rebellious, not the compliant;
they attacked the perilous, not the easy;
they attacked the excessive, not the timely.
Within the four borders,
they governed with correctness;
in assemblies of feudal lords,
they achieved influence through strategy.
For those nearby who did not submit,
they troubled them with territory;
for those distant who did not obey,
they threatened them with form.
To attack after repeated offenses
is martial;
to spare those who submit
is civil;
when both civil and martial are fully present,
that is virtue.
As for the forms of weight, lightness, strength, and weakness,
feudal lords united become strong,
isolated become weak.
Even a steed's talent,
if a hundred horses replace it,
the steed will surely tire;
a state strongest in its generation,
if the world attacks it,
will surely weaken.
Strong states gain by gathering the small,
they lose by relying on strength;
small states gain by exercising restraint,
they lose by alienating the strong.
States, large or small, have their strategies;
strength and weakness have their forms.
Subduing the near and strengthening against the far
is the form of a kingly state.
To unite the small to attack the large—
this is the situation of rival states;
to use those backed by the sea to attack those backed by the sea—
this is the situation of the central states;
to humble oneself and serve the strong to avoid blame—
this is the situation of small states.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been
anyone who could first initiate troubles,
defy the times and alter circumstances,
and thereby achieve merit and fame;
there has never been any
who first initiated troubles,
defied the times and altered circumstances,
and did not meet with failure.
Now, to subdue rulers and
pacify the four seas,
one cannot rely solely on military force
to seize them.
One must first establish plans and strategies,
make advantageous use of terrain,
ensure favorable balance of power,
befriend allied states,
and act in accordance with the times—
this is the method of a true king.
Now, the campaigns of the former kings
were always righteous in their justification,
and fierce in their execution;
they assessed the situation to know what was feasible,
measured their strength to know what to attack,
and examined gains to know the right timing.
Therefore, in the campaigns of the former kings,
they would first engage in battle and then attack,
first attack and then seize territory.
Thus, those skilled in attack
evaluate the enemy's numbers to attack their numbers,
evaluate their provisions to attack their provisions,
evaluate their preparedness to attack their preparedness.
When attacking numbers with numbers,
if the enemy's numbers remain intact, do not attack;
when attacking provisions with provisions,
if the enemy's provisions remain intact, do not attack;
when attacking preparedness with preparedness,
if the enemy's preparedness remains intact, do not attack.
Instead, abandon the solid and attack the weak,
abandon the hard and attack the brittle,
abandon the difficult and attack the easy.
Now, governing a state does not lie in adhering to antiquity,
ordering the age does not lie in fine precedents,
achieving hegemony does not lie in established codes.
For, if actions are misguided, the state is endangered;
if punishments are excessive, authority is overturned;
if plans are simplistic, disaster follows;
if strategies are sound, strength is assured;
if achievements are made, fame follows;
if authority is weighty, commands are obeyed—
such is the natural order.
Now, states contending for supremacy
must first contend in strategy, in administration, and in power.
What causes the ruler to alternate between joy and anger—
is strategy;
what causes the state to alternate between lightness and heaviness—
is circumstance;
what causes the army to alternate between advance and retreat—
is power.
Thus, if one is skilled in strategy,
the ruler's desires can be fulfilled,
and his commands can be implemented;
if skilled in circumstances,
the territory of great states can be seized,
and the armies of strong states can be contained;
if skilled in power,
the forces of the world can be marshaled,
and the rulers of the feudal lords can be made to pay homage.
Now, the sage observes the circumstances of the world,
understands the strategies of the age,
knows what the armies will attack,
knows where the lands will be归属,
and knows where commands will be applied.
Now, using military force to attack those one hates
for one's own benefit—
this is what makes neighboring states unfriendly.
Using power to act against what is disliked,
yet with little substantial gain in the end—this is strength.
To single-handedly crush a state,
with strength enduring for later generations—this is kingship.
To single-handedly crush a state,
with strength passing to a neighbor—this is ruin.
In general, when establishing a court,
inquiries should follow fundamental principles.
If ranks are granted to the virtuous,
then great ministers will uphold righteousness;
if emoluments are given to the meritorious,
then officers will hold life and death lightly;
if the leader guides officers with the people's support,
then superiors and inferiors will be harmonious;
if tasks are assigned according to ability,
then people will strive for achievement.
If punishments are carefully applied and fit the crime,
then people will not lightly engage in disputes;
if the altars of soil and grain and the ancestral temples are not disturbed,
then people will have something to revere.
If the aged are not neglected nor kin forgotten,
then great ministers will not resent;
if measures are taken knowing people's urgent needs,
then the masses will not be disorderly.
If this way is practiced,
the state will have constant norms,
and people will know beginning and end—
this is the method of a hegemon or king.
Then proceed with inquiries into affairs,
starting with major achievements in affairs,
but governance begins with the small.
Inquire about the orphans of those who died in service—
are there any who have no fields or houses?
How many are the young men in the gates who have not yet borne armor and weapons?
Inquire about the widows of those who died in service—
what are their grain rations like?
Inquire about those of great merit to the state—
what officials are they?
Inquire about the grand masters of the regions—
from which villages are the officers?
And now, how are the current officials distinguished?
Inquire whether judgments and punishments follow constant norms in practice,
which cannot be altered,
and why some cases are long delayed?
Inquire whether the five offices have regulations and systems,
and whether the capital officials have constant decisions,
and what is awaited when affairs are stalled?
Inquire how many are the solitary men, widows, orphans, destitute, and sick?
Inquire which clans' sons and brothers are the state's outcasts?
Inquire among the good families of the villages—
how many people do they employ and support?
Inquire among the poor of the towns—
how many families eat by borrowing?
Inquire how many families eat by tending gardens and orchards?
How many families open land for farming?
How many officers personally farm?
Inquire among the poor of the villages—
which clans' branches are they?
Inquire among the clan heirs who support their brothers—
how many families follow their brothers due to poverty?
How many are the younger sons who hold office and have fields and towns,
and now contribute their income?
How many are the sons and brothers known for filial piety in the villages?
How many are the younger sons whose parents are alive,
yet do not support them and live apart?
How many officers have fields but are not employed?
What affairs do the officials dislike?
How many officers have fields but do not farm?
What do they do personally?
How many ministers have positions but no fields?
How many families are outsiders who have come to follow but have no fields or houses?
How many are the state's sons and brothers traveling abroad?
How many are the poor scholars indebted to the grand masters?
How many are the low-ranking officials who engage in trade,
or leave their posts to be replaced by family servants?
How many are the assistant officials and clerks with no field rations yet manage affairs?
How many ministers hold positions serving the grand masters?
How many are the outsiders who have come to travel,
staying in the houses of grand masters?
How many in the villages are the sons and brothers who farm diligently and set an example?
How many are the state's sons and brothers with no proper occupation,
unrestrained in food and clothing,
leading the young to not farm but hunt?
Are there those who disrupt the village sons and brothers
with disorderly relations between men and women?
Inquire how many families have borrowed grain and rice
with separate contracts?
Inquire about the state's hidden resources—
how many places can respond to people's emergencies?
What things harm people
in the villages?
Inquire how many officers have fields and houses
but are themselves in the ranks?
How many of the younger sons are fit for armor and weapons and in formation?
How many men and women possess ingenious skills that can benefit and supply needs?
How many maidens are engaged in handicraft work?
How many people in the state are consumers who eat without producing?
How much food does one person have to sustain several individuals?
What is the total number of war chariots?
How many private horses and carts are available for requisition?
How many scholars of integrity and conduct are capable of teaching others,
leading the masses, and governing the people?
How many gentlemen can be deployed in times of crisis?
How many skilled artisans are there whose work,
when deployed, benefits the military ranks,
and when at home, can repair city walls and fortify defenses?
For how many years can the grain in the city and military provisions last?
How many officials can be assigned in emergencies?
Officials should inventory their equipment:
How many sets of armor, weapons, chariots, banners, drums, cymbals, tents, and commander's vehicles are there?
Inventory stored weapons:
The tension of crossbows, the sheaths of blades, the mechanisms of triggers, and the shafts of spears and halberds—
how well-maintained are they?
For those that should be repaired but are not,
what is the reason for neglect?
And the offices responsible for manufacturing and repair,
the tools for issuing and storing equipment—
why are necessary tasks delayed?
The maintenance tools for local and commandant's supply vehicles—
how are they being serviced?
The Minister of Works should not harvest materials during the three busy seasons.
Only after all materials are grown can instruments be made. By winter,
excellent and fully equipped tools must be sufficient.
If individuals have surplus weapons,
they should not display them recklessly,
to maintain the state's norms.
Regularly inspect the fatness or leanness of the commandant's horses and oxen;
those that are old or dead should all be reported.
How many graze in mountains, forests, marshes, and grasslands?
What are the numbers of births, deaths, and movements?
As for the thickness of city walls,
the depth of moats,
the height of gates and doors—
if they should be repaired but are not,
the ruler must assess the guard units.
Ensure tools and equipment are not lacking,
and each has a storage place during heavy rains.
Ask about the military officials and
the state's heroic figures—
how many can take the lead in crises?
Military affairs are perilous;
winning at the wrong time or
gaining through unjust means
does not bring blessing.
Failure due to poor strategy
endangers the state;
prudent planning preserves the country.
What methods are used to educate and select personnel?
Ask those holding high office—
how many years have they served?
How much reclaimed wasteland has benefited households and towns?
What measures have been taken to mark and enhance people's livelihoods?
Which constructed walls, repaired barriers, blocked passages, fortified gates, and built ditches
have improved territorial defense?
How many bandits have been captured to eliminate public threats?
The ruler who governs the land said:
"The way to administer a state
begins with the virtue of the land.
The rites between ruler and subject,
the affection between father and son,
nurturing all people,
the stores of the government,
strengthening the military to protect the state,
the strategic strength of city walls,
and responding to the four directions—
all derive from the land.
Markets are where the wealth of heaven and earth gathers,
harmonizing and benefiting all people—
this is the correct way.
If the people are not oppressed in times of famine,
and everyone fulfills their duty to the land,
the state will be preserved.
Let each hold their proper position,
not allowing slanderers to cause chaos,
so virtue nurtures closeness throughout the armies.
Border passes are the narrow paths of the feudal lords,
the gateways for external wealth,
and the routes for all travelers.
Clearly announce the rules:
those taxed at the pass
shall not be taxed in the market;
those taxed in the market
shall not be taxed at the pass.
Do not levy empty carts,
nor tax those carrying burdens on foot,
to attract distant people—
all sixteen routes follow this principle.
Handle external affairs cautiously:
listen to their reputations,
observe their expressions,
verify their actions,
and examine their virtue
to assess their outward conduct.
Then, do not be deceived by manipulators
who undermine true virtue.
The state will then be free of confusion,
fulfilling its duties.
Instruct the border officials:
"Petty gains harm trust,
minor angers damage righteousness,
broken promises injure virtue.
Foster harmony with the four neighboring states,
cultivate complete virtue,
and face the four directions."
Order the law-abiding officials:
"Enforce regulations clearly,
without deviating from constant norms."
A section is lost.
The Duke was about to travel east and asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"I plan to travel east via Zhuǎnhú,
south to Lángyá.
The Minister of War said,
'This resembles the travels of the former kings.'
What does this mean?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"The travels of the former kings—
in spring, they went out
to inspect the foundation of farming,
called 'excursions';
in autumn, they went out
to supplement people's shortages,
called 'tours'.
When an army marches and consumes the people's grain,
it is called 'ruin';
indulging in pleasure without return
is called 'decadence'.
The former kings had the purpose of excursions and tours for the people,
but no ruinous or decadent behavior in themselves."
Duke Huán retreated, bowed twice, and said:
"A precious principle!"
Guǎn Zhòng further said to Duke Huán:
"What flies without wings is sound;
what stands firm without roots is emotion;
what becomes noble without position is life.
You should also solidify emotions, guard speech carefully,
and respect life sternly—
this is called the glory of the Way."
Duke Huán retreated
and bowed twice:
"I shall follow these words."
Guǎn Zhòng again said to Duke Huán:
"No burden is heavier than one's self,
no path more fearful than the mouth,
no term longer than the years.
To bear heavy burdens, tread fearful paths, and reach distant terms—
only a noble person can achieve this."
Duke Huán withdrew,
bowed twice, and said:
"You have repeatedly taught me these words, Master."
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Flavors and activities,
nurture life;
preferences, aversions, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure,
are the changes of life;
acuity in responding to things,
is the virtue of life.
Therefore, the sage harmonizes flavors and regulates activities timely,
masters the changes of the six vital energies,
prohibits excess in sounds and sights,
so that improper conduct does not reside in the body,
and contrary words do not remain in the mouth.
Calmly stabilizing life,
is sageliness.
Benevolence arises from within,
righteousness manifests outwardly.
Thus, with benevolence, one does not exploit the world for gain;
with righteousness, one does not seek fame from the world.
Out of benevolence, one does not usurp the throne;
out of righteousness, one retires from governance at seventy.
Hence, the sage esteems virtue and belittles achievement,
honors the Way and disdains material things.
With the Way and virtue embodied,
one is not deluded by external matters.
Therefore,
even dwelling in a thatched hut,
one feels no intimidation;
facing south to rule the world,
one shows no arrogance.
Only then
can one become the king of the world.
What is called virtue
acts swiftly without movement,
understands without being told,
accomplishes without action,
arrives without being summoned—
this is virtue.
Thus, though Heaven does not move,
the four seasons proceed, and below
the myriad things transform;
though the ruler does not move,
decrees are issued, and below
all achievements are completed;
though the heart does not move,
the limbs, ears, and eyes are employed,
and the myriad things are understood.
Having few interactions but many affections
is called knowing people.
Achieving success with few efforts
is called knowing how to act.
Hearing one saying that connects all things
is called knowing the Way.
Speaking much but inappropriately,
is worse than speaking little;
being widely learned but not self-reflective,
must lead to error.
Filial piety and fraternal duty,
are the roots of benevolence;
loyalty and trustworthiness,
are the standards for interactions.
If one does not examine filial piety and fraternal duty inwardly,
nor rectify loyalty and trustworthiness outwardly,
yet delves into the four classics and recites learning,
such a person is one who loses themselves."
The next day, Duke Huán was shooting arrows at the granary,
when Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng came to court.
The Duke saw the two men,
laid down his bow and removed his archer's thumb ring
to greet them, saying:
"Now the swans fly north in spring and south in autumn,
never missing their season—
is it not because they have wings to convey their intent across the world?
Now that I am not successful in the world,
is it not the concern of you two?"
Duke Huán repeated his words,
but the two did not respond.
Duke Huán said:
"I have spoken;
why do you not reply?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Now the people suffer from toil,
yet the ruler employs them untimely;
the people suffer from hunger,
yet the ruler heavily taxes them;
the people fear death,
yet the ruler hastens punishments.
Under such circumstances,
and with sensuality favored nearby
while virtue is kept at a distance,
even if you had the wings of a swan,
or a boat to cross great waters,
what could they do for you, my lord?"
Duke Huán stepped back in alarm.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"In the past, when the former kings governed people,
if people suffered from toil
and the ruler employed them seasonally,
then people did not suffer from toil;
if people suffered from hunger
and the ruler lightened taxes,
then people did not suffer from hunger;
if people feared death
and the ruler relaxed punishments,
then people did not fear death.
Under such conditions,
with virtue favored nearby
and sensuality kept at a distance,
then within the four borders,
the people would regard you as their parents!
Beyond the four directions,
they would flock to you like flowing water!"
The Duke ceased shooting, took the reins, and mounted his chariot.
He drove himself,
with Guǎn Zhòng on the left,
and Xí Péng as the third rider.
After fasting for three days,
he brought the two men to the ancestral temple,
bowed twice and kowtowed, saying:
"Upon hearing your words,
my ears have become sharper and my sight clearer.
I dare not keep them to myself alone;
I present them to my ancestors."
Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng bowed twice and kowtowed, saying:
"As for your kingship,
these are not our words,
but your own teachings."
Thereupon, Guǎn Zhòng and Duke Huán made a covenant and established decrees:
"The old and weak shall not be punished;
only after three considerations of leniency shall judgment be passed;
checkpoints shall inspect but not levy taxes;
markets shall be regulated without fees.
For mountains, forests, weirs, and marshes,
prohibit or allow access according to the season,
without imposing taxes."
Those who returned to cultivate lands and produce salt
were treated like market-goers.
In three years, the people were educated;
in four years, the worthy were selected as leaders;
in five years, chariots were first deployed.
Then they campaigned south against Chǔ,
reaching Fùshī City.
They campaigned north against the Shānróng,
bringing back winter scallions and pulse,
distributing them throughout the world.
Indeed, they thrice upheld the Son of Heaven and nine times assembled the feudal lords.
Duke Huán stayed outside his palace
without having his cauldron meal served.
The palace women and attendants said to the court ladies:
"Why not follow him out?
The lord is about to undertake a journey."
The court ladies all went out to follow.
The Duke angrily said:
"Who said I was going on a journey?"
The court ladies replied:
"We heard it from the palace women and attendants."
The Duke summoned the palace women and attendants and said:
"How did you know I was going on a journey?"
They replied:
"We heard that
when the lord stays outside without his cauldron meal,
if it is not due to internal worries,
it must be because of external threats.
Now you are staying outside without your cauldron meal,
and since there are no internal worries,
we thus knew you were about to undertake a journey."
The Duke said:
"Good.
This was not something I had discussed with you,
yet your words have hit the mark.
So I will tell you:
I wish to summon the feudal lords, but they do not come.
What should I do about it?"
The women of the inner chambers said:
"Since I myself have not been personally attended to,
I have never received others' woven cloth.
Could it be that my appearance is not carefully considered?"
The next day,
Guǎn Zhòng went to court,
and the Duke told him about it.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"These are the words of a sage,
you must act upon them, my lord."
When Guǎn Zhòng lay ill,
Duke Huán went to inquire about him, saying:
"Your illness is severe, Father Zhòng,
as if it cannot be avoided.
If unfortunately you do not recover from this illness,
to whom shall I transfer the governance of the state?"
Guǎn Zhòng did not reply.
Duke Huán said:
"What kind of person is Bào Shū?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Bào Shū is a noble man.
A state of a thousand chariots,
if not given to him
in the right way,
he would not accept it.
However, he is not fit to govern.
His character
loves goodness but hates evil too intensely;
once he sees an evil, he never forgets it for life."
Duke Huán said:
"Then who is suitable?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Xí Péng is suitable.
Péng's character
is such that he excels in understanding those above and inquiring of those below.
I have heard that
those who give through virtue
are called benevolent,
those who give through wealth
are called good.
Those who overcome others with goodness
have never been able to make people submit;
those who nurture others with goodness
have never failed to make people submit.
In the state, there are matters of governance he does not know;
in the family, there are affairs he does not understand;
he must then seek clarity!
Moreover, Péng's character is such that
while at home, he does not forget the public court;
while at court, he does not forget his home;
he serves his lord without duplicity of heart,
yet does not forget his own person.
He raised the currency of the entire state of Qí,
supporting fifty households along the roads,
yet the people were unaware of it.
How greatly benevolent,
is Péng!"
The Duke asked further:
"If unfortunately I lose Father Zhòng,
can the several great officers
still be able to keep the state tranquil?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"My lord, please examine yourself!
Bào Shūyá's character loves uprightness,
Bīn Xūwú's character loves goodness,
Nìng Qī's character is capable in affairs,
Sūn Zài's character is skilled in speech."
The Duke said:
"These four men,
who among them can be unified? They are the best of men.
If I employ them all as ministers,
then why would the state not be tranquil?"
He replied:
"Bào Shū's character loves uprightness
but cannot yield for the state's sake;
Bīn Xūwú's character loves goodness
but cannot yield for the state's sake;
Nìng Qī's character is capable in affairs
but cannot rest when sufficient;
Sūn Sù's character is skilled in speech
but cannot remain silent with trustworthiness.
I have heard that
to wax and wane, to fill and empty,
to yield and extend with the common people,
only then can the state be tranquil.
If it must be someone,
could Péng be suitable?
Péng's character is such that
in action he must gauge his strength,
in raising he must gauge his skill."
When his words ended,
he sighed deeply and said:
"Heaven gave birth to Péng
to be my tongue;
when my body dies,
how can the tongue live on!"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The states of Jiāng and Huáng are near to Chǔ;
when your servant dies,
you must return them to Chǔ and entrust them;
if you do not return them,
Chǔ will surely take them for itself.
If it takes them and we do not rescue them,
that would not do;
if we rescue them,
then disorder will begin from this."
Duke Huán said:
"Yes."
Guǎn Zhòng further said:
"There is a dog at the eastern gate barking fiercely,
day and night wanting to bite;
I shackle it and do not let it.
Now as for Yì Yá,
if he cannot love his own son,
how can he love you, my lord?
You must dismiss him."
The Duke said:
"Yes."
Guǎnzǐ further said:
"There is a dog at the northern gate barking fiercely,
day and night wanting to bite;
I shackle it and do not let it.
Now as for Shù Diāo,
if he does not love his own body,
how can he love you, my lord?
You must dismiss him."
The Duke said:
"Yes."
Guǎnzǐ further said:
"There is a dog at the western gate barking fiercely,
day and night wanting to bite;
I shackle it and do not let it.
Now as for Wèi's Prince Kāifāng,
he left his position as heir of a thousand chariots
to serve you as minister;
this is what he desired. What he gains from you, my lord,
is something he wishes to exceed his thousand chariots.
You must dismiss him."
Duke Huán said:
"Yes."
Guǎnzǐ then died.
Ten months after his death,
Xí Péng also died.
Duke Huán dismissed Yì Yá, Shù Diāo, and Wèi's Prince Kāifāng.
When the five flavors were not attained,
then he reinstated Yì Yá;
when the palace fell into disorder,
he reinstated Shù Diāo;
when pleasing words and humble speech were not at his side,
he reinstated Wèi's Prince Kāifāng.
Duke Huán internally did not measure his strength,
externally did not gauge his alliances,
and exerted himself to attack the four neighbors.
The Duke passed away.
Six sons all sought to be established.
Yì Yá and the Prince of Wèi,
allied internally with Shù Diāo,
thereby together killed the officials
and established Prince Wúkuī.
Thus, the Duke's body lay uncoffined for sixty-seven days,
and unburied for nine months.
Duke Xiào fled to Sòng,
Duke Xiāng of Sòng led the feudal lords to attack Qí,
fought at Yǎn,
greatly defeated the Qí army,
killed Prince Wúkuī,
established Duke Xiào, and returned.
Duke Xiāng was established for thirteen years,
Duke Huán had been established for forty-two years.
All military leaders
must first thoroughly understand maps.
The dangers of Huányuán's defiles,
the waters that submerge chariots,
the locations of famous mountains, accessible valleys, traversable rivers, elevated lands, and hills,
the lushness of grasslands, forests, cattails, and reeds,
the distances of roads,
the sizes of city walls,
and the conditions of renowned cities, abandoned towns, and barren or fertile lands
must be completely known.
The intricacies of terrain's exits and entrances
should all be stored in mind.
Only then can one march troops and attack cities,
determine the sequence of actions,
not lose geographical advantages,
which is the constant principle of map usage.
The number of troops,
the quality of soldiers—elite or crude,
the efficiency of weapons—effective or flawed, must all be known;
this is understanding the form.
But understanding the form is not as good as understanding capability,
and understanding capability is not as good as understanding intent.
Thus, those who command troops must possess all three aspects.
Having an enlightened ruler, a knowledgeable minister, and a capable general is called possessing the three.
So when the general issues orders and mobilizes troops,
a specific timeframe is set;
the target state for conquest is predetermined,
preventing ministers, high officials, elders, and close attendants from debating success or failure—
this is the responsibility of the ruler.
Evaluating achievements,
carrying out rewards and punishments,
daring not to obscure the worthy or show favoritism;
managing resources,
supplying the army's demands,
ensuring all officials are solemn and respectful,
daring not to be negligent or act corruptly,
awaiting the ruler's commands—
this is the responsibility of the minister.
Maintaining weaponry,
selecting and training soldiers,
implementing drills and discipline,
organizing squads and units,
comprehending the world's affairs,
and carefully controlling strategies and tactics—
these are the tasks of the military leader.
Now, for any ruler,
if fierce and resolute, they will be attacked;
if timid and weak, they will be eliminated.
What is meant by fierce and resolute?
Being quick to execute is called fierce and resolute.
What is meant by timid and weak?
Being hesitant to execute is called timid and weak.
Both are errors in opposite ways.
Those quick to execute often kill the innocent,
while those hesitant to execute let the guilty escape.
Thus, if the ruler kills the innocent,
the upright will feel insecure;
if the ruler fails to punish the guilty,
the corrupt will not reform.
If the upright feel insecure,
then talented people will flee;
if the corrupt do not reform,
then ministers will form cliques.
If talented people flee,
external calamities are likely;
if ministers form cliques,
internal chaos is inevitable.
Hence it is said: the fierce and resolute are attacked,
the timid and weak are eliminated.
The factors that determine a ruler's status—high or low,
and a state's condition—safe or perilous,
none is more crucial than the military.
Thus, to punish violent states, one must use the military;
to restrain wicked people, one must use penalties.
Therefore, the military externally punishes violence,
and internally prohibits evil.
Thus, the military is the means to honor the ruler and secure the state,
and cannot be abandoned.
However, mediocre rulers do otherwise:
externally, without using the military,
they wish to punish violence,
but their territory will surely be diminished;
internally, without using penalties,
they wish to prohibit evil,
but their state will surely fall into chaos.
So, in all military calculations,
three alerts equal one advance,
three advances equal one army,
three armies equal one battle.
Thus, a single campaign's forces
can exhaust ten years of accumulated supplies;
the cost of one battle
can deplete the achievements of generations.
Now, to seek advantage only after engaging in combat
is to ensure self-defeat in battle.
In besieging cities and towns,
if the defenders resort to cannibalism and
burning bones for fuel,
then the attack will cause self-destruction.
Therefore, the sage conducts minor campaigns but achieves major stability,
not missing heavenly timing,
not wasting earthly advantages,
using days and dreams for planning,
his strategies never straying from calculation.
Thus, plans must be set first before troops cross the border.
If plans are not set and troops cross the border,
then battle leads to self-defeat,
and attack to self-destruction.
To have masses but not their hearts
is equivalent to acting alone;
if weapons are not sharp and effective,
it is like having none;
if armor is not strong and tight,
it is like being unarmored;
if crossbows cannot reach far,
they are like short weapons;
if arrows shot do not hit,
it is like having no arrows;
if they hit but do not penetrate,
it is like having no arrowheads;
leading untrained men
is like being maimed;
using short weapons against distant arrows
is like sitting and awaiting death.
Therefore, in all military assessments,
one must first evaluate the weapons,
evaluate the soldiers,
evaluate the general,
and evaluate the ruler.
Hence it is said:
"With crude and ineffective weapons,
one gives one's soldiers to the enemy;
with unusable soldiers,
one gives one's general to the enemy;
with a general ignorant of warfare,
one gives one's ruler to the enemy;
with a ruler not devoted to military affairs,
one gives one's state to the enemy."
Thus, when the first type of weapon is perfected,
and the vanguard is ready,
the world loses the will to fight;
when the second type is perfected,
and the shock troops are ready,
the world has no defensible cities;
when the third type is perfected,
and the mobile forces are ready,
the world cannot assemble masses.
What is meant by no will to fight?
Knowing that battle is unwinnable,
thus no will to fight;
what is meant by no defensible cities?
Knowing that cities will surely fall,
thus no defensible cities;
what is meant by unable to assemble masses?
Knowing that masses will surely disperse,
thus unable to assemble masses.
In all military priorities,
sages and worthy men
do not serve for noble titles,
those with wisdom and ability
do not serve for official posts,
the skilled and courageous
do not serve for high salaries,
the sharp-eared and clear-sighted
do not serve for wealth.
Thus, Bóyí and Shūqí
did not become famous only on the day of their death,
for their previous conduct was highly virtuous;
King Wǔ did not achieve victory only on the morning of Jiǎzǐ,
for his prior governance was largely excellent.
Therefore, in minor campaigns, one must know everything within a thousand lǐ.
Even a wall built of dirt
or a gathering of ten people
should be inspected five times a day.
In major campaigns,
one must know everything under heaven.
By observing through five intervals,
one disperses gold and wealth
to employ intelligence and clarity.
Hence, those skilled in using troops
have no trenches or ramparts but possess eyes and ears.
Troops do not shout alarms,
do not gather hastily,
do not act recklessly,
and do not advance forcibly.
Shouting alarms alerts the enemy to be cautious,
hasty gatherings render the masses ineffective,
reckless actions exhaust the soldiers,
and forced advances blunt the elite troops.
Therefore, all who employ troops
attack strong points with persistence, yet they are resilient; flaws become divine.
Attacking strong points makes flaws firm,
while exploiting flaws turns strong points into weaknesses.
Thus, fortify what is strong,
and expose what is flawed.
Tú Niú Tǎn butchered nine oxen in a morning,
and his knife could still shave hair,
for the blade moved through the gaps.
Thus, if the heavenly way does not prevail,
yield and do not follow insufficiency;
if human affairs are neglected and chaotic,
use ten to break a hundred;
if weapons and equipment are not effective,
use half to strike double.
Hence, in military contention,
one does not act against intact city walls,
and those with the Way do not act against rulerless states.
Thus, none know when they will arrive,
and upon arrival, they cannot be resisted;
none know when they will depart,
and upon departure, they cannot be stopped.
Even if the enemy is numerous,
they cannot halt or await.
Order leads to wealth,
but order does not necessarily bring wealth;
one must understand the affairs of wealth,
then one can become wealthy.
Wealth leads to strength,
but wealth does not necessarily bring strength;
one must know the methods of strength,
then one can become strong.
Strength leads to victory,
but strength does not necessarily bring victory;
one must understand the principles of victory,
then one can achieve victory.
Victory leads to control,
but victory does not necessarily bring control;
one must know the distinctions of control,
then one can exercise control.
Therefore, governing a state requires tools,
enriching a state requires affairs,
strengthening a state requires methods,
victorious states require principles,
and controlling the world requires distinctions.
As a ruler,
cultivate the way of overseeing officials,
without speaking of internal matters;
as a minister,
attend to affairs within the office,
without speaking of external matters.
If the ruler's way is not clear,
those receiving orders will be doubtful;
if standards and measures are not uniform,
those following duty will be confused.
If the people have doubts and divided hearts,
and the ruler cannot rectify it,
then the commoners' involvement
is like holding up a sign and ordering them to stop.
Thus, one who can embody this way in the state,
apply it to the people,
and sufficiently guide officials and transform the masses
is an enlightened ruler.
One who can fully advise the ruler above,
devote efforts to the people below,
and sufficiently uphold duty and follow orders
is a loyal minister.
If the ruler favors the way,
and the people diligently pursue their tasks,
with upper and lower levels mutually supporting,
as if observing aligned markers,
then the corrupt can be identified.
The official Sèfū is responsible for affairs,
the people's Sèfū is responsible for education.
Education lies with the people,
judgment in impartiality,
rewards in trustworthiness,
embodied in the roles of ruler and minister,
its sincerity
is for defense and warfare.
Thus,
the duties of the people's Sèfū are fulfilled.
The official Sèfū fully oversees assessments, regulations, and laws,
deliberates on legal codes,
weights, measures, dou, and hú,
and documents, without personal bias,
but with affairs as the standard.
Thus,
the duties of the official Sèfū are fulfilled.
After the people's Sèfū completes education
and the official Sèfū establishes laws,
then even the sincere and faithful
cannot claim undue merit,
while the frivolous and negligent
cannot cause ruin.
Thus,
the ruler's affairs are fulfilled.
Therefore, as a ruler,
follow their occupations,
leverage their affairs,
and examine them with standards.
For those who do good,
reward them with the honor of ranks and titles,
the richness of land,
and the people will not envy.
For those who err,
punish them with the disgrace of dismissal and exile,
the penalty of execution,
and the people will not resent.
Life and death decisions are not violated,
and none of the people abandon their kin,
this is only because above there are clear laws,
and below there are constant duties.
Heaven has constant phenomena,
earth has constant forms,
humans have constant rites,
once established, they do not change—
this is called the three constants.
Unifying and integrating them
is the way of the ruler;
dividing and assigning duties
is the task of the minister.
If the ruler loses the way,
they cannot maintain the state;
if the minister fails in their duties,
they cannot retain their position.
Thus, the ruler's nurturing of the subjects is not arbitrary,
and the subjects' service to the ruler is not hollow.
The ruler's nurturing not being arbitrary (those who issue laws and systems)
means that those who issue laws and systems
are clear;
the subjects' service not being hollow
means that those who follow duty and orders
are careful.
With clarity above and care below,
upper and lower levels share virtue,
succeeding in order.
The ruler does not lose authority,
the subjects do not neglect their production,
and none boast of virtue.
Therefore, those above focus on virtue,
and those below uphold integrity, duty
and rites take form above,
and goodness permeates the people below,
then the commoners turn to and cherish the ruler above,
and devote themselves to farming below.
Hence it is said:
"If the ruler is enlightened, ministers trustworthy, officials respectful, scholars incorrupt, farmers simple, merchants and artisans honest,
then upper and lower levels are united,
and internal and external are distinguished;
the people's nature is settled,
and the three clans are regulated."
As a ruler,
one shelters virtue among the people;
as a minister,
one looks up for livelihood from above.
As the superior,
measure achievements and provide sustenance sufficiently;
as the minister,
accept appointments and fulfill them with reverence.
When governance is equitable,
and the people have sufficient wealth,
then the state prospers.
When rewards are given according to labor,
the people do not rely on mere survival.
When punishments are impartial,
the subjects harbor no resentment.
When names are correct and distinctions clear,
the people are not confused about the Way.
The Way is
what the ruler uses to guide the people.
Therefore,
the Way and virtue emanate from the ruler,
decrees are transmitted by the ministers,
tasks are regulated by officials,
and the strength of the common people
moves in accordance with orders.
Thus, for the ruler,
nothing is more valuable than his words;
for the ministers,
nothing is more cherished than their efforts.
Words descend and efforts ascend,
completing the Way of ruler and subject.
Hence,
the ruler plans,
and the ministers execute;
the ministers plan,
and the officials execute;
the officials plan,
and the people serve.
Moreover, there are tallies, seals, laws, and records to verify them.
This is the method to illuminate public justice and eliminate deceit.
Assessing talent, measuring ability, considering virtue, and promoting accordingly—
this is the ruler's Way;
focusing wholeheartedly,
maintaining duty without weariness—
this is the subject's task.
If a ruler
descends to meddle in official affairs,
then the responsible officials cannot fulfill their roles;
if a minister
usurps the ruler's authority,
then the ruler loses his majesty.
Therefore,
a ruler who follows the Way
rectifies his virtue to oversee the people,
without boasting of wisdom or cleverness.
Wisdom and cleverness
are the duties of the subjects;
how to employ wisdom and cleverness
is the Way of the ruler.
When the superior
clarifies his Way,
and the inferior
adheres to their duties,
their distinct roles differ,
yet they unite as one body.
Thus,
to recognize goodness
is the ruler's role.
To embody goodness
is the servant's role.
If the ruler embodies goodness personally, it becomes unfair.
If the ruler is unfair,
often indulgent in rewards,
and reluctant in punishments,
then the state lacks law.
Governing without law,
the people form cliques and collude below,
crafting deceit for private gain.
If laws and institutions are constant,
the people do not scatter but unite with the ruler,
offering their loyalty wholeheartedly.
Thus, without speaking of wisdom,
court affairs are ordered, and state crises resolved—
this is the responsibility of the great ministers.
Without boasting of cleverness,
the good are promoted,
the deceitful punished—
because there are many who observe and listen.
Therefore, the ruler
sits at the source of all things,
overseeing the duties of all officials.
Selecting the worthy and assessing talent,
he treats them according to law.
If appointments are made with the right people,
he sits and reaps blessings
beyond measure.
If officials are incompetent,
running about in service, their failures
are beyond saving.
Yet the state is never lacking in competent men;
it is the ruler's insight that falls short of recognizing them.
Thus, an enlightened ruler carefully identifies competent ministers.
Hence it is said:
When the ruler's Way is attained,
worthy talents flourish,
and the people are well-governed.
Order or chaos lies with the ruler alone.
Therefore it is said:
The ruler's person
is the root of rectifying virtue;
official governance
is the system of eyes and ears.
When the ruler establishes himself, the people are transformed;
when virtue is rectified, officials are well-governed.
Governing officials and transforming the people—
the key lies with the superior.
Thus, the noble man does not demand from the people.
Hence, the superior interfering in inferior affairs
is called presumption;
the inferior meddling in superior affairs
is called usurpation.
For the superior to presume
is perverse;
for the inferior to usurp
is rebellious.
If the state has perverse and rebellious conduct,
the ruler who holds the land and people has lost his order.
Therefore,
distinguishing associations and correcting roles is called principle;
following principle without error is called the Way.
When the Way and virtue are established, the people have a path to follow.
A ruler who follows the Way
is skilled at clearly establishing laws
and not allowing personal interests to obstruct them.
While a ruler without the Way,
having established laws,
then abandons them to act on personal interests.
If the superior
discards laws to act privately,
then the ministers will use private interests as public justice.
If public justice is not upheld,
then private ways are not restrained.
Practicing public justice while harboring selfishness—
if this continues long unnoticed,
how can deceitful intentions not accumulate?
When deceitful intentions accumulate,
the great ones lead to the calamity of encroachment and regicide,
the small ones to the chaos of cliques and internal strife.
This happens because
the ruler's virtue is not established,
and the state lacks constant laws.
If the ruler's virtue is not established,
even women can manipulate his will;
if the state lacks constant laws,
then ministers dare encroach on his power.
Ministers borrow women's skills
to gauge the ruler's sentiments;
favored consorts, borrowing men's wisdom,
to pull in external power.
Thereupon, alienating the wife and endangering the heir,
armed rebellion arises within,
summoning external invaders.
This is the sign of a ruler in peril.
Therefore,
a ruler who follows the Way
has five offices above
to shepherd the people,
so the masses dare not transgress and act recklessly;
and five inspectors below
to oversee the officials,
so the responsible officers dare not deviate from the law in their duties.
The court has fixed measures and standards,
to honor the ruler's position,
robes and regalia
all follow regulations,
then the ruler establishes himself through law.
The ruler bases his orders on law,
officials carry out tasks by command,
the people follow the superior and form customs,
becoming habitual over time,
and those who violate customs or defy teachings
are opposed by all,
then the ruler can be at ease.
The Son of Heaven issues decrees to the world,
feudal lords receive decrees from the Son of Heaven,
ministers receive orders from their lords,
children receive instructions from their parents,
the lower obey their superiors,
younger brothers obey their elder brothers—
this is the ultimate in orderliness.
With standardized weights in weighing stones,
uniform measures in dou and hú,
consistent lengths in zhàng and chǐ,
unified specifications for weapons,
identical writing characters,
and matching axle widths for carts—
this is the ultimate in correctness.
When all follow order and one alone rebels,
when all uphold correctness and one alone deviates,
it is like seeking fire in the night and finding it—
deceitful and fraudulent individuals
have nowhere to hide.
This is how the ancient kings unified the people's hearts.
Therefore, when the Son of Heaven achieves good,
he attributes the virtue to Heaven;
when feudal lords achieve good,
they credit it to the Son of Heaven;
when ministers achieve good,
they dedicate it to their lord;
when common people achieve good,
they trace it to their fathers,
and credit it to their elders.
This is the origin of the Way and laws,
the foundation of governance.
Hence, annual pronouncements
are made by the ruler;
seasonal reviews
by the chancellor;
monthly audits
by officials;
exerting the strength of limbs,
cultivating farming to await orders—
this is the role of commoners.
Thus, the people measure their efforts within family relations,
heed words in the context of ruler-subject duty,
and officials assess their virtue and capability for appointment.
Ministers manage internal affairs of office,
not speaking beyond them;
while the chancellor provides constant support.
The chancellor oversees essentials,
officials and advisors
evaluate realities and deliberate on merits,
rectifying and inquiring about doubts.
The ruler issues clear laws and tokens to verify,
standing on the three-tiered steps,
facing south to receive reports.
Thus, the ruler has surplus time,
and officials fulfill their duties;
seasonal orders are not excessive,
and the people are diligent.
Only when above there are laws and systems,
and below there are divided responsibilities.
The Way completes human life,
it does not reside in humans.
Sage kings and enlightened rulers are those skilled in knowing and guiding it.
Therefore, governing people has a constant Way,
and generating wealth has constant methods.
The Way
is the essence of all things.
The ruler of men
holds this essence and awaits—
then even if those below harbor deceitful hearts,
they dare not test it.
The Way is an abstract setup,
existing when the right person is present, blocked
when they are gone.
Without this,
there is no means to govern people;
without this,
no way to generate wealth.
With people governed and wealth nurtured,
the benefits return to the ruler.
Thus, it is known that enlightened rulers value the Way and laws,
and lightly regard their state.
Hence, he who rules a state
does so through the Way of rulership;
he who kings the world
does so through the Way of kingship.
Great, to king the world;
small, to rule a state—
the Way presides over both.
Therefore, what they desire
can be obtained from the people,
what they detest
can be eradicated among the people.
Desires obtainable from the people,
thus worthy talents flourish.
Detestables eradicable among the people,
thus deceit and fraud diminish.
Like the smith working metal,
the potter molding clay—
control lies with the craftsman.
Therefore, to bestow rewards,
excessive generosity cannot suffice;
to execute punishments,
severe authority cannot intimidate.
Authority failing to intimidate,
generosity failing to suffice—
there is a gap between name and reality.
For the good, rewards are not delayed,
so people do not covet private gain;
for the faulty, punishments are not postponed,
so people do not resent authority.
The system of rewards and punishments
does not bypass the people,
thus they turn and cling to the ruler.
Like heaven's rain,
soaking down one chǐ,
life springs up one chǐ.
Therefore, to oversee others without being overseen,
to manage affairs without being managed,
standing alone without audit—
this is the position of the ruler.
When the ancient kings were in the world,
the people compared them to divine virtue.
The ancient kings excelled at gathering from the people.
For the people, heard individually are foolish,
heard collectively are wise.
Even with the virtue of Tāng or Wǔ,
they still combined with the words of the marketplace.
Thus, enlightened rulers follow the people's hearts,
pacify their natures,
and act from what gathers in public opinion.
Hence, decrees issued are not resisted,
punishments established go unused.
The ancient kings excelled at becoming one body with the people;
becoming one body with the people
means using the state to guard the state,
using the people to guard the people.
Then the people find no advantage in wrongdoing.
Even an enlightened ruler,
beyond a hundred paces,
hears nothing;
beyond a wall's gap,
sees nothing.
Yet one called an enlightened ruler
is so because the ruler excels at employing ministers,
and ministers excel at offering loyalty.
Trust begets trust,
goodness transmits goodness.
Thus, within the four seas,
order can be achieved.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler promotes subordinates,
he fully knows their strengths and weaknesses,
knows what they cannot improve,
as if assigning tasks accordingly.
When worthy people serve their ruler,
they fully know their own shortcomings
and the limits of their abilities,
as if measuring capability to receive office.
The superior thus nurtures the inferior,
the inferior thus serve the superior—
both sides aiming for correctness,
then all people, men and women, participate in governance.
In ancient times, there was no distinction between ruler and subject, high and low,
no union of husband and wife in marriage,
people dwelled like beasts in groups,
contending by force—
then the wise deceived the foolish,
the strong bullied the weak,
the old, young, orphaned, and alone
had no place to belong.
So the wise borrowed public strength to prohibit violence and cruelty,
and the brutal were stopped.
To benefit the people and eliminate harm,
rectify their virtue,
and they will take you as their teacher.
Thus, the ways and methods, virtues and conduct
originate from the worthy.
When righteousness and principle
take shape in the people's hearts,
the people will return to the Way.
When names and things are properly placed, right and wrong distinguished,
then rewards and punishments can be implemented.
When hierarchy is established,
the people have order,
and the capital is founded.
Therefore, the reason a state is a state
lies in the people's order making it a state;
the reason a ruler is a ruler
lies in rewards and punishments making him a ruler.
Excessive rewards lead to depletion,
excessive punishments lead to cruelty.
Wealth depleted and orders cruel—
this is how one loses the people.
Hence, an enlightened ruler carefully examines the teachings of governance,
so that the people can be made to live in order,
win in battle, and defend firmly.
If rewards are too heavy, the ruler cannot supply them;
if punishments are cruel, the subordinates will not trust.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler adorns the rites of feasting and mourning the wounded,
and thereby unites all things.
Thus, by encouraging with the eight administrative affairs,
distinguishing with garments,
enriching with state provisions,
and honoring with royal prohibitions,
the people will be close to the ruler
and can be employed.
When the people are usable,
then the world can be attained.
If the world follows its Way,
it will come;
if it does not follow its Way,
it will not come.
Water
forms waves and rises,
exhausts its turbulence and falls back down—
such is its natural tendency.
Thus, by embracing them with virtue,
and awing them with authority,
the world will submit.
In a state that has the Way,
when commands and decrees are issued,
even husbands and wives fully devote their allegiance to the ruler;
when laws and statutes are proclaimed,
the worthy and scholars exhaust their talents and efforts for the ruler.
Within a thousand miles,
the fines of bundled cloth,
the taxes on each acre of land,
can all be known.
Those administering punishments dare not neglect their duties,
those conferring honors dare not neglect rewards,
harmonious as if children of one father,
as if the substance of one family—
such is the clarity of righteousness and propriety.
If the people do not support their superiors,
ministers do not support their ruler,
then the worthy will not come.
If the worthy do not come,
then the common people will not be usable.
If the common people are not usable,
then the world cannot be attained.
Hence it is said:
If virtue is encroached upon, the ruler is endangered;
if judgment is encroached upon, the meritorious are endangered;
if commands are encroached upon, officials are endangered;
if punishments are encroached upon, the common people are endangered.
And an enlightened ruler
carefully prohibits such excessive encroachments.
If the ruler has no excessive or encroaching judgments,
then the people will have no hopes of luck.
As for the ruler,
to betray the Way and abandon laws,
indulging in personal favoritism,
is called chaos.
As for the minister,
to alter established ways and change constants,
using clever words to flatter the ruler,
is called insolence.
Chaos leads to cruelty,
insolence leads to defeat.
If any of these four occurs,
ruin follows, and enemies will plot.
Thus, by granting amnesty and being generous to quell disorder,
the people will be pleased.
Selecting the worthy and promoting the capable,
and showing respect to filial piety and fraternal duty,
then deceit and falsity will cease.
Restraining licentiousness and excess,
distinguishing men and women,
then promiscuity and disorder are blocked.
When nobility and humility have righteousness,
and social ranks are not overstepped,
then the meritorious are encouraged.
When the state has constant norms,
and laws are not concealed,
then the people have no resentment.
These five
are the ways to promote virtue, correct errors,
preserve the state, and stabilize the people.
If the ruler has great faults,
the minister has great crimes.
The state
is what he possesses,
the people
are whom he rules;
to possess the state and rule the people
yet let them be controlled by what they hate—
this is the first fault.
The people have three duties;
if not assigned to the people,
they are not his people.
If the people are not his people,
they cannot defend or fight—
this is the second fault of the ruler.
As for the minister,
receiving high rank and heavy salary from the ruler,
managing important offices,
yet betraying his duties,
neglecting his responsibilities,
pleasing the ruler's countenance,
indulging his desires,
flattering and overpowering him—
this is the great crime of a minister.
If the ruler has faults and does not correct them,
it is called inversion;
if the minister deserves punishment and is not executed,
it is called chaos.
