The ruler being an inverted ruler,
the minister being a chaotic minister—
the decline of the state
can be awaited sitting down.
Therefore, a ruler with the Way holds the root,
the prime minister holds the essentials,
the high officials uphold the laws
to govern their subordinates,
and the subordinates exhaust their wisdom and strength
to serve their superiors.
If these four upholders are correct, there is order;
if altered, there is chaos.
Thus, they must be clearly established and firmly maintained.
In ancient times, the sage kings based themselves on enriching the people's livelihood,
carefully understanding the origins of calamity and blessing.
Hence, they were cautious in small matters and subtleties,
seeking out errors
and investigating them to the root.
Thus, the restless, deceitful, evil, and fraudulent dared not test them.
This is the way to rectify the people.
In ancient times, there were two sayings:
"Walls have ears,
hidden enemies are by your side."
"Walls have ears"
means that secret plans may leak out.
"Hidden enemies are by your side"
means that those who harbor doubts may win over the people.
If secret plans are leaked,
cunning women will exploit the ruler's requests
and aid wandering villains.
Those who harbor doubts win over the people
by driving those formerly noble but now humble.
When an enlightened ruler is on the throne,
sycophants cannot sway his will—
punishments reach even the close ones;
ministers cannot encroach on his power—
those forming cliques are executed,
such is his clarity.
For a ruler,
to be able to distance himself from slander and flattery,
abolish cliques and factions,
and keep those who engage in debauchery, rebellion, and corrupt practices
from holding official positions at court
is the way to stop deceit, restrain villainy,
strengthen the state, and preserve oneself.
For one who is above others,
controlling ministers
and the common people
depends on guiding the central figures.
Therefore, these central figures
are the intermediaries between the ruler and his subjects.
The promulgation of decrees to the people
must pass through these central figures.
If the central figures
treat what is slow as urgent,
urgency can be used to assert authority;
if they treat what is urgent as slow,
slowness can be used to bestow favors on the people.
When authority and favors are transferred downward,
then the one above is in danger.
The ruler's knowledge of who is worthy or unworthy
must come through the central figures.
The tribute of wealth and resources to the ruler
must pass through the central figures.
They can exchange the worthy for the unworthy and form cliques below.
If they are able to use the people's wealth to entice the ruler above
and can claim merit for themselves,
manipulating both above and below for their private gain,
with the system of ranks unable to restrain them,
then the one above is in danger.
Those who anticipate the ruler in doing good
are encroaching on his rewards and seizing his grace.
Those who anticipate the ruler in doing evil
are encroaching on his punishments and seizing his authority.
Those who spread false rumors outside
are coercing their ruler.
Those who suppress decrees and not issue them
are imprisoning their ruler.
If these four occur and the ruler remains unaware,
then the state's peril can be awaited while sitting idle.
The divine and sagely become kings,
the benevolent and wise become rulers,
the martial and brave become leaders—
this is the way of heaven,
the nature of humanity.
The way of heaven and human nature: those who understand them become substance,
those who are destitute follow,
this is the principle of numbers.
Therefore, those who begin with worries
do not participate in affairs,
those who participate in affairs
do not dictate the way.
Thus, the one above worries but does not labor,
while the common people labor but do not worry.
When the distinction between ruler and subject, above and below, is plain,
then ritual and order are established.
Therefore, using people to serve the superior,
using strength to serve the enlightened,
using punishment to serve the mind—
this is the principle of things.
The way of the mind involves advancement and retreat,
while the way of punishment involves vastness and迂回.
Advancement and retreat are mastered by control,
vastness and迂回 are mastered by labor.
What masters labor is square,
what masters control is round.
The round moves,
movement brings penetration,
penetration brings harmony.
The square holds fast,
holding fast brings solidity,
solidity brings trust.
The ruler uses benefit to harmonize,
the subjects use integrity to be trusted,
then above and below are without deviation.
Hence it is said:
The ruler practices benevolence,
the subjects uphold trustworthiness.
This speaks of the ritual between above and below.
The ruler in the capital
is like the mind in the body.
When virtue and dao are established above,
then the common people are transformed below.
When caution is shaped within,
then appearance and demeanor move without.
Correctness
is what illuminates one's virtue.
Knowing what is gained from oneself,
knowing what is gained from the people,
follows its principle.
Knowing what is lost among the people,
withdraw and cultivate it in oneself,
returning to the root.
When what is sought from oneself is much,
then virtuous conduct is established.
When what is sought from others is little,
then the people find it easy to provide.
Therefore, the ruler focuses upward,
the subjects focus downward.
Focusing upward means
recording the seasons of heaven,
directing the people's strength.
Focusing downward means
developing the earth's benefits,
ensuring ample resources.
Thus, being able to adorn great righteousness,
examine the seasons and nodes,
above to ritualize the spirits and gods,
below to righteously assist and support—
this is the way of an enlightened ruler.
Being able to adhere to law without flattery,
above to correct the ruler's faults,
below to relieve the people's sufferings—
this is the conduct of a loyal minister.
With an enlightened ruler above
and loyal ministers assisting him,
then governing the people with administration and punishment,
guided by the benefits of food and clothing,
they become honest and easy to command,
simple and easy to control.
The gentleman is nourished by the dao,
the small man is nourished by labor—
this is the division.
Authority without power
has nothing to stand on,
affairs without action
have nothing to generate.
If so,
then the state is peaceful and villainy reduced.
When the gentleman is nourished by the dao,
then righteousness is detailed and ritual clear.
When righteousness is detailed and ritual clear,
then hierarchical order is not transgressed;
even if there are ministers with partial forces,
they dare not harbor opportunistic minds,
then the ruler is without danger.
When the common people are nourished by labor,
they focus on fundamental work;
when many focus on fundamental work,
farmers obey commands.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler establishes his era,
the people being controlled from above
is like vegetation being controlled by the seasons.
Thus, when the people are stagnant, guide them;
when the people are flowing, stabilize them.
Open a path, and they will move;
block it, and they will stop.
Only an enlightened ruler
can open it
and also block it.
Opening it
allows the gentleman to practice ritual;
blocking it
makes the small man devoted to farming.
When the gentleman practices ritual,
then the ruler is honored and the people obedient.
When the small man is devoted to farming,
then wealth is abundant and supplies sufficient.
With the ruler honored and the people obedient,
wealth abundant and supplies sufficient,
these four fully embodied,
becoming a king in a short time is not difficult.
The four limbs and six passages
are the body of the person.
The four rectitudes and five offices
are the body of the state.
If the four limbs do not connect,
the six passages do not reach,
it is called deficiency.
If the four rectitudes are not correct,
the five offices do not function,
it is called chaos.
Therefore, when a ruler takes a wife from a different clan,
he establishes the system of nieces and younger sisters (as secondary wives),
appoints ladies with titles,
and palace women,
all according to established regulations,
to govern the inner quarters.
He clarifies the distinction between men and women,
and illuminates the boundaries to avoid suspicion,
to prevent illicit relations.
Thus, there is no communication between inner and outer courts,
no slander or wickedness arises,
women's words do not touch upon affairs of state,
and officials' sons do not form connections within the palace.
This is how the ancient kings manifested virtue and guarded against corruption,
making public authority clear and suppressing private interests.
Clearly establishing favored consorts' positions,
without banishing sons, preserves righteousness.
When personal affection brings joy,
it should not override proper relationships.
Though noble rank is esteemed,
rituals must never be neglected.
For capital officials,
they are distinguished by robes,
honored with insignia banners,
to enhance their authority.
Thus, brothers remain without discord,
and slanderers dare not act.
Therefore, when appointing ministers,
they evaluate achievements and add virtue,
assess service and illuminate with laws,
compare merits through thorough investigation,
honoring position while demonstrating trust.
Thus, subordinates have no fear of dying for remonstrance,
and the assembled officials harbor no resentful hearts.
In this way,
the state is peaceful, and the people are without wickedness.
In selecting the worthy and promoting talent,
they recommend the virtuous to positions,
not associating with the virtueless;
they appoint the capable to offices,
not associating with the incompetent.
Virtue covers service,
not harming seniority.
Thus,
the ruler faces no difficulties,
and the people do not rely on luck for livelihood.
There are four causes for a state's disorder,
and two reasons for its downfall.
When inner quarters have consorts challenging the wife,
this is palace chaos.
When common lines have sons challenging the heir,
this is family chaos.
When court has ministers challenging the chancellor,
this is state chaos.
When officials hold posts without ability,
this is public chaos.
If these four are not distinguished,
the ruler loses proper governance.
Officials form cliques for private gain,
then he loses his kin support.
The state's key ministers
secretly plot against each other,
then he loses external aid.
Losing kin internally,
losing aid externally—
these are the two downfalls.
Thus, the wife must be settled,
the son must be legitimate,
the chancellor must be upright in administration,
officials must be loyal and diligent.
Hence it is said:
There is chaos in the palace,
chaos among brothers,
chaos among high ministers,
chaos among middle-class people,
and chaos among commoners.
If any one arises,
the ruler is endangered.
Palace chaos is called jealous strife,
brotherly chaos is called factional bias,
ministerial chaos is called usurping authority,
middle-class chaos is called cunning deception,
commoner chaos is called resource scarcity.
Scarcity breeds meanness,
deception breeds negligence,
usurpation, bias, and jealousy breed rebellion.
Therefore, rectify titles and investigate doubts,
execute swiftly those close,
then internal stability is achieved.
Guide ministers by merit,
guide middle-class by conduct,
guide commoners by tasks,
then the state prospers.
Examine heavenly seasons,
assess earthly products,
to organize people's strength;
banish excessive crafts,
encourage farming,
to employ the idle,
then commoners are well-governed.
The ruler checks by numbers,
subordinates organize in squads for service,
accelerating promotions
to secure their commitment;
establish teachers in villages
to further their learning.
Appoint officials based on ability,
and promote when time comes,
then scholars return to virtue.
Evaluate virtue and measure achievement,
encourage according to capability,
as if testing with public customs,
as if entrusting with state responsibilities.
Thus,
scholars return to true nature.
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Worry about your own faults,
not that others don't know you.
Cinnabar and azurite in mountains—
people know and extract them;
beautiful pearls in deep waters—
people know and retrieve them.
So if I have faults,
people won't misjudge me.
People's observation is sharp—
one cannot escape
by doing wrong.
Thus when I do good
they immediately praise me,
when I err
they immediately condemn me.
Facing public judgment,
one needn't consult family opinions.
Therefore ancient kings revered the people.
Holding reputation that attracts people—
none fail to strengthen;
holding reputation that repels people—
none fail to weaken.
Even as Son of Heaven or feudal lords,
if people hold reputation and leave them,
they abandon lands and flee.
Thus ancient kings revered the people.
In the body, what brings benefit?
Ears and eyes bring benefit.
Sages gain benefit through them,
thus people respect them and fame follows.
I too rely on them.
Sages project likable qualities,
I project detestable ones—
projecting detestable qualities
to seek fine reputation,
is that possible?
Even love cannot make me capable.
Máoqiáng and Xīshī,
beauties of the world,
if filled with resentment on their faces,
cannot be considered attractive.
Suppose I have an ugly face
filled with resentment.
Resentment showing on face,
harsh words from mouth—
removing ugliness to seek beauty,
is that possible?
How profound!
People's hatred for those with excessive flaws.
Thus the long is cut short,
the short is extended,
the full is drained,
the empty is filled."
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Those good at blaming themselves—
people won't blame them;
those unable to blame themselves—
people will blame them.
So acknowledging one's faults shows strength;
cultivating personal discipline shows wisdom;
not attributing faults to others
shows benevolence."
Thus, when an enlightened king errs,
he reflects it upon himself;
when he achieves good,
he attributes it to the people.
Reflecting errors upon himself
makes him vigilant,
and attributing good to the people
brings them joy.
Sending forth joy to the people,
receiving vigilance for himself,
this is how the enlightened king governs the people.
Now, Jié and Zhòu were not so;
they attributed good to themselves,
and errors to the people.
Attributing errors to the people
angers them,
while reflecting good upon themselves
makes them arrogant.
Sending forth anger to the people,
receiving arrogance for themselves,
this is why they lost themselves.
Therefore, the enlightened king
fears sounds that affect the ears,
and fears influences that affect the eyes.
By attending to these two,
he can possess the world;
how can he not be cautious?
The craftsman has a feel for his axe and adze,
so the guideline can be measured.
Yì had a feel for his bow and arrow,
so the shot could hit the mark.
Zàofǔ had a feel for the reins and whip,
so swift beasts could be caught up with,
and distant roads could be reached.
The world is not perpetually chaotic,
nor perpetually orderly.
When the unworthy are in power, there is chaos;
when the worthy are in power, there is order,
depending on their virtue, which influences it. "
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Cultivate respect, deference, reverence, love,
humility, eliminate resentment, and avoid contention,
to treat each other reciprocally,
then you will not fail in human relations.
If instead there is much resentment and contention for gain,
and mutual disrespect,
then one cannot preserve oneself.
How great is the way of respect, deference, reverence, and love!
For auspicious events, it allows participation in sacrifices;
for inauspicious events, it allows observance of mourning.
On a grand scale, it governs the world without excess;
on a small scale, it governs one person without deficiency.
Try applying it in the Central States,
the various Xià states, and the barbarian countries,
even to birds, beasts, and insects,
all depend on this for order or chaos.
Embodying it brings honor,
abandoning it brings disgrace.
If you earnestly practice it without slack,
even the people of the Yí and Mò tribes
can be transformed to love.
If you earnestly abandon it,
even brothers and parents
can be transformed to hatred.
Thus, the self is what inspires love or hatred;
reputation is what brings honor or disgrace.
This transformation of names and things
is as vast as heaven and earth,
hence the ancient kings called it the Dào. "
Guǎn Zhòng fell ill,
and Duke Huán went to ask him, saying:
"Zhòngfù's illness is severe;
if it should prove fatal and you do not recover,
what instruction will you leave for me? "
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Even without your command,
I would have sought to advise you.
However,
you may still be unable to act on it. "
The Duke said:
"When Zhòngfù ordered me east,
I went east;
ordered me west,
I went west.
How would I dare not follow Zhòngfù's commands? "
Guǎn Zhòng straightened his clothes and cap, rose, and replied:
"I wish you to keep distant Yì Yá, Shù Diāo, Táng Wū, and Gōngzǐ Kāifāng.
Yì Yá served you with his culinary skills,
and you said:
'Only the taste of a steamed infant I haven't tried.'
Thereupon, he steamed his firstborn and presented it to you.
By human nature, one cannot but love one's child;
if he does not love his own child,
what regard will he have for you?
You delighted in the inner chambers but were jealous,
so Shù Diāo castrated himself to manage your harem.
By human nature, one cannot but love one's own body;
if he does not love his own body,
what regard will he have for you?
Gōngzǐ Kāifāng served you for fifteen years
without returning to see his parents,
though between Qí and Wèi,
it is not even a few days' journey.
I have heard that
forced efforts do not last,
and falsehoods cannot endure.
Those whose lives are not virtuous
will surely not die a natural death. "
Duke Huán said:
"Well said. "
Guǎn Zhòng died,
and was buried.
The Duke, detesting the four, dismissed them from office.
But after expelling Táng Wū, he fell ill with a vexing disease;
after expelling Yì Yá, flavors lost their taste;
after expelling Shù Diāo, the palace fell into disorder;
after expelling Gōngzǐ Kāifāng, the court became ungovernable.
Duke Huán said:
"Alas!
Even the sage can be mistaken! "
So he reinstated the four.
After a year,
the four rebelled,
besieging the Duke in a room so he could not escape.
A woman
entered through a drain
and reached the Duke.
The Duke said:
"I am hungry and wish to eat,
thirsty and wish to drink,
but cannot get anything.
Why is this? "
The woman replied:
"Yì Yá,
Shù Diāo,
Táng Wū,
and Gōngzǐ Kāifāng
have divided the state of Qí among themselves,
and the roads have been blocked for ten days.
Gōngzǐ Kāifāng has taken seven hundred shè to Wèi,
so you will get no food. "
The Duke said:
"Oh, how profound!
The sage's words are indeed far-sighted!
If the dead have no awareness, it is one thing;
but if they do,
what face have I to see Zhòngfù underground! "
Then he took a plain headscarf, wrapped his head, and died.
Eleven days after his death,
maggots crawled out the door,
and only then did people know Duke Huán had died.
He was buried with a gate leaf from Yángmén.
The reason Duke Huán lay dead for eleven days,
with maggots emerging and no one to collect his body,
was his failure to consistently employ the worthy.
Duke Huán,
Guǎn Zhòng,
Bào Shūyá,
and Nìng Qì once drank together,
and in their merriment,
Duke Huán said to Bào Shūyá:
"Why not rise and offer me a toast? "
Bào Shūyá raised his cup and said:
"May you not forget when you fled to Jǔ,
may Guǎnzǐ not forget when he was bound in Lǔ,
and may Nìng Qì not forget when he fed oxen under a cart. "
Duke Huán left his mat, bowed twice, and said:
"If I and these two great officers do not forget your words,
the state's altars will surely not be endangered. "
Duke Huán asked Guǎnzǐ:
"I am young, weak, and ignorant,
unversed in the principles for dealing with the feudal lords and neighboring states.
Should not Zhòngfù tell me all about the virtuous rulers of old?
That I may learn from them. "
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"What Yíwú can and cannot do,
is all known to you, my lord.
Why do you trouble to command me?"
Duke Huán asked further:
"Zhòngfù,
I am young, weak, dull, and foolish,
and do not understand the principles of dealing with the neighboring feudal lords.
Shouldn't you, Zhòngfù, fully inform me about the virtuous rulers of the past?
I wish to learn from them."
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Yíwú has heard from Xú Bó that,
the virtuous rulers of the past
revered their mountains, rivers,
ancestral temples, and altars of the land and grain,
and even the old, former great ministers,
gathering them with virtue and enriching them greatly.
They secured their military officers,
and appropriately employed their strength.
With sages in the forefront,
and loyal, honest men by their side,
all competed in righteousness,
and both high and low were well-ordered.
Their forms were upright, their insight clear,
and the four seasons passed without error,
so the people had no worries,
and the five grains multiplied.
Internal and external harmony prevailed,
the feudal lords submitted,
the state was peaceful and stable,
with no need for weapons or armor.
They received tributes of silk and cloth,
embracing their virtue;
clearly accepted their decrees,
and used them as models.
This can indeed be called the virtuous rulers of the past."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent!"
Duke Huán continued:
"Since you have told me about the virtuous rulers of the past, Zhòngfù,
shouldn't you also fully inform me about the unvirtuous rulers of the past?
I wish to learn from them as well."
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Now, with your excellence and wisdom, my lord,
already holding office and practicing the beautiful way,
why should you hear about evil?"
Duke Huán said:
"What kind of talk is that?
If black is edged with black,
how can I know what is beautiful?
If white is edged with white,
how can I know what is good?
If you, Zhòngfù, have told me about the good,
but not about the evil,
how can I know that good is truly good?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Yíwú has heard from Xú Bó that,
the unvirtuous rulers of the past
enlarged their palaces,
raised high their towers and pavilions,
did not employ good ministers,
but housed slanderers and villains.
They did not govern their states,
relying on others for plans,
their policies and decrees were not good,
dark as night,
like wild beasts,
with nowhere to settle.
They did not follow the way of heaven,
nor reflect on the four directions,
did not manage their households,
as if born mad,
cursed by the masses,
rarely avoiding destruction.
They promoted jesters and actors,
multiplied bells and drums,
indulged in gambling,
and amused themselves with artisans and blind musicians.
They executed their good ministers,
were licentious with women,
engaged in excessive hunting with nets and arrows,
brutally treated their elders,
galloped without restraint,
joked and laughed in play.
Their governance was corrupt,
and punishments were severe.
They oppressed their people internally,
to wage wars,
like a leaking cauldron,
how could it not run dry?
This can indeed be called the unvirtuous rulers of the past."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent!"
Duke Huán said:
"Since you have told me about the virtuous rulers and
the unvirtuous rulers of the past, Zhòngfù,
shouldn't you also fully inform me about the virtuous ministers of the past?
I wish to learn from them."
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Yíwú has heard from Xú Bó that,
the virtuous ministers of the past,
having pledged themselves as ministers,
did not serve those close to the ruler,
serving if the ruler recognized them,
withdrawing if not.
If there were affairs,
they always planned for the state,
fully applying their abilities.
They followed the virtues of their ancestors,
distinguished between obedience and rebellion,
promoted and nurtured worthy men,
so that slander and evil did not arise.
They served their ruler with righteousness,
treated subordinates with courtesy,
bringing high and low close together,
like brothers.
Loyal to the state,
high and low were well-ordered.
In residence, they pondered;
in speech, they deliberated;
in action, they accomplished.
In the state, they brought wealth;
in the army, they achieved victory;
facing difficulties, they took charge,
never regretting even unto death.
Close to the ruler, they corrected him;
distant, they assisted him,
associating with righteousness,
and dwelling with integrity.
In office, they governed well,
declined wine and food,
did not slander their ruler,
nor conceal their words.
If the ruler had faults,
they advised without hesitation;
if the ruler had worries,
the ministers bore them.
This can indeed be called the virtuous ministers of the past."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent!"
Duke Huán said:
"Since you have told me about the virtuous ministers of the past, Zhòngfù,
shouldn't you also fully inform me about the unvirtuous ministers of the past?
I wish to learn from them as well."
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Yíwú has heard from Xú Bó that,
the unvirtuous ministers of the past,
having pledged themselves as ministers,
served those close to the ruler;
advancing with flattering words,
not seeking to forget themselves;
they pressed forward without retreating,
using favor to sell influence,
valuing their bribes,
belittling their official ranks;
in public, they claimed to assist,
in private, said it was impossible,
ruining their ruler,
yet all denying it was their fault.
They gathered in unrighteous groups,
attacking the worthy,
treating the esteemed as commodities,
the lowly as passersby.
Greedy for bribes,
competing in feasts,
not associating with good people,
only serving their own interests.
Arrogant and disrespectful,
not befriending virtuous scholars,
but communicating with slanderers and villains.
They did not resolve disputes,
only urged people to litigate,
Indulging excessively in wine,
they do not follow righteous conduct.
They do not cultivate the ways of the past,
altering the constant laws of the state,
arbitrarily creating decrees,
bewildering and confusing their ruler,
seizing his governance while he lives,
preserving their own nobility and flaunting their pride.
They dismiss good scholars,
supporting and aiding corrupt individuals.
In court, they form cliques;
outside, they band together in factions.
Bribes flow between them,
they bond over wine and food,
collectively bringing chaos to their ruler.
If the ruler faces calamity,
each saves only themselves.
This also refers to the ministers without virtue in ancient times."
Duke Huán said:
"Well said!"
The chapter is lost.
Short Sayings Nine.
The question is:
Are the times of old and the times of today the same?
The answer:
"They are the same.
Are the people the same
or different?"
The reply:
"They are different,
and this affects governance and punishments.
In the time of Kù and Yáo,
the finest talents of Hùnwú were among the common people.
Their way was not uniquely superior to others."
Mountains differed yet provided ample resources,
marshes were not exhausted and sustenance was sufficient.
People farmed to support themselves,
and with the surplus, they provided for the Son of Heaven,
hence there was peace.
The grazing of oxen and horses did not interfere,
the customs of the people were not mutually known,
without going beyond a hundred lǐ, their needs were met.
Thus, officials were established but not meddlesome,
it was tranquility.
In their courts, one missing leg and one missing sandal sufficed for a death penalty.
Now, the Duke of Zhōu judges with full records,
records full of beheadings,
records full of amputations,
yet the people do not submit even in death.
It is not human nature,
but exhaustion.
The land is overburdened and people are weighed down,
ruins and exhaustion lead to insufficient support,
trivial tasks arise and the people pursue them,
hence names are devalued and substance is exalted.
The sage,
examines the roots and indulges in pleasures,
it is like a great dusk,
a vast night.
The question is:
How to adapt to the changes of the times? Nothing is better than extravagant consumption.
Devalue what is substantial,
revere what is useless,
then people can be disciplined.
Thus, devalue grain and revere pearls and jade,
favor rituals and music but disdain productive work,
this is the beginning of the root.
Pearls are the yang within yīn,
thus they overcome fire;
jade is the yīn within yáng,
thus it overcomes water.
Their transformation is like divinity.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven stores pearls and jade,
feudal lords store metals and stones,
officials keep dogs and horses,
common people store cloth and silk.
Otherwise,
the strong can seize them,
the wise can manage them,
devaluing what is precious and valuing what is cheap.
Otherwise,
widowers, widows, the solitary, and the aged will not obtain anything.
At the beginning of equality,
which is more urgent: governance or education?
Guǎnzǐ said:
Governance and education are similar but differ in method.
As for education,
it is ethereal like distant autumn clouds,
stirring sorrow in people's hearts;
gentle like the calm clouds of summer,
reaching people's bodies;
profound like the stillness of a bright moon,
moving hearts to lament;
flowing broadly like running water,
making people reflect on it,
where life aspires to go.
At the start of education,
one must embody it fully,
likened to the first appearance of autumn clouds,
transforming both the worthy and the unworthy.
Respect and await it,
cherish and employ it,
as if fencing a sacred mountain for sacrifice.
The worthy are few,
the unworthy are many;
if the worthy are employed,
how can the unworthy not be transformed?
Now, governance is slightly different,
it is like the manifestation of authority and form.
If removed, can it still command people?
In dealing with the poor and the rich,
how should one proceed?
The answer: The extremely rich cannot be commanded,
the extremely poor know no shame.
Water level without flow,
without a source, quickly dries up;
clouds even but rain slight,
without accumulated clouds,
rain soon ceases;
governance even but without authority
cannot be implemented.
Love without intimacy leads to dissipation.
Favoring those close, employing
the useless, is like
making each other blind, breeding resentment.
Short above and long below,
using without measure,
endangers the root. Not matching
yet offering excessive sacrifices, dishonors ancestors.
Violating oaths and breaking alliances wounds trust.
Revering ancestors and parents,
honors the beginning.
The trust in agreements,
assesses conduct.
Honoring the principles of heaven and earth,
is how authority is discussed.
Meager virtue is the decay of human relations.
One must rely on authority and punishments to judge people,
this is how governance is carried out.
Can one thus become king?
May I ask how to apply this?
One must discern the ways of heaven and earth,
then achievements and fame can grow.
Understand the benefits of the land,
and the people can be enriched;
master extravagant consumption,
and scholars can be won over.
The ruler personally engages in good deeds,
strong in making decisive judgments,
benevolent in appointing others.
The ruler's longevity extends his years,
the people do not die prematurely or suffer plagues,
the six domestic animals thrive,
the five grains ripen abundantly,
then the people's strength can be utilized.
If the rulers of neighboring states are all unworthy,
then one can become king.
What if they are all worthy?
The answer:
Swiftly change ministers and shift,
swiftly alter affairs and transform,
change sufficiently to establish fame.
Compassionately rescue from corruption and encourage with reputation,
cultivate and the people grow rich;
respond to changes and await stimuli,
grow together with all things,
emulate the brightness of the sun and moon,
move in response to wind and rain,
what heaven covers,
what earth supports,
these are the sustenance of the people.
To possess nothing and yet rival heaven and earth,
is not the affair of the Son of Heaven.
If the people are about to change but cannot change,
it is like attaching leather to a club—
having the leather but being unable to tan it,
one cannot make
the people submit with trust.
When the feudal lords submit through transformation,
may I ask how to transform the feudal lords' corrupt practices?
Corrupt practices
stem from the households.
Households
act based on what people value.
If our ruler loves hunting, value the skins of tigers and leopards;
if the ruler values labor and effort, value gold, jade, and currency;
if the ruler is fond of war, value armor and weapons.
The foundation of armor and weapons
must begin with fields and homes.
Now, if our ruler wages war, then please implement what the people value.
Food and drink,
extravagant pleasures—
these are what the people desire.
Satisfy their wants,
fulfill their wishes,
then you can employ them.
If you make them wear animal skins and horned hats, eat wild plants,
drink from wild streams,
who could employ them?
Those with broken hearts cannot achieve merit.
Thus, offer them the finest flavors
and,
provide the ultimate music
and,
boil eggs only after carving them,
burn firewood only after carving it.
If the cinnabar mines are not blocked,
then merchants will not settle.
The wealthy consume extravagantly,
the poor work to provide it.
This is how the common people sustain their livelihoods, striving and then eating—
not solely for themselves,
but to foster transformation.
In employing ministers,
give to them and then take away,
appoint them and then dismiss them,
enrich them through relocation,
bind them like fathers and subdue them,
grant them empty titles to make them arrogant,
confiscate their spring and autumn harvests to diminish them,
surround them with mixed rituals and righteousness,
and occasionally promote the strong to praise them.
The strong can then be made to serve:
the eloquent with debate,
the wise with counsel,
the upright with setting examples.
If they are stubborn and oppress subordinates,
broaden their virtue to lessen their high status,
or if incapable, exile them.
This is called the crack through which a state perishes.
Thus, uphold laws and maintain constants,
honor rites and transform customs,
value trust and disdain embellishment,
prefer frugality and dislike extravagance—
this is the method to establish a state.
To govern a state,
go against the people's nature,
then you can share closeness with them.
When the people desire ease,
teach them through toil;
when the people seek life,
teach them through death.
When the teaching of toil is established, the state grows rich;
when the teaching of death is established, authority prevails.
The sage
balances yīn and yáng,
thus appearing calm outwardly while being profound inwardly.
So, indulging emotions harms the spirit,
embellishing substance mars the pattern,
the beauty of transformation lies in matching its name,
the beauty of change lies in seizing its time:
those who cannot foresee the beginnings will suffer disaster.
Thus, follow the benefits of the land,
comply with the directives of heaven,
humbly honor the deceased,
open the state's gates,
and understand the order of the spirits. Following the land's benefits
aligns with the auspicious principles of heaven and earth.
Complying with heaven's directives
ensures actions are enlightened.
Humbly honoring the deceased
unites them with their ancestors;
in public affairs, the Way will be practiced.
Opening the state's gates
means engaging with good counsel.
Understanding the order of the spirits
involves handling sacrifices with jade tablets,
to hold the ritual wine vessel.
Minimize minor harms,
use small to overcome large,
round within.
Square without,
yet fear strength,
expand its emptiness,
and rectify things by examining their inner truth.
The duke said:
"If the state's gates are blocked,
and the people are clamoring and unruly,
how to prepare for it?"
Select those favored by heaven,
chosen by ghosts,
and supported by the people,
and swiftly entrust them with responsibility—
this is how to pacify them.
How to establish
the state of Qí with the strong and the weak?
Grant them high honors and promote them,
give them weighty offices and test them,
then demand ability accordingly.
If too close, distance them,
lest others plot against them;
if too distant, draw them closer,
lest others distort them—
this is how to manage it.
If a minister is too powerful,
and may turn harmful,
I wish to prevent trouble and remove harm,
to discern the great through the small—
how to do this?"
Do not cut the deep roots,
do not loosen the firm stems,
do not drain the deep soil, nor
assist the towering peaks,
do not dim the bright,
do not lose the flourishing.
Ten words cannot surpass this one principle:
even in misfortune, there will be good fortune,
thus balance leads to fullness. When at peace
and unified, how to prepare for turmoil?
How to act then?
Accumulators hoard excess grain for luxury,
adorn carriages and horses for display,
stockpile wine for waste—
for a thousand years, do not deplete food stores;
this is called the root task.
When county revenues have a master,
and are used for governance,
yet not fully managed,
accumulate them in the market.
Some accumulate below,
some accumulate above—
this is called profit having no constancy.
The people have no treasure,
they prioritize profit.
Rising and falling,
they follow where profit lies.
With profit, they can circulate,
and circulation builds the state.
If profit stagnates without transformation,
observe its outflow,
and shift accordingly.
See those who are unusable,
and classify them among the common people.
Select those who love reputation,
and make them leaders of the people;
if their goodness persists,
they become the state's guiding principles.
Those whose achievements are incomplete
cannot claim sole fame;
those whose tasks are unfinished
cannot speak of reputation.
Only after success can one claim sole fame,
only after completing tasks can one speak of reputation—
then they can receive the sacrificial toast.
To prioritize the scholar-officials is to invite offense upon oneself,
and to neglect the common people is to deplete one's own resources.
Those who take the state's position lightly will surely lead the state to ruin,
and those who alienate the nobility will see their plans leaked.
Do not appoint people from other states to office,
for this is to lose the proper way.
Do not frequently change policies,
for this is to ruin accomplishments.
When high officials commit offenses,
do not exile them beyond the borders,
for this is to leak information.
Do not repeatedly drink at the homes of high officials,
for this will cause the state to greatly decline.
If decline persists,
hidden in the wilderness,
returning repeatedly,
following such ways will surely lead to collapse and ruin!
It is like a ritual wine vessel (zūnzhì) where the tip outweighs the base,
flowing downward uncontrollably
and unable to balance.
If orders are issued but not properly implemented,
those of high and low status cannot rely on each other,
this is called destruction.
Why is it that established affairs crumble?
What is the reason?
Why do troops stationed far away become fearful?
What is the cause?
Why do gathered people disperse?
What is the reason?
Why does peace turn to danger?
What is the cause?
Achieving success without gaining trust
is perilous;
having strong forces without righteousness
leads to brutality;
neglecting what is near while seeking what is far
causes troops to be untrustworthy;
overlooking close ministers and aligning with distant ones,
then established affairs will crumble.
When the foundation of a state is lost,
and its clans are destroyed,
then troops far away will not fear it.
A small state acting like a great one,
benevolent but without benefit,
still has those contending for fame,
how burdensome this is!
Taking pleasure in amassing one's own strength,
to overpower others' might,
awaiting their harm,
even if gathered, will surely disperse.
If the great king does not rely on the masses but relies on himself,
the people will gather spontaneously;
provide for them and then benefit them,
achieve success without harm.
Alienating relatives and favoring outsiders,
aspiring to benevolence yet plans are leaked,
despising the few and favoring the great,
this is what leads to danger.
Having many but binding them with agreements,
taking in reality while speaking of yielding,
acting in secret while speaking openly,
benefiting from others' misfortunes,
harming those without troubles,
if I alone wish to possess these,
what should be done?
Therefore, in such times,
the way of displaying wealth
can be implemented.
Now, if benefits are scattered and the people scrutinize,
they must be let go, and then it can proceed.
The duke asked: What does this mean?
Prolonged mourning to consume their time,
lavish funerals to expend their wealth,
one relative going,
one relative coming,
this is how kinship is maintained.
This is called binding the multitude.
Question: How is this applied?
Large burial pits
are used to employ the poor;
beautifying grave mounds
is to employ artisans;
massive inner and outer coffins
are to stimulate woodworking;
abundant burial garments and quilts
are to promote women's work.
If this is still not enough,
then there are secondary floats,
differing enclosures,
and buried treasures.
By doing these, they feed each other,
then the people benefit mutually,
and preparations for defense and offense are complete.
If villages have different customs,
and states have different rites,
then the people will not roam;
with different laws,
the people will not be distressed;
if village elders do not interact widely,
and vagrants are punished,
then people will not gaze afar.
Content with their villages and homes, enjoying sacrifices
and singing praises with distinct titles,
this is how customs are preserved.
Determine the numbers of the well-field system,
calculate the multitude of horse-drawn fields,
and regulate them;
establish ghosts and spirits on hills and streams and offer careful sacrifices;
all are provided for according to their abilities,
showing the importance of fundamentals.
Thus, for a lord with a territory of a thousand li,
emoluments are heavy and sacrifices are revered.
If the ruler has no extra land,
and the land is as one,
then follow and reduce it.
If the ruler initially
reduces as one,
then follow with reduction.
Those involved in reduction, as one,
if followers reduce as one,
then follow with reduction.
Those involved in reduction, as one,
begin with no enfeoffment.
The true king
attends to higher affairs,
the hegemon generates achievements,
emphasizing fundamentals
is called the ten correspondences;
dividing land without contention,
means putting others first and oneself last.
The administration of official rites,
the separation of Zhao and Mu ancestral lines;
merit and tools in order,
affairs well managed,
revering spirits and preserving traditions;
military responsibilities,
valuing merit over death;
in fundamental affairs, rewarding merit and limiting profits;
encouraging ministers, upholding righteousness and not granting petty benefits.
When the five officials
compete in their duties,
then the ruler is informed.
Observe this, for it is the time
for elevating the worthy.
Thus, ruler and ministers share control.
When ruler and ministers share control,
then high and low are balanced,
this shows that elevating the worthy is of no benefit,
and its loss is inevitable.
Elevating the worthy leads to ruin,
while employing the worthy leads to prosperity.
Uphold righteousness to prohibit violence,
honor ancestors to respect lineage,
gather the clan for court sacrifices,
showing not to take lordship lightly.
With the sacrificial vessel clearly set,
Gāo Zǐ heard of it,
and informed the various sons of the inner chamber.
The various sons of the inner chamber informed me,
that you skipped court and did not dine with the ding cauldron.
The various sons of the inner chamber told the women in the palace:
The duke is about to travel,
so we did not see him off.
The duke said he is not traveling,
how did you hear this?
They said:
We heard it from the various sons of the inner chamber.
I summoned the various sons of the inner chamber and asked them,
I am not traveling,
how did you hear this?
I heard from my ancestors,
when feudal lords skip court and do not dine with the ding cauldron,
if there is no external affair,
there must be internal trouble.
The lord said,
"I do not wish to engage with you and your kind,
yet your words have reached me,
so I cannot avoid speaking with you and your kind.
I desire to summon the feudal lords,
but if they do not come, what then?
You, sir, do not debate on summoning the feudal lords.
Since I refrain from befouling myself by serving others through wrongful executions,
I cannot even obtain cloth to wear.
Thus, even if there were a sage, how could he be of use?"
"Can one follow both old and new ways,
stabilize the state and its families, and then transform the times?
If the capital is poor while the borders are rich,
nothing is more admirable than the court;
if the capital is rich and the borders poor,
nothing is better than the market."
"The market
encourages activity.
Encouragement
is the foundation from which things arise.
When the foundation is sound, secondary affairs flourish.
Without some extravagance,
the fundamental enterprises cannot be established."
"If selecting the worthy and promoting the capable is unattainable,
how can one subdue the unruly?
A hundred men without a leader
cannot be overseen;
a state with a thousand chariots that follows the Way
cannot be invaded.
Under the rule of Zhòu,
how could he subdue the unruly?"
"When equally matched, they fight;
when defending, they attack.
A hundred roofs without foundations,
a thousand gatherings without altars—
this is called destitution,
and it can be taken in one move."
"In times when the world faces turmoil,
if all feudal lords are equal,
and the myriad people have none to heed,
those in high positions cannot achieve merit or reform institutions—
can they then rule as kings?
By following tradition and refining laws,
governing with political order,
then the balance of power shifts to
our lord; hence, I, Yíwú, advocate for change."
The lord asked:
"What should be done?"
The reply was:
"Through unity.
If such governance endures long,
results can be expected to stand promptly.
Spirits and gods are not manifest,
yet offerings in sacks go unrewarded—
this illustrates profound virtue.
To sink or float
demonstrates轻视财富.
First establish symbols and set fixed periods,
then the people will follow.
Thus, in prayers
and court rituals with fine silks,
they show轻视财富而重视名誉."
The lord asked about governance?
"What is called 'unity'
relies on the wisdom of prioritizing and sequencing.
Equality leads to strife,
doubling brings persuasion;
tenfold yields compliance,
ten-thousandfold transformation.
When success is achieved yet unrecognized,
and the people await a sovereign, once form is set and names changed, governance is established."
"May I ask how to manage the borders?"
The reply:
"The borders change daily,
and cannot be viewed with constant knowledge.
If the people have not begun to change, yet you force change,
this is self-disorder.
I suggest observing all borders and assessing their turmoil,
entrusting tasks accordingly,
adapting to their plans."
"In a territory of a hundred lǐ square,
with markers visible to each other,
men rush to avert disasters, women prepare food,
internal and external preparations mutual.
In spring and autumn, a single day
can incur losses of a thousand gold,
acting in accordance with the root."
"Envoys cannot be heavily relied upon;
only through communication with superiors
can one ensure the borders' reports.
Should messengers have private interests?
No. Private interests
lead to internal conspiracies.
Let the capable have authority, await
and handle internal affairs."
"A state lasting ten thousand generations
must have a treasure for ten thousand generations.
It must follow the ways of heaven and earth,
nurturing its interior
rather than its exterior,
cultivating the small
not the large."
"Abandoning the state's treasure
to focus externally,
brings loss and failure; valuing the treasure
and focusing on the small
can lead to the Way."
"With ability, specialize;
specialization brings ease.
If rafters can overreach,
then let them overreach.
If capable in office,
then without guarding, they won't scatter.
Multitude of abilities brings leadership;
otherwise, opposition will appear."
"The noble person
strives to correct others,
not to correct themselves.
Thus, the light is treated lightly,
the heavy heavily,
without partiality
in precedence."
"Generally, the light
handles substance;
with lightness, they can be directed,
but heaviness cannot lift
lightness—light and heavy have their measures.
Use heaviness to stabilize the state,
lightness to handle mortality."
"Do not grant full salaries, lest the state grow poor
and resources insufficient;
do not give full rewards, lest virtue be prized
but motivation wane."
"May I ask how to align with all under heaven without private grudges,
confront the strong without personal harm,
and accomplish this?"
The reply:
"Though the state is strong,
decrees must be loyal and righteous;
though the state is weak,
decrees must be respectful and compassionate.
If strong and weak do not transgress,
then people will wish to obey."
"Putting others first and oneself last
does not constitute benevolence;
adding merit to others without claiming credit,
one's influence extends far,
and conflicts remain external.
Clearly, without private alliances,
there are no internal grudges."
"Aligning with the great brings victory;
private alliances multiply, leading to怨恨杀戮. As for Yíwú,
rather than giving wealth to others,
it's better not to rob them of their time;
rather than giving food to others,
it's better not to deprive them of their work.
This is called having no troubles, internal or external."
"Loyalty and respect
define the relationship between ruler and minister;
ritual and righteousness
are the divine essence of a ruler.
Moreover, the bond between ruler and minister is righteousness;
the love among relatives
is innate."
"Making the bond between ruler and kin seek the same, it belongs to respect.
What unsettles a ruler
belongs to scrutiny,
and must be handled with care.
The worthy cannot be intimidated,
the capable cannot be detained.
To prevent affairs beforehand
is ease."
Where springs gush forth,
people gather;
where land is fertile,
people die for it.
Like the vast rivers and lakes,
those seeking pearls and shells never cease.
Pursuing spirits while avoiding heat,
those exchanging ceremonial cups do not linger,
yet elder brothers discard benefits—
alas! Affairs lie with the people of the central states;
observing perilous nations and misguided rulers while preying on their abilities—
is this not nearly endangering the altars of the state?
Profit cannot be regulated,
so the people drift;
spirits cannot be regulated,
so they are served.
Heaven and earth cannot be halted,
thus they move, transforming
and thus following the new.
Therefore, those who attain heaven
stand high without collapse,
those who attain the people
are lowly yet invincible.
Hence, the sages value this,
and rulers value it.
Thus, utmost integrity begets utmost trust,
utmost trust begets deepest bonds.
Generating these inherently follows the Way,
not striving to let ornament overcome substance,
nor to let abundance overpower scarcity.
Without action, one hopes for walls,
yet personally acts within ten days.
Laws, institutions, and measures
are the vessels of kings.
Holding to old righteousness and ways,
one fears change.
Heaven and earth are like the movement of spirits—transformative and changing,
the ultimate of heaven and earth.
Those who can rise with transformation and skillfully use it
cannot be stopped by the Way.
The benevolent use it skillfully,
the wise use it skillfully;
if not the right person,
they are lost with the spirits.
Clothing and food for people
cannot be forsaken for a day,
while kin may be left at times.
Thus, sages stand firm amid the hardships of the myriad people.
Death is easy to speak of,
life is hard to harmonize.
So, once is a reward,
twice is routine,
thrice is taken for granted.
Practicing it minimally
is desire,
over time
it becomes ritual and righteousness.
Therefore, do not let subordinates take it as due;
superiors must practice it before changing.
Merchants in the state
are not to be employed.
They dwell without choosing their locale,
serve without choosing their ruler,
go out for profit,
return without guarding.
The state's mountains and forests,
they take and profit from.
Where markets reach,
they double their capital.
Hence, if those above are extravagant, those below are wasteful,
and if ruler, ministers, and subordinates are close,
then wealth is not privately hoarded by ruler and ministers,
thus they labor and obtain food.
Moving cities and shifting markets
is also a strategy.
The question is:
Can many worthies be spoken of?
The reply:
Turtles and fish that do not take bait
do not leave their depths;
trees that withstand frost and snow
do not heed heaven;
scholars who can govern themselves
do not follow sages.
How can they be spoken of?
What I, Yí Wú, have heard is:
Without desire, the strong cannot be subdued;
with wisdom but not governed.
Like the moon's cycle over ten days,
or musical pitches arising from one source, clearly,
then one can dwell in it.
So, constrain the path and scant what is given,
then scholars will be content.
Giving without choosing the person
is called being fond of people;
taking without choosing the person
is called being fond of profit.
Examining these two,
using them to dwell and act,
then it is said.
Unprincipled governance
cannot rule a state;
crooked, quiet words
cannot constitute the Way.
Regulating time in governance,
move with the times.
Inaction as the Way,
uniformity as conduct,
the path of avoiding the world
cannot advance and achieve.
The yang aspect advances plans,
the subtle responds to stimuli,
a second reduction brings alignment,
then operation follows. (May I ask) What does this mean?
The reply:
"Those who operate plans [deal with] the emptiness and fullness of heaven and earth,
their union and separation,
the succession of spring, autumn, winter, and summer.
Yet knowing where strengths and weaknesses lie,
then responding to the feudal lords to form alliances,
thus understanding where the safety and peril of the state reside.
Serve heaven according to the season,
serve spirits through heaven,
serve ghosts through spirits,
so the state incurs no punishment, the ruler lives long,
and the people suffer no
plague; wisdom operates plans and stays clear of weapons.
Fullness is stimulation,
emptiness is loss;
the union of fullness and emptiness
sometimes becomes substance,
sometimes becomes movement.
Yin and yang lend by season;
if winter is harsh, summer is hot;
if yang is strong, yin is cold.
Thus, the king is cautious about the solstices,
knowing where emptiness and fullness lie, to issue decrees.
After life and death decisions,
when united but not dispersed,
matters can be decided.
As they are about to unite, one can anticipate
their following actions to raise troops,
dividing their numbers
for specific governance.
May I ask if forms change with time?
The reply:
When the division of yin and yang is set,
sweet and bitter grasses grow.
Following what is fitting,
sour and salty harmonize,
and forms and colors are fixed,
used for music and sounds.
The advance and retreat of yin and yang,
the timeliness of fullness and emptiness,
their dispersion and union can indicate the year.
Only the sage does not weary over the year,
knowing fullness and emptiness,
taking from excess,
supplementing deficiency,
to streamline governance,
and sustain the people's livelihood.
The changing qi of earth
responds to its sources;
the changing qi of water
is met with essence,
received with preparation;
the changing qi of heaven
is met with correctness.
Moreover, the essential qi of heaven and earth has five aspects,
not necessarily obstructing
its urgency or reverting
to its heaviness. The advance and retreat of movement and destruction,
this is the difficulty in grasping these numbers,
this is the temporal change of forms.
To calm the vital energy's yang aspect,
how can one achieve tranquility through words?
When residual energy stirs imperceptibly,
and cherished energy grieves silently,
how can one govern such movements?
The reply states:
Obtain it in times of decline,
observe it from its position—
true beauty then radiates brilliance. Cultivate
the heart,
which moderates through mutual interaction,
hence the energies of fullness, emptiness, grief, and joy arise.
Thus, in records of the Eight Emperors,
Shénnóng is not included,
because he held no position,
and could not be utilized.
Question: Where lies the convergence of fortune's fullness?
At twenty years, it may expand;
at twelve years, it narrows;
by a hundred years, the spirit is harmed.
When the rituals of Zhōu and Zhèng shift,
the laws of Zhōu are abandoned,
then flora of the central states may migrate to inaccessible wilds.
Thus, if the ruler's music and attire change,
ministers may possess wealth of a thousand steeds,
women govern affairs,
and iron's weight surpasses bronze.
Music favors descending melodies,
foods crave salty bitterness—
hastily, the ruler's influence wanes daily.
Then sacrifices to mountain valley spirits alter,
and responding states' titles change likewise.
Observe celestial transformations,
watch the winds and energies.
Ancient sacrifices
sometimes honored stars,
sometimes blazing heat,
sometimes smoldering embers,
sometimes gentle warmth.
The rodent responds to expansion's reality—
this is the number of yīn and yáng;
blossoms like falling
names are appellations for sacrifices.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven governs the state
by charting its trees and objects.
The heart within the body
holds the ruler's position;
the nine orifices with their functions
reflect official duties.
If the heart follows the Dào,
the nine orifices adhere to order;
if desires overflow,
eyes see no colors,
ears hear no sounds.
Hence it is said:
"When superiors deviate from the Dào,
subordinates neglect their tasks."
Do not run for the horse—
let it exhaust its strength;
do not fly for the bird—
let it wear its wings;
do not move before things—
observe their patterns.
Action loses position,
stillness brings self-attainment.
The Dào is near yet hard to reach fully,
coexists with humans yet hard to obtain.
Empty your desires—
the spirit will enter its abode;
if impurities remain uncleansed,
the spirit will not stay.
All seek wisdom
yet none inquire its source.
Wisdom, oh wisdom—
cast it beyond the seas, none can seize it.
Those who seek it fall short of those who empty themselves.
The sage seeks nothing,
thus achieves emptiness.
Emptiness without form is called Dào;
nurturing all things is called Dé;
ruler-minister, father-son, human affairs are called Yì;
ritual bows and deference,
noble and humble ranks,
kinship distinctions are called Lǐ;
unifying small and great in one path,
executions and prohibitions are called Fǎ.
The great Dào can be followed but not described.
The speech of true persons—
neither biased nor partial—never leaves their lips,
nor appears in their expression.
People under heaven,
who can know their principles?
Heaven is emptiness,
Earth is stillness—
thus they never err.
Cleanse the palace,
open the gates,
discard selfishness, speak not—
the divine light will endure.
Chaotic as if disordered,
calm it, and order arises spontaneously.
Strength cannot establish everything,
wisdom cannot plan exhaustively.
Things inherently possess form,
forms inherently possess names—
whose names align are called sages.
Thus one must know wordless speech, actionless deeds,
then comprehend the Dào's essence.
Though shapes and grasps differ,
their principles align with all things—
thus they can begin governing the world.
Humans can be executed
because they fear death;
they can be deprived
because they crave gain.
Thus the noble person is not seduced by cravings,
nor pressured by aversions—
serene and joyful, non-acting,
discarding cleverness and artifice.
Their responses
are not premeditated;
their actions
are not prearranged.
Fault lies in self-assertion,
guilt in forced transformations.
Therefore,
the noble person embodying the Dào
dwells
as if unknowing,
responds to things
as if coinciding.
This is the way of stillness through accordance.
"The heart within the body
holds the ruler's position;
the nine orifices with their functions
reflect official duties."
Eyes and ears
are organs of sight and hearing—
if the heart does not interfere with seeing and hearing,
the organs maintain their duties.
When the heart harbors desires,
objects pass unseen by eyes,
sounds arrive unheard by ears.
Hence it is said:
"When superiors deviate from the Dào,
subordinates neglect their tasks."
Thus it is said:
The art of the heart
governs orifices through non-action.
Hence called
"the ruler."
"Do not run for the horse,"
"do not fly for the bird"—
this means not usurping abilities
nor competing with subordinates.
"Do not move before things"—
for the shaking remains unsettled,
the restless never calm—
meaning action prevents true observation.
"Position" refers to
where one stands.
The ruler stands in the yīn,
and yīn is tranquil,
hence it is said "movement leads to loss of position".
Yīn can control yáng,
tranquility can control movement,
hence it is said "tranquility brings self-attainment".
The Dào exists between heaven and earth,
so vast it has no exterior,
so minute it has no interior,
hence it is said "neither distant yet difficult to reach its extremity".
Emptiness and humanity are without separation,
only the sage attains the way of emptiness,
hence it is said "coexist yet difficult to obtain".
What ordinary people focus on is essence.
Eliminating desires leads to openness,
openness leads to tranquility,
tranquility leads to essence.
Essence leads to independence,
independence leads to clarity,
clarity leads to spirituality.
Spirituality is most noble,
thus if the lodging is not cleansed,
the noble one will not dwell there.
Hence it is said "without purity, spirit does not reside".
All people desire knowledge but do not seek it;
that by which they know, what they know is that;
that by which they know, is this.
Without cultivating this,
how can one know that?
Cultivating this,
one can achieve emptiness.
Emptiness means having no storage.
Therefore
eliminating knowledge, what is there to seek?
Having no storage, what is there to establish?
Without seeking or establishing,
there is no deliberation,
without deliberation, one returns to emptiness.
The way of heaven
is empty and formless.
Emptiness is inexhaustible,
formlessness has no opposition,
having no opposition,
thus it flows through all things without change.
Dé is the abode of Dào.
Through it, things obtain life
and life, knowledge attains the essence of Dào.
Thus dé is attainment.
Attainment means
that by which what is obtained becomes so.
Non-action is called Dào,
its embodiment is called dé,
thus Dào and dé are without separation,
so those who speak of them do not distinguish them.
The principle of separation
refers to that which embodies them.
Yì
means each being in its proper place.
Lǐ
follows human feelings,
aligns with the principle of yì,
and establishes regulations and refinements.
Thus lǐ means having pattern.
Pattern
clarifies distinctions to illustrate the meaning of yì.
Hence lǐ comes from pattern,
pattern comes from yì,
and yì is based on appropriateness.
Fǎ is that which uniformly issues forth,
making it necessarily so,
thus killing, punishing, prohibiting, and executing to unify it.
Therefore affairs are supervised by fǎ,
fǎ comes from authority,
authority comes from Dào.
Dào,
in motion shows no form,
in bestowal shows no dé,
all things obtain from it,
yet none know its limit.
Hence it is said
"can be relied upon but not explained".
"Zhēnrén",
speaks of utmost attainment.
"Not forcing",
speaks of response.
Response
is not something we contrive,
thus it can be without forcing.
"Not partial", speaks of
following.
Following
is not something we (deliberately choose),
thus there is no partiality.
"Not issuing from the mouth,
not appearing in the countenance",
speaks of formlessness;
"people within the four seas,
who knows their rule?",
speaks of profound containment.
The way of heaven is empty,
the way of earth is tranquil.
Emptiness is inexhaustible,
tranquility is unchanging,
unchanging means without fault,
hence it is said, "not impaired".
"Cleanse its palace,
open its gates":
palace
refers to the heart,
the heart
is the abode of wisdom,
hence called "palace".
Cleansing it
means removing preferences and faults.
Gates
refer to ears and eyes.
Ears and eyes
are for hearing and seeing.
"Things inherently have forms,
forms inherently have names",
this means names must not exceed reality,
reality must not extend names.
Examine forms through forms,
use forms to ascertain names,
supervise speech and correct names,
hence called "shèngrén".
"Wordless words",
are responses.
Response
is because it acts for others.
Grasp its name,
focus on
how it is accomplished,
this is the way of response.
"Actionless actions", follow naturally.
Following naturally
means neither adding nor subtracting.
Based on its form
assign it a name,
this is the method of following.
Names
are what the shèngrén uses to record all things.
Ordinary people stand on strength,
strive for goodness,
focus on ability,
act based on past experiences.
The shèngrén lacks these.
Lacking these
makes them different from things.
Different means empty,
emptiness is the beginning of all things,
hence it is said "can be the beginning of the world".
People pressured by evil
lose what they prefer;
tempted by preferences,
forget what they dislike.
This is not the Dào.
Hence it is said:
"Not tempted by preferences,
not pressured by aversions."
Aversions do not lose their principle,
desires do not exceed their nature,
hence it is said:
"Jūnzǐ." "Serene and joyful without action,
eliminating knowledge and past experiences",
speaks of emptiness and simplicity.
"Its response is not premeditated,
its movement is not self-initiated" —
this speaks of accordance.
Accordance means
setting aside oneself and taking things as the standard.
Responding only after being stimulated,
it is not premeditated;
moving along with principle,
it is not self-initiated.
"The fault lies in self-will,
the crime lies in alteration" —
self-will leads to lack of emptiness,
lack of emptiness then conflicts with things;
alteration gives rise to fabrication,
fabrication then leads to disorder.
Therefore, the Dào values accordance.
Accordance means
speaking of utility
based on their capabilities.
"The noble person's abiding is as if unknowing" —
this speaks of ultimate emptiness.
"His response to things is as if coincidental" —
this speaks of timely suitability,
like a shadow resembling the form,
an echo responding to the sound.
Thus when things arrive, he responds;
when they pass, he lets go.
Letting go means
returning to emptiness.
If the form is not upright, virtue will not come;
if the center is not refined, the heart-mind will not be ordered.
Upright form and adorned virtue,
and all things are completely attained.
Swiftly they come of themselves,
even the spirits do not know their limit.
Illuminatingly knowing all under heaven,
penetrating to the four extremes.
Therefore it is said:
Do not let things扰乱 the senses,
do not let the senses扰乱 the heart-mind —
this is called inner virtue.
Thus when the will and qì are settled,
then one returns to correctness.
Qì is
what fills the body,
and action is the meaning of correctness.
If the filling is not beautiful,
then the heart-mind is not attained;
if action is not upright,
then the people will not submit.
Therefore
the sage is like heaven,
covering all without partiality;
like earth,
bearing all without partiality.
Partiality
is what disorders all under heaven.
All things come bearing their names,
the sage accordingly assesses them,
and all under heaven is ordered;
essence is not harmed, not disordered in all under heaven,
and all under heaven is ordered.
Focused in intention,
unified in heart-mind,
ears and eyes straight,
knowing the far as near.
Can you focus?
Can you unify?
Can you know fortune and misfortune without divination?
Can you stop?
Can you cease?
Can you, without asking others,
attain it by yourself?
Therefore it is said,
think about it.
If thinking does not attain it,
the ghostly and divine will teach you.
Not through the power of ghosts and spirits,
but through the ultimate of essential qì.
That which can transform one thing is called essence,
that which can transform one affair is called wisdom.
Impartial selection
is how to rank affairs,
ultimate transformation
is how to respond to things.
Impartial selection without disorder,
ultimate transformation without vexation.
The gentleman who holds to the One
holds to the One without losing it,
can lord over the myriad things,
with the sun and moon shares their light,
with heaven and earth shares their principle.
The sage judges things,
is not driven by things.
Heart-mind at peace
means the state is at peace;
heart-mind ordered
means the state is ordered.
Order lies in the heart-mind,
peace lies in the heart-mind.
Ordering the heart-mind lies within,
ordered speech comes from the mouth,
ordered affairs are applied to the people,
thus achievements are made and the people follow,
then the hundred clans are ordered.
What is used to control is not punishment,
what is used to intimidate is not anger.
The people are controlled,
the hundred clans are ordered,
the Dào is their root
reaching the ultimate.
Reaching the ultimate reaches the nonexistent,
not something humans can disorder.
All systems held by officials who enforce regulations
are not the Dào.
The Dào of the sage,
seeming to exist, seeming not to exist,
yet when taken up and used,
does not perish through the ages.
Changing with the times yet not transforming,
responding to things yet not shifting,
used daily yet not being used up.
One who can be upright and still
will have supple sinews and strong bones,
can uphold the great circle, embody the great square,
mirror the great clarity, see the great illumination.
Not losing uprightness and stillness,
daily renewing one's virtue,
illuminatingly knowing all under heaven,
penetrating to the four extremes.
A whole heart-mind within cannot be concealed,
externally appearing in the body and countenance,
can be known through the complexion.
A good qì meeting others
feels as close as brothers;
an evil qì meeting others
harms more than weapons.
The wordless word
is heard louder than thunder drums.
The form of a whole heart-mind
is brighter than the sun and moon,
more discerning than parents.
In the past, the enlightened king loved all under heaven,
thus all under heaven could adhere;
the tyrannical king hated all under heaven,
thus all under heaven could depart.
Thus rewards are insufficient to show love,
punishments are insufficient to show hatred.
Rewards are the branch of love,
punishments are the branch of hatred.
All people's lives
must be based on uprightness and balance.
What causes its loss
must be joy, pleasure, sorrow, and anger.
Nothing better than music to moderate anger,
nothing better than rites to moderate pleasure,
nothing better than reverence to maintain rites.
Externally reverent and internally still,
one will certainly return to one's nature.
How could there be no beneficial affairs?
But I have no beneficial heart-mind;
how could there be no peaceful abodes?
But I have no peaceful heart-mind.
Within the heart-mind, there is again a heart-mind.
Intention precedes speech,
intention then takes form,
form then leads to thought,
thought then leads to knowledge.
All forms of the heart-mind
surpass the knowledge of former kings.
Therefore, gather inwardly to make it the source.
A spring that does not run dry,
inside and outside thoroughly connected;
The spring never dries up,
the four limbs remain firm.
When able to employ it,
its reach extends to all corners.
Thus, the sage unravels it with a single word,
observing above to the heavens,
observing below to the earth.
Twelve brief sayings. Establish constancy and set the foundation,
taking tranquility as the essence,
valuing timeliness as treasure,
using governance as the standard,
harmony then ensures longevity.
If it is not my standard,
even if beneficial, I will not act;
if it is not my duty,
even if advantageous, I will not proceed;
if it is not my way,
even if profitable, I will not take.
The highest follows heaven,
the next follows humanity.
If people do not initiate, I do not respond;
if heaven does not begin, I do not follow.
Thus, his words
are never discarded,
his affairs
never fall into ruin.
Trace the origins and assess the reality,
return to the root of their birth.
Know its appearance
and seek its form; follow
its principle
and understand its nature;
seek its beginning
and know its name.
Thus, what envelops all things is nothing greater than heaven and earth;
what transforms myriad things is nothing more abundant than the sun and moon;
what people urgently need,
nothing is more urgent than water and fire.
Yet, heaven does not alter its timing for any single thing,
and the enlightened ruler or sage does not bend the law for any one person.
Heaven acts according to its course
and all things receive its benefits,
the sage also acts according to his way
and the common people receive his benefits.
Thus, all things are balanced and all boasts are humbled.
Therefore, in governing, the sage
quiets himself and awaits.
When things arrive, their names naturally govern them.
With correct names, they govern themselves,
with distorted identities, names are abandoned.
When names are correct and laws are complete,
the sage has no affairs to manage.
One cannot dwell in permanence,
nor can one abandon rest;
judge matters according to change,
understanding timing as the measure.
The great is broad,
the small is confined,
things have their surpluses
and their deficiencies.
The emergence of arms
comes from people;
their invasion
enters one's own person.
Victory in battle
depends on the enemy;
the arrival of virtue
stems from oneself.
Hence it is said:
What is auspicious to spirits is righteous to people;
arms without righteousness are impermissible.
The strong who are arrogant diminish their strength;
the weak who are arrogant hasten to their demise;
the strong who are humble
preserve their strength;
the weak who are humble
avoid calamity.
Thus, arrogance leads to humility,
humility leads to arrogance.
The Dào,
used by one person,
is not heard to be excessive;
practiced by all under heaven,
is not heard to be insufficient.
This is what is called the Dào.
Take it in small measure
and gain small blessings;
take it in great measure
and gain great blessings;
practice it fully
and all under heaven submit;
if none is taken from it
then the people rebel,
and one cannot escape harm.
The left signifies emergence;
the right signifies entrance.
Emergence without harming others,
entrance harms oneself.
Without counting days or months,
affairs follow accordingly;
without divination or casting lots,
one carefully knows fortune and misfortune.
This is called leniency in punishment,
dwelling simply and attaining renown.
Speak good words,
do good deeds,
yet when deeds are accomplished, turn back without seeking fame.
The capable are without fame,
engaging in affairs without seeming to act.
Examine the input and output,
and observe what things carry.
Who can govern without governing?
Begin without beginning?
End without ending?
Be weak without weakness?
Hence it is said: How splendid, the rolling hills!
Thus, without center there is a center;
who can grasp the core of this center?
Therefore it is said:
Those who achieve success face downfall,
those who gain fame face loss.
Hence it is said,
who can abandon fame and merit,
and return to be one with the masses?
Who can discard merit and fame
and revert to having no achievement?
Having no achievement values the achievement within,
having achievement values the state of no achievement.
The sun at its zenith declines,
the moon at its fullness wanes.
The extreme leads to decline,
the full leads to wane,
the immense leads to extinction.
Who can forget the self?
Emulate the order of heaven and earth.
If people speak well,
do not listen;
if people speak ill,
do not listen.
Hold and wait,
empty and undivided,
purely clear of itself.
Do not rely on hearsay for accomplishing tasks,
investigate and verify,
do not heed arguments,
all things return to it,
beauty and ugliness then reveal themselves.
Heaven may uphold it,
earth may support it.
If nothing upholds heaven,
then heaven would fall;
if nothing supports earth,
then earth would sink.
That heaven does not fall,
earth does not sink,
must be because something upholds and supports it!
How much more so for humans?
When humans govern it,
it is like the movement of thunder drums.
What cannot move by itself,
something must shake it.
What is that "something"? It is as it is.
Look, and it is not seen;
listen, and it is not heard;
it spreads throughout the world,
yet no blockage is seen.
It gathers in the complexion,
known in the skin and flesh,
demanding its comings and goings,
none know its timing;
subtle as a square,
encompassing as a circle,
endlessly, without finding its gate.
Thus, the mouth is for speaking,
the ear for listening,
the eye for seeing,
the hand for pointing,
the foot for treading,
and things have their comparisons.
"What should live, lives;
what should die, dies,"
means there is west and east,
each dying in its own direction.
Establish constants and set standards,
can one preserve integrity?
Constant affairs penetrate the Way,
can one govern people?
Hence, record the wicked,
speak of the shallow.
The supremely sagely person
utters no idle words,
makes no pointless gestures,
but responds as things arrive.
Manifested in reputation and sound,
solidified in bodily expression,
these can be explained.
Not manifested in reputation and sound,
not solidified in bodily expression,
these cannot be explained.
When reaching the ultimate,
teaching existence is acceptable,
teaching non-existence is acceptable.
Therefore it is said:
He who aids boats harmonizes with water;
he who is righteous to people is auspicious to ghosts.
Affairs have appropriateness,
yet without forcing appropriateness, there is appropriateness;
like untying a knot, without forcing it, it then becomes appropriate.
When a knot exists, it cannot be untied until it is untied.
Thus, those skilled in handling affairs
leave the state unaware of their solutions.
In doing good,
do not be ostentatious;
in doing wrong,
you will fall into punishment.
Good and not good,
stop when trust is gained.
Whether left or right,
central correctness suffices.
Suspended like the sun and moon, ceaseless.
The unpretentious do not worry about the world,
the contentious do not take all things as strategy; who can
abandon contentiousness for unpretentiousness?
Hard to articulate are constitutional methods,
they must emerge through consensus.
No excessive words, no deficient words,
thus one can avoid harm.
Hence it is said:
What knowledge is knowing?
What planning is planning?
Those who examine before acting
attract others naturally.
Knowing oneself is called examination,
knowing others is called success.
