If knowledge is appropriate, one may
become ruler of the world;
consolidated within, unified,
one can endure long;
discuss and employ it,
one may become king of the world.
Heaven sees with precision,
the four directions understand its will,
soil grants life.
Can one be like wind and waves?
Following only what they desire.
Thus, a son replacing his father is called righteousness,
a minister replacing his ruler is called usurpation.
How can usurpation be praised?
Yet King Wǔ was such.
Therefore it is said:
Who can discard debate and cunning,
returning to share the path with the masses?
Hence it is said:
Excessive refinement in thought diminishes clarity,
cultivation of virtue narrows the kingly way,
lying in fame and profit endangers life,
knowledge encompassing all within heaven and earth
reveals life's obstacles.
Grasping and filling it
leads to peril.
Fame filling the world
is better ceased.
Fame advances, but retreat personally,
such is the way of Heaven.
An overfull state
should not be served;
an overfull household
should not marry into;
arrogant, violent people
should not be befriended.
The Way is vast as heaven,
broad as earth,
heavy as stone,
light as feather.
What people follow,
few understand.
Thus it is said:
Why is the Way so near
yet none can follow it?
Abandoning near for far
wastes effort.
Therefore it is said:
To cherish my body,
first know my essence.
Survey all directions,
to examine within.
Thereby understand appearances,
then know conduct's nature.
Knowing conduct's nature,
one knows nurturing life.
Left, right, front, back,
cycle and return.
Hold rituals, embody forms,
respectfully welcome what comes.
What comes
must follow its path,
without deviation or excess,
thus life endures.
Harmony returns to center,
form and nature preserve each other.
Singleminded, without duality,
this is called knowing the Way.
To master it,
focus on its origin,
and solidify your hold.
Observe its comings and goings,
unknowing of its timing,
seek it from Heaven,
set a date with it,
miss not the date,
then you may attain it.
Hence it is said:
I tell you the ultimate brilliance,
the brilliance of great brightness
is not吝惜, but people do not give.
Agreement leads to following,
opposition to distance.
I observe opposition's distance,
thus I know agreement in following.
Earth is
the origin of all things,
the root of all life,
where beauty, ugliness, worthiness, unworthiness, folly, and brilliance arise.
Water is
earth's blood and energy,
flowing like channels and vessels.
Thus: water possesses all qualities.
How is this known?
Answer:
Water is soft and clear,
cleansing others' filth—
this is benevolence.
Appearing dark yet being white—
this is essence.
Measured, it cannot be leveled,
stopping when full—
this is correctness.
Flowing without cease,
stopping when level—
this is righteousness.
All head for heights,
alone it seeks lows—
this is humility.
Humility is
the dwelling of the Way,
the vessel of kings,
and water makes it its home.
The level is the ancestor
of the five measures.
The plain is the substance
of the five colors.
The bland is the mean
of the five flavors.
Thus, water is the standard of all things,
the blandness of all living beings, and the substance
of right and wrong, gain and loss.
Therefore, there is nothing it does not fill, nowhere it does not dwell.
It gathers in heaven and earth
and is stored within all things,
produced from metal and stone,
and collected in all living beings.
Hence it is called the divine water.
When it gathers in plants and trees,
their roots attain proper measure,
their blossoms achieve their due number,
and their fruits reach their full quantity.
When birds and beasts obtain it,
their bodies grow plump and large,
their feathers become luxuriant and abundant,
and their patterns appear clear and distinct.
All things fully realize their potential;
those that return to their normal state
do so because the internal measure of water is appropriate.
What makes jade valuable is that
the nine virtues emerge from it.
Jade is warm, smooth, and lustrous—
this is benevolence.
Dense and well-veined—
this is wisdom.
Hard yet not cramped—
this is righteousness.
Sharp-edged but not cutting—
this is conduct.
Fresh and unsoiled—
this is purity.
It can be broken but not bent—
this is courage.
Flaws and perfections both visible—
this is genuineness.
Splendid, radiant, and glossy,
mutually penetrating without encroaching—
this is tolerance.
When struck,
its sound is clear, rising, penetrating, and far-reaching,
pure and unmixed—
this is resonance.
Therefore, rulers value it,
store it as treasure,
and carve it into tokens of auspicious signs,
for the nine virtues emerge from it.
Humans
are water.
When the vital energies of male and female combine,
water flows and takes form.
At three months, it is like chewing; what is chewing?
It is the five flavors.
What are the five flavors?
They are the five organs.
Sour governs the spleen,
salty governs the lungs,
pungent governs the kidneys,
bitter governs the liver,
sweet governs the heart.
When the five organs are fully formed,
then the internal parts are born.
The spleen produces the diaphragm,
the lungs produce bones,
the kidneys produce the brain,
the liver produces skin,
the heart produces flesh.
When the five internal parts are complete,
then the nine orifices develop.
The spleen manifests as the nose,
the liver as the eyes,
the kidneys as the ears,
the lungs as the orifices.
It forms in five months,
and is born in ten months.
Upon birth, the eyes see,
the ears hear, the heart reflects.
What the eyes see
is not only mountains and hills,
but they perceive the faint and vague.
What the ears hear
is not only thunder and drums,
but they discern the whispers and chirps.
What the heart reflects on
is not only the coarse and obvious,
but it contemplates the subtle and minute.
Thus, when water gathers in jade,
the nine virtues emerge.
When it congeals and solidifies into a human,
the nine orifices and five senses appear.
This is its essence,
coarse, turbid, and solid,
able to exist but not to vanish.
Those that lie hidden in darkness, able to exist and vanish,
are the yarrow, tortoise, and dragon.
The tortoise is born in water,
revealed through fire,
thus it precedes all things,
and rectifies fortune and misfortune.
The dragon is born in water,
adorned with five colors and roams,
hence it is divine.
If it wishes to be small, it transforms like a silkworm or caterpillar;
if it wishes to be large, it encompasses heaven and earth;
if it wishes to ascend, it soars above the clouds;
if it wishes to descend, it enters the deep springs;
it changes without a fixed day,
rises and falls without a set time,
and is called divine. The tortoise and dragon,
lying hidden in darkness, are able to exist and vanish.
Some are seen in an age,
some are not seen in an age,
such as the Wēi and Qìngjì.
Thus, in marshes that have dried up for centuries,
where valleys do not shift,
and water does not cease, Qìngjì is born.
Qìngjì
has a form like a human,
four inches tall,
dressed in yellow clothes,
wearing a yellow crown,
topped with a yellow canopy,
riding a small horse,
fond of swift galloping.
Call it by its name,
and it can report back from a thousand miles away in one day.
This is the essence of dried-up marshes.
The essence of dried-up rivers
is born as the Wēi.
The Wēi has one head and two bodies,
its shape like a snake,
eight feet long.
Call it by its name,
and it can fetch fish and turtles.
This is the essence of dried-up river water.
Therefore, the essence of water, coarse, turbid, and solid,
able to exist but not to vanish,
gives birth to humans and jade.
Those lying hidden in darkness, able to exist and vanish,
are the yarrow, tortoise, and dragon.
Some seen in an age
or not seen
are the Wēi and Qìngjì.
Thus, all people submit to it,
but Guǎnzǐ takes it as a standard;
all people possess it,
but Guǎnzǐ utilizes it.
So what is that which embodies it?
It is water.
Nothing fails to live by it,
and only those who know its reliance can rectify it.
That which embodies it
is water.
Hence it is said:
What is water?
It is the root and origin of all things,
the ancestral home of all living beings,
and that which produces beauty and ugliness, worthiness and unworthiness, folly and brilliance.
How do we know it is so?
The water of Qí
is forceful, restless, and recurring,
hence its people are greedy, coarse, and fond of bravery.
The waters of Chǔ
are soft and clear,
thus its people are light-hearted, resolute, and daring.
The waters of Yuè
are turbid and heavy, stagnating,
thus its people are foolish, quick-tempered, and filthy.
The waters of Qín are murky and accumulate,
clogged and mixed,
thus its people are greedy, cruel,
deceitful, and fond of troublemaking.
The waters of Qí and Jìn
are dry and swirling,
clogged and mixed,
thus their people are flattering, sycophantic, hypocritical, and deceitful,
cunning, artful, and fond of profit.
The waters of Yān
gather low and are weak,
stagnant and mixed,
thus its people are foolish, simple-minded, and fond of integrity,
frivolous, hasty, and easily perish.
The waters of Sòng
are light, strong, and clear,
thus its people are straightforward, uncomplicated, and fond of righteousness.
Therefore, when a sage transforms the world,
the key lies in the water.
Thus, when water is unified, people's hearts are upright;
when water is clear, people's hearts are easily influenced.
When people's hearts are upright, desires are not defiled;
when people's hearts are easily influenced, actions are without evil.
Hence, when a sage governs the world,
he does not inform each individual,
nor persuade each household,
the pivot lies in the water.
Guǎnzǐ said:
Commands must have their timing.
Without timing,
one must observe and follow the way of Heaven's manifestations,
the five are vast and boundless,
the six are dim and obscure, who can know them?
Only the sage knows the four seasons.
Not knowing the four seasons,
means losing the foundation of the state.
Not knowing the reasons of the five grains,
the state will decline.
Thus, Heaven is called truly bright,
Earth is called truly sage,
the four seasons are called correct.
If the king is truly bright and sage,
his ministers will be upright.
How to know that the king is truly bright and truly sage?
Answer: Carefully employ the capable and wisely listen to truth. Employing the capable is called bright,
listening to truth is called sage,
those who are truly bright and sage,
all receive Heaven's rewards.
Employing the incapable is called dim,
those who are dim and forgetful,
all suffer Heaven's calamities.
Therefore, if the superior sees accomplishments and values merits,
then the people's affairs will be diligently undertaken without complaint.
If the superior sees merits and despises them,
then those below will become lazy,
and those above will become arrogant.
Thus, yin and yang
are the great principles of Heaven and Earth,
the four seasons
are the great patterns of yin and yang,
punishments and virtues
are in harmony with the four seasons.
When punishments and virtues harmonize with the seasons,
blessings arise;
when they deviate, calamities arise.
Then, what should be done in spring, summer, autumn, and winter?
The east is called the stars,
its season is spring,
its energy is wind,
wind gives rise to wood and bones.
Its virtue delights in growth,
issuing forth and regulating the seasons.
Its affairs: commands
to repair and tidy the spirit altars,
carefully pray and remove obstacles,
honor the full yang,
repair dikes and embankments,
plow, weed, plant, and cultivate,
mend bridges and crossings,
dredge ditches and canals,
repair roofs and manage water flow,
resolve grievances and pardon crimes,
open communications in all directions.
Then gentle winds and sweet rains will arrive,
the people will live long,
all creatures will multiply,
this is called the virtue of the stars.
The stars govern issuance, issuance becomes wind.
Therefore, if spring follows winter's governance, there is withering;
if it follows autumn's governance, there is frost;
if it follows summer's governance, there is desire.
Thus, in the three months of spring, on the days of Jiǎ and Yǐ, issue five policies.
First policy: Care for the young and orphaned,
pardon the guilty.
Second policy: Confer ranks and titles,
grant emoluments and positions.
Third policy: As ice thaws, dredge ditches and canals,
repatriate those who have fled.
Fourth policy: Clear dangerous obstacles,
repair borders and boundaries,
straighten paths and fields.
Fifth policy: Do not kill fawns or young animals,
do not break flowers or cut buds.
If these five policies are timely,
spring rains will come.
The south is called the sun,
its season is summer,
its energy is yang,
yang gives rise to humans and energy.
Its virtue bestows gifts and cultivates joy.
Its affairs: commands
for rewards and gifts, conferring titles,
granting emoluments, appeasing the villages.
Carefully perform sacrifices to spirits,
evaluate achievements and reward the worthy,
to assist the yang energy.
Great heat will then arrive,
seasonal rains will fall,
the five grains and hundred fruits will ripen,
this is called the virtue of the sun.
The sun governs rewards,
rewards become heat.
If summer follows spring's governance, there is wind;
if it follows autumn's governance, there is flood;
if it follows winter's governance, there is decline.
Thus, in the three months of summer, on the days of Bǐng and Dīng, issue five policies.
First policy: Seek those with achievements and exerted labor and promote them.
Second policy: Open long-stored goods,
clear out old houses,
open old cellars
for lending.
Third policy: Order to remove fans and hats, do not bare feet or head,
clear urgent leaks in field huts.
Fourth policy: Seek those with virtue who bestow alms upon the people and reward them.
Fifth policy: Order to prohibit setting traps for birds and beasts,
do not kill flying birds.
If these five policies are timely,
summer rains will come.
The center is called earth,
earth's virtue truly assists the four seasons in their coming and going,
regulating wind and rain, earth increases strength.
Earth gives rise to skin and flesh.
Its virtue is harmonious, peaceful, and evenly applied,
impartial and selfless,
truly assisting the four seasons:
in spring, fostering growth,
in summer, nurturing development,
in autumn, gathering the harvest,
in winter, storing and concealing,
great cold then reaches its peak,
the state prospers,
all directions submit,
this is called the virtue of the year.
The year governs harmony,
harmony becomes rain.
The west is called the constellations,
its season is autumn,
its energy is yin,
yin gives rise to metal and armor.
Its virtue is sorrowful, mournful,
tranquil, upright, stern, and obedient,
dwelling without daring to be licentious or excessive.
Its affairs: commands
not to let the people be licentious or violent,
follow the mustering and gathering of the harvest,
measure the people's resources to store and accumulate.
Gather the various stems,
collect the various materials,
all things are then harvested,
make the people not be idle.
To scrutinize what is detested,
and to obtain what is desired without fail,
upholding righteousness and trust leads to victory,
this is called the virtue of Chén.
Chén governs harvest,
and harvest belongs to yīn.
If spring governance is applied in autumn, it causes lush growth;
if summer governance is applied, it leads to floods;
if winter governance is applied, it results in depletion.
Therefore, during the three months of autumn, issue five policies on the days of Gēng and Xīn.
The first policy: prohibit gambling,
restrict petty arguments,
and prevent disputes and slander.
The second policy: do not display the blades of the five weapons.
The third policy: encourage seasonal farming,
and hasten the gathering of harvests.
The fourth policy: repair deficiencies and seal cracks.
The fifth policy: mend walls and enclosures,
and secure the gates and alleys.
If these five policies are timely,
all five grains will be stored.
The north is called Yuè,
its season is winter,
its energy is cold,
and cold gives rise to water and blood.
Its virtue is pure and far-reaching,
gentle and forgiving, thorough and meticulous.
Its affairs: issue decrees
to regulate restrictions and relocate the people,
ordering them to remain still,
so the earth does not lose its essence.
Enforce judgments and carry out punishments,
showing no mercy to the guilty,
to align with the yīn energy.
Then the great cold arrives,
armor and weapons strengthen,
the five grains ripen,
the state prospers,
and the four directions submit,
this is called the virtue of Yuè.
Yuè governs punishment,
and punishment is associated with cold.
If spring governance is applied in winter, it causes leakage;
if summer governance is applied, it leads to thunderstorms;
if autumn governance is applied, it results in drought.
Therefore, during the three months of winter, issue five policies on the days of Rén and Guǐ.
The first policy: care for the orphaned and solitary,
and show compassion to the elderly.
The second policy: harmonize with the yīn energy,
maintain divine sacrifices,
grant ranks and emoluments,
and appoint to appropriate positions.
The third policy: audit accounts,
and do not exploit the hidden treasures of mountains and rivers.
The fourth policy: suppress evildoers and fugitives,
reward those who capture thieves and bandits.
The fifth policy: prohibit relocation, stop the flow of refugees, and restrict divisions.
If these five policies are timely,
winter affairs will not go awry,
what is sought will be obtained,
and what is detested will be subdued.
Thus, spring withering, autumn lushness,
winter thunder, summer frost and snow,
these are all disruptions of energy.
If punishments and virtues shift seasons and lose order,
disruptive energy swiftly arrives;
when disruptive energy arrives swiftly,
the state faces many disasters and calamities.
Therefore, the sage king focuses on timing in governance,
establishes teachings to embed martial prowess,
and conducts sacrifices to embed virtue.
These three are how the sage king aligns with the movements of heaven and earth.
The sun governs yáng,
the moon governs yīn,
and the year governs harmony.
Yáng represents virtue,
yīn represents punishment,
and harmony represents affairs.
Thus, when a solar eclipse occurs,
states that have lost virtue dread it;
when a lunar eclipse occurs,
states that have lost punishment dread it;
when a comet appears,
states that have lost harmony dread it;
when wind contends with the sun for brightness,
states that have lost correctness dread it.
Therefore, the sage king cultivates virtue during a solar eclipse,
cultivates punishment during a lunar eclipse,
cultivates harmony when a comet appears,
and cultivates correctness when wind contends with the sun.
These four actions are how the sage king avoids the punishment of heaven and earth.
If faithfully implemented,
the five grains will multiply,
the six livestock will thrive,
and armor and weapons will strengthen.
Accumulation of order leads to prosperity,
accumulation of tyranny leads to ruin. . : , . : , , , . : , . : , . : , , . , , , .
The Dào gives birth to heaven and earth,
virtue brings forth wise men.
Dào produces virtue,
virtue produces correctness,
correctness produces affairs.
Thus, the sage king governs the world,
where exhaustion leads to reversal,
and endings lead to beginnings.
Virtue begins in spring,
grows in summer;
punishment begins in autumn,
and flows in winter.
If punishment and virtue do not err,
the four seasons remain consistent.
If punishment and virtue deviate from their course,
the seasons will reverse.
Efforts will not succeed,
and great calamity will surely follow.
The moon has three policies,
ensuring the king's affairs are managed,
and stability is maintained.
Those who fail to align will perish,
those who lose order will fall.
The state has four seasons,
firmly upholding the king's affairs,
with four guardians in place,
and three policies to assist.
The first is the foundation,
the second is the vessel,
the third is fulfillment,
the fourth is governance,
the fifth is education,
the sixth is preservation,
the seventh is establishment,
the eighth is advancement,
the ninth is completion.
These nine aspects,
then complete the five organs within the six repositories,
and the five tones within the six pitch standards.
When the sixth month and the solstice arrive,
thus humans have six yáo,
which serve to connect heaven and earth.
The way of heaven is governed by nine,
the principles of earth by eight,
and human affairs by six.
Taking heaven as father,
earth as mother,
to open up all things,
and unify the whole.
Mastering the nine regulations,
six repositories, and three fulfillments,
one becomes an enlightened Son of Heaven.
Regulate water and soil,
awaiting the celestial mandate;
reflect on the five viscera,
to examine what is not intimate;
under the governance of sacrifices,
observe the position of earth;
honor the divine abode,
harmonizing with the essence of energy.
Once harmonized, constancy is achieved,
with constancy comes principle.
Carefully attune the sounds,
refine the twelve bells,
to regulate human emotions.
Once human emotions are grasped,
all things have their limits,
and only then is virtue attained.
Thus, by comprehending yáng energy,
one serves heaven,
aligning the sun and moon,
applying it for the people;
by comprehending yīn energy,
one serves earth,
By observing the stars and calendars,
one discerns their movements.
Only when the Way is comprehended can actions be taken;
then divine divination becomes unnecessary,
the sacred tortoise need not be consulted,
and the Yellow Emperor's wisdom permeates all,
achieving the pinnacle of governance.
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor obtained Chīyóu and understood the Way of Heaven,
obtained Dàcháng and discerned the advantages of the earth,
obtained Cānglóng and distinguished the East,
obtained Zhùróng and distinguished the South,
obtained Dàfēng and distinguished the West,
obtained Hòutǔ and distinguished the North.
With these six ministers, the Yellow Emperor brought order to the world,
reaching the height of divine brilliance.
Chīyóu understood the Way of Heaven,
so he was made the Director of Seasons;
Dàcháng discerned the earth's benefits,
so he was made the Granary Keeper;
Cānglóng distinguished the East,
so he was made the Chief Artisan;
Zhùróng distinguished the South,
so he was made the Minister of Education;
Dàfēng distinguished the West,
so he was made the Minister of War;
Hòutǔ distinguished the North,
so he was made the Chief Justice.
Thus, spring corresponds to the Chief Artisan,
summer to the Minister of Education,
autumn to the Minister of War,
winter to the Chief Justice.
In the past, the Yellow Emperor, according to the urgency of seasons,
created the five tones,
to regulate the five bells.
He decreed these five bells:
the first called the Green Bell
with a grand sound,
the second the Red Bell
centering the heart,
the third the Yellow Bell
sprinkling light,
the fourth the Bright Bell
dimming its brilliance,
the fifth the Black Bell
concealing its constancy.
Once the five tones were harmonized,
he then established the five phases
to rectify the heavenly timing,
and the five offices to set human positions.
When humans harmonize with Heaven,
the beauty of heaven and earth is born.
When the sun reaches
and the jiǎzǐ day is observed, the Wood phase governs.
The Son of Heaven issues decrees,
ordering the left and right officials and inner attendants.
He distinguishes and arranges ranks,
evaluating worthy and unworthy scholars and officials;
distributes treasures, bestowing rewards within the four borders.
He releases stored grain according to farmland acreage.
Leaving the capital, the衡
inspects the mountains and forests,
forbidding people from cutting trees,
to cherish the plants and trees.
Then, ice melts and frost thaws,
plants and trees sprout in clusters.
Redeeming dormant insects and eggs,
spring plowing should not miss its time,
ensuring seedlings have strong roots,
no pests harm the fledglings,
no premature death for fawns.
Do not hasten growth,
do not harm the swaddled young.
Then the season will not wither.
This lasts seventy-two days and concludes.
Observing the bǐngzǐ day,
the Fire phase governs.
The Son of Heaven issues decrees,
ordering the messengers and inner attendants.
He commands the digging of ditches and canals, clearing old paths.
Distributes stored goods, granting rewards as the ruler sees fit.
Nobles engage in excursions to stimulate the earth's energy.
Issues leather and currency,
ordering messengers to practice the spring and autumn rites throughout the land,
so that feudal lords communicate,
and all under heaven who meet harmonize together.
Then, no harsh winds blow from heaven,
plants and trees flourish vigorously,
stagnant air dissipates,
people suffer no illness, and splendor multiplies.
This lasts seventy-two days and concludes.
Observing the wùzǐ day,
the Earth phase governs.
The Son of Heaven issues decrees,
ordering the left and right Ministers of Education and inner attendants.
No executions for unfaithfulness,
revering agricultural affairs.
Greatly promoting benevolent words,
leniency in capital punishment,
pardoning criminals.
Leaving the capital, the Minister of Education orders
the people to exert their efforts in farming to nurture the five grains.
Nobles reside peacefully,
while farmers devote their utmost to labor.
Then, heaven becomes a nurturing canopy,
plants and trees grow and flourish,
the five grains bloom, bear fruit, and swell large,
sacrificial animals from the six livestock are prepared;
people have ample wealth,
the state is prosperous,
superiors and inferiors are close,
feudal lords are harmonious.
This lasts seventy-two days and concludes.
Observing the gēngzǐ day,
the Metal phase governs.
The Son of Heaven issues decrees,
ordering the prayer officials to select forbidden禽兽
and the first-ripened of the five grains,
offering them in the ancestral temple and to the five sacrifices,
so that ghosts and spirits enjoy their essence,
and nobles taste their flavors.
Then, cool winds arrive,
white dew descends,
the Son of Heaven issues decrees,
ordering the left and right Ministers of War
to prepare armor and sharpen weapons,
forming squads and platoons, training within the four borders,
solemnly informing the people of impending events,
to prepare for heaven and earth's season of harvest and killing.
Then, the day scorches with sun,
evening brings down dew,
the earth competes in fertility,
the five grains ripen in succession,
plants and trees are lush with fruit,
the farmers' year is abundant,
the harvest exceedingly plentiful.
This lasts seventy-two days and concludes.
Observing the rénzǐ day,
the Water phase governs,
the Son of Heaven issues decrees,
ordering the left and right envoys and inner attendants; if the energy
is sufficient, it is released and then stopped,
if the energy is insufficient,
then suppress ditches and punish thieves.
Repeatedly cut bamboo arrows,
fell sandalwood and mulberry trees,
order the people to go hunting,禽兽
regardless of size, kill them without release,
to honor what heaven and earth have closed and stored.
Then, those with feathered eggs do not break,
those with furry fetuses do not miscarry,
pregnant women do not suffer loss or abandonment,
plants and trees have beautiful roots.
This lasts seventy-two days and concludes.
Observing the jiǎzǐ day,
the Wood phase governs,
if the Son of Heaven does not levy taxes
nor bestow rewards,
but instead engages in great cutting and harm,
the ruler will be in danger,
otherwise,
the crown prince will be in danger,
the household members or the lady will die,
otherwise,
the eldest son will die.
This lasts seventy-two days and concludes.
Observing the bǐngzǐ day,
the Fire phase governs,
if the Son of Heaven hastily implements urgent policies,
drought and pestilence will occur,
seedlings will die, and people will suffer plagues.
This lasts seventy-two days and concludes.
When the Wùzǐ day appears
and Earth's cycle prevails,
the Son of Heaven renovates palaces and halls,
builds terraces and pavilions,
endangering the ruler;
constructing outer walls and battlements
causes ministers to perish.
This lasts seventy-two days and concludes.
When the Gēngzǐ day appears
and Metal's cycle prevails,
the Son of Heaven attacks mountains and quarries stone,
leading to military conflicts and defeat, soldiers dying,
and loss of governance.
This lasts seventy-two days and concludes.
When the Rénzǐ day appears
and Water's cycle prevails,
the Son of Heaven breaches barriers, stirring great floods,
causing the queen and consorts to pass away,
or else
bird eggs to break,
furry embryos to miscarry,
pregnant women to lose their fetuses,
and plants' roots and foundations to wither.
This lasts seventy-two days and concludes.
To fear water in battle
is called the extinction of courage. In small matters, there is no compliance;
in great affairs, there is no auspiciousness.
To fear danger in battle
is called confusion within.
Dividing one's troops and masses,
when people are bewildered and lost,
surely leads to the path of the commander's demise.
Those overly still are likened to the dead,
those overly active to ghosts,
those overly trusting to resistance,
those overly yielding to avoidance.
Stillness and action,
at times take the role of host,
at times that of guest,
valuing the attainment of measure.
Knowing the preparation in stillness,
one dwells and benefits oneself;
knowing the follow-through in action,
every move achieves merit.
Thus it is said, "The one who does nothing becomes emperor,"
which refers to this.
When rebellious tendencies sprout,
and heaven and earth have not yet taken form,
to initiate governance beforehand
will lead to the affair not succeeding,
and wrongly suffering its punishments.
Heaven acts through humans,
the sage acts through heaven. When heavenly timing does not arise,
do not be the guest;
when human affairs do not stir,
do not be the initiator.
Harmonize and unite the masses,
following the course of heaven and earth.
Humans initiate it,
heaven and earth shape it,
the sage completes it,
thus aligning with heaven's ultimate principle.
Correct and still without contention,
acting without error,
plain essence without residue,
aligning with earth's ultimate principle.
If not yet attaining heaven's ultimate,
then conceal oneself in virtue;
having attained heaven's ultimate,
then exert one's strength.
Once the achievement is complete,
follow and preserve its course,
and no one can replace it.
The way to success
values expansion and contraction as treasures.
Do not forget heaven's ultimate,
exhaust the numbers and stop.
If affairs are not yet accomplished,
do not alter their form,
do not lose their beginning,
calm the people and observe the timing,
await the command and then arise.
Therefore it is said,
"Follow the course of yin and yang,
and embody the constancy of heaven and earth.
Expanding and contracting,
act accordingly and appropriately;
dying and being born,
follow the forms of heaven and earth.
Heaven and earth shape it,
the sage completes it,
small pursuits yield small gains,
great pursuits yield great gains,
those who fully practice it possess the world.
Thus, the worthy are sincere and trustworthy to be benevolent,
kind and gracious to show love,
upright in governance and example
dare not to precede others.
Centered stillness without lingering, abundant virtue without seeking,
manifest in feminine charm.
Their disposition is soft,
tranquil and joyful, practicing
virtue without contention,
awaiting the turmoil under heaven to arise.
Hence, the worthy are calm, composed, correct, and still,
with gentle restraint predetermined,
acting in timidity,
and establishing in incapability,
holding to weak points and firmly abiding by them.
Thus, they do not violate heavenly timing,
nor disrupt the people's labors.
Seize the time to nurture the people,
virtue first, punishment later.
Comply with heaven,
subtly measure humans.
Those skilled in encompassing,
clarity cannot perceive them;
those skilled in clarity,
encompassing cannot obscure them.
Great clarity overcomes great encompassing,
then the people lack great encompassing;
great encompassing overcomes great clarity,
then the people lack great clarity.
The precursor of great encompassing
can inspire trust;
the ancestor of great clarity
can substitute for heaven: below
search and not find,
seek it under the beckoning and waving.
Beasts weary of running, yet there are hidden nets. One lies down, one turns aside,
otherwise, it cannot be obtained.
Great civility thrice layered,
values righteousness and virtue;
great martiality thrice layered,
lays down arms and strength.
Deciding and executing the five punishments,
each fitting its name,
the guilty bear no resentment,
the good feel no alarm,
this is called punishment. Correcting it,
subduing it, overcoming it, adorning it,
must enforce its commands strictly,
and the people follow them, this is called governance.
Like the four seasons without error,
like the stars unchanging,
like night like day,
like yin like yang,
like the brightness of sun and moon,
this is called law.
Loving them, giving them life,
nurturing them, completing them,
benefiting the people without taking,
the world draws close to them,
this is called virtue.
Without virtue without resentment,
without preference without aversion,
all things honor the one,
yin and yang share the same measure,
this is called the Way.
Punishment to judge them,
governance to command them,
law to restrain them,
virtue to nurture them,
the Way to enlighten them. Punishment to judge them,
do not forfeit the people's lives;
command them to cut off their desires,
do not let the people take shortcuts;
restrain them to eliminate their ambitions,
do not let the people rely on luck;
To nurture them and transform their vices,
one must start with oneself;
one must enlighten them to observe their lives,
following the natural order.
When penalties are enforced, the people
will be diligent in heart and reverent;
when governance is established, the people
will trust and obey;
when virtue is promoted, the people
will be harmonious and tranquil;
when the Way is attained, the people
will entrust themselves without contention.
Punishing the guilty appropriately is called justice,
issuing decrees at the right time is called rectitude,
adhering to established rules without change is called law,
loving the people selflessly is called virtue,
gathering what the people converge upon is called the Way. In establishing norms and administering governance,
can one inspire trust?
With balance, harmony, caution, and reverence,
can one renew daily?
With balanced standards and unified stillness,
can one maintain caution?
Abandoning selfishness for public good,
can one recommend others?
In governing officials and the people,
can one put oneself last?
Being able to inspire trust,
this is called upholding discipline.
Being able to renew daily,
this is called practicing principle.
Maintaining caution and rectifying names,
deceit and fraud cease on their own.
Recommending others without selfishness,
the virtue of ministers is all guided by the Way.
Being able to put oneself last,
one assists the Son of Heaven from above.
The reasons why the people defend and fight to the death without expecting reward from their superiors
are several and lead to this outcome. They say:
The greatest is
the location of their parents' graves and ancestral homes,
with ample wealth and property to dwell in.
If not,
then the bonds of state, county, village, and clan are enough to cherish and delight in.
If not,
then the ruler's teachings and instructions,
customs, and deep benevolence toward the people
make it unthinkable to seek elsewhere.
If not,
then the resources of mountains, forests, marshes, and valleys suffice for livelihood.
If not,
then the terrain is perilous and difficult,
easy to defend and hard to attack.
If not,
then punishments are severe and fearsome.
If not,
then rewards are clear and sufficiently encouraging.
If not,
then there is deep enmity toward the enemy.
If not,
then there are great merits owed to the ruler.
These are why the people defend and fight to the death without expecting reward from their superiors.
Now, relying on untrustworthy people
and seeking wisdom from them; employing
undisciplined people,
yet desiring stability;
leading troops who do not fight,
yet hoping for victory;
these are the three follies of warfare.
The sage ruler relies on law, not on cleverness;
relies on methods, not on rhetoric;
relies on public good, not on private interests;
relies on the great Way, not on trivial matters;
thus, the ruler is at ease while the world is well-governed.
The failed ruler does otherwise,
abandoning law for cleverness,
so the people neglect duties and seek fame;
abandoning methods for rhetoric,
so the people forsake substance for empty words;
abandoning public good for private interests,
so the people deviate from law and act recklessly;
abandoning the great Way for trivial matters,
thus the ruler is burdened and troubled,
the people are confused and lost,
and the state is not well-governed.
The sage ruler does otherwise,
upholding the essence of the Way,
dwelling in ease and joy,
galloping in hunting,
with bells, drums, pipes, and lutes,
the pleasures of the palace,
unrestricted and unconfined.
Without anxious thoughts or schemes,
without worries or plots,
benefiting the body,
easing the form,
nurturing longevity,
the ruler governs the world with folded hands.
Therefore, if a ruler can apply this Way, there is no need to strain the mind,
labor the will,
or exert strength,
yet the land expands on its own,
granaries fill themselves,
stores accumulate abundantly,
armor and weapons strengthen themselves,
ministers are free of deceit,
officials are without treachery,
and those with unusual skills or arts
dare not boast or act recklessly
to exceed their true roles
or manipulate their ruler.
In ancient times, when Yáo governed the world,
it was like clay in the potter's hands,
shaped only as the potter willed;
like metal in the furnace,
molded as the smith chose to cast.
His people were drawn to come,
pushed to go,
made to achieve,
and restrained to stop.
Thus, Yáo's governance
was simply skilled at clarifying laws and prohibitions.
When Huángdì governed the world,
his people came without being drawn,
went without being pushed,
achieved without being made,
and stopped without being restrained.
Thus, Huángdì's governance
established laws unchanged,
allowing the people to abide peacefully by them.
What are called benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music all stem from law.
This is how the ancient sages unified the people.
The "Zhōu Shū" says:
"If the state's laws are not uniform,
it bodes ill for the ruler;
if the people do not follow the law, it bodes ill; if the state frequently changes laws to govern the people, it bodes ill;
if ministers do not use ritual and righteousness in instruction, it bodes ill;
if officials in service govern apart from the law, it bodes ill."
Therefore, it is said:
Law
is not to be constant,
but it is the source of survival, ruin, order, and chaos,
the great standard by which the sage ruler governs the world.
Rulers, ministers, superiors, inferiors, noble, and base all emanate from it,
hence it is called
"law." In ancient law,
there were no people seeking office through petitions or recommendations,
no idly knowledgeable, widely learned, or argumentative scholars,
no extravagant attire,
no peculiar conduct,
all were encompassed by the law in serving their ruler.
Thus, what the enlightened king consistently upholds are two things:
first, clarifying the law and firmly adhering to it,
second, prohibiting private interests among the people and mobilizing them,
these two
are what the ruler consistently maintains.
Now, law
is what the ruler uses to unify the people and command subordinates;
private interests
are what subordinates use to undermine law and disrupt the ruler.
Therefore, the sage ruler establishes standards and sets laws, firmly upholding them,
so that even talented, learned,
widely knowledgeable, and erudite individuals cannot cause disorder,
the powerful, wealthy, noble, or privately brave cannot encroach,
the trusted, close, and beloved cannot alienate,
rare and exotic treasures cannot bewilder,
and all things and affairs not within the law's scope cannot sway.
Thus, law is the ultimate Way of the world,
the precious tool of the sage ruler.
Nowadays, the world is not like this.
All have good laws but cannot uphold them.
Thus, talented and learned individuals,
those with broad knowledge and deep understanding,
can use their wisdom to disrupt the laws and confuse their superiors;
the powerful, wealthy, and privately brave
can use their influence to violate the laws and oppress others;
neighboring feudal lords can use their authority to install sons and appoint ministers;
high officials can use their personal interests to win over the common people,
diverting public wealth to reward private followers.
Under such circumstances, to expect the laws to be implemented
and the state to be well-governed
is impossible.
A sage ruler, however, is not like this.
Ministers and chancellors cannot divert resources for private gain,
and officials cannot appoint their close associates.
The sage ruler also clarifies the laws and firmly upholds them.
Officials cultivate harmony and gather around to serve their ruler,
while the people live in peace, obey orders, follow the laws, and carry out their duties. Hence it is said:
There are those who create the laws,
those who uphold the laws,
and those who are governed by the laws.
The one who creates the laws is the ruler;
those who uphold the laws are the ministers;
those governed by the laws are the people.
When rulers, ministers, superiors, inferiors, noble, and humble all follow the law,
this is called great order.
Thus, a ruler has three methods:
To love others without rewarding them privately,
to dislike others without punishing them privately,
but to establish standards and laws and judge by measure—
this is the superior ruler.
To love others and reward them privately,
to dislike others and punish them privately,
to turn against high ministers,
alienate close aides,
and rely solely on one's own mind to judge—
this is the mediocre ruler.
When ministers reward those they favor privately
and punish those they dislike privately,
violating public laws,
corrupting upright intentions,
and the ruler relies solely on these ministers—
this is the endangered ruler.
Therefore, as a ruler,
one should not excessively love others,
nor excessively dislike others.
Excessive love is called losing virtue,
excessive dislike is called losing authority.
If both authority and virtue are lost,
the ruler is endangered.
Thus, the enlightened king wields six powers:
to give life, to take life,
to enrich, to impoverish,
to ennoble, to debase.
These six handles
are what the ruler controls.
The ruler occupies four positions:
first, civility; second, martial prowess; third, authority; fourth, virtue.
These four positions
are where the ruler stands.
To lend others what one controls
is called losing the handles;
to lend others where one stands
is called losing one's position.
Losing the handles and position,
yet expecting orders to be carried out,
is impossible.
Laws not being impartial,
orders not being complete,
this too is the path to losing handles and position.
Thus, there are those who twist the law,
and those who destroy orders—
these are what the sage ruler prohibits in himself.
Hence, the noble cannot intimidate him,
the wealthy cannot bribe him,
the lowly cannot serve him obsequiously,
the close cannot gain undue intimacy,
the beautiful cannot seduce him.
Firmly rooted and unmoving,
deviant and wicked schemes then fear him;
when strangeness is transformed and wickedness corrected,
orders go forth and the people follow.
Thus, the sage ruler establishes measures,
sets standards and laws,
firm as heaven and earth,
steady as the constellations,
bright as the sun and moon,
trustworthy as the four seasons.
Thus, orders go forth and the people obey.
But a failing ruler is not like this:
he establishes laws only to abolish them,
issues orders only to reverse them,
twists the law to follow private interests,
and destroys orders, leaving them incomplete.
Thus, the noble can intimidate him,
the wealthy can bribe him,
the lowly can serve him obsequiously,
the close can gain undue intimacy,
the beautiful can seduce him.
If these five
are not restrained in oneself,
then officials and common people alike
will harbor selfish intentions
and seek to manipulate their ruler.
If they succeed in their aims,
the ruler's power is daily eroded.
If they fail in their aims,
resentment grows daily.
With daily erosion and growing resentment,
this is the path of a failing ruler.
Any ruler who cannot apply his laws,
cannot follow his own intentions,
but acts according to his ministers,
deviating from the law to heed the noble—
this is what is called being intimidated by the noble.
When the wealthy use gold and jade to serve the ruler and make requests,
and the ruler deviates from the law to heed them,
this is what is called being bribed by the wealthy.
When the lowly use submissive, humble, and sorrowful expressions to appeal to their ruler,
and the ruler thereby deviates from the law to heed them,
this is what is called being served obsequiously by the lowly.
When the close use their proximity and intimacy to make requests of their ruler,
and the ruler thereby deviates from the law to heed them,
this is what is called gaining undue intimacy with the close.
When the beautiful use clever words and charming appearances to petition their ruler,
and the ruler thereby deviates from the law to heed them,
this is what is called being seduced by the beautiful.
In a well-governed age, it is not like this:
without distinguishing between close or distant, near or far, noble or humble, beautiful or ugly,
judgment is made by measure.
Those who are executed bear no resentment,
those who are rewarded feel no personal gratitude.
Acting through the legal system,
it is as impartial as heaven and earth.
Thus, officials have no private debates,
scholars have no private discussions,
the people have no private opinions—
all empty their hearts to heed their superiors.
The superior judges with fairness,
decides by the legal system,
thus bearing the weight of the world without burden.
But a disorderly ruler is not like this:
he has private vision,
so there are things he does not see;
he has private hearing,
so there are things he does not hear;
he has private thoughts,
so there are things he does not know.
For private interests
are the path to obstruction and loss of position.
When the ruler abandons public law and heeds private opinions,
then officials and common people all establish private standards
to teach in the state,
forming cliques and factions
to promote their private interests,
using petitions and recommendations
to disrupt public law,
each employing their schemes
to curry favor with the superior.
If the superior lacks measures to prohibit this,
private opinions will daily increase,
while public law daily declines.
The state's lack of order
arises from this.
For the relationship between ruler and minister
is like the positions of heaven and earth;
the people
are like the images of all things.
Each should stand in their appointed roles and await the ruler's commands—how can officials and people each use their private minds and establish selfish interests?
Thus, those who follow the ruler's orders in their actions,
even if they cause harm or failure, shall not be punished;
those who act without the ruler's orders,
even if they achieve merit and benefit,
shall be guilty and sentenced to death.
Therefore, subordinates serving their superiors
are like an echo responding to a sound;
ministers serving their ruler
are like a shadow following a form.
Hence, when superiors issue orders, subordinates respond;
when the ruler acts, ministers follow—
this is the way of orderly governance.
If one acts without the ruler's orders
and achieves merit and benefit,
yet is rewarded for it,
this teaches reckless action;
if one follows the ruler's orders in action,
causes harm or failure,
and is punished for it,
this leads the people to weigh gains and losses and deviate from the law.
If all officials and the common people consider their own interests
and act based on their selfish intentions,
then legal institutions will be destroyed, and orders will not be carried out.
What is called a well-governed state
is one where the ruler's way is clear;
an enlightened ruler
possesses methods and strategies and cannot be deceived,
is meticulous about laws and prohibitions so they cannot be violated,
and discerns duties and responsibilities so they cannot be disrupted;
thus, officials dare not act out of selfishness,
the noble cannot oppress the lowly,
the close cannot block the distant,
the orphaned, widowed, elderly, and weak do not lose their proper place,
and within the borders, clarity prevails without overstepping boundaries—
this is what is called a well-governed state;
thus, the Ming Fǎ states:
"What is called a well-governed state
is one where the ruler's way is clear."
What is called a disordered state
is one where ministers' methods prevail.
An enlightened ruler
is what the superior uses to unify the people and command subordinates.
Selfish methods
are what subordinates use to encroach upon the superior and disrupt the ruler.
Thus, if laws are abandoned and selfish actions prevail,
the ruler becomes isolated and alone,
while ministers form cliques and factions;
in such a case,
the ruler is weak and the ministers are strong—
this is what is called a disordered state;
thus, the Ming Fǎ states:
"What is called a disordered state
is one where ministers' methods prevail."
Honoring the ruler and humbling the ministers
is not due to affection,
but because the ruler holds the power to prevail;
when an enlightened ruler is in position,
possessing an inevitable authority to govern,
then officials dare not do wrong;
thus, the reason officials dare not deceive the ruler
is not out of love for the ruler,
but out of fear of the ruler's authority;
the people's willingness to serve
is not out of love for the ruler,
but out of fear of the ruler's laws and orders;
therefore, an enlightened ruler wields certain means of victory
to govern the people who must be used;
occupies a position of inevitable respect
to control ministers who must submit;
thus, orders are carried out and prohibitions are heeded,
the ruler is honored and the ministers are humble;
thus, the Ming Fǎ states:
"Honoring the ruler and humbling the ministers,
is not a matter of affection,
but of prevailing through authority."
Officials being diligent
is not due to kindness,
but because punishments are certain.
In the governance of an enlightened ruler,
he suspends ranks and emoluments to encourage the people;
the people see benefit in serving the superior,
so the ruler has means to employ them;
he establishes punishments to intimidate subordinates;
subordinates fear the superior,
so the ruler has means to control them;
thus, without ranks and emoluments, the ruler has no way to encourage the people;
without punishments, the ruler has no way to intimidate the masses;
therefore, ministers who act rationally and obey orders
do so not out of love for the ruler,
but to pursue benefit and avoid harm.
Officials who uphold the law without deceit
do so not out of love for the ruler,
but to receive ranks and emoluments and avoid punishments;
thus, the Ming Fǎ states:
"Officials performing their duties,
is not due to kindness,
but because punishments are certain."
Thus, if ruler and ministers share the same way, there is disorder.
The ruler
holds exclusive power over life and death,
occupies a position of authority,
wields the handle of issuing orders and enforcing prohibitions,
to command his officials—
this is the way of the ruler.
Ministers,
occupying humble positions,
follow the ruler's orders,
adhere to their fundamental duties,
and manage their assigned responsibilities—
this is the way of ministers;
thus, if the ruler practices the way of ministers, there is disorder;
if ministers practice the way of the ruler, there is peril;
so if there is no distinction between superior and subordinate,
and ruler and ministers share the same way,
it is the root of disorder;
thus, the Ming Fǎ states:
"If ruler and ministers share the same way, there is disorder."
Delegating exclusive power leads to loss.
The reason ministers fear and serve the ruler diligently
is that they desire life and dread death;
if people did not desire life
or dread death,
they could not be controlled;
if the power of life and death rests solely with high ministers,
and the ruler is not endangered,
such a thing has never occurred;
thus, if order and disorder are not decided by law but determined by powerful ministers,
and the power of life and death is not controlled by the ruler but lies with subordinates,
this is a parasitic ruler;
therefore, if a ruler exclusively delegates his authority to others,
he will inevitably face the calamity of being overthrown and killed;
if he exclusively delegates his legal system to others,
he will inevitably encounter the disaster of chaos and ruin;
such actions
are the way of a perishing ruler.
Thus, the Ming Fǎ states:
"Delegating exclusive power leads to loss."
There are four ways a state perishes:
If orders fundamentally do not issue forth,
it is called extinction.
Whenever a ruler cannot enforce his orders,
abandons the law and allows officials to act arbitrarily,
his majesty already abolished,
his authority already seized,
orders cannot be issued,
officials do not serve him,
the people are not directed by him,
the masses within the borders are uncontrolled,
then the state is not his state,
and the people are not his people;
in such a case,
it is the way of an extinct ruler;
thus, the Ming Fǎ states:
"Orders not issuing forth is called extinction."
If orders issue forth but are obstructed along the way,
it is called blockage.
The way of an enlightened ruler
allows the lowly to be seen without waiting for the noble,
high ministers to advance without relying on court attendants,
all officials to communicate directly,
and all ministers to be clearly visible.
Those who are to be punished,
the ruler sees their crimes.
Those who are to be rewarded,
the ruler knows their merits.
When knowledge and insight are not confused,
rewards and punishments are not misapplied,
and there exist methods that remain unobscured,
then there is no danger of obstruction;
a disorderly ruler, however, is not so,
for laws and decrees do not reach the people,
the distant are isolated and blocked,
and cannot be heard,
such is the way of obstruction,
thus the Ming Fǎ states:
"When decrees are issued but delayed,
it is called obstruction."
When the sentiments of the people are not conveyed upward,
it is called blockage.
The means by which ministers seize power to commit treachery
is usurping the ruler's authority;
when ministers usurp the ruler's authority,
then the ruler's commands cannot be carried out,
and the sentiments of the people are not conveyed upward,
the power of ministers
can separate ruler and subject, preventing the truth of good and evil from being known,
and keeping news of fortune and misfortune from penetrating through,
leaving the ruler bewildered with no way to understand,
such is the way of a blocked ruler;
thus the Ming Fǎ states:
"When the sentiments of the people are not conveyed upward,
it is called blockage."
When the sentiments of the people are conveyed upward but the path is halted,
it is called infringement.
An enlightened ruler
hears widely yet decides alone,
opening many channels;
the way of ministers
allows the lowly to inform the high,
the humble to advise the noble,
thus treacherous men dare not deceive;
a disorderly ruler is not so,
listening without method or calculation,
deciding matters without cross-examination,
so the incapable gain access above,
while corrupt ministers monopolize the state,
the ruler's vision is obscured and hearing blocked,
loyal ministers wishing to remonstrate cannot advance,
such is the way of an infringed ruler;
thus the Ming Fǎ states:
"When the sentiments of the people are conveyed upward but the path is halted,
it is called infringement."
Thus the origins of extinction, infringement, blockage, and obstruction
stem from the failure to establish laws.
When a ruler governs the state,
there must be laws and decrees;
with rewards and punishments in place,
so his laws and decrees are clear,
and where rewards and punishments are established appropriately,
then the ruler is honored and treachery does not arise;
if his laws and decrees are perverse,
and where rewards and punishments are established inappropriately,
then ministers establish private interests and obstruct them,
forming cliques to seize and kill;
thus the Ming Fǎ states:
"The origins of extinction, blockage, infringement, and obstruction
stem from the failure to establish laws."
Therefore, when the ancient kings governed the state,
they did not indulge whims outside the law,
for legal measures
are what the ruler uses to control the world and prohibit treachery,
and to govern the realm and serve the ancestral temple.
Private whims
are what create chaos, nurture treachery, and harm public justice,
leading to obstruction, loss of correctness, and perilous decline;
thus when legal measures are practiced, the state is orderly,
when private whims are practiced, the state is chaotic.
An enlightened ruler, even toward those he loves in heart,
does not reward if they have no merit;
even toward those he hates in heart,
does not punish if they are without crime;
he examines according to legal standards to verify gains and losses,
and does not pay attention to anything outside the law;
thus the Ming Fǎ states:
"When the ancient kings governed the state,
they did not indulge whims outside the law."
Nor did they bestow favors within the law.
When an enlightened ruler governs the state,
he acts according to what is appropriate,
practicing correct principles,
so those deserving reward
cannot be refused by the ministers.
Those deserving punishment
dare not be avoided by the ministers.
For rewarding merit and punishing crime
is how to bring benefit and eliminate harm for the world.
If weeds are not removed,
they harm the grain.
If bandits are not punished,
they injure good people.
To abandon public law and practice private favor
is to benefit treachery and encourage violence.
Practicing private favor and rewarding the unmerited
makes the people opportunistic and expectant of the ruler.
Practicing private favor and pardoning the guilty
makes the people disrespectful of superiors and prone to wrongdoing.
To abandon public law
and use private favor
is what an enlightened ruler does not do;
thus the Ming Fǎ states:
"Do not bestow favors within the law."
To act without anything unlawful
is how to prohibit errors and exclude private interests.
All rulers desire their people to be usable,
to make the people usable,
laws must be established and decrees enforced;
thus for governing the state and employing the masses, nothing compares to law,
for prohibiting excess and stopping violence, nothing compares to punishment;
thus the poor may desire to seize the wealth of the rich,
yet dare not,
because the law does not allow it.
The strong may be able to bully the weak,
yet dare not,
for fear of legal punishment;
thus in the affairs of all officials,
if examined by law,
then treachery does not arise.
Violent and arrogant people,
if punished by penalty,
then disaster does not occur.
When ministers advance together,
if measured by standards,
then private interests have no place to stand;
thus the Ming Fǎ states:
"To act without anything unlawful
is how to prohibit errors and exclude private interests."
Authority should not be placed in two hands,
government should not come from two gates.
What the ruler uses to control ministers
is authority and power;
thus if authority and power lie below,
then the ruler is controlled by ministers.
If authority and power lie above,
then ministers are controlled by the ruler;
for an obstructed ruler,
it is not that his gates are blocked,
or his doors guarded,
yet his commands are not carried out,
prohibitions not stopped,
his desires unfulfilled,
because he has lost his authority and power;
thus if authority and power reside solely with the ruler,
then ministers fear and respect.
If laws and governance issue solely from the ruler,
then the world submits to virtue;
thus if authority and power are divided among ministers,
then commands are not carried out.
If laws and governance issue from ministers,
then the people do not obey;
thus when an enlightened ruler governs the world,
authority and power reside solely with the ruler,
and are not shared with ministers,
laws and governance are controlled solely by the ruler,
and do not follow from ministers;
thus the Ming Fǎ states:
"Authority should not be placed in two hands,
government should not come from two gates."
Governing the state by law
is simply a matter of action and restraint.
An enlightened ruler,
unifies standards and measures,
establishes models and norms,
and firmly upholds them,
so that when orders are issued, the people follow.
The law is
the standard of the world,
the model for all affairs.
Officials are
those on whom the people's lives depend;
Thus, in the governance of an enlightened ruler,
those who conform to the law are rewarded,
and those who violate the law are punished.
Therefore, punishing crimes according to the law
makes the people accept death without resentment.
Measuring achievements by the law,
then the people receive rewards without feeling indebted,
this is the effect of applying the law in actions;
hence the Mingfǎ states:
"Governing the state by law
is simply a matter of proper application."
Therefore, where there is a system of laws and standards,
one cannot be tricked by deceit and falsehood;
where there are scales for weighing,
one cannot be deceived about lightness or heaviness;
scales are
what determine the measure of lightness and heaviness,
yet people do not manipulate them,
not because they dislike profit in their hearts,
but because the weights cannot alter the measure of quantity,
and the balance cannot change the measure of weight;
people know that manipulating the scales is useless,
so they do not do it;
thus, when an enlightened ruler is in power,
officials cannot bend the law,
clerks cannot act for private gain,
the people know that currying favor with clerks is useless,
so wealth and goods are not offered to clerks,
the scales are impartial and just in dealing with matters,
thus treacherous and deceitful people cannot carry out their selfish schemes;
hence the Mingfǎ states:
"Where there are scales for weighing,
one cannot be deceived about lightness and heaviness."
Where there are measures of xún and zhàng,
one cannot err in length;
cùn, chǐ, xún, and zhàng are
what ascertain the true length,
so using cùn and chǐ to measure shortness and length,
then every action will be without error;
thus, the measure of cùn and chǐ,
even for the wealthy, noble, and powerful,
does not increase the length;
even for the poor, humble, and lowly,
does not decrease the length,
it is fair and without bias,
so treacherous and deceitful people cannot cause error;
hence the Mingfǎ states:
"Where there are measures of xún and zhàng,
one cannot err in length."
If the ruler abandons the law and promotes based on reputation,
then ministers will turn away from the ruler and form cliques below;
if officials are appointed based on factions,
then the people will focus on social connections rather than seeking usefulness.
The reason the state falls into disorder
is neglecting actual affairs and relying on false praise,
thus an enlightened ruler, when hearing reports,
holds speakers accountable for the facts,
tests those praised by assigning them to office,
punishes those who speak without substance,
punishes officials who disrupt governance,
so that empty words dare not be presented;
the unworthy dare not accept office.
A disorderly ruler is not like this,
hearing words without verifying their truth,
so ministers use false praise to advance their clique,
appointing officials without demanding achievements,
thus foolish and corrupt officials remain in court;
in this way,
ministers recommend each other with fine reputations,
lend each other credit for achievements,
strive to expand their cliques,
and are not used by the ruler,
hence the Mingfǎ states:
"If the ruler abandons the law and promotes based on reputation,
then ministers will turn away from the ruler and form cliques below;
if officials are appointed based on factions,
then the people will focus on cliques rather than seeking usefulness."
Thus, when officials fail in governance,
it is because the ruler rewards based on praise,
and punishes based on slander.
A disorderly ruler does not examine ministers' achievements,
rewarding those with much praise,
not scrutinizing their faults,
punishing those with much slander.
In such cases,
treacherous ministers gain rewards without merit,
while loyal ministers are punished without crime.
Thus, with much achievement but no reward,
ministers will not strive to exert themselves;
with upright conduct but punishment,
the wise and sage cannot fully use their abilities;
if wealth and goods can obtain ranks and emoluments,
then corrupt and disgraceful people hold office;
if unworthy proteges hold high positions,
then the people betray public law and flock to the powerful,
in this way,
honest people lose their posts,
and incorrupt officials lose their governance;
hence the Mingfǎ states:
"When officials fail in governance,
it is because the ruler rewards based on praise and punishes based on slander."
Then those who love rewards and fear punishment
abandon the public way and practice private arts.
When impartial officials govern,
enforcing the law without selfishness,
then treacherous ministers cannot gain benefits,
this is what treacherous ministers strive to undermine.
If the ruler does not verify their faults,
punishing them based on unsubstantiated words,
then treacherous ministers will inevitably flatter the powerful and seek recommendations,
to avoid punishment and receive emoluments and rewards;
hence the Mingfǎ states:
"Those who love rewards and fear punishment
abandon the public way and practice private arts."
Colluding to conceal for each other,
they forget the ruler and die for friendships, to enhance their reputation.
Treacherous ministers ruin their ruler
gradually and subtly,
causing the ruler to be deluded without self-awareness;
above, they watch for the ruler's inclinations for each other,
below, they buy reputation among the people,
praising their clique to make the ruler honor them,
slandering the uncooperative to make the ruler dismiss them;
what they consider beneficial or harmful,
the ruler hears and acts upon.
Thus,
all ministers forget the ruler and rush to private cliques.
Hence the Mingfǎ states:
"Colluding to conceal for each other,
thus they forget the ruler and form private cliques to enhance their reputation."
Therefore, those with many connections have much praise,
forming cliques inside and out,
even if greatly treacherous,
they obscure the ruler greatly.
If the ruler lacks methods and strategies,
ministers can easily deceive him;
if the state lacks clear laws,
the people will lightly do wrong,
thus when treacherous and evil people handle state affairs
then ministers look to personal gain and harm
in this way
there are many who watch and listen for treacherous people
even with great righteousness the ruler cannot know it hence the Mingfǎ says those with many cliques have much praise
forming cliques inside and out even if greatly treacherous they obscure the ruler greatly
thus loyal ministers die for non-crimes,
and evil ministers rise without merit.
All who are called loyal ministers
strive to clarify laws and methods,
assisting the ruler day and night,
understanding the principles of measures to govern the world.
Treacherous and evil ministers,
knowing that clear laws and methods will bring order,
and order will trap treacherous ministers while revealing masters of law and method,
therefore what treacherous and evil ones
strive to accomplish is to keep the law unclear
and the enlightened ruler unawakened,
so they can obtain what they desire.
Thus when upright ministers are employed,
treacherous ministers are trapped and harmed;
this is the situation where the upright and the treacherous cannot both advance.
When treacherous and evil ministers are by the ruler's side,
they cannot but be detested. Only by detesting them
can harm be avoided; otherwise, they will inevitably wait for
the ruler's moments of negligence to endanger him day and night. If the ruler
does not scrutinize and instead adopts their words,
then loyal ministers will be without fault
yet die in distress, while treacherous ministers will achieve no merit but enjoy wealth and honor.
Therefore, the "Illuminated Laws" state:
"Loyal ministers die though not guilty,
and evil ministers rise though without merit."
Those who die are not guilty,
and those who rise are without merit.
Thus, as ministers, they prioritize the private over the public.
Wealth, honor, dignity, and prominence,
long-lasting possession of the realm,
are things no ruler fails to desire.
Orders carried out and prohibitions heeded,
unmatched within the seas,
are things no ruler fails to desire.
Deception, encroachment, and oppression,
are things no ruler fails to detest.
Losing the realm,
and the destruction of the ancestral temples,
are things no ruler fails to detest.
Loyal ministers wish to clarify laws and methods to achieve the ruler's desires and eliminate what he detests,
but treacherous ministers who control the ruler
use private interests to endanger them,
so loyal ministers have no way to advance their just and impartial strategies.
Therefore, the "Illuminated Laws" state:
"Those who die are not guilty,
those who rise are without merit,
thus as ministers, they prioritize the private over the public."
Ten visits to private doors,
not one to the court;
the disordered ruler's distribution of ranks and emoluments
does not follow laws and decrees to assess achievements;
his imposition of punishments
does not follow laws and decrees to examine faults,
but instead heeds the words of powerful ministers;
thus, if a minister wishes to reward someone,
the ruler rewards them;
if a minister wishes to punish someone,
the ruler punishes them,
abandoning public laws,
and exclusively listening to powerful ministers.
In this way,
all officials strive to form cliques,
valuing powerful ministers and forgetting their ruler,
flocking to the doors of powerful ministers instead of the court.
Therefore, the "Illuminated Laws" state:
"Ten visits to private doors,
not one to the court."
A hundred plans for their families,
not one for the state.
The enlightened ruler governs
by clarifying duties and responsibilities,
and supervising the completion of tasks;
those capable of their posts hold office,
those incapable are dismissed;
thus, all officials exhaust their abilities and efforts to manage their affairs.
The disordered ruler is not so,
so officials hold positions,
receive generous emoluments,
but none focus on governing the state,
aiming instead to control the state's important matters and monopolize their benefits,
preying on the people to enrich their families.
Therefore, the "Illuminated Laws" state:
"A hundred plans for their families,
not one for their state."
Though the number of subordinates is large,
it is not to honor the ruler;
though the officials are complete,
it is not to serve the state.
This is called the state having no people.
When an enlightened ruler is in power,
all within the borders strive to serve their ruler,
officials divide duties to achieve order,
and secure the state and families.
The disordered ruler is not so,
though there are brave and strong men,
powerful ministers privatize them,
and they do not serve the ruler;
though there are wise and intelligent men,
powerful ministers privatize them,
and they do not govern the state;
thus, though the number of subordinates is large,
they cannot advance;
though the officials are complete,
they cannot exercise control.
In such a case,
there is the name of a ruler but not the reality.
Therefore, the "Illuminated Laws" state:
"Though the number of subordinates is large,
it is not to honor the ruler.
Though the officials are complete,
it is not to serve the state,
this is called the state having no people."
The state having no people
does not mean the court officials are few,
but that families strive to benefit each other,
not striving to honor the ruler.
The enlightened ruler
makes subordinates exert effort and abide by legal duties,
so officials strive to honor the ruler and dare not care for their families.
The distinction between ruler and minister is clear,
the positions of superior and inferior are defined,
so powerful ministers each stay in their place and dare not esteem each other.
The disordered ruler is not so,
laws and institutions are abandoned and not implemented,
so officials strive to benefit their families,
there is no distinction between ruler and minister,
no difference between superior and inferior,
so officials strive to esteem each other.
In such a case,
it is not that court officials are few,
but that the multitude is not of use.
Therefore, the "Illuminated Laws" state:
"The state having no people
does not mean court officials
are few,
but that families strive to benefit each other,
not striving to honor the ruler,
powerful ministers strive to esteem each other,
and do not serve the state."
Powerful ministers strive to esteem each other and not serve the state;
minor officials hold onto emoluments to cultivate connections,
not taking office as their duty,
so offices lose their function.
When the ruler establishes offices and appoints officials,
it is not merely to honor them personally,
or to provide them generous support.
It is to make them uphold the ruler's laws,
carry out the ruler's orders,
govern the common people,
and punish bandits and thieves.
Therefore, those appointed to high office
receive noble rank and ample emoluments;
those appointed to low office
receive humble rank and meager emoluments.
Ranks and emoluments
are what the ruler uses to make officials govern their duties.
The disordered ruler's governance,
placing them in honored positions,
giving them generous emoluments,
they nurture their associates
and do not focus on official duties.
In this way,
offices lose their function.
Therefore, the "Illuminated Laws" state:
"Minor officials hold emoluments to nurture associates,
not taking office as their duty,
so offices lose their function."
Thus, the ancient kings in governing the state
used laws to select people,
not promoting on their own.
The enlightened ruler in selecting the worthy
tests those claiming courage in the army,
tests those claiming wisdom in office.
Those tested in the army and achieving merit are promoted;
those tested in office and governing effectively are employed.
Thus, through military achievements, courage and cowardice are determined;
through governance in office, foolishness and wisdom are determined.
So the appearance of courage, cowardice, foolishness, and wisdom
becomes as distinct as black and white.
The disordered ruler is not so,
hearing words but not testing,
so boastful speakers gain employment.
Appointing people without official testing,
thus the unworthy are not constrained.
Thus, the enlightened ruler uses laws to examine words and seek their substance,
appoints officials to positions and assesses their achievements,
relying solely on laws without promoting based on personal judgment;
therefore, the Mingfǎ states:
"When the former kings governed the state,
they used laws to select people,
not promoting based on personal judgment;"
they used laws to measure achievements,
not evaluating based on personal estimation.
All that is called achievement
is what stabilizes the ruler and benefits the myriad people;
destroying enemy armies and killing their generals,
winning battles and capturing territories,
ensuring the ruler has no worry of peril or destruction,
and the common people suffer no harm of death or captivity
—this is how military officers achieve merit.
Upholding the ruler's laws,
governing within the borders,
ensuring the strong do not bully the weak,
the many do not oppress the few,
the myriad people joyfully exhaust their strength to support and serve their ruler,
—this is how officials achieve merit.
Correcting the ruler's errors,
remedying the ruler's faults,
clarifying principles of righteousness to guide the ruler,
so the ruler has no depraved conduct,
no worry of being deceived or obscured,
—this is how ministers achieve merit;
thus, when the enlightened ruler governs,
he clarifies duties and assesses achievements,
rewarding those with merit,
punishing those who disrupt the laws,
applying punishments and rewards
each appropriately,
without the ruler personally intervening;
therefore, the Mingfǎ states:
"Using laws to measure achievements,
not evaluating based on personal estimation."
Thus, ability cannot be hidden nor failure concealed;
failure cannot be disguised.
When the enlightened ruler governs,
he examines right and wrong,
investigates actual circumstances,
applying standards to assess them,
acting in accordance with laws,
refraining when not in accordance;
rewarding when achievements fulfill promises,
punishing when they do not;
thus, those claiming wisdom and ability
must demonstrate achievements before being promoted;
those deemed wicked or failing
must show faults before being dismissed;
in this way,
the worthy advance without being envied,
the incompetent are hindered and dismissed without being promoted;
therefore, the Mingfǎ states:
"Ability cannot be hidden,
and failure cannot be disguised."
Praise cannot promote anyone,
and slander cannot demote anyone.
The way of the enlightened ruler
establishes what the people desire,
to seek their achievements,
hence creating ranks and emoluments to encourage them.
It establishes what the people dislike,
to prohibit their wickedness,
hence instituting punishments to intimidate them.
Thus, assessing achievements to bestow rewards,
assessing crimes to impose punishments;
in this way,
among the officials, those without merit dare not advance,
and slandering the innocent cannot cause demotion,
therefore, the Mingfǎ states:
"Praise cannot promote anyone,
and slander cannot demote anyone."
Then, between ruler and minister, there is clear distinction,
clear distinction makes governance easy,
controlling the officials,
monopolizing life and death,
is the ruler's role.
Looking up to the system,
is the minister's role.
Majestic authority and honor,
are the ruler's role.
Lowly status and fearful respect,
are the minister's role.
Issuing commands and enforcing prohibitions,
is the ruler's role.
Upholding laws and obeying,
is the minister's role.
Thus, the interaction between ruler and minister
involves positions of high and low.
Like heaven and earth,
their roles are as distinct
as white and black.
Hence, with clear distinction between ruler and minister,
the ruler is honored, the minister humble,
in this way,
the subordinates follow the superior
like an echo responds to sound;
the ministers model the ruler
