like a shadow follows the form;
thus, the superior commands and the subordinate responds,
the ruler acts and the ministers follow,
with commands, they are executed,
with prohibitions, they cease,
with pursuits, they are attained,
this is called easy governance;
therefore, the Mingfǎ states:
"Between ruler and minister,
clear distinction makes governance easy."
Although the ruler does not personally act below,
adhering to the laws suffices for action.
The enlightened ruler employs methods to command ministers,
making the officials contribute their wisdom and ability,
offer their specialized skills,
so the wise present their strategies, the capable
advance their achievements,
using earlier words to supervise
later deeds; what is presented
if fitting, reward; if not fitting,
then punish. Establishing offices,
appointing officials to govern the people,
examining them by law, testing their performance, succeeding by upholding the law,
thus the ruler avoids toil while duties are fulfilled;
therefore, the Mingfǎ states:
"Although the ruler does not personally act below,
adhering to the laws suffices for action."
In ancient times, those who wished to rectify the age and harmonize the world would first observe state governance,
evaluate affairs,
examine folk customs,
trace the origins of order and chaos,
understand where successes and failures lie,
then proceed to act. Thus, laws could be established and governance implemented.
If the myriad people are not harmonious,
the state is not stable,
the fault lies not with the superior,
then the error is with the subordinates.
If the ruler acts contrary and does not follow the Way,
executes and kills unreasonably,
imposes heavy taxes,
exhausts the people's wealth,
issues urgent commands,
wears out the people's strength,
when wealth is exhausted
they cannot but plunder,
when strength is exhausted
they cannot but become negligent and rebellious.
Once the people are plundering and rebellious,
if laws are then applied to punish them,
this means punishments are severe but chaos increases.
When the people are weary, troubled, and lacking,
they disregard prohibitions and treat crimes lightly,
in such a case
the fault lies with the superior.
If the fault lies with the superior
and the superior does not reform,
then the myriad people have nowhere to entrust their lives.
If the ruler lightens punishments and governance,
is lenient with the百姓,
reduces taxes,
relaxes commands,
yet the people become licentious, unruly, act selfishly
and do not follow control,
adorn themselves with cunning and employ deceit,
rely on force and contend,
then the error lies with the subordinates.
When passing below,
if the ruler is not incorruptible and changes,
then violent men cannot be subdued,
and wicked chaos does not cease.
If violent men are not subdued,
and wicked chaos does not cease,
then the ruler's power is harmed
and his authority daily declines.
Therefore, for a ruler,
nothing is more valuable than victory.
What is called victory
means that laws are established and commands are implemented.
When laws are established and commands implemented,
then all ministers uphold the laws and adhere to their duties,
and the hundred officials have constancy.
"Laws do not harbor complexity,"
the myriad people become honest and sincere,
returning to fundamentals and conserving their strength.
Thus, rewards must be sufficient to motivate,
authority must be sufficient to overcome,
only then will the people follow.
Therefore, the wise rulers of ancient times
were not of one kind.
Their establishment of rewards ranged from meager to generous,
their setting of prohibitions from light to severe,
their actions and practices not necessarily the same,
not intentionally opposed,
but all changing with the times,
moving according to customs.
When the people are restless and conduct themselves perversely,
then rewards cannot but be generous,
and prohibitions cannot but be severe.
Thus, when sages establish generous rewards,
it is not extravagance;
when they set severe prohibitions,
it is not cruelty.
If rewards are meager,
the people gain no benefit;
if prohibitions are light,
the wicked do not fear them.
Establishing what brings no benefit to the people,
yet wishing to employ them,
then the people will not exhaust their efforts;
setting up what people do not fear,
yet wishing to prohibit,
then the wicked will not cease.
Therefore, when laws are proclaimed and commands issued,
the people do not follow.
Thus, if rewards are insufficient to encourage,
then officers and people will not be of use;
if punishments are not fearsome,
then violent men will lightly violate prohibitions.
The people submit to威慑 and execution
only then do they follow,
see benefit
only then are they employed,
are governed
only then are they rectified,
obtain security
only then are they tranquil.
If robbers and thieves are not subdued,
and wicked chaos does not cease,
the strong plunder the weak,
the many oppress the few,
this is what worries the world,
what the myriad people suffer from.
If worries and sufferings are not removed,
then the people cannot dwell in peace;
if the people cannot dwell in peace,
then the people's hope in the ruler is cut off.
No benefit is greater than order,
no harm greater than chaos.
The reason the Five Emperors and Three Kings succeeded in achievements and established fame,
becoming illustrious to later generations,
is that they brought benefit to the world and removed harm.
Their actions did not necessarily相同,
but their focus was one.
If the people are greedy and restless in conduct, yet punishments are light,
and offenses are not exposed,
then this encourages debauchery and facilitates wickedness.
Having a heart that loves the people,
yet in reality harming them.
These two must not be unexamined.
If robbers and thieves are not subdued,
then good people are endangered;
if laws and prohibitions are not established,
then奸邪 abound.
Thus, no task is more urgent than attending to current duties,
no governance more valuable than achieving balance.
If controlling the people is too harsh, they feel pressured,
if pressured, they become distressed,
if distressed, they lose what they preserve;
if too lenient, they become indulgent,
if indulgent, they become dissipated,
if dissipated, they act selfishly,
if acting selfishly, they deviate from the public good,
if deviating from the public good, they are hard to employ.
Therefore, the reason governance is not established
is that balance is not achieved. If balance is not achieved,
then governance is difficult to implement.
Thus, in balancing the governance of the people,
one must not fail to examine it.
The sage
understands the way of order and chaos,
and is familiar with the beginning and end of human affairs.
In governing the people,
he aims at benefiting them and that is all.
Therefore, in achieving balance, he does not admire antiquity,
nor does he linger in the present,
but changes with the times,
transforms with customs.
The way of ruling people
values nothing more than victory.
Victory establishes the way of the ruler;
the way of the ruler established,
then the people follow;
the people following,
then teaching can be established and transformation accomplished.
If the people are not convinced in heart and obedient in body,
they cannot be taught the refinements of ritual and righteousness.
The ruler must not fail to examine this.
In all ways of governing a state,
one must first enrich the people,
for when the people are rich, they are easy to govern;
when the people are poor, they are hard to govern.
How do we know this is so?
When the people are rich, they cherish their homes and value their families,
cherishing homes and valuing families,
they respect superiors and fear punishment,
respecting superiors and fearing punishment,
they are easy to govern.
When the people are poor, they endanger their communities and轻视 their families,
endangering communities and轻视 families,
they dare to defy superiors and violate prohibitions,
defying superiors and violating prohibitions,
they are hard to govern.
Therefore, a well-governed state is always rich,
while a chaotic state is inevitably poor.
Thus, those skilled at governing a state
must first enrich the people,
then govern them.
In the past, the rulers of seventy-nine dynasties,
though their legal systems varied,
their commands differed,
all became kings under heaven—why?
Surely because their states were rich and grain abundant.
Wealthy states and abundant grain
are born from agriculture,
hence the former kings valued it.
Among urgent tasks for governing a state,
the foremost is to prohibit non-essential crafts and elaborate luxuries,
for if non-essential crafts and luxuries are prohibited,
the people have no means to idle for food,
and having no means to idle for food,
they must farm.
When the people are engaged in farming,
then fields are cultivated,
fields cultivated,
then grain is abundant,
grain abundant,
then the state is rich,
a rich state has strong soldiers,
strong soldiers win battles,
victors in battle expand territory.
Thus, the former kings knew that increasing population, strengthening the military,
expanding territory, and enriching the state necessarily arise from grain,
therefore they prohibited non-essential crafts,
stopped奇巧,
and benefited agricultural affairs.
Nowadays, those engaged in non-essential crafts and ingenious devices
work one day and have food for five.
Yet farmers who toil all year round
cannot produce enough to feed themselves.
Consequently, the people abandon fundamental endeavors and turn to peripheral trades.
When they forsake essential work for non-essential activities,
the fields become barren and the state impoverished.
Generally, farmers experience monthly shortages but annual surpluses.
If the authorities impose sudden and untimely levies,
the people must borrow at double interest to meet these demands.
Plowing and weeding are seasonal tasks,
but rainfall is not always sufficient,
forcing the people to borrow at double rates to hire labor.
Buying grain in autumn at five units
and selling in spring for ten,
this again constitutes double interest.
Thus, due to government exactions, the people face quadruple exploitation,
with market tolls,
treasury levies,
a tenth of grain,
and labor services
—these four items also amounting to double interest.
With one person supporting four masters,
even punishments for fleeing
cannot stop the exodus,
for grain is scarce and the people have no reserves.
East of Sōng Shān,
between the Hé and Rǔ rivers,
where crops sprout early and wither late,
the five grains flourish and ripen.
With four plantings, five harvests are reaped.
In an average year, one mǔ yields two shí,
and one man produces two hundred shí of grain.
Yet now granaries are empty and the people have no stores,
with farmers selling their children—
a sign that the rulers lack methods to balance this.
Thus, the ancient kings ensured that farmers,
scholars, merchants, and artisans exchanged skills and labors,
so that annual profits
did not excessively diverge.
Hence, the people, focused on one task, achieved equity.
When the people concentrate on one endeavor,
the land is cultivated,
and deceitful crafts do not arise.
With land cultivated,
grain abounds;
with abundant grain,
the state grows rich.
Without deceitful crafts,
the people are orderly. Wealth
and order—this is the way of true kings.
A state that produces no grain perishes;
one that produces grain but it perishes becomes a hegemon;
one that produces grain and preserves it attains kingship.
Grain is
what the people gravitate toward;
grain is
where wealth converges;
grain is
what the land yields.
With ample grain, all things under heaven arrive.
Thus, Shùn, with one move, formed a town;
with two, a capital;
with three, a state.
Shùn did not rely on harsh punishments
or severe prohibitions,
yet the people followed him,
for to leave meant harm,
and to follow meant benefit.
The ancient kings
excelled at removing harms and promoting benefits for the people,
so all under heaven turned to them.
Promoting benefits means
advancing agriculture;
removing harms means
prohibiting what harms farming.
When farming prospers, grain income increases;
with more grain, the state grows rich;
a rich state makes people secure in their homes and value their families,
and when they are secure and value their families,
even if customs are changed,
crowds driven, or people relocated,
to the point of execution,
they will not resent it.
This is the achievement of focusing on grain.
If the rulers do not benefit agriculture,
grain becomes scarce;
scarcity leads to poverty;
poverty makes people disregard their homes;
disregarding homes, they easily leave;
if they leave easily, the ruler's commands cannot be enforced,
and if commands are not enforced,
prohibitions cannot be upheld,
leading to
uncertain victory in battle
and insecure defense.
When commands are not obeyed,
prohibitions not upheld,
battles not won,
and defenses not firm,
such a ruler is called a parasitic sovereign.
This stems from not benefiting agriculture
and the harm of grain shortage.
Grain is
the king's fundamental task,
the ruler's great duty,
the means to attract people,
and the way to govern the state.
All essence of things,
when concentrated, gives life.
Below, it produces the five grains;
above, it forms the constellations.
Flowing between heaven and earth,
it is called ghosts and spirits;
stored within the breast,
it is called the sage.
Therefore, this vital force
shines brightly as if ascending to heaven,
recedes deeply as if entering an abyss,
spreads vast as if in the sea,
yet suddenly rests within oneself.
Thus, this vital force
cannot be restrained by force
but can be settled with virtue;
it answers not to calls
but may be met with harmony.
Guard it reverently without loss,
and this is called perfected virtue.
With virtue perfected, wisdom emerges,
and all things are attained.
The nature of the mind
is to fill and overflow of itself,
to generate and complete itself.
What causes its loss
is surely worry, joy, anger, desire, and profit.
If one can rid oneself of these,
the mind returns to wholeness.
The true state of the mind
thrives in tranquility and peace,
free from disturbance and chaos,
so harmony naturally arises.
Clearly, it seems close at hand;
fleetingly, it seems elusive;
boundlessly, it stretches to infinity.
This examination is not far—
daily employ its virtue.
The Way is what fills the form,
yet humans cannot hold it fast.
It goes without returning,
comes without lingering.
Silently, no sound is heard;
suddenly, it resides in the heart;
darkly, its form unseen,
continuously, it is born with us.
Unseen in form,
unheard in sound,
yet it orders completion—this is called the Way.
The Way has no fixed abode;
it dwells where the heart is good and loving.
When the mind is calm and the vital force orderly,
the Way can settle.
That Way is not distant;
through it, the people produce;
that Way does not depart;
through it, the people know.
Therefore,
abruptly, it seems within reach;
subtly, it seems to have no end.
The nature of the Way
dislikes noise and sound;
cultivate the mind and quiet the tones,
and the Way may be attained.
The Dào is that which the mouth cannot speak,
the eyes cannot see,
the ears cannot hear;
it is that by which we cultivate the heart and rectify the form;
it is that which, when lost, causes humans to die,
and when obtained, enables them to live;
it is that which, when lost, causes affairs to fail,
and when obtained, enables them to succeed.
In general, the Dào
has no root and no stem,
no leaves and no blossoms.
All things are born from it,
all things are completed by it;
we name it Dào.
Heaven governs uprightness,
Earth governs levelness,
Humanity governs tranquility.
Spring, autumn, winter, and summer
are the seasons of Heaven;
mountains, hills, rivers, and valleys
are the materials of Earth;
joy, anger, taking, and giving
are the plans of Humanity.
Therefore, the sage changes with the times but is not transformed,
follows things but does not shift.
Being able to be upright and tranquil,
then one can achieve stability.
With a stable heart within,
the ears and eyes become clear and sharp,
the four limbs become firm and strong,
and it can serve as the abode of the essence.
Essence is
the quintessence of qì.
With qì, the Dào is generated;
generation leads to thought,
thought leads to knowledge,
knowledge leads to cessation.
In general, the nature of the heart,
if it overreaches in knowledge, loses its vitality.
That which can transform a single thing is called spirit;
that which can change a single affair is called wisdom.
Transformation does not alter the qì,
change does not alter the wisdom;
only the gentleman who holds fast to the One can accomplish this!
Holding fast to the One without losing it,
one can rule over all things.
The gentleman employs things,
he is not employed by things;
this is the principle of attaining the One.
With the heart governed within,
governed words issue from the mouth,
governed actions are applied to people;
then the world becomes orderly.
With one word obtained, the world submits;
with one word settled, the world listens;
this is what is meant.
If the form is not upright,
virtue will not come;
if the center is not tranquil,
the heart will not be governed.
Rectify the form and attract virtue,
like Heaven's benevolence and Earth's righteousness,
then it will abundantly arrive of its own accord.
At the ultimate of spiritual clarity,
one illuminates and knows all things.
Maintaining the center without error,
not allowing things to disturb the senses,
not allowing the senses to disturb the heart,
this is called attaining the center.
There is a spirit naturally present in the body,
coming and going,
beyond anyone's ability to conceive.
Losing it inevitably leads to chaos,
obtaining it inevitably leads to order.
Reverently cleanse its abode,
and the essence will come of itself.
Reflect on it with concentrated thought,
calm the mind to govern it,
with a solemn demeanor and reverent awe,
the essence will reach perfect stability.
Once obtained, do not abandon it,
and the ears and eyes will not be excessive.
With the heart free from other distractions,
and an upright heart within,
all things attain their proper measure.
The Dào fills the entire world,
pervasive in the people's domain,
yet the people cannot know it.
A single word's understanding
extends upward to inspect Heaven,
downward to reach the Earth,
and spreads throughout the Nine Provinces.
What is the key to understanding it?
It lies in the governance of the heart.
When my heart is governed,
the senses are governed;
when my heart is tranquil,
the senses are tranquil.
That which governs them is the heart,
that which tranquilizes them is the heart.
The heart stores the heart,
within the heart there is yet another heart.
That heart within the heart
is the intention that precedes speech.
Intention then takes form,
form then leads to speech.
Speech then leads to command,
command then leads to order.
Without order, there must be chaos;
chaos leads to death.
When essence is preserved, life arises spontaneously;
externally, there is peace and flourishing;
internally stored, it becomes a springhead,
vast and harmonious,
forming an abyss of qì.
When the abyss does not run dry,
the four limbs become firm;
when the spring is not exhausted,
the nine orifices become unobstructed.
Then one can penetrate Heaven and Earth,
and cover the Four Seas.
With no confused thoughts within,
and no evil calamities without,
the heart is whole internally,
the form is whole externally,
one does not encounter heavenly disasters,
nor meet with human harm;
such a one is called a sage.
If a person can be upright and tranquil,
the skin becomes ample and relaxed,
the ears and eyes become clear and sharp,
the sinews stretch and the bones strengthen.
Then one can support the great circle (Heaven),
and tread upon the great square (Earth),
reflect with great clarity,
and see with great brightness.
Reverent and cautious without error,
daily renewing one's virtue,
comprehending all under Heaven,
reaching to the four extremes.
Reverently express this inner fullness,
this is called attaining internally.
If, however, one does not return (to this),
this is the error of this life.
In general, the Dào must be all-encompassing and meticulous,
must be broad and relaxed,
must be firm and solid.
Hold fast to the good without abandoning it,
expel excess and dilute the superficial;
once you know its ultimate,
return to the Dào and virtue.
With a whole heart within,
it cannot be concealed or hidden;
it is known through one's appearance and form,
visible in one's skin and complexion.
A welcoming aura of good qì
feels closer than brothers;
a welcoming aura of evil qì
is more harmful than weapons of war.
The sound of no-word
is swifter than thunder or drums.
The form of the heart's qì
is brighter than the sun and moon,
more discerning than one's parents.
Rewards are insufficient to encourage goodness,
punishments are insufficient to punish transgressions.
When the qì and intention are attained, the world submits;
when the heart and intention are settled, the world listens.
Concentrate the qì like a spirit,
and all things are present in fullness.
Can you concentrate it?
Can you unify it?
Can you know fortune and misfortune without divination?
Can one stop?
Can one cease?
Can one refrain from seeking it from others and attain it within oneself?
Ponder it, ponder it,
and ponder it again.
If pondering does not bring understanding,
spirits and deities will enlighten you.
It is not the power of spirits and deities,
but the ultimate state of vital energy.
When the four limbs are aligned,
and blood and breath are calm,
with unified intent focusing the mind,
ears and eyes not distracted,
even the distant seems near.
Reflection gives birth to wisdom,
negligence gives rise to worry,
arrogance breeds resentment,
melancholy begets illness,
and severe illness leads to death.
If one ponders without respite,
internally exhausted and externally pressured,
without early planning,
life will depart from its abode.
In eating, nothing is better than not being full,
in thinking, nothing is better than not forcing it;
moderate and harmonize them appropriately,
and it will come naturally.
For all human life,
Heaven provides the essence,
Earth provides the form,
combining these to make a person.
Harmony brings life,
disharmony brings no life.
Examining the way of harmony,
its essence is not visible,
its signs are not apparent.
Serenity fills the chest,
balanced governance resides in the heart,
this leads to longevity.
When anger exceeds its measure,
one should plan for it.
Moderate the five desires,
eliminate the two evils,
neither delighting nor angering,
serenity fills the chest.
For all human life,
it must be based on serenity.
What causes its loss,
must be joy, anger, worry, and distress.
Thus, to stop anger, nothing is better than poetry;
to remove worry, nothing is better than music;
to moderate music, nothing is better than ritual;
to uphold ritual, nothing is better than reverence;
to maintain reverence, nothing is better than stillness.
Inner stillness and outer reverence,
enable one to return to one's nature,
and the nature will be greatly stabilized.
The way of eating:
overfilling,
harms and the body does not thrive;
undereating,
withers bones and congeals blood.
Between fullness and restraint,
this is called harmonious achievement,
where essence finds its abode,
and wisdom is born.
When hunger and fullness lose their measure,
one should plan for it.
When full, move vigorously;
when hungry, broaden thoughts;
when old, engage in deep contemplation.
If full without vigorous movement,
energy does not reach the extremities;
if hungry without broad thinking,
fullness does not cease;
if old without deep contemplation,
exhaustion swiftly depletes.
Expand the heart and make it open,
relax the breath and make it broad,
the body remains tranquil and unmoved,
able to hold to one and discard all vexations,
seeing profit without being lured,
seeing harm without fear,
relaxed and benevolent,
finding joy within oneself alone,
this is called cloud-like energy,
the will moving as if in heaven.
For all human life,
it must be with joy.
Worry disrupts order,
anger disrupts harmony.
With worry, sorrow, joy, and anger,
the Way finds no place.
Calm love and desires,
correct encounters with chaos,
neither pulling nor pushing,
fortune will come of itself.
That Way comes naturally,
one can align with it and consult it,
stillness attains it,
agitation loses it.
The spiritual energy is in the heart,
coming and going,
so fine it has no inside,
so vast it has no outside.
What causes its loss,
is the harm of agitation.
If the heart can hold stillness,
the Way will settle of itself.
Those who attain the Way,
have regulated pores and discharging hairs,
with no decay in the chest.
The way of moderating desires,
ensures no harm from all things.
The Duke convened the feudal lords at Kuíqiū,
and wished to perform the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"In ancient times, seventy-two families performed the Fēng sacrifice on Tài Shān and the Shàn sacrifice on Liángfù,
and of those, I remember twelve.
In the past, Wúhuáishì
performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Yúnyun;
Fú Xī performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Yúnyun;
Shénnóng performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Yúnyun;
Yándì performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Yúnyun;
Huángdì performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Tíngtíng;
Zhuānxū performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Yúnyun;
Dì Kù performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Yúnyun;
Yáo performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Yúnyun;
Shùn performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Yúnyun;
Yǔ performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Kuàijī;
Tāng performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Yúnyun;
Zhōu Chéngwáng performed Fēng on Tài Shān,
and Shàn on Shèshǒu.
All received the Mandate before they could perform Fēng and Shàn."
Duke Huán said:
"I campaigned north against Shānróng,
passing through Gūzhú;
west against Dàxià,
crossing Liúshā,
binding the horses and suspending the chariots,
ascending Bēi'ěr Mountain;
south to Zhàolíng,
climbing Xióng'ěr Mountain
to gaze upon the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
I held three military assemblies,
and six peaceful gatherings,
uniting the feudal lords nine times,
rectifying the world once,
and no feudal lord defies me.
In the past, the three dynasties received the Mandate;
how is this any different?"
Thereupon, Guǎn Zhòng saw that the Duke could not be swayed by words,
so he used facts to illustrate, saying:
"In ancient Fēng and Shàn ceremonies,
millet from Hàoshàng,
and grain from Běilǐ,
were used for the offerings;
from between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
a three-ridged grass,
was used as the mat.
The Eastern Sea presented flatfish,
the Western Sea presented birds that share wings,
and then, fifteen kinds of things arrived without being summoned."
Now that phoenixes and qilins do not come,
fine grains do not grow,
while weeds and tares flourish,
and owls frequently arrive,
yet you wish to perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
is it not inappropriate?"
Thereupon, Duke Huán stopped.
Duke Huán asked Guǎnzǐ:
"To govern without chaos,
to be enlightened without obscurity,
how can this be achieved?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Clearly define duties and appoint officials accordingly,
then there will be governance without chaos,
enlightenment without obscurity."
The Duke said:
"May I ask how to enrich the state?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Work the land diligently and act in accordance with the seasons,
then the state will surely be enriched."
The Duke asked further:
"I wish to practice broad benevolence and great righteousness,
to benefit all under heaven,
what must be done to achieve this?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Punish the violent and prohibit wrongdoing,
preserve the perishing and restore the severed,
and pardon the innocent,
then benevolence will be broad and righteousness great."
The Duke said:
"I have heard that,
to punish the violent, prohibit wrongdoing, and pardon the innocent,
one must possess the instruments of victory in war,
and the strategies for attack and conquest,
before one can punish the violent, prohibit wrongdoing, and pardon the innocent.
May I ask about the instruments of victory in war?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Select the heroes of all under heaven,
gather the finest materials from all under heaven,
attract the skilled craftsmen of all under heaven,
then you will have the instruments of victory in war."
The Duke said:
"What about the strategies for attack and conquest?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Destroy their defenses,
disperse their stockpiles,
seize their food supplies,
then they will have no secure cities."
The Duke said:
"Then how should we recruit scholars?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Treat them with respect and courtesy,
be generous and do not deceive them,
then the scholars of all under heaven will come."
The Duke said:
"How to gather the finest materials from all under heaven?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Offer five for six,
nine for ten,
without fixed rates."
The Duke said:
"How to attract craftsmen?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Triple their pay,
and they will come without regard for the distance."
Duke Huán said:
"I already know about the instruments of victory in war,
and the strategies for attack and conquest.
May I ask how to conduct military campaigns, assault cities,
and make moves with knowledge of what comes first and what follows,
without losing the advantages of terrain?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Use wealth and examine maps."
The Duke said:
"How to be certain of victory in open battles?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Through surprise tactics."
The Duke said:
"I wish to know all under heaven thoroughly, how can this be done?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"If you, in your small capacity, do not understand,
then all under heaven cannot be fully known."
The Duke said:
"In defense, battle, and foresight, there are concerns.
If the people are not willing to die,
then you cannot rely on them to overcome the difficulties of defense and battle;
if they are not trustworthy,
then you cannot depend on them for external intelligence.
To rely on people unwilling to die
and expect them to defend and fight,
to depend on untrustworthy people
and seek external intelligence from them,
these are the three blindnesses in military affairs.
How to make the people willing to die and trustworthy?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Clarify the three foundations."
The Duke said:
"What are the three foundations?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"The three foundations are:
first, stability;
second, honor;
third, hostages."
The Duke said:
"What does this mean?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Thus, the location of the state's ancestral graves provides stability;
fields, homes, ranks, and emoluments provide honor;
wives and children serve as hostages.
When these three are in place,
then amplify your authority,
strengthen their resolve,
and the people will be willing to die and not deceive us."
Duke Huán asked Guǎnzǐ about governing the people.
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"For all who shepherd the people,
they must understand their hardships,
and care for them with virtue,
not intimidate them with punishment,
nor restrain them by force.
Be cautious in these four aspects,
and you will be capable of governing the people."
Duke Huán said:
"I see the goodness in this,
but why is the population small?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"A small population is not the worry of those who possess a state.
In the past, the Son of Heaven stood at the center,
with a territory of a thousand lǐ square,
and the four statements encompassed it all;
why would the population be small?
If shepherding the people without understanding their hardships
leads to their suffering,
not caring for them with virtue
leads to much resentment among the people,
intimidating them with punishment
leads to much deceit among the people,
restraining them by force
causes those who leave not to return,
and those who come to keep their distance.
Therefore, when a sage king shepherds the people,
it does not lie in their numbers."
Duke Huán said:
"Good.
If it does not cease,
how then should it be implemented?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Be genuine, trustworthy, extremely benevolent,
and strict yet courteous,
be cautious in these four aspects,
and this is how to implement it."
Duke Huán said:
"Please explain this further."
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Trustworthiness
makes the people trust you;
benevolence
makes the people cherish you;
strictness
makes the people fear you;
courtesy
makes the people praise you.
As the saying goes,
'not changing one's mandate despite favors,'
this is trustworthiness;"
What one does not desire for oneself,
do not impose on others,
this is benevolence;
firm in both inner and outer integrity,
this is strictness;
sincere in substance and yielding in manner,
this is propriety."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent!
What should come first in governing the people?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Sometimes administration takes precedence,
sometimes virtue takes precedence.
When violent winds and torrential rains
cause no harm to the people,
droughts bring no disaster to the populace,
all rivers flow smoothly,
the grain harvest is abundant,
prices for buying and lending are low,
birds and beasts gather with people
to share their food,
and the people suffer no epidemics.
At such times,
the people are wealthy and arrogant.
Those who govern should heavily collect from the good harvests
to fill the granaries,
restrict access to marshes and lakes,
this is called putting affairs first,
following with punishments,
and restraining their excesses with ritual and music
to correct their dissipation.
This is called giving priority to administration.
When violent winds and torrential rains harm the people,
droughts bring disaster to the populace,
the grain harvest fails,
the year is famine-stricken
prices for buying and lending are high,
and the people suffer from epidemics.
At such times,
the people are poor and exhausted.
Those who govern should open the granaries, mountains, forests, marshes, and lakes
to provide them with resources.
Putting affairs afterward,
and forgiveness first,
to relieve their exhaustion.
This is called giving priority to virtue.
In gathering resources,
do not seize the people's wealth;
in distributing them,
do not fail those with virtue.
Enriching the ruler while satisfying the subjects,
this is the ultimate achievement of sage kings." Duke Huán said:
"Good."
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"I wish to become hegemon,
with the efforts of you few gentlemen,
I have already achieved hegemony.
Now I desire to become king,
is it possible?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"You should summon Yì Yá and ask him."
When Bào Shū arrived,
the Duke asked him again.
Bào Shū replied:
"You should summon Bīn Xūwú and ask him."
Bīn Xūwú hurried forward,
and the Duke asked him again.
Bīn Xūwú replied:
"The kings of ancient times,
had abundant virtue themselves,
while their ministers were restrained.
Now, your ministers are abundant."
The Duke hesitated, standing distantly in silence.
The three men then advanced slowly.
The Duke said:
"In the past, King Tài was worthy,
King Jì was worthy,
King Wén was worthy,
King Wǔ was worthy;
King Wǔ attacked the Yīn and conquered it,
but died seven years later,
and Zhōu Gōng Dǎn assisted King Chéng in governing the world,
barely maintaining control within the four seas.
Now my son is not as capable as I am,
and I am not as capable as you few gentlemen.
From this perspective,
it is certain that I cannot become king."
Duke Huán said:
"I wish to subdue the people,
how should I do it?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"These are not the words of a ruler.
Subduing the people is easy.
The way of subduing the people
is not the great Way of the world.
If you wish to subdue the people,
then have your officials meticulously try cases,
demand compensation from the guilty,
frequently inspect and punish severely,
thus, the people will be subdued.
However, the way of subduing the people
is not the great Way of the world.
Making the people fear the ruler
without feeling close to him,
disaster will quickly befall him.
Even if he can manage, it will not last long,
then people will hold back, and no one
will assassinate him,
but it is perilous.
Your state, oh, is in danger!"
Duke Huán was inspecting the stables,
and asked the stable official:
"What is the most difficult task in the stables?"
The stable official did not answer.
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Yí Wú once was a groom,
and erecting horse stalls was the most difficult.
If you set the crooked wood first,
the crooked wood will require more crooked wood,
once the crooked wood is set,
the straight wood has no place to apply.
If you set the straight wood first,
the straight wood will require more straight wood,
once the straight wood is set,
the crooked wood also has no place to apply."
Duke Huán said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"I wish to attack the great states that do not submit,
how should I proceed?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"First show love within the four borders,
then you can oppose the unvirtuous beyond the borders;
first stabilize the families of the ministers and high officials,
then you can threaten the enemy states nearby.
Therefore, the former kings necessarily had what to establish,
before having what to abolish;
necessarily had what to benefit,
before having what to harm."
Duke Huán ascended the throne,
and ordered a sacrifice at the altar with prayers for protection.
Zhù Fú Yǐ Bì presented the sacrificial meat,
and prayed:
"Remove the ruler's harsh ailments and his tendency towards much emptiness and little substance."
Duke Huán was displeased,
and stared angrily at Zhù Fú Yǐ Bì.
Zhù Fú Yǐ Bì offered wine and sacrificed, saying:
"And also with the ruler's seeming worthiness."
Duke Huán was enraged,
and intended to execute him, but did not.
He reported this to Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng then knew that Duke Huán could achieve hegemony.
Duke Huán was riding a horse,
and a tiger saw him and crouched down.
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"Just now I was riding a horse,
and the tiger saw me but dared not move,
what is the reason?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I suppose
you were riding a dappled horse and circling about,
galloping towards the sun?"
The Duke said:
"Yes."
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"This is the image of the bó.
The bó eats tigers and leopards,
so the tiger was suspicious."
Chǔ attacked Jǔ,
and the ruler of Jǔ sent someone to seek help from Qí
Duke Huán. He was about to rescue them,
when Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Do not rescue them, my lord."
The Duke said:
"What is the reason?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"When I spoke with his envoy,
I insulted his ruler three times,
yet his expression did not change.
I had our officials reduce the ceremonial honors
three times with insistence,
yet his envoy argued unto death.
The ruler of Jǔ is a petty man.
Do not send aid, my lord."
Duke Huán indeed did not send aid, and Jǔ perished.
Duke Huán was enjoying spring,
viewing the fields in the third month.
Duke Huán said:
"What thing can be compared to the virtue of a noble man?"
Xí Péng replied:
"The millet grain,
wrapped in armor within,
has a coiled fortress at its core,
and bears weaponry without.
Yet it dares not be presumptuous,
humbly naming itself 'sù' (millet).
This might be compared to the virtue of a noble man!"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The sprout, in its youth,
sways tenderly like an infant!
As it matures,
it stands dignified like a scholar!
When it ripens,
it bows gracefully in humility,
how like a noble man!
The world is secure with it,
imperiled without it,
hence it is named 'hé' (grain, harmony).
This may be compared to the virtue of a noble man."
Duke Huán said:
"Well said."
When Duke Huán marched north against Gūzhú,
ten lǐ from Bēi'ěr Gorge,
he abruptly halted.
Staring wide-eyed,
he drew his bow to shoot,
but held back without releasing.
He asked his attendants:
"Do you see that figure ahead?"
The attendants replied:
"We see nothing."
The duke said:
"Will our campaign fail?
I am greatly perplexed.
Just now I saw a person
one chǐ tall but fully formed:
crowned, with right sleeve tossed back,
swiftly running before my horse.
Will our campaign fail?
I am greatly perplexed.
How could there be such a being?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I have heard of a mountain spirit named Yú'ér,
one chǐ tall yet completely human in form.
When a hegemon king arises,
the mountain spirit appears.
His running swiftly ahead
indicates the path.
The tossed sleeve
signals water ahead.
The right sleeve tossed back
shows we should cross from the right."
Reaching Bēi'ěr Gorge,
a guide to the waters
said:
"Crossing from the left,
the depth reaches your crown;
crossing from the right,
it only reaches your knees.
If you cross from the right,
you will succeed greatly."
Duke Huán immediately bowed to Guǎn Zhòng before his horse, saying:
"How profound is Zhòngfù's wisdom,
while I have long been deserving of punishment."
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I, Yíwú, have heard that
sages foresee the formless.
Now that it had form, and I recognized it thereafter,
I am no sage,
but merely skilled at receiving teachings."
Duke Huán sent Guǎn Zhòng to recruit Nìng Qì,
who responded with:
"Vast and boundless!"
Guǎn Zhòng did not understand,
and worried through his midday meal.
A serving maid asked:
"What troubles you, sir?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"This is beyond your understanding."
The maid said:
"Do not dismiss the young,
nor despise the lowly.
During the Wú-Gān war,
those whose baby teeth remained couldn't enter the army gates.
Guǒ Zǐ knocked out his teeth,
thus gaining entry,
and contributed much to the Gān state.
Bǎilǐ Xī
was a cowherd of Qín.
Duke Mù elevated him as minister,
and he helped hegemony over the lords.
Thus we see,
should the lowly be despised?
Should the young be dismissed?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"True. The duke sent me to recruit Nìng Qì,
who answered: 'Vast and boundless!'
I cannot decipher it."
The maid said:
"The Odes say:
'Vast are the waters,
teeming are the fish;
without a home,
why summon me to dwell?'
Perhaps Nìng Zǐ desires marriage."
When Duke Huán and Guǎn Zhòng closed their doors to plan an attack on Jǔ,
though not yet launched,
it was already known throughout the state.
Why was this?
Guǎn Zhòng said:
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The state must have a sage."
Duke Huán said:
"Indeed.
Among the servants,
one holding a mat and food kept looking up—
could it be him?"
So he ordered the servants to resume duties,
without substitution.
Soon after,
Dōngguō Yóu arrived.
Duke Huán had ushers escort him up,
stood with him on equal steps,
and asked:
"Was it you who spoke of attacking Jǔ?"
Dōngguō Yóu said:
"Yes,
it was I."
Duke Huán said:
"I never spoke of attacking Jǔ
yet you did;
how did you know?"
Dōngguō Yóu replied:
"I have heard that
noble men excel at planning,
while commoners excel at intuiting—
I intuited it."
Duke Huán said:
"How did you intuit it?"
Dōngguō Yóu said:
"Joyful cheer
reflects the hue of bells and drums;
profound serenity reflects the hue of mourning;
vibrant fullness,
with hands and feet subtly stirring,
reflects the hue of arms and armor.
The other day, I saw you two lords on the terrace,
mouths agape—
that meant 'Jǔ'; your raised hands pointed
directly toward Jǔ.
Moreover, I observed that among the small states defying you,
only Jǔ remains.
Thus
I said you would attack Jǔ."
Duke Huán said:
"Marvelous!
From subtle signs discerning the obvious—
this describes it!
Please be seated,
I shall share counsel with you."
A visitor sought an audience with Duke Huán of Qí,
requesting an official position and
a salary of a thousand zhōng.
The duke informed
Guǎn Zhòng, who said:
"Grant it to him."
Upon hearing this, the visitor said:
"I will not take office."
The duke asked:
"Why?"
He replied:
"I have heard that those who employ others based on others' recommendations
will also dismiss others based on others' words.
I will not take office."
Some, through impartial inquiry, discussed the ways of the seven types of rulers,
identifying six faults and one merit,
using it as a mirror for self-reflection
to understand gains and losses. Applying this to the seven types of ministers,
they also found six faults and one merit.
How admirable!
The matter is accomplished.
The Diligent Ruler: Relies on circumstances and adheres to principles as the norm,
widely listens to both near and far to maintain clarity.
If all essentials are scrutinized,
then laws and decrees are firm;
if rewards and punishments are certain,
then subordinates abide by the rules.
Without preparation, harmony is achieved,
and the people return to simplicity.
Thus, the ruler is content and secure,
officials are solemn and stern,
the people are honest and affectionate,
there are no corrupt officials,
no treacherous courtiers,
no encroachments or conflicts below,
and no criminals in the world.
The Indulgent Ruler: Lavishes rewards and generous gifts, exhausting the treasury,
pardons the wicked and overlooks faults, damaging the law.
When the treasury is exhausted, the ruler's authority declines;
when the law is damaged, the gates for wickedness open.
Hence it is said:
"Excess leads to failure." The Encroaching Ruler: Violates the law with personal likes and dislikes, harming himself,
delights in resolving obscure matters, obstructing clarity.
Follows spies and favors petty investigations,
acts without consistency, and laws are dragged down.
If not rectified,
the state loses its power.
The Frivolous Ruler: Eyes indulging in the five colors,
ears constantly filled with the five sounds,
disregarding the four borders,
ignoring the reports of officials,
then ministers act recklessly,
and the state's authority greatly topples.
If not rectified,
what he detests will befall him.
The Laboring Ruler: Fails to clarify duties and roles,
causing confusion between superior and subordinate,
ministers and ruler share the same standards.
Punishments are excessive and severe,
severity leads to harshness.
Abandoning them brings chaos,
facing them brings peril,
what then can future generations attain?
The Agitated Ruler: Joy and anger know no bounds,
severe punishments without pardon,
ministers tremble with fear,
not knowing what to do,
then people revert to their old ways.
If not rectified,
laws and methods decline daily,
and the state loses its stability.
The Doomed Ruler: Suspects others based on human feelings,
so ministers have no trust.
Trying to manage all affairs personally
leads to numerous tasks,
numerous tasks cause confusion,
confusion means both urgent and slow matters are neglected.
If not rectified,
he sees only the undesirable,
exhausts his strength, loses self-control, and incurs punishment. , , , , , , .
Thus, the order or chaos of an individual lies in their heart,
the survival or demise of a state lies in its ruler.
The gains and losses of the world,
emanate from one person.
If the ruler values agriculture,
the people will cultivate wastelands;
if the ruler favors goods,
people will engage in trade;
if the ruler enjoys palaces,
craftsmen will become skillful;
if the ruler loves ornate patterns,
women's work will become extravagant.
The King of Chǔ preferred slender waists,
so beauties reduced their food;
the King of Wú favored swords,
so warriors of the state disregarded death.
Death and starvation
are what all under heaven detest,
yet why do people do it?
To follow the ruler's desires.
How much more so with the influence of music and pleasure?
If men do not farm,
women do not weave,
and artisans focus on useless skills,
yet expect the land to yield crops,
granaries to be full,
it is unattainable.
If the land yields no crops,
the people will be in want;
if the people are in want,
rebellious spirits arise;
if rebellious spirits arise,
orders will not be obeyed.
Then when a powerful enemy rises and attacks,
even the capable cannot preserve the state.
How to verify this?
The answer is:
In the past, Zhòu was such an example.
He executed the worthy and loyal,
drew close to slanderous and treacherous men,
and prized women,
enjoyed killing but lacked courage,
loved wealth but forgot the poor.
He hunted without end,
reveled in music without satiety,
found jade terraces and gardens insufficient to dwell in,
a thousand chariots insufficient to ride,
had three thousand skilled female musicians,
with the sounds of bells, stones, strings, and bamboo never ceasing.
The people were exhausted and destitute,
the noblemen had no loyalty,
ultimately, there was no support,
and people harbored rebellious hearts,
until they encountered King Wǔ of Zhōu,
and he was captured by the Zhōu.
This is due to being engrossed in material things and losing touch with reality,
indulging in debauchery and forgetting future troubles.
Thus, if expenditures are without measure,
the state will collapse,
and if actions are untimely,
it will surely suffer calamity.
Granaries are not empty for no reason,
trade and officialdom are not ruined without cause,
laws and decrees are not disordered without reason,
states do not fall without cause.
There are spring and autumn seasons,
years of abundance and famine,
governance has urgency and leniency.
Since governance has urgency and leniency,
goods have light and heavy values;
since years have abundance and famine,
the people have surplus or shortage;
since there are spring and autumn seasons,
grain has high and low prices.
If the ruler does not regulate excess,
traveling merchants can multiply their capital ten or a hundredfold.
The people not farming,
the disparity between rich and poor unmeasured,
all stem from this.
City walls not defended,
soldiers not used,
all begin from this path.
Those who lose states and ruin families
do not lack territory;
what they engage in is not fruitful.
In years of drought and thunder,
it is not that there is no rain or dew;
the dryness and moisture are just untimely.
In chaotic times with oppressive governance,
it is not that there are no laws and decrees;
it is that those punished or rewarded are not the right people.
Tyrannical and deluded rulers
do not lack close advisors;
it is that their choices and rejections are not based on proper methods.
Thus, an enlightened ruler has six priorities and four prohibitions.
What are the six priorities?
The first is frugality in expenditures,
the second is worthy assistants,
the third is laws and regulations,
the fourth is certainty in punishment,
the fifth is heavenly timing,
the sixth is terrestrial suitability.
What are the four prohibitions?
In spring, do not engage in killing or attacking,
do not cut into large burial mounds,
strip great marshes,
fell large trees,
level great mountains,
spread great fires,
execute high officials,
or collect grain taxes.
In summer, do not block waterways
or obstruct famous rivers,
close off great valleys,
undertake earthworks,
or shoot birds and animals.
In autumn, do not pardon faults, release criminals, or delay punishments.
In winter, do not grant titles, rewards, or stipends,
nor harm or deplete the five stored provisions.
Thus, if spring governance is not prohibited,
the hundred growths will not sprout;
if summer governance is not prohibited,
the five grains will not ripen;
if autumn governance is not prohibited,
wickedness and evil will not be overcome;
if winter governance is not prohibited,
the earth's energy will not be stored.
If all four are violated,
then yin and yang will be disharmonious,
wind and rain will be untimely,
great floods will wash away regions and sweep through cities,
great gales will topple houses and break trees,
fierce fires will scorch the land and burn grasses;
in winter, thunder will sound in the sky,
and the earth will quake;
grasses and trees will wither in summer and bloom in autumn;
hibernating insects will not hide away,
those meant to die will live,
those meant to hibernate will chirp;
marshes will teem with locusts and toads,
mountains will swarm with pests and vermin;
the six domestic animals will not multiply,
the people will die young in great numbers;
the state will be impoverished and laws chaotic,
rebellious energies will arise from below.
Therefore it is said:
Terraces and pavilions facing each other
are the corridors of a perishing state;
chariots filling the country
are the horses for pursuing invaders;
feathered arrows and pearl-adorned swords
are the axes that cut down life;
embroidered silks and ornate ribbons
The enlightened king knows this to be so,
thus he keeps them at a distance and does not draw near.
If he can reject these and choose those,
then the way of the ruler is complete.
Now, laws
are what promote achievements and deter violence,
statutes
are what define duties and stop disputes,
decrees
Laws, statutes, and government orders
are the compass and square for officials and people.
If the square is not true,
one cannot seek right angles;
if the line is not straight,
one cannot seek straightness.
Laws and decrees
are established jointly by ruler and ministers;
authority and power
are what the ruler alone maintains.
Thus, if the ruler loses his maintenance, there is danger;
if ministers and officials lose theirs, there is chaos.
If crimes are decided by officials, there is order,
if authority is determined by the ruler, there is majesty,
if the people trust the laws, there is closeness.
Therefore, the enlightened king examines laws carefully and is cautious with power,
so that superior and inferior have their distinctions.
Now, wherever private interests arise,
they must originate with the ruler.
If the ruler values fundamentals,
then upright scholars will be before him;
if the ruler prefers profit,
then slanderous and flattering men will be at his side.
If the ruler frequently bestows rewards for goodness,
not according to actual merit,
then scholars will not serve him;
if he repeatedly imposes severe laws,
but cannot overcome crimes,
then wickedness will not cease.
The enlightened king knows this to be so,
thus he implements inevitable governance,
and establishes inescapable punishments.
Therefore, the people know what they must pursue,
and know what they must avoid;
push them and they go,
call them and they come,
like a heavy object falling from a height,
like water flowing across the ground.
Thus, laws are not burdensome and officials are not wearied,
the people do not violate prohibitions,
and so, all and the common people hold no grudges against the ruler.
The legal minister: with laws,
he decides cases and settles names,
without slander or praise.
Thus, if the ruler follows the law, his position is secure;
if ministers follow the law, bribery ceases
and the people are without wickedness.
How excellent it is,
when names are decided and words are smooth!
The ostentatious minister: he curries favor with the noble and esteemed to make a name,
and is nonchalant about titles and stipends to appear lofty.
Loving fame, he lacks substance;
acting lofty, he is uncontrollable.
As the old record says:
"Without substance, there is no power;
if the reins are lost, how can the horse be controlled?"
The encroaching minister: he nitpicks small matters to bend laws and decrees,
and favors cronies to carry out private requests.
Thus, when private ways prevail, laws and regulations are encroached upon;
when punishments are numerous, wickedness cannot be prohibited.
If the king strictly punishes, he loses the people's hearts first.
The flattering minister: when numerous, they build bells and drums,
and adorn women lavishly to delude the ruler.
Thus, when the ruler is deluded, the neighboring states are not considered,
and the office of music receives salaries directly.
Hence, flattering ministers are esteemed and legal ministers are despised;
this is called subtle isolation.
The foolish minister: he considers severe accusations and heavy punishments as conduct,
imposes heavy taxes and levies,
and offers many expedient ways to please the ruler,
causing himself to be detested and the ruler to suffer slander.
As the old record refers to it: "Foolish loyalty is slanderous villainy,"
this is what it means.
The treacherous minister: he exaggerates human sentiments to alarm the ruler,
and exposes criminal factions to eliminate enemies
for the ruler.
Eliminating for enemies leads to punishing the innocent;
punishing the innocent
means dwelling with enemies.
Thus, he skillfully speaks of detestable things to win trust,
and the ruler loses intimacy.
The subversive minister: he secretly claims achievements and stipends for himself,
while openly requesting generous rewards for subordinates.
In repose, he is the mother of wrongdoing,
in action, the pillar of apparent goodness.
He buys fame with wrongdoing,
injures the ruler with rightness,
and the masses do not realize it.
This is called subtle attack.
If prohibitions are stored within the breast and ribs,
calamity will be avoided beyond ten thousand miles.
The ability to use this to control that
lies only in being able to understand others through oneself.
Not bathing in winter
is not due to loving ice;
not warming oneself in summer
is not due to loving fire.
It is because what is unsuitable does not comfort the body.
The enlightened ruler does not embellish his palaces and chambers,
not because he prefers smallness;
he does not listen to bells and drums,
not because he dislikes music.
It is because they harm fundamental endeavors and hinder education.
Thus, he first exercises caution in himself and then in others;
officials also prioritize internal affairs before external ones,
and the people focus on essentials while discarding non-essentials.
Settle the people where they find joy,
employ them in what benefits them,
reward them for what they do well,
punish them for what they detest,
trust them with their surplus wealth,
and credit them where no blame is due.
When there is no one to punish below,
it is because punishment is certain;
when there are those to punish,
it is because punishment is not certain.
To progress from having punishments to having none—
such laws are simple, and the people remain whole;
to regress from having no punishments to having them—
such penalties become oppressive, and wrongdoing multiplies.
What begins easy ends difficult,
what begins difficult ends easy—
all things are like this.
The enlightened ruler knows this principle,
hence he punishes without pardon,
rewards without delay—
not because he enjoys giving or delights in killing,
but to bring benefit and eliminate harm for the people.
In nurturing the aged and raising the weak,
preserving and sustaining all people,
nothing is more illuminating.
To govern without law is to govern lawlessly.
Law is
the standard of the world,
that which resolves doubts and clarifies right and wrong,
upon which the lives of the common people hang.
Thus, the enlightened ruler is cautious of it,
not altering the law for relatives or the privileged;
officials dare not use their authority to endanger lives,
and the people do not violate prohibitions for pearls, jade, or treasures.
Hence, the ruler regards the law as stricter than kin, officials uphold orders
with more reverence than for teachers,
and the people receive instruction
with more weight than divine treasures. Thus, laws are established but not used,
penalties are set but not enforced.
If rewards are uneven,
though the position is high,
few will serve;
if pardons are inconsistent,
though virtue is deep,
many will not praise;
if actions are mistimed,
though strength is exhausted,
the task will not succeed;
if judgments are unjust,
though executions are many,
violence will not be restrained.
Where justice is applied,
though the penalty is heavy,
the people bear no resentment;
where favoritism is applied,
though rewards are ample,
scholars feel no joy.
If laws are implemented unrighteously,
the masses cannot comply;
if measures are inappropriate,
the masses cannot achieve.
Those who neither correct nor prepare
should be deemed fools.
Therefore, in managing affairs, the sage
can restrain palaces and chambers,
moderate carriages to enrich stores—
then the state will surely prosper,
and his position be honored;
he can moderate clothing,
abandon frivolities to support fundamentals—
then resources will suffice,
and his person be secure;
he can shift useless efforts,
unproductive expenses,
to facilitate trade and rituals—
then allies will multiply,
and bonds grow close.
Most people excessively pursue material things,
straining their strength,
wearying their minds,
thus trapped and insufficient—
the great lose their states,
the small endanger themselves.
Human nature is such:
achieving desires brings joy,
encountering dislikes brings sorrow—
this is common to all, noble and base.
What is near, they cannot help but desire;
what is far, they cannot help but remember—
such is human nature.
Yet likes and dislikes differ;
each follows their desires,
and safety or peril varies,
revealing the forms of worthiness and unworthiness.
Things vary in abundance,
yet emotions cannot be equal;
affairs meet success or failure,
yet intentions cannot align;
actions advance or retreat,
yet strength cannot do both.
Thus, stand firm in the middle,
nourish with moderation:
palaces and chambers enough to avoid damp and dryness,
food and drink enough to harmonize blood and breath,
clothing enough to suit cold and warmth,
rituals enough to distinguish noble and base,
recreation enough to evoke joy,
coffins enough to decay the bones,
burial shrouds enough to decay the flesh,
graves enough to mark remembrance.
Undertake no efforts without benefit,
engage in no deeds without gain,
so the mind is settled and emotions unagitated.
When emotions are unagitated,
the ears and eyes are clear,
clothing and food sufficient;
with clear ears and eyes,
sufficient clothing and food,
conflict and strife do not arise,
resentment and anger are absent,
superiors and inferiors cherish each other,
and weapons are unused.
Thus, by aligning oneself with righteousness,
being frugal, modest, and respectful—
if not blessed,
misfortune will not come either;
through arrogance, extravagance, and excess,
deviating from norms and violating reason—
if not stricken by misfortune,
blessings will not arrive either.
Therefore, the superior man looks upward at those who violate reason
to caution himself,
and downward at those who fall short
to reflect on himself.
Hence it is said:
"Praise does not emerge without cause,
and calamity does not arise alone;
blessings do not choose families,
misfortunes do not seek people out"—
this refers to this.
If one can observe with what one hears,
then affairs will surely be clear.
Thus, all conditions of order and disorder
originate from above. Therefore, the adept restrains with harm,
guides with benefit—
those who can balance benefit and harm
will have abundant resources and few faults.
Now, human nature is such:
seeing benefit, none can avoid pursuing it;
seeing harm, none can avoid evading it.
The merchant in trade,
traveling double the distance,
continuing day into night,
covering a thousand lǐ without considering it far—
benefit lies ahead.
The fisherman venturing into the sea,
depths of ten thousand rèn,
facing turbulent currents,
braving peril for a hundred lǐ,
staying out day and night—
benefit lies in the water.
Thus, where benefit resides,
even a mountain of a thousand rèn—
there is no height not scaled;
in the depths beneath abysses— there is no place not entered.
Therefore, the adept ruler holds fast to where benefits lie,
and the people naturally find beauty and peace;
without pushing, they go forth,
without pulling, they come forward,
without vexation or disturbance,
and the people enrich themselves.
Like a bird covering its eggs,
without form or sound,
one only sees their completion.
The foundation of governing a state lies in,
seizing the timeliness of Heaven as the warp,
gaining the hearts of the people as the weft,
with laws and decrees as the guiding threads,
officials as the net,
organizing in squads and tens as ranks,
rewards and punishments as the civil and martial means.
Repairing farming tools
serves as weaponry,
farming serves as attack and defense,
pushing plows and hoes
substitutes for swords and halberds,
wearing straw raincoats substitutes for armor,
bamboo hats substitute for shields.
Thus, when farming tools are complete, war equipment is ready;
when agricultural tasks are practiced, combat skills are refined.
In the three months of spring,
repair houses and air them out,
drill wood for fire and change the fire,
draw water from wells and change the water,
to eliminate lurking toxins.
Hold spring sacrifices,
fulfill long-standing prayers,
use fish as offerings,
use sprouted grain to make wine,
summon one another,
to bind relatives together.
Do not kill livestock,
do not take eggs,
do not cut down trees,
do not harm young blooms,
do not break off shoots,
to let all living things thrive.
Aid the widowed and solitary,
relieve the orphaned and alone,
lend to those without seed,
exempt those without means from taxes,
to encourage the weak among the people.
Issue the five decrees,
pardon minor offenses,
release detained people,
reconcile enemies,
to establish timely achievements
and promote grain growth.
In summer, reward the five virtues,
fill ranks and emoluments, promote officials, honor filial piety and fraternal duty, restore the capable and strong,
to encourage merit.
In autumn, carry out the five punishments,
execute the severely guilty,
to curb depravity and evil,
and stop thieves and bandits.
In winter, gather the five stores,
collect all things,
to internally prepare the people.
When the affairs of the four seasons are complete,
the people's achievements multiply a hundredfold.
Thus, spring embodies benevolence, summer loyalty,
autumn urgency, winter closure,
following Heaven's timeliness,
conforming to Earth's suitability,
harmonizing with human accord,
hence wind and rain come timely,
the five grains are full,
plants and trees flourish abundantly,
the six domestic animals thrive,
the state grows rich and the army strong,
the people are talented and orders are obeyed,
internally free from vexatious governance,
externally without the threat of powerful enemies.
When actions and stillness align, then harmony is achieved;
not missing the timing leads to wealth;
not losing the method leads to order.
Thus, a state does not become rich in vain,
nor the people governed in vain.
To prosper without governance,
or to perish without chaos,
from ancient times to the present
has never occurred.
Therefore, a state with much private bravery
has a weak military;
officials with much private cunning
lead to chaotic laws;
people with much self-interest
result in a poor state.
Thus, virtue should be as broad and deep as possible,
making the people willing to die for it;
rewards and punishments must be certain and inevitable,
making the people trust them.
Those skilled at shepherding the people
do not rely on city walls,
but assist them with squads,
manage them with units of five.
In the units, none are out of place,
among the people, none are outside their villages,
in the villages, none are outside their homes.
Thus, fugitives have nowhere to hide,
migrants have nowhere to settle,
without seeking, they are restrained,
without summoning, they come.
Hence, the people have no thought of fleeing,
and officials have no worry of pursuit.
Thus, the ruler's governance can reach the people,
and the people's hearts can be tied to the ruler.
The way laws control the people
is like the potter with clay,
or the smith with metal.
Therefore, examine where advantages and harms lie,
the people's choices to flee or follow,
are like fire towards dryness or dampness,
water towards high or low.
What the people live on
is clothing and food;
what produces food
is water and soil.
Thus, to enrich the people, there is an essential method;
to feed the people, there is a standard:
thirty mu per person suffices for a year's needs.
Considering the year's good and bad harvests,
taking one dan per mu,
then each person has thirty dan;
fruits and vegetables count for ten dan,
chaff and livestock for ten dan,
so each person has fifty dan,
with cloth, silk, hemp, and silk,
and additional odd profits,
not included herein.
Thus, the state has surplus stores,
and the people have extra food.
The steelyard is for measuring more or less,
scales are for assessing weight and lightness,
household registers and land records
are for knowing wealth and poverty without mismeasure.
Therefore, the adept ruler must first know the land,
then understand the people,
and with land prepared, the people can be satisfied.
All who possess the world,
those who conquer through empathy become emperors,
through deeds become kings,
through governance become hegemons.
And there are five strategies for achieving merit.
First, observe whom they love,
to divide their authority;
if one person has two minds,
their inner strength must decline.
If ministers are not used,
the state may be endangered.
Second, observe those they secretly hate,
enrich them with bribes,
to deeply grasp the situation.
If internally close but externally distant,
the state's condition can be known.
Third, indulge their decadent pleasures,
to broaden their indulgences.
Present them with yu pipes, se zithers, and beautiful women,
to堵塞 their inner senses;
present them with flattering ministers and decorated horses,
to blind their external senses.
When both internal and external are blocked,
success or failure can be determined.
The fourth says: One must deeply befriend them,
as if sharing the same life.
Secretly introduce skilled debaters
to plot their strategies;
introduce brave warriors,
to boost their morale.
Introduce agents into other states,
to make them break their alliances,
sever their diplomatic relations,
and contradict their intentions,
so that they will inevitably fight each other.
When two states are in conflict,
one must take advantage of their exhaustion.
The fifth says: Deeply investigate their plans,
be cautious of their loyal ministers,
estrange their envoys,
causing internal distrust,
so that they develop intentions to defect.
When intentions to defect cannot be reconciled,
they will inevitably harm each other internally.
Once the loyal ministers are dead,
the governance can thus be seized.
These five are
the ways to achieve strategic success.
Upon entering a state for forty days,
implement the teachings of the nine benefactions.
The first is called honoring the aged,
the second is called caring for the young,
the third is called comforting the orphaned,
the fourth is called supporting the disabled,
the fifth is called uniting the solitary,
the sixth is called inquiring about the sick,
the seventh is called aiding the destitute,
the eighth is called relieving the distressed,
the ninth is called commemorating the deceased.
What is called honoring the aged:
In every state and capital, there are officials in charge of the aged.
For those aged seventy and above,
one son is exempt from corvée,
and they receive meat every three months;
for those aged eighty and above,
two sons are exempt from corvée,
and they receive meat monthly;
for those aged ninety and above,
the entire household is exempt from corvée,
and they have wine and meat daily.
Upon death,
the state provides the coffin.
Encourage the younger generation: to prepare fine meals,
ask about their desires,
and seek what they enjoy.
This is called honoring the aged.
What is called caring for the young:
In every state and capital, there are officials in charge of the young.
If common people have children,
and the children are too young and weak to be raised, becoming a burden,
those with three young children
have no levy on the wife,
those with four young children have the entire household exempt from corvée,
those with five young children are additionally given a nurse,
receiving food for two people,
until they can manage on their own.
This is called caring for the young.
What is called comforting the orphaned:
In every state and capital, there are officials in charge of the orphaned.
When common people die,
and their children are orphaned and young,
with no parents to raise them,
unable to support themselves,
entrust them to their village community,
acquaintances, and old friends.
Those who raise one orphan
have one son exempt from corvée,
those who raise two orphans
have two sons exempt from corvée,
those who raise three orphans
have the entire household exempt from corvée.
The official in charge of the orphaned frequently visits and inquires,
must know about their food, drink, hunger, and cold,
and pity their emaciated bodies.
This is called comforting the orphaned.
What is called supporting the disabled:
In every state and capital, there are officials in charge of supporting the disabled.
The deaf, blind, mute, lame, paralyzed, and those with contorted limbs,
who cannot support themselves,
the state takes them in and cares for them
in institutions for the disabled,
providing them with clothing and food.
This continues until their death.
This is called supporting the disabled.
What is called uniting the solitary:
In every state and capital, there are officials in charge of matchmaking.
A man without a wife is called a widower,
a woman without a husband is called a widow.
Take widowers and widows and unite them harmoniously,
grant them land and housing to establish households,
and after three years, assign them duties.
This is called uniting the solitary.
What is called inquiring about the sick:
In every state and capital, there are officials in charge of the sick.
When common people are ill,
the official in charge of the sick, by order of the superior, inquires about them.
For those aged ninety and above,
inquire once a day;
for those aged eighty and above,
inquire once every two days;
for those aged seventy and above,
inquire once every three days;
for the general populace, inquire once every five days.
For those severely ill, report it
to the superior, who personally inquires.
The official in charge of the sick travels throughout the state,
with inquiring about the sick as his duty.
This is called inquiring about the sick.
What is called aiding the destitute:
In every state and capital, there are officials in charge of aiding the destitute.
If there are impoverished couples without shelter,
or poor guests without food,
those in their village community
who report it are rewarded,
those who do not report it are punished.
This is called aiding the destitute.
What is called relieving the distressed:
In years of famine,
when people suffer from epidemics,
and many die;
relax punishments,
pardon the guilty,
and distribute granary grains to feed them.
This is called relieving the distressed.
What is called commemorating the deceased:
When common people die in service of the state
or in battle,
have their acquaintances and old friends
receive funds from the state
to offer sacrifices to them.
This is called commemorating the deceased.
Be calm and composed,
with gentleness and restraint as the foundation,
empty the mind and pacify the will to await what is necessary.
Above is about the ruler's position.
The eyes value clarity,
the ears value acuteness,
the mind values wisdom.
Using the eyes of the world to see
then nothing remains unseen;
using the ears of the world to listen
then nothing remains unheard;
using the minds of the world to ponder
then nothing remains unknown.
Like spokes converging and advancing together,
then clarity will not be blocked.
Above is about the ruler's clarity.
The method of listening is:
Do not reject upon first impression,
nor approve upon first impression.
Approving hastily leads to loss of control,
rejecting hastily leads to obstruction.
High mountains, looking up at them
cannot reach their peaks;
deep abysses, measuring them
cannot fathom their depths.
The virtue of divine intelligence,
with correctness and tranquility as its ultimate.
Above is about the ruler's listening.
In using rewards, sincerity is valued;
in using punishments, certainty is valued.
If punishments and rewards are trustworthy and certain in what is seen and heard,
then even in what is unseen, none will not be subtly transformed.
Sincerity, flowing through heaven and earth,
connecting with divine intelligence,
how could deceit and falsehood exist?
Above is about the ruler's rewards.
First is that of Heaven,
second is that of Earth,
third is that of Humanity.
In the four directions, above and below, left and right, front and back,
where does the confounding influence lie?
On the right is the ruler's inquiry.
If the mind does not interfere with the nine orifices,
the nine orifices function properly;
if the ruler does not interfere with the five officials,
the five officials govern well.
For those who do good,
the ruler grants rewards;
for those who do wrong,
the ruler imposes punishments.
The ruler follows their inherent tendencies,
and accordingly bestows upon them,
thus avoiding toil.
The sage follows this principle,
hence is able to control it.
By following it and adhering to reason,
thus it can endure long.
On the right is the ruler's adaptation.
The ruler must not be unencompassing,
if the ruler is unencompassing,
then the ministers below will fall into disorder.
Silent and without apparent beginning or end.
If internal and external do not communicate,
how can grievances be known?
If barriers are closed and not opened,
good and bad have no origin.
On the right is the ruler's comprehensiveness.
First is called long eyes,
second is called flying ears,
third is called establishing clarity.
Clearly knowing beyond a thousand miles,
within the hidden and subtle,
is called detecting treachery.
When treachery is detected, it can be changed.
On the right is the ruler's reference.
Follow the name to supervise the reality,
examine the reality to determine the name.
Name and reality generate each other,
and in turn reflect the true situation.
When name and reality correspond, there is order;
when they do not correspond, there is chaos.
Name arises from reality,
reality arises from virtue,
virtue arises from principle,
principle arises from wisdom,
wisdom arises from appropriateness.
On the right is supervising names.
Duke Huán of Qí asked Guǎnzǐ:
"I wish to possess and not lose,
to gain and not let perish,
is there a way to achieve this?"
He replied:
"Do not initiate or create,
but follow when the time comes.
Do not let personal likes and dislikes harm public justice.
Observe what the people detest, to caution yourself.
Huángdì established the discussions at the Bright Terrace,
to observe the worthy from above;
Yáo had inquiries at the Crossroads House,
to listen to the people below;
Shùn had the banner for reporting goodness,
so the ruler was not blinded;
Yǔ set up a drum at court,
to prepare for inquiries;
Tāng had the court at the main street,
to observe people's criticisms;
King Wǔ had the restoration at the Spiritual Terrace,
so the worthy were advanced.
These are how the ancient sage emperors and enlightened kings possessed without loss,
gained without forgetting."
Duke Huán said:
"I wish to emulate this,
what should it be called?"
He replied:
"It is called the discussion chamber of earnest voices.
That is to say: laws simple and easy to implement,
punishments careful and not violated,
affairs concise and easy to follow,
demands few and easily satisfied.
If someone criticizes the ruler's faults,
they are called an upright scholar,
and included in the discussions of the earnest chamber.
Officials in charge all perform their duties faithfully, without neglect.
This is the affair of the earnest chamber,
I request that Dōngguō Yá be put in charge.
This person can dispute with the ruler on matters of principle."
Duke Huán said:
"Good."
Formerly, Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"I venture to ask about measuring the terrain to establish a state,
what must be done to succeed?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"From what Yíwú has heard,
those capable of being hegemon kings,
are sages of the world.
Therefore, when a sage establishes a state,
it must be on stable ground,
choosing fertile and rich terrain,
