Thus, they take heaven and earth,
the sun and moon,
the four seasons as their master
and substance,
to govern the world.
Heaven covers without exclusion,
its virtue reaching everywhere;
earth carries without abandonment,
stable and unmoving.
Therefore, all things grow and multiply.
Sages emulate this to cover and carry the myriad people,
so none fail to fulfill their duties and natures.
When they fulfill their duties and natures,
all become useful.
Hence it is said:
"Imitate heaven in combining virtue,
model earth in showing no favoritism."
The brightness of the sun and moon is impartial,
so all receive light.
Sages emulate this
to illuminate the myriad people,
thus able to scrutinize thoroughly,
leaving no good unrecognized,
no evil hidden.
With no good unrecognized,
no evil hidden,
then punishments and rewards are trustworthy and certain.
When punishments and rewards are trustworthy and certain,
goodness is encouraged and evil ceases.
Therefore it is said:
"Align with the sun and moon."
The progression of the four seasons
is trustworthy, certain, and clearly manifest.
Sages emulate this
to serve the myriad people,
thus not missing timely achievements.
Hence it is said:
"Coordinate with the four seasons."
In general, regarding the masses,
love them and they draw close,
benefit them and they gather.
Thus, enlightened rulers set up benefits to attract them,
and demonstrate love to draw them near.
If only benefits without love,
the masses gather but do not draw close;
if only love without benefits,
the masses draw close but do not gather.
When love and benefits are both applied,
it pleases ruler and minister,
pleases friends,
pleases brothers,
pleases father and son.
Where love and benefits are established,
even fourfold fortresses cannot hold.
Therefore it is said:
"Delighting the masses lies in love and benefits."
The reason a ruler holds the masses
is the virtue of love and benefits.
If love is diverted,
benefits monopolized,
then one cannot fully possess them.
Hence it is said:
"Holding the masses lies in abolishing selfishness."
Even if the virtue of love and benefits is practiced selflessly,
if inner conduct is not cultivated,
one cannot make distant rulers pay homage.
Therefore, rectify the principles between ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
adorn the duties of father and son, elder and younger brother, husband and wife,
distinguish the separation between men and women,
differentiate the measures of closeness and distance,
so that the ruler is virtuous and ministers loyal,
fathers kind and sons filial,
elder brothers loving and younger brothers respectful,
with ritual and righteousness clearly evident.
Thus, those nearby will be affectionate,
and those afar will submit.
Hence it is said:
"Summoning the distant lies in cultivating the near."
Preventing disaster lies in eliminating resentment;
it is not that resentment exists and then removed,
but that in all actions, there should normally be no resentment.
All disasters and chaos arise
from resentment and blame;
resentment and blame arise
from irrationality.
Thus, an enlightened ruler in dealing with the masses must be consistent,
in employing them must follow the Way,
in giving rewards and retributions must be just,
in speech must be appropriate,
in punishments must be reasonable.
Then the masses will have no pent-up resentment,
no regret or hatred.
Thus, disasters and chaos do not arise,
and the ruler's position is not endangered.
Therefore it is said:
"Preventing disaster lies in eliminating resentment."
The reason a ruler is esteemed and secure
lies in worthy assistants.
With worthy assistants, the ruler is honored,
the state secure,
the people orderly;
without them, the ruler is humbled,
the state endangered,
the people chaotic.
Hence it is said:
"Preparedness for longevity lies in appointing the worthy."
All people,
without exception, desire benefit and detest harm.
Therefore, those who share benefits with the world
are upheld by the world;
those who monopolize the world's benefits
are plotted against by the world.
Those plotted against by the world,
even if established, will surely fall.
What the world upholds,
though lofty, is not perilous.
Hence it is said:
"Securing heights lies in sharing benefits."
Those who can use what they do not benefit from to benefit others—
Shùn was such a man.
Shùn farmed at Lìshān,
made pottery by the riverbanks,
fished at Léizé,
yet took no profit for himself,
instead teaching the common people,
who thereby gained advantage.
This is what is called using what one does not benefit from to benefit others.
Those who can give what they do not possess to others—
King Wǔ was such a man.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
the soldiers who followed him
each received land and community.
Upon entering Yīn's capital,
he distributed grain from Jùqiáo granaries,
scattered coins from Lùtái treasury,
greatly pleasing the people of Yīn.
This is what is called giving what one does not possess to others.
Duke Huán said to Guǎnzǐ:
"Now you teach me to emulate heaven's virtue,
which brings enduring harmony.
With harmonious virtue embracing all, all things receive their mandate.
Imitate earth's impartiality,
which brings stable security.
With impartiality bearing all, all living things flourish.
Align with sun and moon,
selflessly preserving radiance.
With selfless illumination, beauty and ugliness remain unconcealed.
Then should a gentleman cultivate himself
merely without preferences or aversions?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Not so.
Learning serves to transform oneself,
and to comfort oneself.
Thus the gentleman dislikes exposing others' faults,
detests disloyalty with resentment and jealousy,
abhors unfair criticism while seeking fame,
despises holding high position without merit,
and rejects neglecting outsiders while indulging inwardly.
These five things the gentleman fears to practice,
yet are why petty men perish.
How much more should a ruler heed them?"
An enlightened ruler,
possessing statecraft cannot be deceived,
being well-versed in laws and prohibitions cannot be violated,
and discerning in the division of duties cannot be thrown into chaos.
Thus, ministers dare not pursue their private interests,
the noble cannot obscure the lowly,
the near cannot block the distant,
the orphaned, widowed, old, and weak do not lose their means of livelihood,
and within the borders, clarity prevails without overstepping.
This is what is called a well-governed state.
Hence, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"A well-governed state means
the ruler's way is clear."
Clear laws are
what the ruler uses to unify the people and command the subordinates;
private schemes are
what the subordinates use to encroach upon the ruler and create chaos.
Thus, if laws are abandoned and private actions prevail,
the ruler becomes isolated and alone,
while ministers form cliques and factions.
In this case, the ruler is weak and the ministers are strong,
which is called a disordered state.
Hence, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"A disordered state means
the ministers' schemes prevail."
When an enlightened ruler is in power,
with an inevitable grip on governance,
ministers dare not do wrong.
Therefore, the reason ministers dare not deceive the ruler
is not out of love for the ruler,
but out of fear of the ruler's authority;
the people's willingness to serve
is not out of love for the ruler,
but out of fear of the ruler's laws and decrees.
Thus, the enlightened ruler holds the key to certain victory,
governing the people who must be utilized;
occupies a position of certain respect,
controlling ministers who must submit.
Hence, orders are followed and prohibitions heeded,
the ruler is honored and the ministers are humble.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Honoring the ruler and humbling the ministers
is not due to personal affection,
but because authority prevails."
In governing, the enlightened ruler
suspends ranks and emoluments to encourage the people,
and since the people benefit from the ruler,
the ruler has the means to employ them;
establishes punishments to intimidate the subordinates,
and since the subordinates fear the ruler,
the ruler has the means to control them.
Thus, without ranks and emoluments, the ruler has no way to encourage the people,
and without punishments, the ruler has no way to intimidate the masses.
Therefore, ministers who act rationally and obey orders
do so not out of love for the ruler,
but to seek benefit and avoid harm;
officials who uphold the law without deceit
do so not out of love for the ruler,
but to receive ranks and emoluments and avoid punishment.
Hence, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Officials performing their duties
is not due to kindness,
but because punishments are certain."
The ruler
monopolizes life and death,
holds authority,
and wields the power of issuing orders and enforcing prohibitions to command the ministers—
this is the way of the ruler.
Ministers,
occupying lowly positions,
obey the ruler's orders,
adhere to their fundamental responsibilities,
and manage their assigned duties—
this is the way of ministers.
Thus, if the ruler acts as ministers do, there is chaos;
if ministers act as the ruler does, there is danger.
Therefore, the absence of distinction between superior and inferior,
with ruler and ministers sharing the same way,
is the root of chaos.
Hence, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"When ruler and ministers share the same way, there is chaos."
The reason ministers fear and serve the ruler diligently
is their desire to live and aversion to death.
If people did not desire life
or fear death,
they could not be controlled.
If the power over life and death
is monopolized by ministers,
and the ruler remains unharmed,
such a thing has never occurred.
Thus, if order and disorder are not determined by law but decided by powerful ministers,
and the power to kill is not controlled by the ruler but lies with the subordinates,
this is a parasitic ruler.
Therefore, if the ruler fully delegates his authority to others,
there will inevitably be the calamity of usurpation and murder;
if he fully delegates his legal system to others,
there will inevitably be the disaster of chaos and ruin.
Such actions
are the path to a fallen king.
Hence, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Full delegation leads to loss."
Any ruler who cannot enforce his orders,
abandons the law and allows ministers to act wantonly,
with his majesty discarded,
authority seized,
orders unable to be issued,
ministers refusing to serve,
the people refusing to be directed,
and the masses within the borders uncontrolled,
then the state is not his state,
and the people are not his people.
Such a situation
is the path to an extinguished ruler.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"When orders fundamentally cannot be issued, it is called extinction."
The way of the enlightened ruler
allows the lowly to be seen without relying on the noble,
ministers to advance without depending on courtiers,
all officials to have clear communication,
and all ministers to be visible.
Those to be punished are seen by the ruler for their crimes,
those to be rewarded are known by the ruler for their merits.
What is seen and known does not conflict,
rewards and punishments are not mistaken.
With methods that prevent obstruction,
there is no worry of blockage.
A chaotic ruler is not so;
laws and decrees do not reach the people,
the distant and isolated are cut off and unable to hear.
Such a situation
is the way of a blocked ruler.
Hence, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"When orders are issued but滞留, it is called blockage."
The means by which ministers seize opportunities to commit treachery
is usurping the ruler's role.
If ministers usurp the ruler's role,
the ruler's orders cannot be carried out,
and the sentiments of the people below do not reach above.
The power of ministers
can create a gap between ruler and ministers,
preventing the truth of good and evil from being heard,
and the matters of fortune and misfortune from being communicated,
leaving the ruler confused with no way to understand.
Such a situation
is the way of a stifled ruler.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"When the sentiments below do not reach above, it is called stifling."
An enlightened ruler
listens widely and decides independently,
opening many avenues.
The way of ministers
allows the lower levels to inform the higher,
and the lowly to speak of the noble.
Hence, treacherous individuals dare not deceive.
A chaotic ruler is not so;
he listens without method,
and decides matters without verification.
Thus, incompetent individuals rise to the top,
wicked and corrupt ministers monopolize the state,
the ruler's clarity is obscured and his hearing blocked,
and loyal ministers wishing to advise cannot advance.
Such a situation
is the way of an encroached ruler.
Hence, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"When sentiments from below are stopped on their way up,
it is called encroachment."
In governing the state, the ruler
invariably has laws, decrees, rewards, and punishments.
Therefore, if his laws and decrees are clear and rewards and punishments are appropriately established,
the ruler is honored and treachery does not arise;
if his laws and decrees are perverse and rewards and punishments are inappropriately established,
ministers will establish private interests and block him,
forming cliques to usurp and murder.
Thus, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Extinction,
stifling, encroachment,
and blockage arise
from the failure to establish laws."
Laws and standards
are what the ruler uses to control the world and prohibit treachery,
and to govern the realm and serve the ancestral temple.
Personal whims
are what give rise to chaos, foster treachery, and harm justice,
leading to obstruction, loss of correctness, and peril.
Thus, when laws and standards are practiced, the state is well-governed;
when personal whims are practiced, the state is in chaos.
An enlightened ruler does not reward those without merit, even if he loves them in his heart,
nor punish those without crime, even if he hates them in his heart.
He examines according to legal standards to verify gains and losses,
and does not entertain anything outside the law.
Hence, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"The ancient kings in governing the state
did not let their minds wander beyond the law."
In governing the state, the enlightened ruler
acts according to what is appropriate,
and follows correct principles.
Thus, those deserving reward
cannot be refused by the ministers;
those deserving punishment
dare not be avoided by the ministers.
Rewarding merit and punishing crimes
is the means by which benefits are brought to the world and harms are eliminated.
If weeds are not removed,
they harm the grain crops;
if bandits are not punished,
they injure the good people.
To abandon public law and practice private favoritism
is to benefit the wicked and encourage violence and disorder.
Practicing private favoritism by rewarding the undeserving
causes the people to rely on luck and expect favors from their superiors;
practicing private favoritism by pardoning the guilty
causes the people to disrespect their superiors and readily do wrong.
To set aside public law and follow private intentions
is something an enlightened ruler does not do.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Do not practice favoritism within the bounds of the law."
All rulers desire their people to be useful.
To make the people useful,
laws must be established and orders enforced.
Thus, in governing the state and directing the masses, nothing compares to the law;
in suppressing excess and stopping violence, nothing compares to punishment.
The poor may wish to seize the wealth of the rich,
yet they dare not
because the law does not permit it;
the strong may be capable of oppressing the weak,
yet they dare not
for fear of punishment by law.
Therefore, in the affairs of all officials,
if they are regulated by law,
then wickedness does not arise;
violent and arrogant individuals,
if punished by law,
then disasters do not occur;
when all ministers advance together,
if they are guided by standards,
then selfishness has no place to stand.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"In all actions, there is nothing not in accordance with the law,
which is the means to prohibit faults and exclude selfishness."
What the ruler uses to control his ministers
is authority and power.
If authority and power lie below,
then the ruler is controlled by the ministers;
if authority and power lie above,
then the ministers are controlled by the ruler.
A ruler who is obscured
is not one whose gates are blocked or doors guarded,
but rather one whose orders are not carried out,
whose prohibitions are not heeded,
and whose desires are not fulfilled
because he has lost his authority and power.
Thus, if authority and power reside solely with the ruler,
then all ministers fear and respect him;
if laws and governance issue solely from the ruler,
then the world submits and obeys.
Therefore, if authority and power are shared with ministers, orders will not be carried out;
if laws and governance come from ministers, the people will not obey.
Hence, an enlightened ruler in governing the world
keeps authority and power solely with himself and does not share them with ministers,
and laws and governance are controlled solely by him and do not originate from ministers.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Authority should not be placed in two hands,
governance should not come from two sources."
An enlightened ruler
unifies standards and measures,
establishes models and examples,
and firmly adheres to them.
Thus, when orders are issued, the people follow.
The law
is the pattern for the world,
the standard for all affairs.
Officials
are what the people's lives depend on.
Therefore, in the governance of an enlightened ruler,
those who violate the law are punished.
Thus, by using the law to punish crimes,
the people face death without resentment;
by using the law to measure merit,
the people receive rewards without feeling indebted.
This is the achievement of applying the law in actions.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"To govern the state by law
is simply to apply it in actions."
An enlightened ruler
has the system of laws and standards,
so all ministers engage in upright governance and dare not commit wickedness.
The common people know that their ruler acts according to the law,
so when officials issue commands,
if they are lawful, the people comply;
if unlawful, they stop.
The people use the law to resist officials,
and subordinates use the law to serve their superiors.
Thus, deceitful individuals cannot deceive their ruler,
the jealous cannot exercise their malicious intent,
and slanderers and flatterers cannot施展 their cunning.
Even a thousand miles away,
none dare to arbitrarily do wrong.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Where there is the system of laws and standards,
one cannot use deceit and fraud."
Scales and balances
are used to determine the measure of light and heavy.
Yet people do not serve them
not because they dislike profit,
but because the scale cannot alter the number of items,
and the balance cannot change their weight.
Knowing that serving the scales is useless,
people do not do it.
Similarly, when an enlightened ruler is in power,
officials cannot twist the law,
clerks cannot act selfishly,
and the people know that serving clerks is useless,
so wealth and goods are not offered to clerks.
The scales are fair and just in treating all things,
so deceitful individuals cannot practice their selfishness.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"With the standard of scales, one cannot be deceived in weight."
Rulers and measures
are used to ascertain the truth of length and shortness.
Thus, by using rulers to measure length,
every attempt is accurate without error.
Therefore, the measure of the ruler,
even for the wealthy, noble, and powerful,
does not increase in length;
even for the poor, humble, and lowly,
does not decrease in shortness.
It is impartial and unbiased.
So deceitful individuals cannot mislead.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"With the measure of length,
one cannot err in long and short."
The reason a state falls into disorder
is that it neglects actual facts and relies on false praise.
Thus, an enlightened ruler, when hearing reports,
holds speakers accountable for the truth of their words,
and tests those who praise others with official duties.
Those who speak without truth
are punished; officials who disrupt governance
are punished. Hence, empty words dare not be presented,
and the unworthy dare not accept office.
A disorderly ruler does otherwise;
he listens to words without verifying their truth,
so ministers use false praise to advance their factions;
he appoints officials without demanding achievements,
thus foolish and corrupt officials remain in court.
In this way, ministers mutually promote each other with fine reputations,
borrow each other's accomplishments,
and strive to increase their cliques without serving the ruler.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"If the ruler abandons the law and promotes based on reputation,
then ministers will turn away from the ruler and form cliques below;
if officials are appointed through factions,
then the people will strive for cliques and not seek to be useful."
A disorderly ruler does not examine the merits of his ministers;
those with much praise
are rewarded;
he does not scrutinize their faults;
those with much slander
are punished.
In such cases,
wicked ministers without merit gain rewards,
while loyal and upright ones without crime suffer punishment.
Thus, if much merit goes unrewarded,
ministers will not strive to exert themselves;
if upright conduct is punished,
the wise and sage cannot fully use their abilities;
if wealth can buy ranks and emoluments,
then corrupt individuals hold office;
if unworthy proteges hold high positions,
then the people betray public law and flock to the powerful.
As a result,
the honest lose their posts,
and廉洁的官员 lose their governance.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"When officials fail in their governance,
it is because the ruler uses praise as reward
and slander as punishment."
When impartial officials govern,
they enforce the law without selfishness,
so wicked ministers cannot gain benefits.
This is what wicked ministers strive to undermine.
If the ruler does not verify their faults
and punishes them based on unsubstantiated words,
then ministers cannot but flatter the powerful to seek推荐 and praise,
thereby avoiding punishment and receiving rewards.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Those who love rewards and hate punishments
will abandon public principle and practice selfish arts."
Wicked ministers undermine their ruler
gradually and subtly,
causing the ruler to be deluded without realizing it.
Above, they spy on the ruler for each other,
below, they buy praise from the people.
They praise their factions to make the ruler honor them,
and slander the unaffiliated to make the ruler dismiss them.
Whatever they deem beneficial or harmful,
the ruler listens and acts accordingly.
In this way,
all ministers forget the ruler and rush to private alliances.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"They collude to cover each other's misdeeds,
hence they forget their ruler and die for their comrades,
to enhance their reputation."
If the ruler lacks strategic methods,
then ministers can easily deceive him;
if the state lacks clear laws,
then the common people will lightly commit wrongdoings.
Therefore, when treacherous individuals handle state affairs,
ministers look up to personal gains and losses,
and thus,
many become the eyes and ears for the wicked.
Even if there is injustice,
the ruler has no way to know.
Hence, "Míng Fǎ" says:
"With many comrades and much praise,
forming cliques inside and out,
even if there are great traitors,
they obscure the ruler greatly."
All who are called loyal ministers
strive to clarify laws and methods,
day and night assisting the ruler in understanding the principles of measures,
to govern the world.
Treacherous ministers know that if laws and methods are clear, order will prevail,
and order will trap the treacherous while revealing those skilled in law and method.
Therefore, what the wicked focus on
is to keep laws unclear,
the ruler unawakened,
so they can achieve their desires.
Thus, when upright ministers are employed, treacherous ones are trapped and harmed,
showing that upright and treacherous ministers cannot both advance.
Treacherous ministers by the ruler's side
cannot but be detested.
Once detested,
they inevitably wait for the ruler's moments of leisure to endanger him day and night.
If the ruler does not scrutinize but heeds their words,
then loyal ministers suffer and die without crime,
while treacherous ones gain wealth and honor without merit.
Hence, "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Loyal ministers die without crime,
and wicked ministers rise without merit."
Wealth, honor, dignity, and prominence,
long-lasting possession of the world—
no ruler fails to desire these.
Orders obeyed and prohibitions heeded,
unrivaled within the seas—
no ruler fails to desire these.
Deception, encroachment, and oppression—
no ruler fails to detest these.
Losing the world,
ancestral temples destroyed—
no ruler fails to detest these.
Loyal ministers wish to clarify laws and methods to achieve the ruler's desires and eliminate his detestations,
but treacherous ministers who control the ruler
use private interests to endanger them,
so loyal ministers cannot advance their just and fair strategies.
Therefore, "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Those who die are not guilty,
those who rise have no merit,
thus, as ministers, they prioritize private over public interests."
A chaotic ruler bestows ranks and emoluments
not based on laws and merits;
he imposes punishments
not based on laws and offenses.
Instead, he listens to powerful ministers.
So, if a minister wishes to reward someone,
the ruler rewards them;
if a minister wishes to punish someone,
the ruler punishes them.
Abandoning public law,
he solely heeds powerful ministers.
Thus,
all ministers focus on their factions,
valuing powerful ministers and forgetting their ruler,
flocking to the doors of powerful ministers instead of the court.
Hence, "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Ten times they go to private doors,
not once to the court."
An enlightened ruler governs
by clarifying duties and responsibilities,
supervising their completion.
Those competent hold office,
those incompetent are dismissed.
Thus, all ministers exhaust their abilities to manage affairs.
A chaotic ruler does otherwise.
So, ministers hold positions,
receive generous salaries,
but none focus on governing the state,
aiming instead to control the state's weight and monopolize its benefits,
preying on the people to enrich their families.
Therefore, "Míng Fǎ" says:
"A hundred plans for their families,
not one for the state."
With an enlightened ruler above,
all within the borders strive to serve him,
officials fulfill duties to bring order and stabilize the state.
A chaotic ruler does otherwise.
Even with brave and strong men,
ministers keep them privately,
not to serve the ruler;
even with wise and intelligent men,
ministers keep them privately,
not to govern the state.
Thus, though subordinates are numerous,
they cannot advance;
though officials are complete,
they cannot control affairs.
In this case,
the ruler has the name but not the reality.
Hence, "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Though subordinates are numerous,
they do not honor the ruler;
though officials are complete,
they do not serve the state.
This is called the state having no people."
An enlightened ruler
makes subordinates uphold laws and decrees with full effort,
so ministers focus on honoring the ruler and dare not care for their families;
the distinction between ruler and minister is clear,
positions of high and low are definite,
so ministers stay in their places and dare not vie for prominence.
A chaotic ruler does otherwise,
laws and systems abandoned and unenforced,
so ministers can focus on enriching their families;
no distinction between ruler and minister,
no difference between high and low,
so ministers strive to outshine each other.
In this case,
it's not that court ministers are few,
but that the many are not utilized.
Therefore, "Míng Fǎ" says:
"The state having no people
does not mean court ministers are diminished.
Families strive to benefit each other,
not to honor the ruler;
high ministers vie for prominence,
not serving the state."
When a ruler establishes offices and appoints officials,
it is not merely to honor them and provide generous support,
but to have them enforce the ruler's laws,
execute the ruler's orders,
govern the people, and punish bandits.
Therefore, those appointed to high office
receive noble ranks and ample salaries;
those appointed to low office
receive humble ranks and meager salaries.
Ranks and emoluments
are what the ruler uses to make officials govern.
A chaotic ruler's governance
places them in high positions,
grants them salaries,
supports their companions,
but does not make office duties a priority.
Thus,
offices lose their function.
Hence, "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Petty officials hold salaries to support companions,
not attending to official duties,
so offices lose their purpose."
An enlightened ruler selects the worthy
by testing the brave in military affairs,
the wise in official duties.
Those proven in battle with merit are promoted,
those effective in office tasks are employed.
Thus, military achievements determine bravery or cowardice,
official performance determines folly or wisdom;
so bravery, cowardice, folly, and wisdom appear
as distinct as black and white.
A chaotic ruler does otherwise,
hearing words without testing,
so boastful speakers gain employment;
appointing people without
evaluation,
so the unworthy face no hardship.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler uses laws to assess words and seek reality,
employs them in office to evaluate achievements,
relying solely on law, not personal promotion.
Hence, "Míng Fǎ" says:
"When ancient kings governed the state,
they used laws to select people, not promoting personally."
All that is called merit
secures the ruler's safety,
benefits the myriad people.
Crushing armies, killing generals,
winning battles, capturing territories,
freeing the ruler from peril and ruin,
sparing the people from death or capture—
this is the merit of soldiers.
Upholding the ruler's laws,
governing within borders,
preventing the strong from oppressing the weak,
the many from bullying the few,
enabling the people to joyfully exert effort in supporting the ruler—
this is the merit of officials.
Correcting the ruler's errors,
rescuing the ruler's faults,
clarifying principles to guide the ruler,
so the ruler avoids wicked conduct,
and the peril of deception—
this is the merit of ministers.
Thus, an enlightened ruler governs...
Clearly defined duties are used to assess achievements,
those who have merit are rewarded,
those who disrupt order are punished.
The application of rewards and punishments
is in each case appropriate,
and the ruler does not personally intervene.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Let the law measure merit,
without personal judgment."
An enlightened ruler governs
by examining right and wrong,
investigating actual circumstances,
and applying standards to evaluate them.
What conforms to the law is implemented,
what does not conform to the law is halted.
When achievements fulfill their words, reward them;
when they do not fulfill their words, punish them.
Thus, those who claim wisdom and ability
must demonstrate achievements before being promoted;
those who are said to be wicked and failing
must be shown to have faults before being dismissed.
In this way, capable officials advance without being envied,
while the incompetent are thwarted and dismissed without being promoted.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Ability cannot be obscured, nor failure concealed."
The way of an enlightened ruler
establishes what the people desire to seek their achievements,
hence titles and emoluments are used to encourage them;
establishes what the people dislike to prohibit their wickedness,
hence penalties and punishments are used to intimidate them.
Thus, based on their achievements, rewards are given;
based on their crimes, punishments are administered.
In this way, ministers who praise the unworthy
dare not promote them;
those who slander the innocent
cannot demote them.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Praisers cannot advance,
and slanderers cannot demote."
Controlling the ministers,
holding the power over life and death,
is the ruler's duty;
submitting to control from above,
is the minister's duty.
Majestic authority and exalted status,
are the ruler's portion;
lowliness and respectful fear,
are the minister's portion.
Issuing commands that are followed, imposing prohibitions that are observed,
is the ruler's portion;
upholding the law and obeying,
is the minister's portion.
Thus, the relationship between ruler and minister,
in their high and low positions,
is like that between heaven and earth;
their distinctions are as clear
as white and black.
Therefore, when the distinction between ruler and minister is clear,
the ruler is honored and the ministers are humble.
In this way,
the subordinates' following the superior
is like an echo responding to a sound;
the ministers' emulation of the ruler
is like a shadow following the form.
Thus, when the superior commands, the subordinate responds;
when the ruler acts, the ministers follow.
Commands are implemented,
prohibitions are observed,
and sought goals are achieved.
This is called
"easy governance."
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"When the distinction between ruler and minister is clear,
governance is easy."
An enlightened ruler employs methods to command his ministers,
making them contribute their wisdom and abilities,
and present their specialized skills.
Thus, the wise offer their strategies,
the capable present their achievements,
using earlier statements to supervise later deeds.
If what is contributed is appropriate, reward it;
if inappropriate, punish it.
Establishing officials and appointing officers to govern the people,
they examine achievements according to the law.
Upholding the law and acting by it,
the ruler is free from toil while duties are fulfilled.
Therefore, the "Míng Fǎ" says:
"Though the ruler does not personally act,
upholding the law achieves it."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ:
"May I ask about the method of harnessing the state?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"The state's lack of reserves
lies in its decrees."
Huán Gōng said:
"What does it mean that the state's lack of reserves lies in its decrees?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"One farmer's capacity
covers a hundred acres of land,
with spring farming tasks within twenty-five days."
Huán Gōng said:
"What does 'spring farming tasks within twenty-five days' mean?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Sixty days after the winter solstice, the surface frost thaws;
seventy-five days after, the deeper frost thaws.
After the deeper frost thaws, millet and sorghum are planted;
if not planted within a hundred days,
hence spring farming must be completed within twenty-five days.
Now you have built the Fú Terrace,
mobilizing crowds from five directions.
If you continue past spring without stopping,
the people lose those twenty-five days,
then the land within the five directions becomes abandoned.
Mobilizing one person for corvée labor,
a hundred acres go uncultivated;
mobilizing ten people,
a thousand acres go uncultivated;
mobilizing a hundred people,
ten thousand acres go uncultivated;
mobilizing a thousand people,
a hundred thousand acres go uncultivated.
Having already lost twenty-five days in spring,
and still initiating summer projects,
this means losing the land in spring,
losing the sprouts in summer,
and starting endless corvée in autumn,
this is called multiple losses of grain land.
Grain missed in its season,
while the lord's exactions continue endlessly,
if the people eat fifteen units of grain,
then the lord has already taken nine as tax.
There are exactions demanding currency.
This is why banditry and violence arise,
and punishments become numerous.
Violence follows,
this is called internal war."
Huán Gōng said:
"Well said!"
Guǎn Zǐ said: "The method of calculating harnessed strength is not fully explained.
Those who would rule do not rob the people of their farming season,
hence the five grains flourish abundantly.
When the five grains flourish abundantly,
then scholars value emoluments lightly,
and the people are sparing with rewards.
Those skilled at governing the state
make farmers plow in cold and weed in heat,
with their labor benefiting the ruler,
women diligent in fine work
with their weaving going to the storehouses,
not because they resent the people's hearts
or harm their will,
but because the strategy of control
follows inevitable principles."
Huán Gōng said:
"How is this done?"
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"The state of Yú mastered the method of calculating harnessed strength."
Huán Gōng said:
"What is the method of calculating harnessed strength?"
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"To a farmer with a hundred acres, give this plan:
'Dedicate twenty-five days to your spring tasks.
We will provide you with currency.'
In great autumn, when your grain is fully harvested,
the state grain price drops by half.
Tell the farmers:
'The currency in your possession
should be converted to grain and stored in state granaries.'
With half the state's grain in the ruler's hands,
the state grain price rises twentyfold.
Order all distant and nearby counties, villages, towns, and officials to supply equipment and provisions,
saying:
'The state has no currency,
grain will substitute for currency.'
The state's grain holdings,
all at ninety percent,
are exchanged for equipment in response,
state equipment is fully supplied,
without imposing on the people.
This was Yú's method of calculating harnessed strength."
Duke Huán asked Guǎnzǐ, saying:
"The Yǒuyú's policy of chariots and horses has already been implemented.
I wish to establish a policy for chariots and horses,
how should it be done?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Warring states focus on the construction of their city walls and moats,
thus their states often lose the utility of their land.
A royal state, however, acts according to the seasons."
Duke Huán said:
"What does it mean to act according to the seasons?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Issue decrees on standards,
hold the land and employ human strategies,
so that opening and closing (of resources) are controlled from above,
with no demands on the people."
"A hegemonic state maintains its share,
with the ruler and the people operating within the bounds of that share, thus resources are sufficient.
A royal state maintains the beginning,
if state expenses fall short by one part,
then add one part,
if state expenses fall short by two parts,
then add two parts,
if state expenses fall short by three parts,
then add three parts,
if state expenses fall short by four parts,
then add four parts,
if state expenses fall short by five parts,
then add five parts,
if state expenses fall short by six parts,
then add six parts,
if state expenses fall short by seven parts,
then add seven parts,
if state expenses fall short by eight parts,
then add eight parts,
if state expenses fall short by nine parts,
then add nine parts,
if state expenses fall short by ten parts,
then add ten parts.
The ruler maintains control over highs and lows,
storing one-third of the annual harvest,
so in ten years there must be a surplus of three years.
If there is a year of drought or flood,
and the people lose their means of livelihood,
then build palaces, towers, and pavilions,
employing those who have neither dog nor pig before or after them.
Thus, building palaces, towers, and pavilions
is not for the beauty of pleasure,
but to balance state policy.
Now, as for those rulers who have lost the policy of chariots and horses,
in spring, autumn, winter, and summer,
they do not know the timing of beginnings and ends,
mobilize labor and raise crowds,
and erect palaces, towers, and pavilions.
The people lose their fundamental occupations,
and the ruler does not realize that he has failed in spring policies,
and also failed in summer and autumn policies.
There are many cases where the people have no choice but to sell their children.
The fierce and resolute become violent and excessive,
the poor and sick
beg for help, and if the ruler applies laws and measures,
then the people suffer punishment and mutilation but do not obey their ruler.
This is the failure of the policy of chariots and horses."
"The standard for chariots and horses
should align with that of the world.
If goods are light, they will be drained away;
if heavy, they will be targeted.
This is how warring states drain each other,
and experts in light and heavy (economics) contend with one another.
As for a royal state,
it maintains the flow and stops it."
Duke Huán said:
"What does it mean to maintain the flow?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"There are cases where one person farms and five eat,
one person farms and four eat,
one person farms and three eat,
one person farms and two eat.
This is to unite strength and work the land.
Land policies complement each other,
this is the timely maintenance of state policy.
If the ruler does not maintain it with policy,
then the people will take control from below,
this is the state policy flowing away."
Duke Huán said: "Is the method of chariots and horses
exhausted here?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Textiles and goods,
all have their prices established.
The prices of goods
fluctuate with the currency.
Grain alone is uniquely expensive or cheap."
Duke Huán said:
"What does uniquely expensive or cheap mean?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"When grain is heavy, all things are light;
when grain is light, all things are heavy."
The Duke said:
"How about the method of cheapening chariots and horses?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"For the fertile land of commanderies and counties,
maintain a certain amount.
For medium land,
maintain a certain amount.
For poor land,
maintain a certain amount.
Thus, by assessing the land and fixing taxes,
the people do not move;
by relieving the poor and supplementing shortages,
the lower classes are pleased with the upper.
Therefore, use the surplus of the upper land
to supplement the deficiencies of the lower land,
regulate the four seasons,
control the openings and closings,
and the people will not move,
like placing a square on the ground.
This is called the method of the policy of chariots and horses."
The chapter is lost.
Duke Huán asked Guǎnzǐ, saying:
"May I hear about the ultimate methods of governance?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"What are the ultimate methods?"
Duke Huán said:
"Bó Shē advised me, saying:
'If curtains and canopies are not well-maintained,
and clothing is not abundant,
then women's work will not prosper.
If the ritual of sacrificial vessels does not include animals,
with feudal lords using the great sacrifice,
and grand officers using the lesser sacrifice,
if not done thus,
then the six domestic animals will not be raised.
If towers and pavilions are not raised high,
and palaces are not beautified,
then various materials will not be distributed.'
What do you think of this?"
Guǎnzǐ said:
"This is not the method."
Duke Huán said:
"What do you mean it's not the method?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"This is the method of fixed land.
According to the system of the Son of Heaven, the land is a thousand li square,
while feudal lords like Qí are a hundred li square,
coastal lords seventy li,
barons fifty li,
like the chest and arms working together.
Thus, by regulating speed and slack, surplus and shortage,
even if below,
it is not the ruler's worry.
For those with narrow land who wish to rise and compete with great states,
where farmers plow in cold and weed in heat,
and their strength returns to the ruler,
and women diligently spin, weave, and embroider,
with their work returning to the treasury,
it is not to resent the people's hearts
or harm their will,
but without accumulated reserves
one cannot employ people,
without accumulated wealth
one cannot encourage the lower classes.
The methods of excess and luxury
cannot be used in constrained and narrow states."
Duke Huán said:
"Good."
Duke Huán again asked Guǎnzǐ, saying:
"Yì Tián told me:
'A good ruler uses what is not his,
and employs those who are not his people.
Why not rely on the power of feudal lords to control the world?'"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Yì Tián's words are incorrect.
Those who excel at governing a state,
when lands are opened up and fully utilized
the people will remain settled,
when granaries are full
they will understand ritual and propriety.
Moreover, without supplies one invites siege,
with fat walls come assaults.
One who cannot stabilize internally,
cannot maintain control over the world.
Yì Tián's words are incorrect."
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Store one-tenth annually,
in ten years you'll have a full year's supply.
Store two-tenths annually,
in five years you'll have a full year's supply.
With ten measures of grain, keep five,
fill with silk fabrics,
five remain in storage.
Thus observe the harvest and store accordingly,
accumulate over years and seasons,
until the state has ten years' reserves.
Then wealth will overcome poverty,
courage overcome timidity,
wisdom overcome foolishness,
subtlety overcome lack thereof,
righteousness overcome its absence,
trained soldiers overcome rabble,
and all ten victories will be achieved.
Thus deploy like wind and rain,
move like thunder and lightning,
act independently in and out,
with none able to stop it,
without awaiting authority or alliances.
Therefore Yì Tián's words are incorrect."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎnzǐ:
"I wish to levy taxes on terraces and shooting ranges,
what do you think?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"This would destroy completed structures."
"What if I levy taxes
on trees?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"This would harm living things."
"What if I levy taxes
on the six domestic animals?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"This would kill living creatures."
"What if I levy taxes
on people,
what then?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"This would conceal true circumstances."
Huán Gōng said:
"Then how should I govern the state?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Only by state monopoly of mountains and seas is it possible."
Huán Gōng said:
"What does 'state monopoly of mountains and seas' mean?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"For a state aspiring to maritime hegemony,
carefully regulate the salt administration."
Huán Gōng said:
"What does regulating the salt administration mean?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"A family of ten
has ten people consuming salt,
a family of one hundred
has one hundred people consuming salt.
In one month, adult males consume five and a half liters of salt,
adult females consume three and a half liters,
children consume two and a half liters.
This is the general measure.
One hundred liters of salt make one fǔ.
If the price of salt increases by half a qiáng per liter,
that's fifty per fǔ.
Increase by one qiáng per liter,
that's one hundred per fǔ.
Increase by two qiáng per liter,
that's two hundred per fǔ,
two thousand per zhōng,
twenty thousand for ten zhōng,
two hundred thousand for one hundred zhōng,
two million for one thousand zhōng.
In a state of ten thousand chariots,
the population numbers ten million mouths.
Calculating accordingly,
the daily revenue is two million,
twenty million in ten days,
sixty million in one month.
For a proper ten-thousand-chariot state,
the population is one million taxpayers.
A monthly tax of thirty coins per person
would yield thirty million coins.
Now without taxing the lords and their children,
we obtain sixty million from two states' revenues.
If the ruler issued an order saying:
'I will tax the lords and their children,'
there would surely be loud protests.'
But by providing salt administration,
hundredfold returns come to the ruler,
and people cannot avoid this -
it's the way of numbers."
"Now the iron officials' calculations say:
each woman must have one needle and one knife,
for her work to be established.
Each farmer must have one plow, one spade, and one hoe,
for his work to be established.
Those making carts and carriages must have one axe, one saw, one awl, and one chisel,
for their work to be established.
To accomplish tasks without these
is impossible under heaven.
If the weight of needles is increased by one unit,
thirty needles equal one person's tax.
If the weight of knives is increased by six,
five times six is thirty,
five knives equal one person's tax.
If the weight of spade-iron is increased by ten,
three spades equal one person's tax.
All other light and heavy items follow this principle.
Thus whenever people raise their arms to work,
none avoid contributing."
Huán Gōng said:
"Then can a state without mountains and seas not achieve hegemony?"
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Borrow from others' mountains and seas.
States that have seas
sell salt to our state -
at fifteen per fǔ, we purchase it
and the government sells it at one hundred.
Without engaging in the basic production,
we handle others' products,
using this method
to leverage weight differentials. This is the way of human numbers."
When the state has ten years' reserves,
but the people lack sufficient food,
they all rely on their skills hoping for the ruler's support;
when the ruler has wealth from mountains and seas,
but the people lack sufficient resources,
they all use their occupations to connect with the ruler.
Thus the ruler controls their food,
maintains their resources,
holding surplus to regulate scarcity,
so the people all depend on the ruler.
The five grains and food rice
are what the people depend on for life;
gold, coins, and currency
are what the people use for exchange.
Thus the skilled ruler controls the medium of exchange
to master their means of subsistence,
so the people's strength can be fully utilized.
The people trust in kinship and die for profit,
this is universal throughout the land.
When given to, the people rejoice;
when taken from, they anger -
such are universal human feelings.
The ancient kings knew this,
so they showed the appearance of giving,
while concealing the reality of taking.
Thus the people's affection could be won by the ruler.
Forced levies
are what constitute coercive demands;
regular taxes
are what people consider and accept.
Kings and hegemons
eliminate coercive demands,
abolish what people resentfully accept,
so the world willingly follows them.
When profits flow from a single source,
the state is invincible;
from two sources,
its military strength is halved;
from three sources,
it cannot raise an army;
from four sources,
the state is doomed to perish.
The ancient kings understood this principle,
hence they blocked the people's excess,
and narrowed their paths to profit.
Thus, giving lies with the ruler,
taking away lies with the ruler,
impoverishing lies with the ruler,
enriching lies with the ruler.
Therefore, the people look up to him like the sun and moon,
and cherish him as parents.
Generally, to govern a state,
without understanding the principles of light and heavy,
one cannot establish control to protect the people;
without being able to balance and regulate the people's profits,
one cannot speak of achieving great order through regulation.
Thus, in a state of ten thousand chariots,
there are merchants with ten thousand gold;
in a state of a thousand chariots,
there are merchants with a thousand gold.
Why is this so?
When the state loses much profit,
then ministers do not exhaust their loyalty,
and soldiers do not exhaust their willingness to die.
The year may have famine or abundance,
hence grain has its price fluctuations;
decrees may be lenient or urgent,
hence goods have their light and heavy values.
However, if the ruler cannot manage this,
it allows hoarding merchants to roam the market,
taking advantage of the people's shortages,
to multiply their capital a hundredfold.
If land is divided equally,
the strong can hold it;
if wealth is divided equally,
the wise can gather it.
The wise achieve tenfold the results of others,
while the foolish fail to recover their capital.
Yet if the ruler cannot regulate this,
the people will have a hundredfold disparity in livelihood.
If the people are wealthy, they cannot be motivated by salaries;
if poor, they cannot be intimidated by punishments.
The failure of laws and decrees,
the lack of governance over the masses,
stem from the disparity between rich and poor.
Moreover, the ruler calculates expenditures,
plows fields and clears grasslands,
and the court obtains its due share;
as for the food consumed by the people,
each has a certain amount of land;
estimating the base and measuring reserves should suffice.
Yet why are there people starving without food?
Because grain is hoarded.
The ruler mints coins and establishes currency,
which the common people use for exchange.
Each person has a certain amount of hundreds or thousands.
Yet why are there unmet needs
and insufficient resources?
Because profits are monopolized and hoarded.
Thus, unless the ruler can disperse accumulations,
balance surplus and deficiency,
and redistribute concentrated wealth and profits
to regulate the people's affairs,
then even if he strengthens agriculture and promotes farming,
and endlessly mints currency himself,
he will only make the people exploit each other—
how can this achieve good governance?
In a year of good harvest,
the market has no buyers for grain,
and dogs and pigs eat human food.
In a year of famine,
grain is sold at ten qiǎng per fǔ,
and there are starving people on the roads.
Is this because the land's productivity is inherently insufficient
and food inherently scarce?
In years when grain is cheap,
dogs and pigs eat human food,
hence the people lack enough the following year.
When goods are too cheap,
they are sold at half the effort with no return,
and the people's labor fails to cover their costs;
when goods are too expensive,
they are unavailable even at ten times the price,
and the people lose their means.
Is this because wealth and goods are inherently scarce
and reserves inherently insufficient?
It is due to missing the timing for people's benefit and the imbalance in goods' value.
Therefore, the adept ruler stores and distributes when the people lack,
and collects when the people have surplus.
When the people have surplus, they undervalue goods,
so the ruler collects them at low prices;
when the people lack, they value goods highly,
so the ruler distributes them at high prices.
Collecting and storing when prices are low,
distributing and selling when prices are high,
thus the ruler surely gains tenfold profits,
and commodity prices can be stabilized.
The great advantage of light and heavy policies
lies in using high prices to draw out low-priced goods,
and low prices to release overpriced goods.
The fullness and emptiness of all goods
change with the season, but through standardization, they remain stable,
and when balance is broken, heaviness reappears.
The ruler knows this principle,
hence maintains it through standardization.
Ensure a city of ten thousand households has a storage of ten thousand zhōng,
with millions in currency reserves;
a city of a thousand households has a storage of a thousand zhōng,
with hundreds of thousands in currency reserves.
In spring, to support plowing,
in summer, to support weeding.
Farm tools and equipment,
grain and food supplies,
all are provided by the ruler.
Thus, great merchants and hoarding families cannot ruthlessly plunder our people.
How is this achieved?
The ruler diligently nurtures the fundamentals.
In spring, provide loans to gather silk and cloth,
in summer, lend to collect autumn harvests,
so the people have no neglected tasks,
and the state loses no profits.
Among all things, the five grains
are the masters.
When grains are expensive, all other goods must be cheap;
when grains are cheap, all other goods must be expensive.
The two are in opposition,
and cannot both be balanced.
Thus, the ruler controls the order of grains to overcome this,
and operates within their imbalance.
Hence, the people pay no taxes,
yet state profits return to the ruler.
Taxing based on housing,
is called destroying achievements;
taxing livestock,
is called halting livelihood;
taxing farmland,
is called prohibiting farming;
taxing individuals,
is called severing emotions;
taxing households,
is called nurturing the wealthy.
These five methods cannot all be used,
so the true king employs them selectively, not exhaustively.
Thus, the Son of Heaven taxes through currency,
the feudal lords tax through food.
In an average year, grain is sold at ten coins per shí.
A grown man eats four shí,
hence a monthly tax equivalent of forty coins;
a grown woman eats three shí,
hence a monthly tax equivalent of thirty coins;
a child eats two shí,
hence a monthly tax equivalent of twenty coins.
In a famine year, grain is expensive,
bought at twenty coins per shí.
Then a grown man has a tax equivalent of eighty coins,
a grown woman sixty coins,
a child forty coins.
This is not the ruler issuing orders to collect harvests or household taxes;
rather, the ruler diligently manages reserves,
and all men, women, and children unavoidably pay their dues.
When one person receives stored grain,
ten others gain surplus;
when ten receive,
a hundred gain surplus;
when a hundred receive,
a thousand gain surplus.
When goods are abundant, they become cheap;
when scarce, they become expensive;
when dispersed, they become light;
when concentrated, they become heavy.
The ruler understands this principle.
Therefore, he observes the surplus and deficiency of the state to manage its wealth and goods.
When grain is cheap, he uses currency to purchase food;
when cloth and silk are cheap, he uses currency to acquire clothing.
He observes the lightness or heaviness of goods and manages them with standards.
Thus, prices can be regulated,
and the ruler gains benefits.
If ahead there is a state of ten thousand chariots,
and behind a state of a thousand chariots,
it is called a "dǐ state."
If ahead there is a state of a thousand chariots,
and behind a state of ten thousand chariots,
it is called a "jù state."
If the territory is square,
facing enemies on all four sides,
it is called a "qú state."
A state of a hundred chariots situated at a crossroads
is termed a ruler who "depends on others for sustenance."
A state of a thousand chariots at a crossroads
will lose more than half its territory.
A state of ten thousand chariots at a crossroads
will lose less than half its territory.
What does it mean for a hundred-chariot state at a crossroads to have a ruler depending on others for sustenance?
With a hundred chariots at a crossroads, it is intimidated and besieged between states of a thousand and ten thousand chariots.
The rulers of large states are at odds,
raising armies to attack each other,
and they will surely use it as a buffer or shield.
It cannot share in the gains and benefits.
Ministers die abroad,
and lands are divided as rewards for achievements;
formations capture prisoners,
and shares of the spoils are given as salaries.
Thus, the land is exhausted by rewards for achievements,
and tax revenues are depleted in supporting orphans.
This is merely having the name of a ruler,
without possessing any territory.
Though nominally having the defense of a hundred chariots,
in reality, there is not an inch of land to use,
hence called a ruler depending on others for sustenance.
However, if a large state is internally impoverished,
and a small state has exhausted its resources,
how can they cope?
The answer:
For a state of a hundred chariots,
official levies and regulated tallies,
utilizing the fluctuations of the four seasons,
managed with the standard of lightness and heaviness,
then a hundred chariots can be sustained.
For a state of a thousand chariots,
it enriches the resources of natural wealth,
the production of tools and weapons,
and the generation of goods and wealth.
Observing the fullness or emptiness of the harvest
and adjusting salaries accordingly,
then a thousand chariots can be adequately supported.
For a state of ten thousand chariots,
it monitors the harvest's fullness or emptiness,
responds to the people's urgency or leisure,
rectifies its commands
and manages with a grand standard,
then ten thousand chariots can be funded.
Jade originates from Yùshì,
gold from Rǔ Hàn,
pearls from Chìyě,
east, west, south, north,
all eight thousand seven hundred lǐ from Zhōu.
Waters cut off, lands broken,
boats and carts cannot pass.
The former kings, due to the distance of the journey,
the difficulty of arrival,
therefore utilized their heaviness,
taking pearls and jade as the highest currency,
gold as the middle currency,
knife and cloth money as the lower currency.
These three currencies
held, do not add to warmth,
eaten, do not add to fullness,
but the former kings used them to preserve wealth and goods,
manage civil affairs,
and balance the world.
Now, rulers impose levies on the people,
ordering that
"if completed in ten days,
then the price of goods drops by one-tenth;"
ordering that
"if completed in eight days,
then the price of goods drops by two-tenths;"
ordering that
"if completed in five days,
then the price of goods drops by half;"
if ordered in the morning and completed by evening,
then the price of goods drops by nine-tenths.
The former kings knew this,
thus they did not seek from the myriad people but relied on commands.
Duke Huán asked Guǎnzǐ:
"May I ask about governing the state?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Fields have their norms,
people have their norms,
expenditures have their norms,
villages have their norms,
human affairs have their norms,
currency has its norms,
counties have their norms,
the state has its norms,
without understanding the norms and calculations
and wishing to govern the state,
it is impossible."
Duke Huán said:
"How does one implement the norms and calculations?"
He replied:
"How much land in a certain village?
What is the standard for human affairs?
How heavy is the grain?
Say:
How many people in a certain county?
How much land?
How much currency is appropriate?
How heavy is the grain for the currency to be suitable?
At year's end, calculate the people's food, how much is left?
Say:
The women in a certain village skilled in work
spin all year, how much is their output?
Valuing the output at current prices,
at year's end, after the people are clothed,
how much clothing remains?
Differentiate the various norms,
assess the suitability of the land."
Duke Huán said:
"What does it mean to differentiate the various norms,
assess the suitability of the land?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"There is land for reeds and cattails,
land for bamboo, qián, sandalwood, and柘 trees,
low-lying marshy land,
waterlogged land for fish and turtles.
Now, if the ruler skillfully manages and controls these four types of land,
then he levies on goods and wealth,
not on the people. For land
yielding ten gǔ,
if the ruler does not control it by norms,
the people will control it.
The people have movable long knives,
not gaining from fundamentals,
this is the ruler's loss."
Duke Huán said:
"Where does the intent of norms come from?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"If not secretly basing on their norms,
all below will control those above."
Duke Huán said:
"What does this statement mean?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
How much land in a certain village?
How many eaters?
How much women's work in a certain village?
How much clothing remains?
Carefully survey the villages and neighborhoods, saying:
'So much land,
so many people,
with many people and land not enough for food, how much?'
Say:
'So much land,
so much surplus food.'
Must obtain the norm and measure.
This is called the great norm.
Then adjust and establish the currency for cyclical transactions.
For the surplus of farmland production beyond what the people consume,
carefully allocate public funds.
Large households contribute more,
small households less.
For mountainous fields and marginal lands,
if the annual food supply falls short of the people's needs by a certain amount,
then public funds are allocated,
to make up the standard amount. In abundant
years, during harvest seasons,
the five grains flourish.
Tell the farmers of highland fields:
'The amount of currency I entrusted to you is such-and-such,
and the local grain price is such-and-such.
Let me reduce your debt by thirty percent.'
Grain is valued higher,
currency lower.
Highland fields are managed, while marginal
mountain lands remain uncultivated, yet grain yields increase tenfold.
Mountain fields, through the ruler's entrusted funds,
relieve their insufficiency,
preventing excessive loss.
Highland fields are timely managed by the authorities,
sitting idle yet increasing by ten percent.
Women contribute woven silk,
if it meets the state's requirements,
all are stored with contracts issued.
Using local market prices as standard
it is said:
'The state has no currency, but has grain.
Use grain as standard for currency.'
Circulate grain to respond to policies,
state provisions are secured. Grain
returns to standard price. Tax-regulated currency,
grain granaries, again increase by ten percent.
Tell wealthy households and contributing families:
'The ruler will soon tour around,
each person must contribute a certain amount of currency.'
Tell neighboring counties:
'Those with stored goods should not distribute them.
If insufficient,
then temporarily provide food for the people on behalf of the cavalry.'
When all surrounding counties control prices, grain
sits idle yet increases tenfold.
The authorities issue orders:
'Wealthy families lending currency,
all must use grain as standard for currency,
calculating the currency value for repayment.'
Grain becomes lower value,
currency higher value.
All cities and counties
follow regulated standards. Grain
sits idle yet increases tenfold.
Circulate grain to respond to currency loans.
Nine-tenths of state currency remains with the authorities,
one-tenth among the people,
currency becomes valuable while goods become cheap,
collect goods,
responding with currency.
When currency is among the people,
all goods are with the authorities,
goods become ten times more valuable.
Government offices use market controls to release
and stabilize goods, then stop.
State economic planning, implemented before situations develop,
based on what has already formed,
advance or retreat according to commands,
without demanding from the people.
This is called state economic planning."
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zǐ:
"Is there a way to sustain the state
without imposing taxes?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"Maintain planning according to the seasons,
manage natural resources officially,
what need is there to demand from the people?"
Huán Gōng said:
"What does managing natural resources mean?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In early spring
the people's labor services,
in midsummer
where the people's orders stop,
where orders are issued.
In early autumn
where the people's orders stop,
where orders are issued.
In midwinter
where the people's orders stop,
where orders are issued.
These are all what the people maintain according to the seasons,
these are times when commodity prices fluctuate,
these are times when people engage in consolidation.
The ruler should maintain these four tasks."
Huán Gōng said:
"What are the four tasks?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In early spring,
what the people will need,
the ruler has already stored;
in midsummer,
what the people will need,
the ruler has already stored;
in early autumn,
what the people will need,
the ruler has already stored;
in midwinter,
what the people will need,
the ruler has already stored.
In early spring when work is distributed daily,
spring lined garments,
summer single-layer clothes,
shovels, baskets, ropes, winnowing baskets, bamboo containers, (󰂏) bags, hampers, bundles,
the work of certain days,
how many people are employed?
Families without means
are all lent tools and equipment.
Bamboo containers, (󰂏) bundles, bags, hampers, public clothing.
When work is completed, return to the government, cancel contracts.
Thus labor comes from the people,
while resources come from the authorities.
Ten days in spring
should not harm plowing,
ten days in summer
should not harm weeding,
ten days in autumn
should not harm harvesting,
twenty days in winter
should not harm field preparation.
This is called timely work."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good,
I wish to establish planning officials,
how should this be done?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"The salt and iron policies
are sufficient to establish planning officials."
Huán Gōng said:
"How so?"
Guǎn Zǐ replied:
"In the Lóng Xià region,
distribute nine thousand units of gold,
using currency to finance gold.
Wealthy families use gold,
poor families use currency.
From Zhōu Qí Shān to the western Sài Qiū of Zhēng Qiū,
these are mountainous region fields,
distribute currency according to wealth and adjust accordingly.
From Zhōu Shòu Líng east to Shào Shā,
these are medium-quality fields,
control them with currency,
wealthy families use gold,
poor families use currency.
When three types of land are managed,
state grain increases twentyfold.
Liáng Wèi, Yáng Suǒ's cattle and horses fill Qí's plains.
Please inspect their age by teeth,
measure their height and strength,
saying:
'The state is raising armies,
war chariots being assembled
require collecting your cattle and horses,
the authorities have no currency,
please accept grain at market price as repayment to you.'
Cattle and horses go to the authorities,
grain goes to two families.
The two families distribute their grain,
returning to standard price. Cattle and horses return to the authorities."
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"Please establish contributions among the people,
those with land double it.
If there is none within,
outside all becomes contributed land."
With a thousand chariots equipped with saddled horses,
and the implements for war chariots of Qí all prepared here,
there is no need to demand from the people.
This is to abolish the registers of hill settlements."
"The state's grain prices at dawn and dusk are controlled by the ruler,
the price levels of mountain forests and granary tools are controlled by the ruler,
the relative values in spring, autumn, winter, and summer are controlled by the ruler.
When cultivating farmland,
if there are trees in the fields,
they are called grain thieves.
In the four corners of the palace,
planting the rest is said to harm women's work.
For palace buildings and tools,
without mountains there is nothing to rely on.
Then the ruler establishes three grades of mountain rents,
saying:
"Those below a handful are considered firewood and branches,
those above a grasp are for building materials,
those above three arm-spans are for coffin materials;
the rent for firewood and branches is such amount,
the rent for building materials is such amount,
the rent for coffin materials is such amount."
Guǎnzǐ said:
"With salt and iron stabilizing the economy,
when grain is stored, one granary yields ten,
the ruler regularly controls nine,
the people have clothing and food while performing corvée labor,
those below remain peaceful without complaints.
Abolish their field taxes,
and rent the mountains instead:
wealthy families who heavily bury their relatives pay heavy rents,
poor families who thinly bury their relatives pay light rents;
wealthy families who beautifully decorate their palaces pay heavy rents,
poor families who build simple huts pay light rents.
The ruler establishes economic controls in the state,
the people's wealth and poverty
are as if measured with a plumb line,
this is called the state's economic regulation."
Duke Huán asked Guǎnzǐ:
"May I ask about strategic calculations?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Heaven uses timing as its strategy,
earth uses resources as its strategy,
people use strength as their strategy,
the ruler uses commands as his strategy.
If one loses Heaven's strategic advantage,
then human and earthly advantages are lost."
Duke Huán said:
"Why does losing Heaven's strategic advantage mean losing human and earthly advantages?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Tāng had seven years of drought,
Yǔ had five years of flood.
People had no grain and sold their children.
Tāng used the metal from Zhuāng Mountain to cast coins,
and redeemed the people who had no grain and sold their children;
Yǔ used the metal from Lì Mountain to cast coins,
and redeemed the people who had no grain and sold their children.
Therefore, when Heaven's strategic advantage is lost,
human and earthly advantages are all lost.
Thus the kingly ruler annually stores three-tenths,
in three years with a small half
completes a year's reserve. In thirty-seven years, eleven years and a small half are stored.
Storing one-third
does not harm the people,
and farmers respectfully attend to their work with effort.
Thus when Heaven destroys and earth fails:
with severe drought and flooding,
no people fall into ditches begging.
This is the way of maintaining timing to await Heaven's strategic advantage."
Duke Huán said:
"Good.
I wish to implement the method of three strategic advantages,
how should this be done?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"On the south side of Liáng Mountain
there are coins of qiànqiàn and night stones,
which are found nowhere else in the world."
Guǎnzǐ said:
"To maintain state grain reserves, store one-tenth annually,
implement this for five years,
then the value of state grain
will be ten times different from before."
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Please establish currency,
using two years' worth of millet to commission the state's copper,
establish settlements.
Implement light and heavy measures to harmonize with the world.
When others are heavy then we are targeted,
when light then we are drained,
thus harmonize with the world.
Draining means losing strategic advantage,
being targeted means losing policy control.
Without preparing for Heaven's strategic advantage,
those below seek preparation from each other,
secretly enslaving each other below standards.
This is the origin of punishments
and the root of chaos.
Thus when balanced becomes unbalanced,
people being rich is not as good as being poor,
accumulations become empty.
This is the loss of the three strategic advantages."
Duke Huán said:
"How to maintain the method of three strategic advantages?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"In great abundance, store a portion,
in scarcity also store a portion."
Duke Huán said:
"Scarcity is for increasing gains.
Why store a portion?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"In scarcity it is easy to increase,
one can become ten,
ten can become one hundred.
Use scarcity to manage abundance,
in scarcity the standard rate rises from one to ten,
in abundance the policy rate drops ten removing nine,
then we have nine as surplus. In calculation
policy for abundance, then all three strategic advantages belong to the ruler,
this is called state strategic advantage."
Duke Huán asked Guǎnzǐ:
"May I ask about state regulations?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"The state has no fixed regulations,
the land has measures."
Duke Huán said:
"What means the state has no fixed regulations, the land has measures?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"High fields yield ten dàn,
medium fields yield five dàn,
poor fields yield three dàn,
the remainder all belongs to wasteland.
Land measure of one hundred mǔ,
is the strength of one man.
Grain price one,
grain price ten,
grain price thirty,
grain price one hundred.
In flowing calculations,
one hundred mǔ follows the calculation of one thousand mǔ.
Thus one hundred chariots follow one thousand chariots,
one thousand chariots follow ten thousand chariots.
Therefore land without measure,
state without calculation."
Duke Huán said:
"Good,
now wishing to become a great state,
a great state wishing to rule the world,
without understanding strategic calculations,
it is impossible."
Duke Huán said:
"How to implement strategic advantage now?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"The ruler understands the numbers of breadth and narrowness,
not fearing breadth because of narrowness;
understands the numbers of lightness and heaviness,
not fearing multitude because of fewness.
This is the great policy of the state."
Duke Huán said:
"Good.
To cover all under heaven,
oversee all within the seas,
achieve lasting praise without end,
is there a way to do this?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"Yes.
It is said: Maintain the measures according to the rules,
balance and stabilize their flow,
act before forms take shape,
and preserve what has already been accomplished.
From one thing,
ten can be derived, thus nine are put to use.
The pace of speed and slowness,
is the strategy of light and heavy,
one can become ten,
ten can become a hundred.
Deduct half of the ten and store away four,
using five to manage affairs,
lies in the ruler's control of opening and closing."
Duke Huán asked:
"What does 'opening and closing' mean?"
Guǎnzǐ said:
"If the ruler does not exalt benevolence,
then the destitute will not be aided;
if the ruler does not honor filial piety and kindness,
then the people will neglect their parents and take faults lightly.
This leads to the utmost chaos.
So, I ask the ruler to use one-tenth of the state's resources
to erect markers and set up high standards,
bestow gifts upon filial sons in the villages,
and whether filial sons and brothers are many or few,
they shall not be involved in military campaigns.
By setting up markers and high standards,
and exalting benevolence and filial piety,
wealth will be distributed and its value lightened.
Seize the opportunity of light value and control it with strategy,
then half of the ten will remain with the ruler.
Operating with these five as if conducting affairs,
like the perpetual cycle of the sun and moon.
This is the way to long possess the world,
called the balanced way."
Duke Huán asked Guǎnzǐ:
"May I ask about the methods of education?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"For those among the people who excel in understanding agricultural affairs,
grant them one jīn of gold,
equivalent to eight shí of grain.
For those who can breed and raise the six domestic animals,
grant them one jīn of gold,
equivalent to eight shí of grain.
For those skilled in planting and cultivation,
grant them one jīn of gold,
equivalent to eight shí of grain.
For those who can grow melons, gourds, onions, and various fruits ensuring their abundance,
grant them one jīn of gold,
equivalent to eight shí of grain.
For those who can cure the people's illnesses,
grant them one jīn of gold,
equivalent to eight shí of grain.
For those who know the seasons:
saying
'the year will be harsh',
or
'a certain grain will fail',
or those who say,
'a certain grain will be abundant', grant them one jīn of gold,
equivalent to eight shí of grain.
For those proficient in sericulture,
ensuring the silkworms do not fall ill,
all grant them one jīn of gold,
equivalent to eight shí of grain.
Carefully listen to their words and record them in the official records,
exempting them from involvement in military campaigns,
this is part of the state's strategy.
The state's needs will be met through mutual support and sufficiency,
(mutually dependent and balanced) balanced and stabilized.
Then set the four limits, adjusting the high and low
to command the pace of speed and slowness, driving and screening
all things, controlling them with strategy,
there are the five official skills."
Duke Huán said:
"What are the five official skills?"
Guǎnzǐ said:
"The Shī is for recording things,
the calendars for recording the years,
the Chūnqiū for recording successes and failures,
conduct for guiding the people in benefits and harms,
the Yì for determining fortune and misfortune, success and failure,
divination for foreseeing good and bad, benefits and harms.
Those among the people skilled in these
shall each receive a field that supports one horse,
and clothing worth one piece of gold.
This is the method to keep the ruler from confusion and error.
These five families,
when their time comes,
should be given the responsibility to anticipate and prepare in advance,
so the ruler never misses the timing,
never errs in strategy,
and all things flourish abundantly;
from their Chūnqiū,
they predict gains and losses from afar,
using it as a secondary teaching;
from the Shī, they record people without improper words;
